Just a note and a thank you to the game programmer who took a moment to read my review and provide a response.  As you read my review below note that while I didn't understand the story, his comment does a great job of summarizing what I missed.  Feel free to read the comments on this review for a proper explaination.  Having someone from the game team read one of my negative reviews always makes me feel a bit self-concious, and I surely didn't mean it to offend someone directly.  With this said, I'm hoping that my review comments will still serve as a unbiased commentary.  And as my comment response back states, I'll still stand firm that "... the game rode that fine line of giving you just enough control over the character to feel like there could have been more, but at the same time obfuscating the artistic direction of making it like a movie."
This is such a disappointing review to write; you can tell that there was a good vision going into the development of this game.  The best summary you can provide here really is that the game is just simply not fully-realized.  I wasn't a Kickstarter backer and I don't have a true sense of the development process that went into this game, but I think there in lies part of the problem.  This game feels like yet another scenario where the developer put a lot of love and thought into an idea, and once he was appropriately backed got bored and decided the game simply needed a beginning and an end with nothing in between.  There really is no story here, and for a majority of the 2 hours it will take to finish this game you will either be pressing the right arrow key or the spacebar.  I got this game for a real steal as part of a game bundle, and even then I couldn't recommend playing this even at a steeply discounted price.  Play this game if you enjoy game design, and maybe want to see something that was a great idea that couldn't be manifested.

Get this game.  It's free, it's got 5 to 8 hours of story-driven content and entertaining puzzles, and is just what you need to sate your thirst for more Portal content.
This sequel-in-spirit to the Portal franchise was lovingly developed by a third party studio, but expands upon the lore of the setting in a realistic way.  You take on the role of Mel, an olympian-turned-test subject who winds up spending a great deal of time in the Aperture Science labs.  The NPCs that aid you on your journey are fully voice-acted by two incredible talents.  That's right, the game's got voice acting for start to finish.  It doesn't skimp on adding story and fills the in-between sections with rich monologuing and universe-expanding detail.  There's probably three or four hours of new audio altogether.
The game's new characters are oozing with personality.  The game's coldly-rational no-jokes villain is a fresh take for the Portal series, which has been dominated by comic foils and calamitous goofballs since its inception.  Your companion through the game delivers the best jokes and seems like a friendly fellow.  Some of the game's humor comes through its posters, artwork, and design choices.  Humor isn't this game's focus, though, and it naturally comes off as a little more severe than its inspirations.  The art and music are fantastic and fit the mood of each chapter of the game perfectly.  I forgot how good Portal-style music can be.
The thing that sets this game apart from Portal's limitless "test chambers" and other mods is its gameplay.  While most mods/levels for Portal focus on purely logical puzzle-solving, this game captures the spirit of the originals by providing "exploration" sections and "outside of the box" solutions using new techniques.  In fact, the vast majority of this game isn't just "solve a puzzle"; only in a couple of the chapters do you get puzzly bits without any in-game explanation (and even those puzzles are pretty incredible).  Rather, the game takes you on a journey, where you slowly remember how portals work and where to place them.  There are sections where you hunt for the best spots to use portals, so you can cross broad gaps.  There's also new puzzle content, which changes how you deal with problems in the game world.
The game has a learning curve, which allows you to get your bearings while enjoying the rich story.  This learning curve is steeper than Portal and Portal 2.  It assumes the player is familiar enough with the gameplay that they're ready for some new challenges.  It's hard to describe them without spoiling the fun.  By the fourth chapter, I was getting a little hung up on a few of the puzzles, in a good way.  I got through the game in a little over six hours.  I was pretty familiar with Portal puzzles, having fairly recently played a lot of test chambers.  I imagine some of the puzzles could take an out-of-practice puzzle-solver an extra 10 minutes or so to crack.  The fact that this game is nearly half as long as an official Valve game makes its price point (a whopping $0) pretty incredible.
You can tell a lot of time, effort, and passion went into this project.  If you've got a bit of spare time to play it, you'd be remiss not to give this new hidden gem a try.

Imagine Dynasty Warriors with guns and bugs, and you have a good idea what this game is about. The first hour of playing was by far the hardest part, as I got used to all four character play styles, the map icons, and that sort of thing. There are roughly 100 missions, with four difficulties. All the missions are relatively straight forward: kill all enemies or do enough damage to unkillable enemy. Tons of fun, especially when played with others.
There are a few issues, of which I will highlight the two most frustrating for me, just as a word of warning.
Multiplayer system: It is far from seamless. Regardless of where you are in the game, if you accept an invite, before joining, you have to return to the main menu. Setting a game as private doesn't exactly work as intended. Instead of reserving all spots, you need to leave spots open to the public that will then be filled by your friends that you invite. If you buy the game (and you should), you will see what I am talking about.
Collision detection: Collision detection for the player is pretty good. However, the enemies have zero collection detection at all. They can shoot you through enemy bodies, but it doesn't work the other way around. So you will massacre dozens of bugs, and have a huge pile of corpses, with one or two survivors hiding in the bodies. On certain maps, enemies can shoot you through the ground.
Those annoying issues aside, this game is loads of fun. Now get out there and do your duty: Save Earth from bugs.

Although Yahtzee placed his "Like God of War But..." stamp on Darksiders, I enjoyed this game, on the whole. The action is fluid, the graphics are pretty, and the game has enough length to keep you occupied for a while. However, in spite of it being a good ACTION game, the story itself falls flat on a few occasions, although it did have a satisfying conclusion. One of the things that irked me was how little you use your horse, Ruin. You get him about 3/4 of the way into the game, and even once you've GOTTEN him, his only real use is moving about more quickly in the overworld, which seems rather contradictory; you're a HORSEMAN of the apocalypse, but you fight on foot more than you fight on your horse. The other thing is that even though the game takes several themes from Zelda, like the"overworld"  the game fdoes't make USE of those themes properly; it feels extremely linear. However, in spite of this, the game was fun; it just didn't reach its full potential.

Narcissu is one of the best Visual Novels I've ever played, which is odd because it lacks a staple feature of the genre in having no choices.Reading the author's notes he states that he wanted this VN to flow like a movie and have good pacing which really adds to it more than it takes away. The story has more meaning behind it than just tear-jerking/FEELS, and the minimalistic art makes you feel like your a bystander listening in instead of looking at talking heads for hours. After playing both Narcissu 1 and 2, I feel that 1 has a better story and has a stronger experience behind it, but 2 is better produced and has a sadder story. Narcissu 2nd definitely makes you feel for Setsumi more in part 1, and gives you some insight into how she feels.
I think I should mention that the author states in the notes he would like people to play 2nd before 1st because it's the chronological order. I personally played 1st before 2nd as I played 1st when it was first translated by insani a few years ago. But it definitely would probably be a more powerful experience if you played 2nd before 1st, knowing what happens kind of gave me a weird feeling, it's hard to explain, but I think it would make the 1st game an even greater experience if you had the build up of 2nd still in your mind.

A charming throwback to the platform games of yesteryear bolstered by a powerful chip tune soundtrack, sharp level design and an oddly endearing story.
Controls are tight and responsive, and when coupled with levels that intuitively introduce obstacles and mechanics to you, result in a consistently enjoyable platform experience in which only you are responsible for your failures.
The music is phenomenal, easily enjoyable outside the game if you're into that sort of thing.
Graphics are bright, colorful and creative, allowing the player to both enjoy the astethics and easily identify everything important in a screen.
The game is difficult in places, but never so much that it becomes a chore to play through.  The difficulty is further adjustible via a unique checkpoint mechanic that allows you to destroy stage checkpoints for additional score/wealth, allowing the player to make the game easier or harder on the fly.
If you were a fan of old 8-bit platformer games like Mega Man or pre Symphony Castlevania, buy this game.  If you ever wondered why the 30 somethings around you rant about games like Mega Man or pre Symphony Castlevania, buy this game.  In a sea of "me too" throwback platformers being churned out on Kickstarter or early access, this game stands out for truly understanding what made those titles so memorable in the first place.

This review will be purely based on multiplayer regular and zombies
I think that overall COD WWII is a good game, not amazing and not terrible. However this was true for the week after launch, after that the problems started piling up for me at least. From about one week after launch the game had huge issues with simply connecting online. It would get stuck in fetching profile information, and if it was not that it would be failing to update. Now these issues i persisted through, but a bit later the dev team made a new patch they implemented that significantly reduced performance for me and everyone i know that play the game. Even the simple headquarters became a laggy mess.
Now i think the game in its core is decent, but with some of the issues i cannot recommend it in good faith. At least not to another player who would have to pay a very high price for a game that only has a decent multiplayer. I believe that some of the earlier call of duty titles have balanced gameplay and made innovation to gameplay. But this is at best a downgrade from COD World at War which i would consider a superior game, even though it was released 9 years ago. It feels like an insult to the franchise that a lot of people already consider garbage. Even for a call of duty title i consider this one bland, the strengths of the franchise were stripped away to simplicity. Even zombies gamemode is a lobotomized version of its former self with too many objectives and things that have to be done. I always believed the strength of zombies was its simplicity, that anyone could play it and enjoy it no matter their knowledge of the map or the game.
Another matter entirely is the influx of cheaters that are gradually increasing and destroying the game. I do not feel confident that this matter will improve over time. I would like to say that I hope most issues with this game will be resolved, but after roughly 40 hours in the game I will most probably not return to play it again after this mediocre title. I entirely respect the people that understand and see the flaws of the game and continue playing, and I for their sake the issues are resolved sooner rather than later. I refrained from playing Call of Duty titles for years in hopes that when I came back the gameplay would feel refreshing. Turns out the type of refreshing I was about to feel is the same type as when you drive towards farmland and you can taste the smell of♥♥♥♥♥♥on your skin.
As far as the game goes i would not recommend it at its current stage. At the very least i'd recommend caution in buying the title unless you know specifically what you are buying it for, like for example zombies or the single player. And even then I would recommend you only buy it when the price drops lower. Which knowing a call of duty title will not be for years.

A couple of weeks ago I was in the mood for some strategic space combat - as I regularly am - and decided to revisit Gratuitous Space Battles. The game promises a straightforward brawl without the complications or delay presented by having any kind of story to get in the way.
First, you design your ships. There's a great deal of customization options available, but many are locked when you first begin the game. In order to unlock them, you'll need to play through the missions (more of "combat scenarios" as there is no story behind any of them). It's rather frustrating, almost feeling like the developer decided there needed to be some sense of progression in the game since there would be no story, but I found it to simply get in the way.
Once you've designed your ships, you select your scenario and plan out your ship deployment. Many times you will see the enemy deployment, but on harder difficulties the enemy deployment will be a mystery. After finalizing your deployment, you press play. And here lies the second central conceit of GSB - the battle plays out in front of you without any control. After starting the scenario, your ships fight the enemy on their own, based on the starting deployment and fairly detailed movement and targeting parameters you can give each ship in the planning phase.
I've found the AI to be - at times - frustratingly stupid, which can cripple your careful deployment. There is an option to retain manual control over your ships, allowing the game to play much more like a traditional RTS, and often times I resorted to that so that I could quickly change targets as the situation warranted. This feels like a concession, though, to unhappy players, as the game is clearly designed to be played in a manner where you set up all the pieces and then see what happens when you press start.
Still, with the ship design and deployment phase leading to you sitting back and watching your work unfold, it's very satisfying when everything works together just the way you envisioned it. GSB does a respectable job capturing what it would be like to be a fleet admiral who set the battle plan but had no direct control over the course of the fight (with the one caveat that the fleet admiral would be able to give orders throughout the fight as necessary).
The main problem I had, though, is that it just didn't hold my interest. While the lack of any story to get in the way of the action may be appealing to some, I found that there was no real reason to keep playing. Stories allow you to become invested in the game world, to identify with a character or a faction. Sometimes the story is just the experience of having explored the map and built your bases - you've invested time and effort into the game world. Here, there is nothing even like that.
Sure, there are some vague hints about the game universe in the faction descriptions, but the scenarios become a matter of simple trial and error. If one ship design doesn't work, just go back to the drawing board and pump out another design. There's no penalty if you fail, and there's no way that you can lead your navy to victory once the tide begins to turn against them...you just have to watch them die.
To be fair, an expansion has been released that adds in a Galactic Conquest mode, where you actually have a persistent campaign. But I'm not going to buy an expansion for a game unless I'm interested in seeing more, and GSB wasn't compelling enough for me to want more.

The sound and music, lifting and recontextualising lines from the films as is the custom in the Lego games, adds a lot too, and even on my knackered old laptop performance is great. All in all, great fun and a great game... just like the idea of a vast theme park with real live dinosaurs.
Just like Jurassic Park, though, it comes with one gigantic problem. Its bugs and glitches are less murderous, but can be hugely annoying. Getting to the end of a lengthy, four-part mission, starting a boss fight only to find that the boss doesn't appear; triggers not triggering; objects disappearing. They don't show up often, but when they do they tend to be at the worst possible moment.
It's a great game, and I've enjoyed it immensely - but maybe wait until they've patched it.

I got this game with a 90% discount (only cost me a dollar).
I had my expectations pretty low after reading other reviews but was somewhat impressed once I got into it.
This is a cute, simple, and at-times beautiful game, as long as you enjoy quirky pixel exploration games. The world reveals itself slowly but gracefully and I found myself wanting to continue until I reached the end.
The story is pretty fresh, quite irreverent and I chuckled a few times at the silliness.  It does a good job of balancing the humor, weirdness and the ghostly references of past adventurers' deeds.  You can tell the writers play a lot of games like this and wanted to bring something new to the table.

Disclaimer: I'm not giving a negative rating because the show isn't good, but simply because I've yet to actually be able to watch it. As a rule, any product I pay for but can't use gets a downvote until the issue is resolved.
Every time I try to start the video, the player spends a couple of minutes trying to "retrieve additional components" before displaying an error message and telling me to try again. The exact same problem, with the exact same show, has been reported before, but then by someone using the beta client in Linux (that user has since confirmed the problem to be fixed). For that user, the problem seemed to be caused by the Widewine DRM system, but I honestly have no idea if that is the case here or if there is some other issue. I've been having connectivity issues, but not so severe as to prevent me from downloading and updating games in my library or using other streaming services.
I'm hoping the issue will be resolved soon, but I figured I'd give others a friendly warning in the meantime: Most people don't seem to have any problems, but with a bit of bad luck, you could have to wait for a while before you get to enjoy the show.
That being said, I do hope I'm not discouraging anyone from giving the show a try. Personally, I'm irrationally excited and very much looking forward to watching it - the casting and concept is promising to say the least, and Alan Tudyk is an amazing actor. It's always a good sign when his name pops up in the credits! It's also encouraging to see more content being developed for streaming services, free of the constraints of old media (though less encouraging to see how eager people are to add new constraints). Well worth investing in, I think, regardless of price-per-minute, technological hick-ups and so on.
Fingers crossed that the problem is resolved soon and I can remove the negative rating! In the meantime, enjoy it on my behalf if you can get it to play.

Flawed as it may be, I can see the potential. With a few more game modes, characters and features, this could be an excellent horror-themed multiplayer game.
Like I said, there are a couple of issues. For one, it's a little too easy for the ghost to find people. The radar sense makes sense for the humans as it builds tension to know that the spirits are approaching as you cower and hide, but it makes hiding much less viable when the ghost can get an accurate read on your location fairly easily with his own radar, which is actually better than the human's.
Another problem is reaping humans. At times it can be difficult to lay your ghostly hands on them, especially when they're moving. It's a 50/50 chance of whether it will actually register your clicks and actually tag them, even when you're basically touching them already.
But again, flawed as it may be, this game really shines when things get chaotic. It's easy to see the potential on display here. I'm eager to see what this game will look like with more additions and a handful of bugs fixed up. Here's hoping this game blossoms into something great. It would be a shame if it turned out to be an overpirced game of tag.

Going to do a casual review for now and update when more is added to the game. On launch, it's a good early access. There's some optimization to be done, and the walking animation is a bit goofy, but the three maps they have currently are all very fun, expansive, & detailed. The two monsters are different and interesting and mix-up how you play, as do the two game modes (the first game mode is basically similar to a Damned/Slender, you need to collect 10 stop watches while the monster is invisible except for on your phone, the second is an 'infection' mode where the monsters kill humans, who turn into malicious spirits to kill more humans).
You can play in a lobby with between 2-8 people, the lobbies are good, don't need to forward ports and hosting is easy, along with some good customization in the lobby for things like time, rounds, etc.
Game is good for a few rounds or hours, but the concept is executed well. I found it less scary and more exciting and fun with some really tense and clutch moments. Both modes out feel different and change the tone of rounds considerably. This game will be made or broke by support to the title, I can see this being a real gem of a multiplayer horror game if they add more maps/monsters/modes at a pretty steady rate, what's there now is quite fun and the seven friends I played with and myself all enjoyed it.
While I personally don't find it hugely scary, I did find it a lot of fun, tense, and I did have panic moments when a monster was on my tail or if I was hiding and hoping to god they wouldn't spot or sense me.
TL;DR - Game is fun, content there currently is fun, needs more of it but a very good Day 1 Early Access, has some kinks but nothing game-breaking, this is a good pick-up-and-play game that is good for a few hour sessions every once in a while, and with more content could get addicting. Look forward to see what it becomes.

Artwork, check. Soundtrack, check. Story, eh, half-check. Gameplay, nope.
While most components of the game were great, the game overall was utterly tedious. The story was so sparsely spread that I wouldn't be surprised if someone forgot it between pieces of the story. It was a terrible struggle to even finish the game, and upon completion, I felt sorely disappointed; my time was completely wasted. The slow walking pace of the character, combined with the snail-pace action animations made for a completely awful experience. The game could do without the obstacles entirely and would become far better than it is now. I get that you intended to slow down the player so they could admire the background art, but it's only pixel art. There are no intricate details that need analyzing. It takes mere seconds to take in the entirety of the scene in all of its detail. So the pace at which the game takes place is horrid. I'm not going to even try playing this game again to get all the achievements or see another ending, because it's just that slow.
But if you don't mind repetitive actions that serve no purpose to the game, and that also make the player want to claw their eyes out because they are animated so slowly, then get this game for the artwork and the soundtrack. Heck, just buy the soundtrack and spare yourself the boredom.
P.S. I changed the controls and started playing with one hand so I could use my phone while playing this game. Yes, its gameplay is that mindless and dull.
P.P.S. Just noticed this game is $10. For the love of all that is holy, don't spend the money here for this game. I got it as part of a bundle of 14 other indie games for $5 on Bundle Stars. If you want to check this game out, get it from there to spare yourself the extra $5. You also get a bunch of way better indie games.

This game is extremely fun. The main issue? It could be better.
PROS;
-Is basically Trouble in Terrorist's Town but scarier. And darker. And more stressful.
-Completely and utterly free (unless you want the DLC or tokens for the in-game customization).
-Both co-op and steam party compatible. The first time I got the game, I made a party with two other players and we had quite the amusing time.
-Different characters to play as, has quite a lot of customization options. There's also the fact that in every game, there is never a player that looks like another. Matches force you to pick different default characters and its a chance thing (with your preferred choice making a slight difference).
-There is a leveling/perk system (though I have yet to get the perk tree to work). Leveling helps seperate the noobs from the skilled players by making a casual and ranked difficulty. Ranked difficulty can only be accessed once you are level ten.
-In-game voice and text chat. Makes things amusing.
CONS;
-Glitchy. Game tends to crash on occassion, main menu tends to freeze. I once got stuck in the floor after dying and being healed; had to completely restart the game. There's also the fact that infected can grab you from two feet away because they're magical and prevent dodging. It's also really easy to get stuck on other players.
-Optimization is poor. I have an average computer (gaming wise) and typically get around twenty-five to thirty FPS. That isn't THAT bad but I have a few friends with craptops who barely reach twenty FPS. There are also a ton of random FPS drops or times when the game completely breaks because of server lag.
-Butthurt players. For some reason, if you shoot another person out of nowhere everyone instantly wants a report button just to get you out of the match.....even if you're the infected and have been obvious about it. I've also come across quite a few sexist pigs who don't know when to disable their mics. But that may not be an issue to some people.
-Limited. There really isn't much to the game. I want more gadgets or ways the infected could trick the normal humans up. Torches, cameras, and ammo can only get you so far.
I'm going to be honest, if this game fixed the majority of the cons, added more gamemodes, and simply tweaked around a few things, I would be willing to pay a good....five to seven dollars for this game.

Without a single doubt, this is the scariest game I've ever experienced. Instead of cheap jump scares, Amnesia messes with your brain, making you think things are there when they aren't, and you dread opening every door...
Amnesia is a standard survival-horror game, in terms of it's gameplay. You've got your inventory, your lantern, your health and sanity meters, your journal, et cetera. However, Amnesia truly shines in its story aspect, having a deep and well-written story that needs to be experienced first-hand. And for once, a game actually has pacing, unlike many "Triple-A" games whose developers assume you'll fall asleep within five minutes if something hasn't already exploded. Instead, it builds up the tension, and by the time you even get to see a monster, you're an absolute nervous wreck. And that's good.
If you are a fan of survival horror, I suggest you buy this game.

This game falls in the extremely rare category of one I did not enjoy but would still definitely recommend, presuming you're someone that enjoys precision platforming.  Despite this, I still finished the game, and went back for a few achievements in New Game Plus.
Shovel Knight is extremely well made, and lovingly crafted -- that much is clear.  In fact, I'd argue it's almost too well made -- it's like when a record label sets out to manufacture a song that uses the absolute most pleasing melody, with the perfect rhythm that only years of cold market research and focus testing could produce -- as opposed to some pure, deep, soulful and meaningful expression of life experience by some aspiring and talented singer-songwriter (e.g. Spice Girls vs. Johnny Cash).  That's not to say either method is "wrong"; they're just different.  This game is
good.
The aesthetic... --I mean, if the modernizing features alone weren't a dead giveaway (e.g. widescreen resolution, extended color range, high quality audio), one might mistake it for an old NES game from the '80s; an absolutely masterful presentation in the retro style from the 8-bit Nintendo era.  I've heard some say that the game would've been right at home on the NES.  Of course, ignoring all of the technical impossibilities of such an assertion, some form of it could've.  However, the way I see it, it both absolutely could not, but already kinda did...
You see, Shovel Knight is a great game in its own right; aside from the fan service and nostalgia for an era of gaming long past, it stands up.  A person of any age, regardless of gaming background, could find a lot to like in it, but it especially caters to those of us that grew up playing games of this style, and boy does it hit all the right notes -- like I said, a bit too well.  ...and for me, this is the part where the argument that Shovel Knight stands on its own breaks down, because the only originality I see in it is the token shovel-wielding player character.  Sure, it crafts a personality for itself with its whimsical aesthetic and interesting bosses, but it feels like it all came together as a product of imitation.
Some of the best systems and mechanics from some of the best, most iconic games of the NES era were carefully selected and combined into Shovel Knight.  The overworld map system from Super Mario Bros. 3, the boss and item progression from Mega Man, and heavy elements of Castlevania playstyle are a few examples.  That's not to say this is a problem, nor would I accuse the developers of plagiarism; game development is a highly iterative process.  You could critically examine most games today and find roots well-established by games the preceded it; that's just progress.
My point though is a counter-argument to the idea that Shovel Knight could've been at home on the NES.  It simply couldn't, because it is a perfection of all of those games that came before it; it just wouldn't exist without them.  It is a modernized adaptation of our best memories from a long-past era of gaming, formed to fit with the conveniences and features we've come to expect today.
As for me?  I mentioned I didn't enjoy it.  I actually found the experience a lot more stressful than I expected it to be.  Not that I necessarily felt cheated, or that I took issue with the difficulty ramp (by the end, I found it extremely challenging, though fair).  My skill and reflexes felt informed by the level design, commensurate to my ability (I did beat the game after all).  There were moments of triumph, where I managed to successfully execute difficult maneuvers on the first try, but there were contrasting moments of trial and error, akin to the Dark Souls experience where you learn enough from each mistake to do better on subsequent attempts.  I got the impression that it was never going to exceed my skill level -- despite how crazy it became at times --that I could find some way to force my way through it, and even when I was sure the game might beat me, sure enough, I found a way through.
The problem for me is that Shovel Knight managed to trigger my anxiety in a way that few games have ever been able.  For me, the execution and platforming would often feel harrowing, is if I was risking and wagering far more than was actually on the line.  I don't know where this feeling came from, because ultimately the death penalty isn't all that impactful, and there are enough checkpoints throughout each level to keep the repetition tolerable.  ...but I felt stressed out and tense the whole time, and it just wasn't a good feeling.  I expect, for most people -- especially for any fans of this genre -- this will not be a problem, but I just couldn't relax, and that made it that much more difficult to just have fun.
My personal edge-case aside, it's a wonderfully made game, and stands as one of the best examples of percision platforming I've seen.  It's well loved and respected for a reason, and I would still easily recommend giving it a shot.

The magic of this game is hard to describe in words. In short, it combined the nostalgia of my childhood passion for gaming while altogether creating something new for the next generation to fall in love with. It's tough to relate to that feeling of opening up a brand new Super Nintendo game for the first time, but this game comes damn close.
Combining all of the elements I used to love about side scrolling platfomers like Duck Tales, Castlevania, Metroid and Megaman, Shovel Knight keeps true to its goal of delivering 8-bit fun without just rehashing a classic.
My only regret is not finding this game sooner. It is an absolute must play for anyone looking to feel that rush from the past or simply to broaden your horizon and try something unique.

So, before anyone has a chance to give you the wrong impression about this game let me set you straight. This is probably the best Call Of Duty campaign since Black Ops. It has characters you actually care about, set in an era which is familiar to some and brand new to the younger Call Of Duty fans. The story is actually interesting, most World War Two games focus on the liberation of Paris and then the drive all the way to Berlin. In this game while you do liberate Paris, takes you on a more average path. You fight in the Battle of the Bulge, and even have a brief stint of infiltration into a Nazi stronghold. There is a lot more stealth in this Call Of Duty, having something like 4-5 different stealth sections in the main campaign. The gameplay is pretty good overall, which is pretty important since this game is a first person shooter. The story does have some dull moments but overall the story is gripping enough to make you want to keep going. I actually really advise you guys to pick up this game up, despite the negative reviews given just because it is Call Of Duty. I think it is also worth mentioning I havent played a Call Of Duty in over 3 years, so this really gave the series the refresh it needed. I hope the next game is as good or better then this one. Other then that, I don't have too much else to say, so pick this game up and try it for your self before boycotting it just because it is Call Of Duty.

So apparently there was an issue in which the game would not launch due to missing files, this issue seems to have been resolved though I get the feeling it would of been bettter off without the fix.
So having not played the 47 previous Destruction games (that or I assume the developer named it Destruction 48 for artistic purposes) I was unsure on what to expect from this game. After the 0.3 hours it took to apparently complete this, I'm still unsure of what the actual ♥♥♥♥ I experienced...
So what to expect from playing this, the level design is at times confusing with where you left the previous screen not really matching up to the next screen you enter. Also parts of the levels you would expect to be blocked off you're able to easily walk through whilst other parts you would think you can walk to are blocked off by invisible walls. In fact a lot of the design lacks consistency. Plus I personally liked the glitch in which the game recognises a baseball bat as an equiable helmet, in which when you try to do so an error message will display and the game starts to act like its about to crash.
The combat is basically face the enemy and attack, at this point you will notice if you're using a gun the bad hit detection. The game gives you a huge amount of melee weapons, most of which you will most likely want to avoid as there doesn't seem to be a way to avoid taking damage in close range (not that it really matters with the 800 odd medkits the game throws at you). All the enemies will basically move towards you, unless they get confused and move off screen for some reason, the only vartiety being is that some enemies have more health than others. I also personally like the grenades in which once thrown, bounce off what ever they hit and head back in the direction they came. There is also a magic system, not that I would know as spending the short amount of time that I did with this was painful enough.
Some areas have a 30 second sound loop of chirping birds which seems to cut out and then start to replay at a lower volume. Other areas have absolutely no sound at all. You will think this is bad until you actually reach areas that do have music, in which feels just as painful as having wisdom teeth removed under local anesthetic, honestly sandpaper is less abrasive.
It's sad but if this game had spent more time in development and was refined, it could of been a fun little game to play. But instead feels like it was thrown together on a lazy Sunday afternoon and chucked up on Steam because the developer had that months rent due or wanted to pay off some of their drug debts. This isn't worth 0.99 cents let alone the $1.99 US the dev is asking.

Some of the hiding spots are as simple as standing in a dark corner, where you can clearly look the monsters in the eye without them noticing you, and others require some creative thinking.

Narcissu is a classic amongs Visual Novels.
This is the story of a guy being terminally ill. Once admitted into the hospital he meets another patient, Setsumi. She is, like him, going to die. However, both of them want to die somewhere else than in the hospital. They will escape, and travel through a few prefectures of Japan. This is their story. Up until the very end.
Do not expect this story to be any kind of funny. This is very emotionnal and you might probably cry. The storytelling is good enough. Two differents translations are available, and you can choose to activate the voices or not.
I read this visual novel a long time ago. Voices and episode 2 were not available at the time.
I do strongly recommend this "game" to anyone wanting to try the Visual Novel genre. This VN, is linear and there are no choices. No interactivity. Technically, this is a subgenre of Visual Novel called a Kinetic Novel. You just read. And do nothing else. Narcissu is however very minimalistic. There are not many pictures compared to other visual novels. Please do not be rebuked, and read, immerse yourself in the story. Like you would for any good book.
This is very close to reading a comic book, except you have music, voice and -- sometimes -- animated pictures. You have to experience at least one visual novel in your life, the same way you should play an RTS or FPS if you haven’t done so. This genre is not well known enough, it's kinda sad.
A lot of other visual novels exists and are masterpieces. This is a good start for anyone not knowing what this media is.
Since Narcissu is Free, do not miss this opportunity, and try it. You will hate it or love it. But, you have to try.

You miss those days when you saw the heart and soul put into a game?
When the game was challenging, but not punishing?
When the game had charm, but wasn't childish?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, then you should definitely look into Shovel Knight. Even if you said no because you weren't old enough to have classic memories of ye games of olde but would be interested then this is still a solid game to play. It's definitely inspired by a lot of older games such as Megaman and Ducktales, but it plays extremely well and is a standout and well made game.
For starters, the gameplay itself is really solid. For the levels, the platforming is solid, controls extremely well, and is overall well designed. Most stages have a gimmick, such as being pitch black and only lightning to show the path, or lava you have to traverse by spreading a gel on it. This makes each level it's own and stand out. For the bosses, the combat is extremely smooth. They do their pattern and you dodge and fight them, and each boss has a bit of a gimmick (One gets a herald of trumpets to cause raining killer confetti, while another sets up a treasure chest that steals your money). Each knight (or boss) has it's own personality to. You got the self-riteous King Knight, the bratty Tinker Knight, and so on.
The items are also interesting, and each bring their own gameplay change (Though you are by no means required to get them, which makes them better). Some have utility (Such as an amulet that gives invulnerability), some give aid to platforming (Such as a knife that pulls you forward), and others just help with combat (Such as a giant anchor that you can throw). Which items are useful or not depends on how the player uses them, though almost all items can be used in most situations.
The death system is also interesting. If you die you lose a large sum of your collected loot, but you can retrieve it by grabbing the floating bags that you leave behind (on the first life after you die). This means while death isn't that punishing, it can cause you to not be able to get some items, so you are still encouraged to keep as much treasure as you can.
There is also one neat little gimmick that levels have: Their checkpoints. While this isn't true for the first level, you can break your checkpoints as you go along for treasure, but remove the check point itself. Checkpoints that have a longer stretch to the next one generally give more treasure. It becomes a measure of risk vs reward!
The music is also quite amazing overall. Though some may not like the chiptune instruments, it is overall well composed.
As every rose must have it's thorns, though, this to has some flaws.
While I said the level design is amazing earlier, the majority of the time the enemies aren't obstacles as much as platforms, and this makes some levels feel like the biggest threat is the instakill pits/spikes/lava, which given a health system seems redundant.
Also most bosses can simply be cheesed by "Scrooge McDucking", ie. Simply bouncing on them over. And over. And over, and that often times is a blind spot on them, so the difficulty of the boss is diminished if you are good at bouncing over and over.
Another issue is a couple bosses have instant kill moves that can catch a player off guard (Snow Knight...), leading to some cheap deaths (Though this is rare).
Finally, the final boss has one flaw I find quite major: You are supposed to bounce off a partner, however there is no implication of this. You can't stand on them like it looks like, you can't hit them or anything... this can lead to frustration of just trying to figure out how to beat the final boss.
Overall a terrific game in almost any aspect, save for a few minor gripes! If you are looking for an entertaining game, look no further!

Tactical Intervention is...interesting. While not being tactical in any way, it does live up to its name; being an intervention. While many people are on a high from Counter Strike, and CS:GO, T.I. seems like a very possible alternative to dive into. However, even with its decent map design and solid mission modes; T.I. fails in many regards. Keep in mind, this is a free game.
Game Play synopsis -
- pay to win does not always win. I found that after a couple hours playing, years back, i could stand my own with an M4 and buying light armor with the in-game points. *Save your GP*
- Shotguns = the noob cannon. I find the best way to deal with these players, is to just stay away. There is always some off chance that a stray bullet with decide to fly across the map and nail you with a headshot. However, the gore and carnage that is left in their path is quite enjoyable to watch.
- invest in a decent pair of boots. Speed is key, and with no universal speed, the ones who can run are the ones who can survive.
- camping is possible but hard to pull off. The feature to spot where your attacker killed you from is a great advantage. *it takes certain skill to defend a corner*
- Spawn time is 10 seconds. Longer than most games, such as C.S. and the instant respawn in a deathmatch.
- The damage stats are garbage. You’ll see damage carry over from previous kills. Upwards of 200, 300, etc. In many cases, 150 damage could be beaten by 140. The number of shots again follows this logic…..oh wait, there is no logic because it makes NO SENSE!
- This game is all about how well you can tolerate those annoying players who live in the middle of nowhere with a ping of +600 and can kill you instantly because they are clipping harder than the Microsoft Word Helper in a paperclip factory.
- You’ll be bombarded by rage quitters, “you’re a 10 yr old boy!” comments, loud music being blasted over the voice chat, and also, the always appreciated, “?how do to change class” stupid questions.

The path ahead is almost entirely linear, brought to life with beautiful vistas crafted through pixel art and supported by a tranquil soundtrack. But there's very little to actually interact with, so what is there ends up feeling very perfunctory. Every tool, save one, is collected before the adventure starts; there's not even any mystery or problem solving there (though I can't imagine the backtracking involved if you did not take your time and speak to everyone). You're encouraged from the beginning to play slowly, but it's difficult to miss an opportunity permanently and it's impossible to die. There's no stress or tension here. It's all replaced with a soothing calm that permeates the whole experience. With as little input or risk as it requires from the player, Qora could have easily been made as a film, but it'd be a film worth watching. Should you feel inclined to spend the time and money on it, you'll likely walk away happier than you were when you started, as brief and straightforward as the game is.

Last time i played a fishing game it was on a PlayStation console. Since then i couldn't find any fishing game which would be interesting and fun. Fishing planet combines simulation with arcade and the result is pretty good. The game is realistic enough to keep you playing, try different baits and lures, time of day etc. and it's arcady enough to be fun for casual players.
Gameplay is pretty basic, you choose the lake or river, pay the money for transportation, buy the licence and go fishing. The are countless baits and lures, rods and reels. You choose the correct ones, cast the rod and wait. If your equipment is low level it can break very fast, but if you use it correctly it wears pretty slow. You can buy equipment to store more things (you can take limited amount of things to the lake with you).
What i don't like is the licence system. I'll try to explain. There is in-game time, you arrive at the lake in early morning and time slowly ticks while you're fishing. You also must buy a licence with in-game money, but licence are valid only for the time you purchase it(1 day, 3 days etc. You can buy unlimited licence but it cost crazy amount of money) so if you purchase a licence for 1 day it is valid for 1 day in real time while game clock stops when you quit the game. I think this is not fair. People after work don't have much time to play, they purchase the licence and play maybe for an hour in the evening and the next day the licence expires. I think licence should be tied to in-game clock and licence time should freeze same as in-game clock when you quit. If developers want money they should make and sell new lakes as DLC instead of items or boosters.
This game is free with in-game purchases for real money, so i guess this is the reason. Developers want people to buy licenses for real money. Anyway you still can fully enjoy the game without spending real money. Leveling is very slow but it wouldn't be fun to level up fast in my opinion. If you're short on money you get some each time you launch a game and there's free lake where you can farm money and exp.
The graphics are acceptable, it could use some work. There are maybe 10 or so maps which are very small so it shouldn't be too difficult for developers to make them look better, after all you stare at the same environment for hours so it would be nice if it looked better. game runs steady 60fps all the time. Water on the other hand looks amazing and realistic. Well you kinda expect that from such game anyway.
Developers made a good work on the sound department. Sounds really add immersion and make you feel closer to the nature.
All in all the game is really fun, a perfect game if you want to relax and listen to the sounds of nature. Try it, it's free :)

Y'know, sometimes there are legitamate reasons to not want to pick up a game. Bugs might be one of them. and boy does EDF have them. stay away if you hate giant insects.
okay, cheesy joke aside, EDF is a blast if you can play it co-op in some form. like, for real. the game is a bit buggy at times in the more proper sense of the term, but nothing game breaking unless your computer isn't up to the sheer amount of things EDF will toss at it. i do reccomend the use of a controller if you have a buddy who likes to come over.
the game's arsenal is... surprisingly diverse. ARs that shoot bouncing bullets, homing rocket launchers that clearly take a page off Macross Missle Massacre, shotguns that shoot in a flat cone rather than a circular one, Limpet Guns which act a lot like stickybomb launchers except reloading disarms the bombs, deployables of all kinds, vehichles from tanks to mechs to helicopters, air strikes of all sorts, a bunch of weapons that if i didn't know better i would say were lifted off Monster Hunter, and even laser targeting sights, allowing those with homing launchers to lock onto bugs and other foes too far or are otherwise incapable of locking onto, and so on and so forth. seriously, other game devs need to play EDF before they can think about "weapon diversity". and you'll want the finest arsenal to fight back the giant insects and the ravagers.
mission wise it'll be the same thing for the most part: kill all enemies. to thier credit they do mix it up by not using bugs all the time. there's some mechanized troops, theres flying units with seemingly generic AI, but one thing unifies the enemies. they are all big, and they all outnumber you when you start the mission.
Voice acting is endearingly both good at times and others just bad enough that you have to chuckle, and it has a "Starship Troopers" vibe to the games story. like, it's cheesy at best, but it's ironically "so bad it's good" at other times. most of the time the story plays absolutely 0 role in the gameplay and is just there to set up the background of the missions or to preface what is happening in said missions.
overall, if you just want an excuse to kill big bugs and lots of them... you really can't go wrong with EDF. unless you don't have friends. in which case you might want to look elsewhere. EDF really sucks as a singleplayer game and it'll show when you're on the wrong end of a horde of ants.

Team Fortress 2 is quite the game to discuss. On one hand, as pointed out by Funke, the learning curve is ♥♥♥♥ed. You have to watch videos and discuss the game if you want to get any good. That might sound like something that's a small gripe and that's because it is. On the whole I love TF2. I puts you in the mind of a psychotic, expendable (spelt wrong I know), and eccentric mercenary in war like setting. The environments I have to complain also are a bit samey as you play longer and longer but the colorful cast of charcters make up for it. I like how Valve puts mechanics over everything else though. Another gripe I have also is that there's no music built into the game, but that is an easy fix with youtube now-a-days. I'm not to sure about what the theme of the game is and might have to look it up, and if there is it gets kind of muddied in the mechanics. That might be because of the mind set of a "gamer" I have built into my brain, and that might actually what this game caters to. Apart from lore that is built up by comics and videos, no story or narrative is brought up other and the characters are kind of there just to contribute to the feel of the game, and that's amazing in my opinion. Just like music or a painting, games don't necessarily have to be about a theme or message. And what makes this game such a game is that it, in my opinon, encourages fantasy and exploration of roleplaying, which I never thought I could get into. Sorry for this being long winded and perhaps pertentious, but that's just me I guess.

I've finished Narcissu 1,2 and 3 before 1 and 2 even got green-lit. Tomo Kataoka did a great job for it. Hopefully this will make people read more visual novels. I see this as an opportunity for more visual novel titles to be up here.
The story was beautifully written and it wasn't in any case forced drama. What I like about this visual novel is it's story is feels almost in touch with reality and not something that is far-fetched. One might think otherwise but it has a natural feel about it. The OST used was also rather smooth and it did great enhancing the mood and atmosphere of the story as it progress. I don't know how well the translations were but Tomo Kataoka did a good job. I hope the translators who translate this don't pull down the quality. It's simply a masterpiece, something not many visual novels could achieve. I for one, recommend this visual novel for visual novel readers. Unless you dislike nakige and utsuge, this visual novel should be a very good read. It isn't very long either so it should be picked up even if one doesn't have loads of spare time as this visual novel is considerably shorter than other visual novels.
I don't want to post any spoilers so I shan't say much about how the story is but I truly recommend this visual novel. I was expecting some tears to flow since this is a nakige and utsuge but I almost never cried anywhere harder. This visual novel took that emotion to a whole new level, something not many visual novel/anime can do.

Even today, Rome: Total War takes the cake as the best Total War title. If nothing else sells you, it is important to note that this game almost NEVER crashes. For those of you new to the Total War series, Total War games love to crash, ruining your hours of hard, strategic work and luck.
Rome is extremely well balanced. Territory development, troop training, technology advances, political maneuvers, unit types...it all works together to make a deep, strategic game with no room to blame broken mechanics.
You pick a house of Rome and start conquering things. Many of the problems that the Roman Empire faced are now obstacles for you to crush. You can spend hours getting sucked into this world and attempting to achieve perfection. Each hour is worth it. Learn lessons, get defeated, try again. The true spirit of combat.

This is a tactics/stats/puzzle game, set in space. Or is it a space admiral sim. Well its really addictive. The gameplay involves setting up a fleet to destroy an ememy fleet. Thats basically it. But the weapon,armor and enemy types are varied enough that you will be required to design your own ships and outfit them with specific components to deal with the current and future challenges. When the battles play out, you have no control over anything except the speed of battle. This allows for alot of trail and eror, which i kinda like.
There are a few gripes i have with this game. The progression system is annoying and requires that you play over and over to get honor so unlock modules, hulls, and races. The modules and hulls not so much a problem, but i do wish the other races were available by default. Also i wish there was a toggle to swap between full screen and windowed when the battles play out. These options do exist in the settings menu, but i did kinda prefer the pre battle stuff to be windowed and the post to be full screen, thats just me though.
If tactics and experimentation are something you want to get into, i suggest you try this one.
Note - If you are visually impared, you may find that the text amounts and stats are abit intimidating. The good news is that this is one of those games that works in windowed mode along with Windows magnifier (At least on Windows 8). Just make sure that when you switch the full screen mode off, you reduce the resolution to the same aspect ratio you are used to, eg. if you play in 1920 by 1080, run it at 1600 by 900. There is also a ticker at the top of the screen during the battle that will explain whats going on, but this is really tricky to read even in windowed mode, however it didn't really stop me from playing through the campaign.

There's a reason why a large number of Total War fans revert back to this game- it's an absolute classic.  Sure, it's an old game, but don't get me wrong- even now this game looks great, and the gameplay is just as good as ever.From commanding Rome's legionares to directing Greece's Spartan hoplites, the one thing that this game does fantastically is create a real authentic feel.  However there are a few drawbacks; the game's strategy is incredibly deep; From managing cities and trade, to Generals and population happiness, the game can not only be daunting to newcomers, but will quickly get out of hand for the seasoned pro when he/she has conquered enough of the world.  In addition to that, the game is not completely balanced; sure the Roman's were overpowered in real life, but when you have a Carthiginian army that outnumbers the Roman army 3:1, it's ridiculous to see the Autoresolve favor of Rome.  Even with this drawbacks however, this game still manages to please, and after almost ten years, it's easy to see why this is one of the greatest strategy games of all time.

A small indie game that some people might find to their liking - I myself got just bored fast.
My main complaint though is how badly this game is coded.
It's a small pixel/sprite game... but launches like a huge AAA game with top graphics engine.
When I first launched it - it started in a window instead of full screen... you hit "space" in the menu instead of "enter" to go to options which is unusual. Options themselves are very basic - full screen, controls, volume and resolution - which only actually means the size of window when you play in windowed mode.
Again, the worst is the coding. UNLESS I leave the whole PC only for this game then the game loads slooooooooooooooooow. And I see "Loading" for few minutes before it starts up.
So by comparison I can launch Skyrim or Dead Space faster than Qora - that's right... that's how badly it's optimized.
In fact since I'm currently copying a lot of files between my external HDDs - playing these small steam games is a way for me to kill time. But THIS game just slows down to a crawl - at times even freezes when I alt-tab.
I mean this is a game on the level of windows games like solitare. Let's be real. My PC has 12GB RAM and i7 CPU. AAA games can all launch faster than this little "snail".
So yeah. Not just I'm not impressed by the game itself - but how badly it's optimized.
On top of that, this is one of those games where Steam detects the time only on exit (or so it seems) and if I play them in windowed - it take muuuuch longer than comparable games to get the cards dropped. I had the same problem with the terrible game called "Retention" which didn't even have full screen mode (had to get 10h on a 10min game just to get cards). But here even with the full screen - it still refuses to drop cards for me and I'm already past 2h, so I think this is related to the full screen thing again. It's always those small, indie games that prefer to work in windowed mode that have issues with card drops for me.
PS. And just as I finished this review and alt tabbed back into the game (at this point my HDD copying finished, so now the game has the whole floor for itself) - and guess what... that's right, the game froze, again. What a turd.

Qora is a game I think everyone likes exploration games should own. It's linear, it's relaxing, and it has an awesome soundtrack.
So, I don't exactly know how to compress my feelings about qora at all. I guess I'll start by the graphics. The graphics design was extremely beautiful. Same goes for the designs, the areas are all extremely well made. Most of them are surreal and unique, and even the plain ones still feel really good. It had a good storyline, I was not expecting the ending at all.
. The soundtrack was pretty good. The music really went well with each location. When it was a dark situation, there was silent eerie soundtrack. When you were in a beautiful area, there was calm or upbeat music. I think you get what I mean.
It has a good athmosphere, there are some very creepy scenes, especially the scene with the hidden bunker. It also has two endings, and multiple ends are always nice! It does leave some questions in your head though. What are the white masked guys? Aliens? Did the deities give anyone else gifts when they moved in, and did they have to go through all that too?
Now, I don't recommend it for everyone. There isn't really much to do in it. There is a lot of exploration, but no puzzles, action sequences or deaths in this case. It's linear, and most of the time you are just heading right. There are some scenes where you have to wake up beasts, break rocks or do a little platforming, but most of the time it's just a game about exploring scenery. If you don't like games like that, then you should probably not buy this. Other than that, it's a pretty great game.
Also, love the credits theme. The quotes people wrote are pretty silly, you guys all make me laugh :3
Sorry for the short review, but like I said, there isn't much to say about qora other than the things I have mentioned.

DISCLAIMER: This is the opinion of someone who recieved the game for free.
This is a very cautious recommendation and I would definitely not recommend this at full price.
Qora is not a fun game to play but rather in my humble opinion presents a compelling enough world to keep exploring.
Qora is very much just a 2d walking sim in terms of gameplay (much of the game is just pushing "space", "up", and "right"). Do not get this game if you are out for a game with any deep mechanics. Then what about the audience that enjoys games like the Stanley Parable and The Beginner's Guide? As someone who can accept a sacrifice in mechanical complexity for a casual but engaging world and story, to me Qora was an enjoyable experience. The aesthetic and chiptune music fit my tastes but if they don't fit yours then this game is probably not the game for you.
Qora started off actually pretty boring until about 5-10 minutes in (this is a short game, max 1-2 hours for 1 playthrough)  when the happenings within the game actually started to become interesting. The bulk of the game has you exploring extremely varied and nicely put together locations as you try to piece together the past of the land. Depending on your actions there are actually multiple endings for some replaybility.
Overall I can safely say that I did infact enjoy my time with Qora but for the usual asking price of 10 USD I cannot recommend it. On sale however, if you are the person who doesn't mind casual failure state free experiences which are essentially more movie than game, then yes this game is worth checking out.
Lastly it has cards and very easy to obtain achievements :P

The trailer has an obvious tie-in to another sci-fi show that was tragically cancelled by a network that just didn't understand what they had, but the show itself doesn't dwell on it. It's a good romp on the life of an actor in a cancelled/ended sci-fi show (so far their life at conventions, but it looks like future episodes have other venues).
The episodes are short (10 1/2 and 11 1/2 minutes for the first two), but the quality is really high. I hope they have many more of the cameo appearances. People just keep popping in and I'm like, "Oh, that's ....!" One interesting thing about being created for streaming is that there doesn't need to be any set length. If it only needs ten minutes, then it's ten minutes. If it runs to 15 minutes, so what? There are no commercials and no time slots. That has to be somewhat freeing for the writers, actors editors etc. If something isn't working, drop it. If they get an idea as they are recording, add it in. As such, there's going to be no excuse for filler or lulls here. I wonder if that adds any pressure to the writers, actors or edtors? With the way my schedule works and with the intensity of these shows, I'm happy with the length. Worth the money already for me.

This game is Fun. I may have only put in about 16 hours so far, but those 16 hours have been over like, a day and a half, to two days. That's how engagingly fun the gameplay is. Another point in favor of the game (at least to my eyes) is the fact that there's an actual text chat supported. It has a hilariously small character limit, but the fact that you can type your own message in and send it is more than you'll see in most console ported games. What shines (at least it has for me so far) is the mic support. That is to say that it actually works just fine in game. Now, you'll have to turn down the back ground music and sound effects to hear people over the gunfire, explosions, and giant monsters you're fighting, but the voice chat itself works properly. Unlike a number of games I've played, it doesn't drop your voice, cut out, or have issues transmitting that seems to plague most in game voice options that I've utilized. And being able to yell about hectors on the horizon and where is incredibly useful when your hands are busy keeping your guy moving and shooting.
The game is not without faults. Some of the dlc is patently ridiculous (human decoy blow up dolls?) the graphics are kind of old looking, and sometimes the equipment menu will lag for mysterious and unknown reasons. But the trade off on those graphics is that you'll be fighting actual armies of giant insects, robots, and flying menaces. It isn't a game where you are sent to fight an army and there's like 4 guys on screen at once for you to do battle with. Swarms look like swarms because they Are and having a full team of four mixed units can really turn the tide of battles, as each class has a different point at which it can shine in missions. Even if you don't get this game on sale, it's worth the price. When it comes to the DLC, however, your milage may vary. The weapon dlcs are very handy for getting a head start with low level weaponry for each of the classes. As a Fencer, I've found the Bloodstorm to be particularly handy even in higher weapon level missions just because of the way that it target locks, tracks targets, and drops a cluster of explosions nearby (or even in mid air against flying units). The vast majority of the weapons in the game, however, drop from missions and none of the dlc weapons are above maybe level 3? (for reference, 50 missions in the cap on weapons you can use in those mission is like, 13? 14?).
Also, there's an entire EDF song that you can sing through the chat menu (with the arrow keys under shout> Sing) set to the tune of Glory, Glory, Hallelujah. The best part about it is that when you have npcs following you, they will sing the next verse back to you. So you sing 1-1, and they sing back 1-2, sing 1-3, and they go to 1-4. It's a nice touch.

Narcissu is a Kinetic Novel - essentially something like reading a novel on the computer, only with music, voicing and background music. It's also considered an 'Utsuge', which basically means it has an incredibly heartwrenching story.
Now, onto the game itself. Without spoilers, by the end of it, you will feel for characters, the music is beautiful, while the amount art is lacking, I personally find that it adds to the themes of the game.
This isn't considered an 'Utsuge' for nothing, however. Excepting those with cold hearts of stone, you will feel sad, you may likely even cry. Though, this is far from a bad thing, and it has some pretty thought provoking themes such as, without spoiling too much, the fate of those with no place in society and suicide.
It is quite short read, it only took me a few hours to complete. So if you're looking for a short, yet powerful read, and aren't afraid to shed some manly(or womanly) tears, then by all means try this out. I can all but guarantee you will not regret it.

There's a reason why a large number of Total War fans revert back to this game- it's an absolute classic. However there are a few drawbacks; the game's strategy is incredibly deep; From managing cities and trade, to Generals and population happiness, the game can not only be daunting to newcomers, but will quickly get out of hand for the seasoned pro when he/she has conquered enough of the world.  In addition to that, the game is not completely balanced; sure the Roman's were overpowered in real life, but when you have a Carthiginian army that outnumbers the Roman army 3:1, it's ridiculous to see the Autoresolve favor of Rome.  Even with this drawbacks however, this game still manages to please, and after almost ten years, it's easy to see why this is one of the greatest strategy games of all time.

Seriously though, Resident Evil 5 has a lot going for it graphically, mechanically, and narratively.
For starters, let's get started:
GRAPHICS: 8.5/10 Runs smooth, and--after dropping the mouse sensitivity--the dizziness once a companion of any movements was gone. Apart from that, this game is gorgeous. The AI movements, the weapon and combat animations, the cutscenes--very well rendered.
GAMEPLAY/MECHANICS: 8/10 It took a little getting used to the new inventory setup. It makes a lot of sense if played through coop, but adds steps to keep track of when solo. Not cumbersome, mind you, but definitely meant for coop play. It's a little inconvenient having you character freeze in his tracks when trying to switch weapons (even more so when surrounded by enemies/bosses). As far as the weapons go, I find myself running out of bullets a whole lot more. In RE4 the game would pause while in menu, allowing smoother transitioning of weapons and strategies; whereas in RE5 you sort of are more guns-blazing and be like, "oh stink, ran out of ammo, let me switch" or "big gun coming! I NEED MORE BPS! (bullets-per-second)... OH WAIT, I GAVE THAT TO MY PARTNER??!?!?!" xD
But that shotgun feels glorious when you get a good knock-back. Still haven't utilized the fighting mechanics as much as the developers intended them to be used, but I like the guns xD
Let's be honest though, if I could be playing through this game with a buddy, the gameplay/mechanics could probably easily hit 9/10.
STORY/NARRATIVE: 9/10 Okay, I'm going to have to break this into two categories: RE5's story, and RE's story (at least from 4 on). The stories are compounding, which is why halfway through I took a break from RE5 to go back and play RE:Revelations 1 and 2. I love the flow between story-archs and characters that Resident Evil has going for it.
RE4 gets a lot more personal on the individual effect upon the virus, but RE5 brings it to a whole new level.
I love storylines that expand your story. Mass Effect 1 and 2 being a prime example. In RE5, I love the direction they took the fall of Umbrella and the corruption of such a lucrative biochemical-market would bear.
And they did awesome is setting that scale, in my opinion, even in the first 5 minutes of the game. I love cultural and political turmoil done right, and they are keeping me interested.
Who else pauses mid-way just to get a richer context on two of the characters mentioned in a game??
Uhmm, me:)

Legitimately excellent game that gives me some renewed hope about the Call of Duty franchise as a whole. The return to classic game mechanics such as limited health and the necessity for health kits brings an intense feeling to the campaign when played on veteran (which you should always do). Playing on lower difficulties makes the game feel disjointed and broken, as you can often times simply charge ahead to trigger various sequences causing the enemies to retreat.
Playing on veteran allowed for an enjoyable 10 hour+ campaign, that had compelling characters and legitimate attachment to your squad. Best campaign since WaW or Modern Warfare, easily.
Multiplayer is pretty rough when you're new as the lack of modifications and better guns definitely shines when matched against prestiged players. The default classes aren't terrible, but I wouldn't call them ideal by any standard.
Zombies introduces a fresh wave of innovation by granting players a linear set of objectives to achieve, which on paper sounds terrible, but in actually gives the survival experience an added layer of tension and achievement beyond turning on the power, getting decent guns, and training zombies unendingly.
Overrall, a great return to what originally made this franchise good, with combat mechanics taken from the gamecube classics, and given the modern twist of beautiful graphics. While not a perfect game, definitely worth the buy.

Never thought that creating ships to blow alien ships up for no apparent reason or logic whatsoever could be so fun! :D
What you basically do is to design ships which, when deployed in battle, will help defeat the enemy fleet. Every victory you win will give you a credit like reward called Honour. You use this 'Honour' to buy new shiny gadgets or weapons that blaze nice looking beams of death onto your enemy.
There is no actual story line. The game is basically composed of about 14 setups (counting the tutorial battle aswell as an additional 9 setups when including all the DLC's, which brings the number up to 23) which all offer a different challenge along with a certain species to go against. This means that just because your ship designs and the fleet you deployed were successful against a certain race in such a scenario, doesn't mean that you will be as successful in another scenario with a different species. Not to mention certain scenarios having something called 'Spartial Anomalies' which can affect how well/poor your ships perform in terms of their weapons and defences.
There is also a multiplayer mode which tbh isnt what you actually think, it isnt a match-up with another player, see who wins and say "HAHA YOU SUCK!" kind of game. No, how it works, is that you mainly pick your map and make your own scenario, deploy your ships that you designed and upload them. The scenario is then uploaded to a vast list of scenarios for the community to try out. Some may even consider retaliating your challenge. However i would just recommend trying out created scenarios to try out since there is a vast list of uploads that there is only a small chance of someone actually trying it out your own.
With every game however, it has its drawbacks...
Not counting the DLC, you may find it fustrating when you find yourself losing and on the recieving end of super intense beams of destruction blowing your stuff to smithereens, again and again. After the battle you are shown stats which are near impossible to understand, so you may end up in a repeating scenario of losing, losing, losing, then after more losing looking at the stats in attempt to study what is wrong, make new ship designs, still lose, go back to the drawing board, still lose and then wondering why the hell you cannot win when you study the stats for almost an hour. Also without the DLC you may end up finding yourself bored with just 4 races at your disposal, one of which you cannot fight on the single player mission scenarios.
As a result you may find yourself thinking that you wasted your money on a game you cannot understand and find out how little content you had. I would advice buying this game when there is some sort of sale or deal going on with this game. Buy with the DLC expansions too to give the game a little more spice to your experience with the game. That and a lot of patience with the losing and looking up for tips on certain situations and you may end up actually coming back to this every now and then.
Despite these flaws, GSB is quite a fun little game to kill an hour or so...just don't expect to fall in love with all the info you are bombarded with at the end of the battle. Again i would advise getting the DLC's as they include an extra 6 races to try and mess around with and a Galactic Campaign, though i would avoid not getting to engrossed in that too much due to the Galactic Campaign having some flaws, but the rest should keep you occupied with this game for even longer.
It may have moments where you say ♥♥♥♥ THIS GAME, ♥♥♥♥ ITS MECHANICS, I WANT MY MONEY BACK!, but stick to it and hopefully in the end you will be glad you bought this game along with the DLC's.
Even though the game may end up annoying you with stats and at times fleets that make you think this is all impossible to understand, it can be really fun to play once you get used to it, maybe you could one day decide to play out of rage and take out your anger on a bunch of aliens who have no reason to be blown up whatsoever, except for your entertainment of zero-g fireworks and act as some sort of stress relief!
