I like the recent tendency towards making resident evil games a co-op-friendly franchise. I honestly think it's high time we abandoned simplistic axioms about what the survival horror genre should be about.
We have to take into account that the game was designed at a time when Capcom decided to make a drift towards a rather action-based style in the RE franchise. I'm quite sure the game still qualifies to be labelled as survival horror and its hybridism should not come as a surprise.
Gameplay-wise, it is somewhat noticeable that the game recycles many of the features shown in RE4 like over-the-shoulder view that switches to first-person when aiming with a rifle and optional physical interactions with small cutscenes when hitting an opponent in certain spots. It's relieving that they kept these, I felt going back to the clunkiness of controlling your character in RE1-3 would have backfired. In many ways, however, it makes you feel as if it lacked originality at times and they had just decided to remake RE4 in Africa. There's something, though, that made me flinch a couple times: bossfights. I think it's fair to say the game has the worst bossfights in the entire saga: forget about wittily using your weapons towards finding a suitable strategy to defeat your boss, most of the times it's all about finding a particular item that's hidden somewhere on the stage and using it against it. Ammo also seemed to be something I constantly found myself running out of at all times, making it a bit more frustrating.
The development of the plot made me frown occasionaly as well. Why is Capcom so hellbent in introducing new female companions and give them backgrounds that are as deep as a banana skin? They didn't learn from that, it seems, since the same thing occurred in RE6. Ashley, Sheva, Excella, Helena... who's next? Only Capcom knows. Apart from that, I guess everything else fits into place somehow, though be prepared to experience bewilderment at certain matrix-like moves in certain how-did-these-storylines-ended-up-tangled-like-this cutscenes.
Still, it's worth a go. Bring along a friend, have a laugh at the silliness of maginis' antics, don't pay much mind to how ridiculously poorly-thought boss fighs are and you will definitely enjoy it.

There is something that works really well in Qora: despite the extremely mundane gameplay, the game strongly feels like a journey. Maybe not an epic one, but a journey none the less in a stranger and stranger land. I think that works because of the pacing, the mundane, a certain sense of wonder and the quantity of content. I mean when I first thought 'I sure travelled a long way' I was maybe half way through the game.
Sadly, it feels the creator was not very confident in the 'contemplative initiatic quest' quality of his game and decided to spice it up with a humorous tone that feels out of place. Worse, the grand finale is a meta humor fest that feels like a kick in the nuts. A bit as if the 'proper' ending of Silent Hill 2 was the dog ending...
I am all for humor and meta, but not when they feel like the creator used them as escape plan. Sometimes you have to dare to tell a story.

First off, let me start this off right! This is, without a doubt, one of the best GAMES I've ever played - forgeting for a moment that it was made by a small team of MODERS, and is available for FREE, with the devs getting
NOTHING from the creation of this game. The fact that both of those things are true, make this game such an acomplishment that they should all be lauded as heros of the video game industry - especially compared to all the S*** people post as early access or greenlight "Games". I sincerly hope this dev team continues making games of this caliber - I'd pay money to play them. Hell, if this game costed money, I'd pay for it. I really cannot state with words how awesome I think this game is considering the size of the dev team. Portal Stories: Mel is a game that tries to tell an interesting story in the Portal universe while not actually being a game in the Valve's main Portal lineup... And it succedes wonderfully. I only have one (Real) gripe on this game. In some places the level design is a bit confusing and it takes you a couple second to figure out were to go, or how to get out of an area. The rest of the time tho, the level design is absolutly fantastic. I also have no complains about the puzzles... they're awesome - to the point were they feel like they were made for Portal 2 instead of for a mod made by a tiny dev team. Even more on par was the music. It NEVER felt out of place and every music piece was phenominal (I never buy music DLCs... but if this one had one (That cost money), I would... both to support the devs AND because the music is actually that amazing... the one it does have... is ALSO free!!!). Also, even more important, I was never bored playing this game... I always wanted to go around the next corner and continue the story - I wanted to know what would happen. This is, in my humble opinion, the mark of a good story driven game - which this is.
+Good story
+Responsive controls (They're the same as Portal 2, what do you expect... of course they're good lol)
+Jokes (I mean, seriously, this game is REALLY funny at some points)
+Atmosphere of the game (It feels like it was professinally done - and well done)
+Level design (Most of the time (Like 99.9 percent of the time - and never in a puzzle room))
+The music
+The puzzles (They're just awesome - all there is to say (Also, some are REALLY hard - but in a good way... Not in a badly designed way.))
+The fact that it's free
-Occasional level design problems
-You can't see your feet
-This isn't Portal 3 (It totally should be tho... It's probably better than whatever Valve's gonna come up with (If they ever do - It's been FAR to long Godd*** it))
I give this game a 9.5/10. And I'm only taking the half point off for the VERY occassional level design problems - which this small of a dev team can't even help - they're just to small to go everything a million times with a fine toothed comb. This game is also FREE!!!! I seriously can't see a reason you wouldn't want to play this (Unless you don't own Portal 2 lol).

The sequel to ACII didn't disappoint, Brotherhood was really fun to play.
The story continues the fight against the Borgia and their Templar agents in Rome, Ezio takes it upon himself to lead the Assassin Order as they try to free Rome from their influence.
This was nicely portrayed as you rebuild your Assassin Order while crippling Templar presence. The story was shorter than the previous game, but it was still very well made and packed with intriguing characters.
The gameplay didn’t change much from ACII, but did add some entertaining side missions like liberating sectors of Rome from Borgia oppression, further develop the city’s economy and various assassination contracts.
Ezio develops his leadership skills while training recruits and managing the Order, this also allows the ability to call assassins as backup or send them on mission across Europe.
The graphics and animations are amazing, the streets, the architecture and monuments and landmarks of Rome are breathtaking and really add to the game’s immersion. The soundtrack itself adds to this, combining some old songs with new ones, really good work.
Definately a game worth buying and a great addition to the series.

Dead Realm is a horror  multiplayer ghost hunting game, where you either run and hide or collect objects to summon a portal to escape.
This is by far the best multiplayer horror game i've ever played. The horrifying environments and scary ghost, makes this game unique, while you are trying to survive with 5-8 other people.
As said before, you can be up to 5-8 players on a map. Currently they have 3 maps, two game modes, two ghost and alot of humans to be. The game has either survival mode for humans like "hide and seek", where you use shield or decoys to escape the ghost. If you die, you become a ghost and hunt the other humans till there isn't anyone. The other game mode is slithly different where you collect 10 clocks, that's spawns a random portal in the map. The first human who enters wins. The clocks are hidden or hanged everywhere on the map, while the ghost is hunting you. If you die in this mode, you cannot hunt the humans, but manipulate props on the map to scare you to death.
The game has lock on mic, by pressing T.  That means you can communicate with the rest of your team and find good hiding spots or where you might think there is a clock. But! Be aware, the ghost can hear you in a range, where you might expose your location. - And yes, if you scream like a little girl, then the one who's playing ghost pisses him self of laughing his♥♥♥♥♥off.
The multiplayer part is really good, and i have to admit that this is by far the best multi-horror game i ever played. It's worth the price. So if you like horror games, collecting items around beautiful, immersive environments with other 7 players with a scary ghost, then this is for you.

Another brilliant Visual Novel with touching, well written story. Narcissu shows that even text can convey the deepest of the emotion.
To play the 'game', you need to sit back, relax, click thru the dialogues slowly and enjoy it. Just don't forget to occassionally save so you won't bang your head against the wall if your machine magically crashes and you need to restart the story all over again.
Replayability is zero. Once you finish once, that's all you need to do. Except if you want to recall the story later.
As an Early Access, Narcissu is pretty much done and polished - except for blank so-called Achievements - and most importantly it's completely translated into English. I'm surprised they didn't charge a dime for this on Steam.
The only purchasable DLC here is OSTs. While I don't own the DLC myself, it's been said that the quality of the OSTs are FLAC, pretty much what we expect nowadays (who likes lossy MP3s now?). Even so, I can vet for the quality of the OSTs in-game, it's very memorable and deep, perfectly blend into the story and I can fully recommend this set for your listening pleasure.
All in all, it's a free stuff with great presentation and story that you can finish in one sitting (at least for each part). Well worth your time. 10/10.

This review focuses on multiplayer.  Your typical COD game with a WW2 skin.  Overall, fun. I would prefer this to exo suits.  Gameplay is more grounded and there aren't enemies in front, to the side, behind, and above you all at once.  Map design still suffers in my opinion.  I think the weak map design is the biggest flaw in COD nowadays.  Most maps in the game are small, circular environments that encourage close quarters combat and force firefights.  I prefer the larger maps in the series such as the quarry map from mw2 and array from black ops 1, but I think I'm in the minority there.  These larger maps made me feel like I had more of a chance especially in modes like search and destroy. I also thought the gameplay was more tactical with that map design.  As a side note, the time limit for S&D was reduced and I'm not a fan of that.  Overall, if you like COD and twitch shooters you will probably enjoy this.  I hope map design improves in dlc/future installments of the series.  No map is memorable to me and gameplay doesn't seem as tactical to me as it used to be.
Simply, recommended if you still find some enjoyment playing past COD titles and not recommended if not.

If you get this game, get the complete pack.  If you already have this game, get the Campaign module.  Without the Campaign aspect, the game is very limited and ultimatey you won't have much to do.
But with the campaign, while it is VERY limited to just building fleets and maintaining them (with no other 4X concerns; all structures are pre-built in any given system), it becomes a completely different game.  Since the fleets are uploaded from players, you'll always hit new interesting configurations for specific systems; add in all the special per-system rules that you need specialized ships and the concern of maintaining supply lines for your fleets, and it becomes a pretty engrossing game that requires far more planning and leaves you with the threat that the next attacking fleet might have your number with a counter.
It's not perfect; I wish there were NPC factions and such in the 4X part with persistant forces for more strategic-level planning, but none the less, I've sunk hours into Campaign long after I previously gave up on the game.  Still this is definitely got a game for people who enjoy designing ships as a central priority.  If you do, it's on my easy list.
And a word on the dev pricing - that I agree on.  The fact only one of the expansions is on a reasonable DLC sale right now is lame.  $6-7 for a new faction is entirely too much and I think he'd earn more from halving the stock price and actually participating in Steam sales more.  Still a fun game, if you grab campaign with the 75% off main game.

A little late to the party, but it happens.  GSB is a blast to play, and I'm a big fan of any strategy or sim games--particularly those that reward careful planning and creativity.  This game is centered around building a fleet and laying out a battle plan; the battles play out according to decisions made prior to the battle.  A 'direct control' option is available to enable RTS-style control during battles, but this feels tacked on and the game shines when one avoids this option altogether.
GSB gives me the impression of building model space-ships from a box of purchased parts and then letting those toy ships destroy each other.  Add in the mix of battling other peoples' fleets via downloadable challenges and a campaign system, and it's the ultimate nerdy space wars game.
Try out the demo; if you enjoy it, buying the full game is a no-brainer.  While the various DLCs add some nice variety, they aren't necessary to play and enjoy the game.

Gratuitous Space Battles is a Pre-planning RTS game where you get to make your own units and make them face the ultimate challenge, blowing the other fleet up. There is no story, plot, or anything like that. There are no politics, and there is absolutely no diplomacy. There is only war, gratuitous war. Btw, it's kinda like Michael Bay made a space combat game. So, let's get to the review.
Pros:
- Graphics are amazing. From the debris to the freaking ship models, they all look great.
- Special effects are also amazing. Every little explosion just makes you jump in satisfaction as your enemies ships go down in an explosion so intense it damages other starships.
- Variety of the races and startships are also great. Every race and every ship in these races have strengths and weaknesses.
- There are only three classes of ship, but the variety is enormous.
- The unit building is spot on, you can customize your ship to be really fast or have weapons so powerful you can almost one-shot kill other starships.
- There is a distinct difference between armor and shields.
- You just have to watch the destruction unfold as the some-what decent AI controlling the ships make their moves.\
- There is a slight bit of humor and slightly racist jokes, but they are pointed towards aliens.
Cons:
- The only strategy in this game is planning ahead of time what your units orders are, meaning that you literally have to watch the battles unfold as you are sitting in your chair waiting for something to happen.
- Only three classes of ship to choose from.
- It's from the 2d perspective. If they made it 3d, I would rate it a lot higher.
- Some classes of ship are almost impossible to customize, like the imperial Gun station.
- For some reason shields don't come back up after they are depleted.
- Some of the ships seem too slow, like the cruisers. you would think that something big in space would still be able to travel fast.
- Get's repetitive really fast, but you have to admit some of you had that thought of 'maybe one more battle'.
- The fact that a squadron of fighters takes 3 frigates to take down, no matter how many anti-fighter weapons you have on them.
- Why does armor have such low health? Isn't armor supposed to help absorb damage taken to the hull rather than be blasted away like it was nothing?
- The DLC's only add races and weapons that can only be used by the race you bought them with.
- Maps are literally the same, except for some debuffs in some of them. The only major difference is the background.
- Some ships are only slightly different from other ships. Some of the modules are also only slightly different.
Overall, it is a decent game that isn't really worth the $15 that it is now. Get it on a sale and try it out. If you love space battles and massive explosioins, you would love this game. If you like plot and story to a game, don't get this game.
I rate this a 7/10 (Decent game). If they added a bit more of a difference between the ships and modules, and they had it 3d, and they added twitch decision making the rating would be much higher.

In fact there is an enormous immersion that let you play the whole game in one sitting, feeling like watching an interactive film and regarding everyone's own adventure as well as the one of the Empress and her followers. The story reveals a plot of serious themes around cult, believe and religion (worship, progress, nature, rock art, burning of whitches, native Americans, Greek myths etc.) peppered with some kind of humour (sometimes too childish).

To sum things up: I had an atmospheric time playing the game two times (to get 100% achievements), for one run you need about 2-3 hours. I'm very glad having discovered this game, and even now I am thinking of some parts of it, which I could understand only some time later - and that's what I like.

It’s a chaotic, challenging game with a fun gameplay, bizarre story, highly destructible environments and criminally low sales. You definitely should buy it if you are into: fight with a whole alien army, along hordes of fully dissectible giant insects, slaying the dragons, bringing an AT-AT style quadruped fortress to its knees, blowing up a Death Star inspired alien mothership out of the sky, punching “Godzilla” in the face, stir up the 50-story hornet nest and then evaporate it with a satellite blaster strike, performing a regicide of Queen of the Ants right in her chambers, challenging King of Spiders, Death Queen, and Dragon King, sometimes all at the same time.


EDF is one of the best games for co-op play out there, it shines the most with 4 friends playing and coordinating their actions. You definitely should buy it, if you are into killing thousands of giant insects (solo or with friends) that want to conquer the Earth and destroy humanity.

You can de describe this game as "Destroy the Earth to stop aliens from destroying the Earth!"
Gameplay has a very simple formula: you're a soldier (solo or part of co-op squad) and your task is to kill every alien invader on the map.
But with fully destructible city environment, fully dissectible insects (given enough firepower) and means of destruction like plasma cannons, laser lances and laser chainsaws, thunderbolt shotguns, bazookas, rotary grenade launchers, high-caliber sniper rifles, powerful shoguns, rocket turrets, landmines, carpet bombings, artillery strikes, ballistic missiles, self-propelled railguns, mechs of various sizes, and a possibility to call an orbital blaster strike, you can't help yourself but smile with each new gib flying around and each piece of city’s' architectural heritage tumbling down. And if you like to get close and  personal, put on the power frame and double-wield Gatling guns, or arm cannons, put a martyr or a guided missile launchers on your shoulders,  slide through hordes of your enemies on the wave from your vibro-hammer, slice them expertly with a force-field blade and deflect their attacks right into their faces with a trusty shield, all while dashing on your rocket boosters like crazy (dash cancelling technique required).

There are four available classes in the game:
Wing diver — very low armor, fast speed, high damage, can fly, but dies fast. She is swift and deadly glass cannon, emergency support, that can fly from one side of a map to another in a moment or die in a second if you don't know what you're doing;
Ranger — medium armor, medium speed, medium damage, can't fly, but can drive vehicles. Effective in almost any battle situation;
Air raider — medium armor, medium speed. It's difficult for him to fight regular enemies due to lack of proper equipment, but he gives hell to powerful ones. Can call for devastating support strikes and order vehicles for delivery to battlefield. Can drive. Dies fast if you don't know what to do or if your teammates don't care about you;
Fencer — heavy armor, either fast as bullet (with dash cancelling) or slow as a sloth taking a♥♥♥♥♥♥(without dash cancelling). Also heavy damage. His main purpose is to get really close and personal with an overwhelming / overpowering enemy, he also usually has enough armor capacity to recover fallen team members over and over (not from the start of the game, though). The only class capable of melee combat;

The game also has a story, which takes it's inspiration from classic alien invasion / monster rampage movies. It's delivered properly, without taking you off of gameplay and doesn't overstay it's welcome. This story mainly supports quick pacing escalation: from small packs of your regular giant enemy ants, to the alien long-range artillery robots covering overwhelming swarms of whatever alien genetic and technical engineers came up with this time. They can get really creative at times.

EDF offers 98 online (or 89 offline) missions in main campaign, and 22 + 23 missions via DLCs, so you'll have plenty of gameplay to experience most part of alien invasion situations you have imagined.
Forget the zombie apocalypse; it’s time to repel an alien invasion!

LEGO Jurassic World is an amazing game, and probably one of the most thought out and well executed LEGO games to date. Unlike some other LEGO games, Jurassic World really does manage to give every main character a completely unique ability which actually makes sense and is enjoyable to use. LEGO Jurrasic World also manages to sucesfully tackle one of the biggest problems LEGO The Movie Video Game had, which was a lack of important characters. Instead of just having all of the levels be played by the same characters over and over again like in LEGO The Movie Video Game, LEGO Jurassic World not only allows the player to control dinosaurs but forces the player to if they want to complete and finish the game, this adds a whole new level of depth to the game and feels very refreshing from the established LEGO video game formula. As with all LEGO video games for the PC, the controls aren't very good and the game plays better if you use a controller. Saying that, the keyboard controlls are noticebly better than the ones in LEGO Marvel Super Heroes. The levels are quite interesting and don't feel too repetitive however the levels for the first and fourth movie are the best and seem to have had the most work put into them. After completing the story, there are many things you can still do, such as complete races, heal dinosaurs and save workers in peril. If you have ever liked a LEGO game before, then LEGO Jurrasic World will be right up your street.

I know it is unfair to judge a game mostly by comparing it with others. But in that very case, RE5 is so close to the fourth entry, and lacks so much of the upgrades from the sixth one, that I can't really talk about it without talking about the other two that surrounds it. Resident Evil 5 is probably the most mediocre experience of the numbered games in the series. And yet, it still is a fun action game, especially in coop.
On its own merits:
Technically speaking the game was gorgeous at release and still looks pretty nice to this day. Here on PC, the resolution and solid framerate makes it even better. Sure the lighting system is a little dated and some choices in the photography look a bit too much (the sunset mostly). But the details in the textures (skins and fabrics) are admirable for a game from 2009. And as far as control goes, even if I'd stick to the controller for the whole franchise, the keyboard+mouse setting works pretty well (you have to put up with a trully horrible crosshair though). The action plays well, thanks to great feedbacks in the gunplay (the sound and visual effects for every shot are superb, like in RE4), and even if newcomers will have a tough time adapting to the tank controls, it feels good shooting stuff in this game once you get around moving without strafe and aiming without moving.
And though its level-design is pretty boring overall (a lot of unimaginative corridors and square arenas), the game manages to renew its action regularly with new little gimmicks (a rotating arena, a vastly more dangerous enemy thrown in the middle of little ones, some crazy turret section/boss, separating the two players etc). Nothing is really brilliant, but it's entertaining as hell, and the game stops right when the variety of enemies, bosses and situations starts to fall, so that you never really feel like it's getting too old. Plus, even if the scenario takes itself way too seriously, some antagonists are so stupidly badass that it is hard not to enjoy fighting them.
In the shadow of a giant:
The real problem with the game actually comes from its ambition, or lack thereof, and the fact that it gets its sorry♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the previous and/or the next entry in the series, depending on what you are looking for.
Because in terms of action, RE5 is good enough, but nowhere near RE4 or 6. The overall structure tries to hit every key moments of RE4, in terms of gameplay situations: and since RE4 was such a good game in terms of pacing (except for the island that dragged on a little too much imho) it still works here. Unfortunately, the setting and the tone, more serious and supposedly grittier, doesn't bode well with the insane action and cutscenes presented. The seriousness is pretty much killed as soon as the protagonists start jumping over each other like sentai to go under a trap door that almost close on them. It's like the story is trying to paint this dramatic search for a partner in the context of a pandemic in Africa while also creating situations for the player to blow as many stuff as possible. You have Wesker fighting like he's in the Matrix, Chris punching a boulder (and actually beating the living crap out of it) or confusing location design (how is there a reffining plant right after an indigenous village, and right before an aztec temple that leads to a Death Star sized laboratory?!?) juxtaposed with tragic deaths of soldier that we are supposed to avenge at some point without knowing them, and characters that take themself really seriously when it's yet again another Umbrella scheme that doesn't make sense (How exactely are you going to sell as a BOW a giant bat that you can't control?). While RE4 had a cocky Leon S. Kennedy (nothing like the one in RE2 but that's beyond the point) that banter with a ridiculous vilain, and who escaped a giant wooden mecha, and RE6 has...pretty much EVERYTHING in the world like german supplex the Terminator X Leatherface above lava and fighting a giant butterfly that was a T-Rex 20 minutes ago, RE5 is stuck between its wish to be serious and the reality of what the game propose as far as action goes. It never really totally embraces the fun and stupidity of its plot and situations; at least never at the rate of the second half ofRE4 or pretty much the entirety of 6.
With the same gameplay, RE4 was a better beast; the story was far more entertaining, starting lowkey with a creepy and stressful atmosphere, and ending up being this giant roller coaster of madness led by goofier protagonists than its successor. And RE6 is like RE5 on steroids; everything about the gameplay suits the rythm and the craziness much better, especially the melee and dodge that cease to be contextual and becomes their very own mechanics. And if the grittier story was what you were looking for, try REmake or RE7, games that actually have a gameplay in direct relation to the story told. Bottom line, there is no place where RE5 is the first choice.
TL;DR
RE5 is a fun enough action game. If you want an entertaining action flick in coop, go for it. But if you haven't played RE4 or 6, I'd say go play these ones first. RE4 has a more solid atmosphere and gets way more inventive in terms of settings and setpieces (especially if you consider playing RE5 solo RE4 is a must play way above the fifth). And RE6 as a much better gameplay (be it coop or solo) with more possibilities and a tone content and great action to boot. If you played both, then RE5 still is a fun action game (again...in coop preferably). I still recommend it, it still is fun. Just not the most fun the action part of the franchise can offer.

Wouldn't say it's worth full price of 15$, and it's disappointing that somehow the DLC isn't cross platform while the original game is.
In this game you can customize 3 classes of spaceships (fighters, frigates and cruisers) and change their weapons loadouts, armor thickness and shield strength (all about the tradeoffs). It comes with a few (10-ish) single player campaign missions and 3 races each with it's own set of ship hulls.
The learning curve is there but it's not steep, you can get away with skipping the tutorial. What you do in this game is you customize your ships, and on a budget with restricted amounts of pilots you deploy them into pre-determined battlezones, you customize the AI a little and then watch the battle ensue. You cannot manually control or micromanage ships while the battle is on-going, you must decide it all before the battle.
It's a unique but cool take on real time strategy. In space. You can expect to get anywhere between 3-10 hours from it depending on how fast you catch on to techniques for easy victories, and how much time you spend customizing your ships. For me, as soon as I'd unlocked all the modules and finished all the campaign missions, it was over. There wasn't even any lore to get into. I didn't have any interest in online play either.
Overall it was a decent and fun game, but I found it lacking in content (both mission quantity and amount of things to do for honor points. Once you've unlocked everything, there's no reward for winning battles any longer), not quite worth a 15$, but if you catch it on sale, it's worth at least one playthrough :)

I love exploration games. Running around a cool, strange world, interacting with fantastic characters and seeing a developer's vision of another universe is one of the most enjoyable parts of gaming. Having read Rock Paper Shotgun's review of Qora, I was excited - maybe I have another Knytt or Journey on my hands! Then I played it.
Qora is absolutely and unequivolcally complete and utter dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ This is an exploration game with no "game". You do nothing but move to the right and press the action button to watch a series of painfully slow animations, dozens of times in a row. It's completely mind boggling how a developer can design a level consisting of nothing more than an enormously long hallway littered with 20 identical short pits that the player must do nothing but hold right and press action to traverse.
This takes upwards of a full minute. For each of the game's 100+ screens.
Every one of the levels are exactly that - whether the obstacle is a pile of grass, a rock, a pit, a ladder, it doesn't matter. You never make any choices, you never wander around. You move to the right. You remove a small obstacle in a mind-numbingly boring way. You move to the right some more. It's all functionally identical, and it's the least fun I've ever  had in a game.
It's inexcusable. There is no way in hell the developer played his own game, because it's tears-streaming-down-your-face boring. Again, please let me reiterate that I love this genre - but Qora is garbage. 0/5 stars. Do not purchase no matter how much you like the aesthetic or world. It's simply not worth the time.

Qora is absolutely beautiful. The music and visuals are perfect. It's less of a game and more of an interactive story, but it really immerses you in its surreal world and is well worth playing.
The movement of your character is very slow and cannot be sped up. In each screen, you are faced with obstacles which will take not skill or imagination, but time and patience to overcome. At times it can feel eternal, and even get a bit frustrating, but you are driven forward by curiosity – what strange and interesting thing will you encounter on the next screen? - as well as a desire to overcome the obstacles and prove your determination. There are countless games out there that test our reflexes or critical thinking skill, but it's rare for a game to test our patience - and to do it well. This game felt like a rare exception.
My only complaint lies with the achievements: in order to get them all, you must play the entire game through twice. I think this was a huge mistake on the part of the developer. This game has no real replay value. There are two endings, but the differences in gameplay between getting one ending and getting the other are minute. Most people will probably get the “good” ending first, then, noticing they are missing an achievement, realize they have to go back and do the whole thing over again while making mistakes. The second playthrough has all the joy and wonder sucked out of it as you race for the finish to get your final Steam achievement. The game would have been much improved without this.
Despite this one criticism, I still recommend getting the game. It's an experience which you will not regret. The visuals and music alone make it worth your time and money, and the ending will make you think differently about how we view certain aspects of our culture.

The OFFLINE: It's a very pretty game but the offline is too short and doesn't tell much of a story. They're probably going to release multfiple WWII games from different theaters of the War. I actually never heard of this Visual novel before i saw it on steam; I saw it on Greenlight, and I voted for it (mainly because I am a HUGE visual novel fan; even to the point of adding Katawa Shoujo to my non-steam steam games). I saw it finally was released and decided to download it immediately. I then sat down and beat the 1st 'side'; and decided to write my review (also apologies if it is vague, I wanted to avoid spoilers, and this is my first in depth review I wrote).
This visual novel is quite amazing in my opinion; it really brought emotion out of me, something most movies, games, and books cannot do (although there have been one or two games and books, and a handful of movies).
There aren't too many images used, but what images are used are amazing looking, and are very beautiful. The dialog is very descriptive, and it is translated amazingly.
The music score/soundtrack to this game is just as amazing as the rest of this visual novel; it fits in perfectly, and both sets and amplifies the mood, making the scenes much more powerful. (The soundtrack is available for purchase, and i recomend picking it up if you have the money)
The impact this game left on me is strong, I even cried at the end [I know; I’m a dork ha-ha] because of its depressing... but strangely satisfying and even somewhat happy ending (I know this seems like a contradicting statement; but it will make sense when you beat it).
I whole-heartedly recommend this to anyone who enjoys visual novels, great stories, or emotionally charged entertainment; best of all is that this amazing experience is free. I give narcissu a 10/10!!

Rarely have I so enjoyed a game that so persistently made me rage,  or made me care for an 8-bit sprite as much as I cared for Shield Knight, but Shovel Knight is just that game. An affectionate homage to the golden age of console gaming, Shovel Knight comes to us from former members of Wayforward Technologies, creators of the Shantae series. The game's incredibly varied stages play out like a greatest hits album of classic platformers. But unlike, say, Ninja Gaiden or Castlevania, Shovel Knight never feels cheap or punishing. The game is filled with a lovable cast of characters, excellent music (courtesy of the ineffable Virt Kaufman, the musical genius behind Contra 4, Scurge: Hive, Shantae, and several other games), useful powerups and hair-pulling jumping puzzles. The controls  are extremely tight, and any mistakes you make are your own damn fault. The game rather mercifully makes use of checkpoints, only depriving you of money when you die, money you have a chance to retrieve when you make it back to where you died. And even if you don't, you can always farm for more, and you will need quite a bit to buy all the upgrades. I had to take a few breaks over the course of playing Shovel Knight to cool off, but I kept coming back until I was done. I do not regret for a second backing this lovely game on kickstarter. If you enjoy platformers and classic NES era gaming in general, then grab yourself a copy of Shovel Knight and prepare to strike the earth!
Plague of Shadows review: I have to commend Yacht Club Games on an excellent addon overall, and though I have some complaints, for what was technically a free dlc (though it was funded by a kickstarter stretch goal) its in a class far above the usual paid fare. Plague Knight plays so completely differently from Shovel Knight that you are essentially playing an entirely new game, despite the fact that the core stages have only been subtley altered from the base game. Unlike the additional character modes in say, the Castlevania games, Plague of Shadows gives the mad alchemist his own unique dialogue, story and motivations, and greatly expands the role of Mona, previously a mere bored mini-game operator. Plague Knight lacks the ability to pogo-jump on enemies and is considerably more fragile then Shovel Knight, with fewer health upgrades overall, and is knocked back much further when hit. Plague makes up for this with an exponentionally larger arsenal of customizable explosives, allowing him to engage almost any enemy from a safe distance, safely dealing with threats that Shovel Knight would often have no choice but to tank damage from. I particularly enjoyed the use of the spark powder, which causes your bombs to emit periodic bursts of electricity as they fly. The beaked bomber can use a number of magic items called "Arcana", which run off a regenerating mana bar rather then the finite numerical mana that Shovel Knight's "Relics" use. You will learn to love the "vat" Arcana, which summons a large purple beaker underneath Plague Knight that acts as a temporary platform, and can save you from an otherwise inescapable fall. Plague excels at airborne combat and has the ability to bomb-jump across large distances, and can jump a second time in the air before or after using a blast jump. This makes several of the games more fiendish jumping segements, especially the pits of Polar Knight, Treasure Knight and Propeller Knight's stages. However, the afformentioned lack of pogo jumping makes some segments that were relatively simple to negotiate, such as the cannonball segments of Propeller Knight's stage and the gears in Tinker Knight's stage, significantly more hair-raising to complete. Plague Knight's movement style is much faster and twitchier then Shovel Knight and I propelled myself into instant-death hazards many, many times over the course of my playthrough, in spite of the use of the slow fall blast jump. In particular, the optional "hazard" stages are completely different in Plague Knight's story and substantially more frustrating, and though Plague Knight laughs at any of the original boss fights, Plague of Shadows throws a completely new final boss at you that I died on so many times that finally killing it felt rather unsatisfying- though the ending cutscene made me smile nonetheless.
Specter of Torment review: I both love and was somewhat disappointed by Specter Knight and his campaign. I sincerely hoped he would be capable of flight as in his boss fight, but I suppose that would have been too easy. Mechanically, he is still easily my favorite character yet, with his ability to wall climb and chain nigh-infinite airborne slashes, targets permitting. He would have made easy pickings of the original stages. The problem is, the devs saw fit to create entirely new stages (I acknowledge that this took a great deal of effort, not to mention the lovely remixes of the orignal stage themes) for Specter that are both designed to exploit his wall-climbing and slash-dashing and be a persitent pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I took significantly more damage as Specter then the other characters thanks to their being noticibly few safe places to stop and catch your breath. With many segments requiring you to hurtle across open pits that would make Plague Knight wince, madly-slash-dashing for survival and careening into whatever enemies or hazards might be in your way, bouncing off of them and then proceeding to continue mashing the attack button in the hopes of finding a footing somewhere. His "Curio" items have very useful functions, but run off a "Darkness" meter that is so limited even at maximum level that you rarely get more then a few uses of the Curios at one time- and most of my Darkness went into the "Will Skull," which recoveres Specter's health, called Will. You are at least able to use some of the Curios to recover dropped gold bags without risk, a welcome addition. I also essentially had to use the "Cloak of Clemency" for the entire run, which spares you a death from pits or spikes at the cost of both Will and Darkness. There seems to be a running theme in gaming with taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of people who wear hooded cloaks and/or use scythes- "Speccy" takes little aside from verbal abuse from a majority of the cast, though it doesn't seem to phase him. If i'm going to dress like a reaper, I should damn well be treated like one. That being said, Specter is straight up the nastiest character so far in direct combat, able to rapidly slash through ordinary enemies often without being damaged in return and effortlessly bouncing off of bosses- though some of the boss fights have a lot more pits then I remember. I'm going to write this review with the assumption that you're not going to buy SR3 without any knowledge of the previous installment, SR2. Everything below is in comparison with Saints Row 2.
Pros:
* The graphics have gotten a massive upgrade. Everything looks so much prettier than in SR2. We now have rain and rain-glistening wet streets.
* There's some great ideas in mission design. When the protagonist was parachuting and was going to be run down by a cargo plane in midair, my jaw dropped at how cool they made the way that she got out of that situation. There's less of these unique "cool" moments than in SR2, but when they're there, they're often really good.
Cons:
* There are much less cinematics. Whereas in SR2, every single mission began and end with a cutscene, and often also had intermediate cutscenes, the majority of missions in SR3 lack cutscenes and only give you the plot by characters speaking dialogue while you can still move around freely. I've found that this drastically lessened my attachment to the characters when I rarely see their faces, and by necessity you can't get as emotionally compelling scenes when you don't have full control of the scene. I felt much more like I was playing a game feeding me dangling carrots than watching interesting characters interact.
* I feel like the writing team hasn't kept characters consistent from SR2. The protagonist in SR2 felt very much like an "all vices go" type who wasn't squeamish about anything -- in this game, she whines about needing hand sanitizer after visiting a BDSM club. Pierce's entire hook in SR2 was about how he constantly gets dismissed and overlooked by others, but here he's suddenly badass and nobody walks over him -- a 180 degree change without any explanation. Shaundi's promiscuity is no longer mentioned at all. Nobody gets high anymore. It's like everybody grew up and became boring adults in comparison to how colorful their characters were in SR2. When you combine the character changes with the new graphics engine making everyone look different, it doesn't really feel like you're hanging with the same gang anymore but entirely new characters.
* There is no more fast travel/taxi, so you have to literally drive everywhere. Fortunately, the map feels a tiny bit smaller than SR2, the cars feel faster and car handling is improved, so driving around is a little easier and a little more fun than it used to be, so driving around does remain fun for a good long while.
* You can no longer go back and re-watch cinematics on the Television system like you could in SR2. I consider this a major shortcoming, as the Television system was one of my favorite things in SR2. Now I feel like I have to have a save point between every single mission if I ever want to go back and re-watch a cinematic play out. Sure, there's always YouTube, but that doesn't have *my* character.
* It's really difficult to make your character look the same as in SR2. The facial structure engine is completely different and a lot of the old hairstyles no longer exist, and don't even dream about finding SR2's clothes anywhere. If you rely on appearance to create attachment to your character, you're going to be disappointed.
Subjective:
* The tone and setting has gotten much more over-the-top and outlandish. SR2 was much more gritty and down to earth with the occasional over-the-top moment (hello, Septic Avenger!), but SR3 goes way out there with an adult toy melee weapon, anime/furry clubs, BDSM clubs, superpowered opponents and such. SR2 was happy with just smoking pot and strippers, but SR3 tackles more specific subcultures. Whether this is a pro or con depends on individual tastes.
* The radios feel less repetitive. Whereas in SR2, I could rattle off half a dozen songs that The Mix keeps playing, coming up with repeated songs in SR3 feels harder. I sort of like the way SR2 did it; I like that I strongly associate Land Down Under and Karma Chameleon with SR2; I don't get that feeling for any songs in SR3. But some people may like the more variety. You decide.
Even though I've listed more cons than pros, I do think that SR3 is still a good game, just not quite as good as its predecessor. I do warmly recommend buying SR3, but I definitely recommend giving SR2 a shot first if you haven't already.

Qora is a short little narrative game where your character is exploring an ancient ruin. You have a "telepathy" power that will let your character see what the areas looked like in the past (or past events that occured in a location) at certain points. As you can see above, the pixel art in the game is beautiful. I don't think there is one bland-looking scene in the game. The music is enjoyable and the story is decent, even if the ending is a bit weird (I got the "good" ending). Some of the dialogue makes it unclear when the game is meant to be taking place, since some of the "ancient" characters talk about (for example) a kitchen sink or a nude beach. The character walks relatively slow and there isn't really a lot of "puzzle" in terms of interaction. The tags call this a platformer, but you can only jump when the context cue is available and there are only a few locations where you actually have to figure out where to go. Your little guy walks along through these pretty locations and you get told a story. If you're okay with that, I'd definitely recommend it.
My only real negative with the game is that after getting the "good" ending, you can't see the "bad" ending without completely replaying a two-hour game. I don't really want to replay the entire thing just to see a "lesser" ending!

The very definition of a walking-simulator. You hold a button to move from left to right, pressing the context-sensitive action button whenever you hit an obstacle (jump, cut grass, break stone, etc.). On your journey you enjoy beautiful scenery and soundtrack. Your character has the ability to use telepathy at specific points, which will allow you to either peer into the future or past. Half of these telepathy sequences have no bearing on the story whatsoever, and show you random animations that will just make you scratch your head. The other half of these sequences are story-related, showing you snippets from the journey of an ancient empress whose footsteps you are following.
Sometimes I am in the mood for a lazy experience where I do not have to do much, but it is hard to recommend Qora because I found the story (and ending) very underwhelming.

I played in both the closed and open betas and can say I'm impressed with the game's progress as of now. It's a gratifying and also frustrating game to play, however. Death comes quick, and a lot of times unexpected via through wall-bangable walls or in some instances from around corners (Ubi pls fix). There's great fun to be had with a group of friends as the roster of operators is diverse in their roles and the way they're meant to be played. The game looks, sounds, and feels great (control wise). Although inconsistent connections, long matchmaking load times in some regions, ping abuse, and outright fukt hit detection keep this game from bursting onto the competitive scene. While the game does have a skill based rank system, the game really is not in a competitive state as of now. The gameplay experience is identical to casual, albeit with more communication and teamplay. No dedicated competitive servers are the most damning thing keeping this game from reaching the famed CS, LoL, DotA or even Overwatch status as a thriving competitive game. On a last note, pick this up on sale, ideally no more than $30.

Singleplayer is short albeit enjoyable. Characters are actually given some time to flesh themselves out. Sledgehammer tries a number of new things to keep gameplay varied between the typical CoD shooting gallery sections.
Multiplayer is one step foward, several steps backward from previous titles. Laggy connections, inconsistent netcode, poor weapon balance, confusing map layouts, and what seems to be a total lack of effective matchmaking system. Removing specialists was a good move foward after Black Ops 3 and the particularly dismal Infinite Warfare but they stripped the rest of what made the post-CoD: MW games so enjoyable, namely the customization.
Hard to recommend at full price to anyone except a diehard Call of Duty fan who can look past the typical faults of a CoD title, but even then so many confused changes have occured in the multiplayer portion that it might not appeal even to them. For everyone else, wait for a sale. The singleplayer doesn't carry the full price of the game and the multiplayer is broken and unbalanced. Unlike most other Free 2 Play games with a shop system, you can actually be good at the game WITHOUT having a full wallet. You get 50k GP for starting out (the game's currency) which you can spend on guns, and equipment. Six players spawn in an isolated place. Two of them are infected and can talk to each other, the others have to perform various tasks to escape while trying to figure out who among them is a monster in disguise. An average round takes about 5 minutes to play. Queue time depends on the server, time of day, and game type (casual or ranked) - usually less than 20 seconds on the English server, rarely going over 60.
Advice for new players:
1) Make sure you have a microphone if you want to play the game. While it's possible to play without one, lack of a mic is a significant handicap for you and your team.
2) Try to find a tutorial or some good players to watch beforehand. The game has no tutorial, only a video that describes the basic rules of the game. Going from begginer to intermediate requires knowledge of a number of details and strategies that might be tricky to figure out from inside the game.
3) Double check that you're playing on a server where everyone speaks a language you know. There are separate servers for each language, and you want to be able to understand what everyone is saying, and to contribute to that discussion.

I was pleased with AC2, and to be perfectly honest AssCreeBro is the same basic game under the hood. But I cannot recommend this installment in the series like I did its predecessor.
The real shame here is that Rome has none of the charm of AC2's brilliant levels. Where Florence was towering and beautiful, Venice labyrinthine and mysterious, and Tuscany open and warm, Rome is just a dissapointment. It feels lifeless and indistinct, even small at times.
Adding to the problem is AssCreeBro's story. AC2 got it right, by telling a straightforward story about the protagonist's journey from simple vengeance to deciphering his role in a larger mystery. AssCreeBro falters, picking up immediately after the admitedly weak finale of AC2 and going nowhere slowly. After the Borgia launch a counter attack that an idiot should have seen coming a mile away, Ezio heads to Rome to regain the Apple and thwart his enemies. The plan includes rebuilding the Assassin order, which plays out in a profoundly boring way. You meet bland, faceless citizens who are under attack, save them, then recruit them to your cause, where they become bland, faceless assassins who do nothing of plot significance. You'll slowly "liberate" Rome by climbing towers (and setting them on fire for some reason), and then buying all the shops in the area.
AssCreeBro adds a few features (like the Assassin recruits). The disappointing part is that most of those new features are bland or unnecessary. The investment minigame seems to exist only to fuel itself. The missions you send your recruits on earn a tiny amount of gold and do nothing for the plot. New "full syncronization" challenges have been added to every mission, further restricting the way you experience this open world adventure (usually in arbitrary ways that don't make any sense and often with bugs).
Without the charm of the setting or story, issues that have plagued Assassin's Creed gameplay since the original begin to take center stage. The controls are atrocious. On PC, the stronger option is to use an Xbox controller rather than wrestle with the horrible keyboard/mouse options. On the controller, one must hold the left trigger to perform all the most common actions. The X and A buttons on the controller are each map to dozens of different (often contradictory) context sensitive commands, and other buttons are under-utilized or outright ignored. Keep in mind, none of these issues is new to AssCreeBro, its just that without the distractions these issues swiftly come to dominate the experience.
Its not that AssCreeBro is bad - its just not good enough to overlook the flaws. If you're already invested in the series, you might want to power through this chapter, but if not, I'd skip right past it.

Great game, I could imagine some people would get scared of this quite easily :D
Overview:
The game is a simple Hide and Seek multiplayer game, with the twist that you can scare hiders (Humans) as a seeker (Ghost and spirit - spirit only seeks in 'Seek and Reap' more). So far there are only two game modes - 'Bounty' and 'Seek and Reap'. In Bounty, the humans have to try find 10 hidden pocket watches while the ghost tries to hunt the humans. Personally, I love how as a spirit in the bounty mode, you can just explore the map and interact with surroundings - gives you the chance to find a new spot for the next round >:] Seek and Reap on the other hand is a little more simple, with the basic element of survival - hide until the time's up. Unlike the bounty mode, humans who have been caught and turrned into spirits can help the ghost find other humans. The game is very straightforward, making it easy to get accustomed to the game and can be enjoyed for hours due to the simple desire to try find the best hiding spots and strategies - a few of which I have discovered myself and I bet you can't get me on the Fireside map >:]
But in all seriousness, the game is definitely worth the money and great fun, especially when you get to talk to the other players - giving the game more suspense and getting some funny moments and reactions from giving someone a jump-scare.
Ideas:
The only thing that I believe need fixing is the mouse sensitivity and for additions to the game it would be great to have an in-game typing chat since some people either prefer to type or don't have a mic or whatever. Also, I think it would create a slightly more scary environment if some of the paintings were animated at random times or when you walk nearby (e.g. eyes following you) or if the statue of Huxley itself could be animated in some way - tbh, Huxley might even be a good additional 'ghost', giving players an extra choice. Since all I can tell from my experience so far, however limited it may be, is that the ghosts only have audio and visual differences, maybe it would be interesting to implement special abilities for each ghost - for example, if the wolf could sniff out the humans or if the baby could place a baby doll or something down as some sort of scare trap. Just random ideas. Perhaps that would make it more interesting and maybe even make certain ghosts better on certain maps, allowing for player strategies to develop.
I also noticed that the ghosts talk when you press 't' but the humans do not, maybe that could be changed so that humans can taunt?
That's all I've got... for now.

Without further ado let's start:
Story - You ''play'' an unnamed 20 year old man, suffering from an terminal illness called lung carcinoma who has been hospitalized and will die because of that illness, they place him in a wing called 7F where he meets a  young woman named Setsumi, 22 years of age. she has a body physique like a child and has a quiet personality. The story properly begins when the protagonists father visits his son in the hospital and leaves his car keys on a table, protagonist takes them and invites Setsumi to go along with him. The two escape the hospital and begin a roadtrip with seemingly no end goal.
Gameplay - The game is a visual novel with little to no interaction if you have autoscroll on the text, so it isn't a ''game'' excactly.
Voice acting and presentation - The ''game'' has very little of the characters and is compromised of a textwindow and a narrow movielike image, the voiceacting is completely optional but i recommend turning it on with autoplay enabled so you don't accidentally skip any speech.
Overall the visual novel is touching and has a very sad undertone driven by the fate of the main characters (incurable illness) so they both know they will die soon or sooner and the novel leaves a bittersweet taste of tears afterwards so i would conclude this with a rating for anyone who loves sad stories of visual novels definetly a 8/10 (would feel again) but for any other person do not expect too much.

I was pleased with AC2, and to be perfectly honest AssCreeBro is the same basic game under the hood. But I cannot recommend this installment in the series like I did its predecessor.
The real shame here is that Rome has none of the charm of AC2's brilliant levels. Where Florence was towering and beautiful, Venice labyrinthine and mysterious, and Tuscany open and warm, Rome is just a dissapointment. It feels lifeless and indistinct, even small at times.
Adding to the problem is AssCreeBro's story. AC2 got it right, by telling a straightforward story about the protagonist's journey from simple vengeance to deciphering his role in a larger mystery. AssCreeBro falters, picking up immediately after the admitedly weak finale of AC2 and going nowhere slowly. After the Borgia launch a counter attack that an idiot should have seen coming a mile away, Ezio heads to Rome to regain the Apple and thwart his enemies. The plan includes rebuilding the Assassin order, which plays out in a profoundly boring way. You meet bland, faceless citizens who are under attack, save them, then recruit them to your cause, where they become bland, faceless assassins who do nothing of plot significance. You'll slowly "liberate" Rome by climbing towers (and setting them on fire for some reason), and then buying all the shops in the area.
AssCreeBro adds a few features (like the Assassin recruits). The disappointing part is that most of those new features are bland or unnecessary. The investment minigame seems to exist only to fuel itself. The missions you send your recruits on earn a tiny amount of gold and do nothing for the plot. New "full syncronization" challenges have been added to every mission, further restricting the way you experience this open world adventure (usually in arbitrary ways that don't make any sense and often with bugs).
Without the charm of the setting or story, issues that have plagued Assassin's Creed gameplay since the original begin to take center stage. The controls are atrocious. On PC, the stronger option is to use an Xbox controller rather than wrestle with the horrible keyboard/mouse options. On the controller, one must hold the left trigger to perform all the most common actions. The X and A buttons on the controller are each map to dozens of different (often contradictory) context sensitive commands, and other buttons are under-utilized or outright ignored. Keep in mind, none of these issues is new to AssCreeBro, its just that without the distractions these issues swiftly come to dominate the experience.
Its not that AssCreeBro is bad - its just not good enough to overlook the flaws. If you're already invested in the series, you might want to power through this chapter, but if not, I'd skip right past it.

[31/07/2015] Update; More serious review.
Ok. I spent a night playing this game with one my friends and honestly it's going to be a hit and miss for some people. that's for sure.
Graphics: The graphics are simple and can be compared to a slightly better version of GMOD but there is still definitely a creepy atmosphere regardless of the quality. I am running everything on ultra and I haven't found anything visually damaging to my eyes.
Mechanics: The current game mechanics are all working pretty well, there are some things which feel a little clunky such as the doors but this is a very minor issue. You can enjoy a game with your friends or even strangers without any frustating problems. Note: There is no text chat feature currently which means the only way to talk is via mic.
Animations: Jump scare animations are quite good, besides that a new animation set could be in order. The current one is fine but I believe they can do much better at a later date.
Gameplay: This is where the hit and miss really comes in. For me, I can scare quite easily on horror games, although some people can't. That being said, I've known my friends to scream often at this game. This is a sort've cross between GMOD Hide n Seek and possibly Slender. (Especially Bounty game mode) The maps are pretty extensive and it's very easy to get lost. There are a lot of hidden doors, passageways and what not. The biggest fear factor of this game is that the enemy is human controlled and you never know when you're going to get jump scared. That being said, I do reccommend this game with friends and not for sole players looking for 'serious' games.
Overall score 8/10, there is room for improvement but things are on a pretty good solid foundation so it should only be up from here ^^

Recommended, but with the caveat that this is an extremely linear, slow game with very little interactivity.
You play the part of the new guy in a village nestled in the mountains of an unspecified (but Asian-flavored) country. A little digging ends up with you being able to see into the past and the spirit world, eventually leading you into an ancient temple and weirder places beyond.
You basically move onwards through a linear path*, hitting the appropriate key (up, down, or space) to deal with obstacles. While the game looks like a platformer, there's no skill involved at all and the morose pace can be off-putting (I groaned every time there was a screen with a lot of pits). If you're thorough it'll last you two to three hours, with very little replayability, though it would be unfair to hold it against a game like this.
So that's the negatives, and it's not too bad as long as you know what you're getting into. Other than that, the presentation is excellent, and the pixel art does a great job of depicting varied, interesting locales; combined with the music and the imaginative setting, it makes the (linear) exploration pretty satisfying. The writing is a lot of fun, alternately clever, evocative and goofy; the game takes itself way less seriously than you'd expect.
*: This is not strictly true - at some points there are short alternate routes or backtracking elements to find optional collectibles, which you need all of to get the "true" ending.

Allow me to introduce you to Narcissu, produced by Stage Nana. There are three visual novels (two being free to play): the Narcissu (the original), Narcissu Side 2nd, and Narcissu 3rd – Die Dritte Welt. (And yes, the story does reference narcissus (daffodils)). I read through the first two and found it very thought-provoking. I will give you a brief summary of the games without giving any spoilers (unless I have no other info), and then I will give you my detailed reviews.
Narcissu:
The story revolves around a character named Yuu Atou, a college-age student (about 21), and a reclusive girl named Setsumi Sakura (age 22). The story is told from the first-person perspective of Atou. The two of them are both sick to the point where they are going to die (there is no known cure for their diseases), and thus they have been confined to the 7th floor of a Catholic hospital, the hospice, where they sit around doing nothing exciting. The boy insists they take off, and opportunity falls in his lap.
Narcissu Side 2nd:
Setsumi returns, but this time, the story is chronologically-earlier than the original. A former-Catholic girl named Himeko, who for a time volunteered at a hospital, ends up meeting Setsumi. Like the first visual novel, the story carries on with the two gallivanting off to various distant places in spite of sickness.
Story:
I played through the original Narcissus first. I’m glad I read it that way – Side 2nd is better in both story and presentation. The first novel is long, and by that I don’t mean text-wise (it’s only four chapters) – I mean it’s dragged out. Not much is really going on. The writer keeps things realistic in that there is no secret source of healing or some new medical technology the characters must find to save themselves. There appears to be no hope period. There isn’t anything to do, hence the characters are seeking something. That’s the ultimate goal – to just get it all over with. But even that goal isn’t existent, or rather, obvious, until the very end. In as much as it lacked direction (Don’t misunderstand me: I appreciated the realism), the little things added up. For instance, how does Setsumi know so much about vehicles (and contrary to other bloggers, it’s not because she’s fascinated with cars)? Why does she have so much money saved up? Why does she want to visit the beach? Questions like these are all answered in Side 2nd. Spoiler: We learn that all of these things are simply ideas inherited from Himeko. Hence, the first story laid the groundwork for the second, chronologically-earlier story.
The story of the second novel is different from the first in a few respects. First, the story isn’t solely centered on Setsumi all the time. It was nice actually being able to see things from Himeko’s point of view concerning her own life. The time given to Himeko as well as her relevance in the story makes the story seem more like it was written about two people, each with their own separate story and each just as significant. Both are the central protagonists, both have their own story, and yet both interact with each other on a very frequent basis. The plot of the second novel develops better than the first: it actually has a direction. Himeko has a list of things that she wants to accomplish, and the mystery as to what those are adds some intrigue to her activities. The presentation of Himeko’s background also adds some variance to the story and is important, given that it shows her lack of faith and helps explain why she no longer refers to herself as Catholic (though she continues to believe in God). Concerning Setsumi, her silent nature is highlighted. Plus, she isn’t portrayed as the reclusive, paranoid character we get in the first novel. Rather, she is simply quiet and polite. Her politeness is not habit, but it isn’t accompanied by the normal cheer typically associated with politeness. Another aspect is that, as Himeko points out, it is hypocritical (note the fries).
Completing both stories in the Side 2nd (Narcissu 1st & 2nd) program reveals tan epilogue and full credits. Rightly so – you wouldn’t understand the epilogue unless you had read both. It was… short, and somewhat rewarding. I wish they would have finished the Himeko story (even though it was implied), but I guess it’s less emotionally straining leaving the ending like this. Note that since the epilogue was created after both stories were made, they didn’t make the same mistake of assuming that walking out with a smile is somehow happy in light of inevitable end.
I can’t emphasize enough how much I appreciated the objectivity in both stories (original and Side 2nd). Let me explain: In the end, I don’t feel a bias towards or against anyone – they are as they are and they believe what they believe. The characters, while I didn’t think of them as real, call for sympathy given their circumstances. They didn’t do anything beyond common human responses. While I don’t agree with Himeko and eventually Setsumi did, I do understand realize that many people see things way and don’t have reason to believe otherwise. Hence, within their own frame of mind, they were justified in doing what they did. As for Yuu Atou, he acted out of the desperateness of his situation. I wasn’t in favor of him escaping from the consequences of his actions, but neither did I condemn him. I was disappointed that he stole things, but it was all in the passing of the moment. Being on the run isn’t justification for acting like a fool, but it is realistic to act like a fool when on the run.
Meh:
As an oddity, Yuu Atou never actually introduces himself. Furthermore, none of the characters really indicate their age. The hints at age occur when Chihiro mentions she went to college and she addresses Himeko as being older. An occasional picture of a character might be shown, but anime-style characters have that funny way of making it difficult to tell what age they are. The images we see of Setsumi seem to indicate she is very young in both the original and Side 2nd novels. She is in the latter since it’s chronologically earlier. However, it seems to me that the story could just as easily have been told if she had hardly aged.
A note should be made about the medical field. The author didn’t do as good a job as he could have about making the world of the hospice realistic. Instead, his primary concern was with story, so the truth about hospitals was neglected to a considerable extent. Care and life in the hospices isn’t as bad as the author made it out to be.
Overall:
Frankly, I rather enjoyed the read. It was very thought-provoking. It was a long-drawn out experience, and it didn’t help that I read it during the only hours I had time each day: between midnight and four in the morning. Take my advice and get some sleep, but if you happen to have a slot for time open between 10 and midnight, let me just say, the cinematic and emotional aura of stories like this is always enhanced at night. Trust me on that.
You should definitely give it a try.

i have nothing good to say about the game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

So, I know I'm not that deep into the story, but there are a few things I'd like to state from the time I've spent (And please, if you're already doing these things, then disregard this completely).
-First off, I like the story. It's a rather sad tale that has a nice setup and a lot of interesting perspective from our protagonist. Just wanted to let you know that.
-However (and I'm assuming this is part of the early access) there are so few pictures or discussions in this visual novel. I'd like to feel the family strain to smile at the protagonist, and have the discussion with the girl whose hair goes to her hips. So much of the story right now just has a blank screen or the background (which is very beautiful, I might add), but the characters need to be there.
-Finally, the story so far is doing a lot of "tell, don't show" with what the protagonist sees, like with the friends playing with her and not coming around as often, or the family around her being as friendly as possible. Simply put, we're told all these things are happening, but I think it would really help to drive the point if we had even a small conversation with some kids when the protagonist is sick, or talking with the family and seeing that smile, wondering why it's so abnormal. This doesn't have to be like adding in minigames and moving around, but just a few slides where the protagonist and characters are having these moments.
All in all, I really can't wait until it's finished. I'm nervous of going further to spoil the story when the whole thing comes out, but I just might have to keep playing! Great work so far!

Kaboom Monsters is a strategy, card battling, adventure game. When you launch the game, you will have the option on 1 out of 3 decks to choose from. There is no clear cut difference, so picking the 'good looking one' is the picking method. The battle screen has a 3x3 game board in the center of the screen and your available cards display on the right of the battle area. Turn based between you and the computer opponent. Kaboom Monsters cards has a series of numbers on each side, which represents its attack/defense strength. You also have another number in the upper left corner, which represents the number of turns a card can remain in play. When you place a card next to an opponent's card, the numbers determine the victor, meaning if the card has the higher value, you will turn your opponent's card to your side. If the value is equal or less than your opponent's card then all stays unchanged. The Smithy will arm or upgrade your cards, the Wizard can combine three of the same cards into a more powerful card.
This game can be play for a little while or you can choose to play at length. For me it was difficult to understand the scoring system in the beginning, but as I played it became easier. The game got quite boring after a while as the computer opponents cards got quite strong, quite fast. Not a game that I would play again in a hurry. Fun to play when there is little time for anything else, but could always find something else to do.
