This game series was one of my favorite as I was growing up and it all starting with EDF 2017 back on the Xbox 360. That was one my favorite co-op games to play with my little brother and have since beat that game on all difficulty modes and got the Genocide Gun to top off messing around with literally the most powerful weapon in the game.
I only played Insect Armageddon on the 360 for so long before despising it for a number of reasons while admittedly it having good segments and enemies to fight and concepts, overally it proved far too short, shoddy in grind, boring, and even with somewhat a unique take on EDF in a lot of ways was instead just feeling too much of a rushed project with difficulty in landing the EDF mark and feelings I was expecting to get from this game.
Focusing back onto this now, EDF 4.1, I'd have to say it massively improves the lot of its replayability in the usual large amounts of missions, 5 difficulty modes, now with 4 classes to try and master with additionally leveling in the form of better gear and grinding for armour, but overall a fun time to be had! (EDF, EDF, EDF!)
While I do love the game very much, let alone the additional mission packs (avoid the DLC guns and such, that stuff is crap and useful for only Easy/Normal really) add a layer of more to be done, sadly I feel the game lacks in playing alone simply because it can feel very sluggish to get going when on your own and not as much of an experience to me honestly. I mean, it is a wonderful game, even for the lot of its simplicity and cheesy humourous cliche nature, but it is not as noticed when alone when you survive the Ravager Alien Invasion.
Lets try to break this down to make it easier to digest:
Singleplayer and its Classes - While fun at first, it is sluggish and not as fun I guess one might say, particularly if solo-ing as a Ranger or Air Raider class since these two don't get going until later on when they get better gear while Wing Divers and Fencers get to enjoy the additional features that are spectacular to their class earlier and are also more effective in a number of ways solo.
Of course, this can be obviously overlooked when working with allies, one in each class, but this is for singleplayer play and their things will be noticeably taking time to accomplish. If anything, one will have to play in bursts to avoid getting burnt out, but if one can keep themselves entertained between beating missions and the rediculous and hilarious story and character dialogue then all power to you.
Missions and Difficulty - One thing I loved EDF 2017 as I do here is the fact of 5 difficulty modes and nearly 100 missions to play through (over 100 if you count DLC missions that, again, add to the game a lot). My memories of 2017 may be hazy and full of nostalgia but if anything Easy was still its own difficulty with enough weapons to be found to keep things interesting and keep you on a powerful spree of destruction against the Ravager alien threat.
However, Easy Mode in this game should NEVER be played in all reality, Normal gives you the exact same progression only with the Ravagers being somewhat more difficult to fight against but even then it is still relatively easy and capable of one's self to get through it without a sweat.
For achievement hunters/completionists/etc., avoid doing it as well as the only thing this mode gives is a Medal towards beating the missions on Easy but no Achievement (do it still if you desire but I fell in thinking it to be like 2017 but didn't and am dissappointed when I got to Normal and saw nearly no difference between the two modes for weapon drops, enemy difficulty, and so forth).
Co-op, Multiplayer, and the Community - Fair to say that this game is MEANT for co-op/multiplayer play, otherwise it will get more stale then you and I would believe (being said from someone who enjoyed, again, the hell out of 2017). It is a fun time, you will feel that EDF HYPE when you get to mowing with your buds together, coordinating attacks, yelling out "FOR THE PRIDE OF EDF!" or even singing out the lyrics of the EDF song that will just get you going even more!
Additionally, with that, playing again through the game makes it all the more fun, and immersive I guess one might say, and always will be one of the definitive features of playing an EDF game. Just be careful though, unless you don't mind this for whatever your reasons, there are those that will tamper forcefully with your savefile in such a way to make you gain everything in the game and whatever else.
If you want to avoid this sad drawback from the online gaming experience, be sure to keep and update a backup save of your progress somewhere so if you need to, you can restore it before it happened, and continue playing. You will have to do this manually and I recommend searching into it.
The playerbase is small, no doubt for its rather niche nature and the likes, but if you can get some personal friends of yours in on this then it can be very much negligible a problem as co-op offline or online is nonetheless a way to play this game.
The DLC Content - Coming back to a lot of mention of DLC, there is such, thankfully to a degree the first mission pack funny enough is made up of the DLC 1 and 2 Packs from the console version, a free 2-in-1 deal sort with Pack 3 made then into Pack 2, and making it somewhat cheaper to get it all. I feel it is definitely worth getting it if you have money to spare and want more challenges and awesome unexpected fights to go through, solo or with friends/online co-op!
Just, please, avoid any and all DLC gear/weapons/vehicles/etc, it is NOT worth whatever it offers and is simply cash grabs, even if minor in price, it is useless these items past Easy/Normal and will make you loathe about spending that money on such rather than say the cards to get yourself maybe a nice Award Medal thing for your Steam Page to show your EDF Pride!

I have played a fair share of Tetris in my day. In the arcade, on the original spinach-green Game Boy, 3D Tetris, every Tetris variation you can name. I mention this because Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm describes itself as Match 4, but it's more like a hybrid between Match 4 and Tetris. Except where it isn't, which is everywhere that matters.
I'm going to assume you have played Tetris, or at least seen someone play Tetris. Different shaped pieces fall one at a time from the top of the screen to the bottom of the screen. You want to arrange the shapes to make lines, which removes the line from the board. If any part of the board fills enough to go past the top of the screen, you lose.
Before we talk about the differences, let's talk about how Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm is similar to Tetris. Different shaped pieces fall from the top of a 4x8 grid to the bottom. You want to match up the shapes to remove them from the board. The game ends if any part of the board gets filled.
In Tetris, shapes fall one at a time and can be moved horizontally around the board, or rotated, to arrange them in a suitable pattern for making lines. In Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm, shapes fall 4 at a time in a horizontal line. You cannot move or rotate the shapes. Instead, you are allowed to replace one shape at a time that is currently falling with an arbitrary shape. Once a shape hits the bottom of the screen, or another shape, it's locked in and cannot be changed. You change shapes by clicking the mouse as a vertical line moves over them, the line moving from left to right across the screen at a speed determined by the tempo of the music.
In Tetris, you know what the next shape is going to beforehand. This allows you to strategize and think ahead. In Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm, you do not know what the next shape will be, so your decisions are entirely reactionary.
In Tetris, the game doesn't end until a shape extends past the top of the board. This means that if one part of the board is getting close to the top, you can move shapes to another part to buy yourself some time. In Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm, a horizontal line of shapes covering the length of the board falls at the same time. Thus every column will increase in height by one with each new row of shapes, no matter what you do. Even if the rest of the board is empty, if a single column is at the top, you are guaranteed to lose, and cannot do anything to stop it.
There are additional game mechanics — score modifiers, special shapes that remove all nearby shapes, etc. None of them change the fact that the game just isn't very well designed, and isn't fun to play. Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm is an excercise in frustration rather than relaxation. You have so little control over the game; you cannot move shapes, you can only change shapes to what the game says you can change them to, you can only change the shapes if the vertical line happens to be over them at that second, and only while they are falling. The closer you get to the top of the board, the more impossible it becomes to change shapes in time.
You do not know what the next shape is, so you are purely guessing what shapes you should change now. Even when you make decisions that seem rational based on the available information, the lack of information and control over the board means you will often fail. Tetris is a game of planning and skill, but this is a game of luck and reaction speeds.
I honestly cannot recommend this game to anyone. From a fundamental design perspective, it's just broken.

A Tetris-style rhythm game? Seems good.
I'll try to explain the gameplay as well as I can:
- You have four tiles falling down, and a vertical line moving from left to right.
- If you press up when the vertical line is over a tile, that tile will turn into the tile showing in the top left corner of the screen.
- When you connect four tiles (or three/five depending on the difficulty) they disappear and you gain points.
- If you press up at the exact right moment matching the beat of the song you can build up a "combo counter" increasing points earned as well as a "supermeter" that can be used to replace a normal tile with an exploding "supertile".
- The campaign mode has no game over, however the amount of points you lose by using a continue will increase by 10 000 each time.
In addition to the "main mode" explained above there is also the free Pure Beat DLC which adds an additional (less complicated but still enjoyable) mode.
The music is a big part of the game, and whether you will enjoy this game or not probably depends a lot on whether or not you will enjoy (or at least don't mind) the music. There were some songs that I enjoyed more than others, and although this is not really the kind of music that I listen to normally I didn't mind listening to it while playing a game like this.
Just a minor warning. The game might feel really hectic at first, and I was just about to give up on it when my first achievement popped, meaning I had to continue playing - and I'm glad I did! The game gets pretty fun once you get the hang of it.
I recommend this game to people who enjoy games like Tetris and to fans of rhythm games. Just remember to give it some time and don't give up on it right away like I almost did.

Summary: Grinding for characters is a chore, but most other aspects of the game are quite enjoyable.
PROS:
-Performance is great, graphics options allow for lots of fine-tuning
-Most guns are satisfying to use (ex: Twitch's 417)
-Sound design is incredible (you can audibly track enemies with very high precision as they move all around you)
-Destructable environments, the defenders' ability to reinfornce walls, and multiple objective locations makes every match feel different
-Default control layout is well-thought-out and may only require minimal tweaking
-Uplay is no longer a grotesque monster of a client
CONS:
-Unlocking characters with Renown is a hefty grind (100-200 per-match, most characters cost 25,000)
-"Complete" edition is ridiculously-priced ($80) and microtransactions for individual characters ($5+) are just as bad
-Guns and gadgets are locked to characters, this limits customization and means you probably won't be 100% satisfied with any character's kit (I'm sure this is for the purpose of better game balance, but it's still annoying)
-AI killcams. Sometimes they'll just start shooting a wall for literally no reason and "just happen kill you"
-Like all competetive games, people in multiplayer live and breathe the game, expect to lose and get flamed
-Being forced to run the game from Uplay instead of Steam is still an annoying and unnecessary step

Developers big and small, please take note: This is how you do dinosaurs.
I could do a regular review of the game, but... it's a LEGO game, so what's the point? You want a short review? Okay, how about this: Blahblah whimsical humor blahblah tons of collectibles blahblah oh, and you can play as dinosaurs, too.
No, I want to take this opportunity to talk about dinosaurs in video games and about how this game gets them right. Y'know, I am a huge dino nerd, and the thing that bothers me is the fact that all recent dino games are more or less about killing them. Yeah, I guess I am a dino-hugging hippie. But I think this approach shortchanges the beauty, the wonder, and, ironically, the danger these animals embody. Players should not be so overpowered that it enables them to kill every prehistoric critter in sight with ease. Where's the danger and the fun in that? Dino games (yes, I have a dedicated folder in my Steam library) should, in my opinion, be about encountering and surviving dinosaurs, not splattering their brains all over the landscape. TheHunter: Primal was great about that... up until the point where I realize that HUNTING them is all the game is really about (I know, duh, considering the title, but still). I also like the original Trespasser because of this. You had weapons, yes, but a) you were a civilian and handled them poorly (a thing where the atrocious control scheme actually worked in the game's favour) and b) there were barely enough of them to keep the pesky raptors at bay long enough to reach the exit, not to leave a trail of dino corpses in your wake.
Like the movies, LEGO Jurassic World is also only about making it through the adventure alive. Sure, there are some brawls where you have to fend off smaller dinos in a fist fight, but even then, you're merely knocking them out. And this is great for a change! I know it goes against the basic impulses of a gamer (myself included) to NOT kill scary-looking creatures the moment they appear. But it works! Nowadays, every game about dinosaurs is either a hunting simulator or a multiplayer title. Also, there hasn't been a decent full-fledged (not counting the official mobile and Facebook games) theme park manager since Operation Genesis some 15 years ago. I haven't played ARK yet, but one of the Steam trailers show the player unloading a dozen revolver bullets into a Ceratopsian's skull, so there you go. Give us some games for dino-hugging hippies! Like a Trespasser remake, for example. Until then, LEGO Jurassic World will have to do. Which is not a bad thing. At all.

For good or bad, video games have trained us to expect and desire violence in our entertainment. We start up a new title, especially action or horror, looking for a gun or a shovel or some blunt object so we can handle the hordes of enemies surely coming our way. When a game not only removes straight-forward combat but takes all fighting options off the table, the fear is very real. Amnesia's design is masterful. This is a game that MUST be played in a dark room, with the headphones on. You cannot defeat the grotesques that haunt the castle, so look for some good places to hide. The visuals are incredibly disturbing and suit the game well, and there's a lively community of modders crafting their own tales of mystery and terror. If you're a horror fan, you owe it to yourself to play Amnesia. Just be prepared to stay awake until dawn.

I'm not entirely sure what to say, other than this game is absolutely fantastic.  I wasn't keen on playing another 2D retro platformer (I was just playing one before I jumped into this one) but I was somehow instantly hooked from the intro level.  The gameplay is basically Mega Man, but with the combat system from Zelda 2 and the dive attack like in Duck Tales.  There are other nods to classic 8 bit games, as well as some modern innovations.  The art design is nice and the levels look fantastic.  The music is probably the main highlight of the game, IMO.  Chiptune music done right!
I only have a few reccomendations for this game (should they make a sequel.)  At some point you will run out of things to buy in the game (upgrades, armor, etc.) and will have absolutely no use for gold.  I wish I could still keep spending it on something useful.  Also, the game is rather short; I keep wishing there were some extra levels.  Fortunately, free DLC will be released sometime in the future.
Also, I should mention that if you are considering buying this game...I might not reccomend the Steam Version.  The console versions (Xbox One and PS4 specifically) came out earlier this year and they each include an extra boss battle that rewards special equipment.  For the Xbox One version, you fight the Battletoads.  For PS4, you fight Kratos (from God of War.)  The Steam, Wii U, and Nintendo DS versions of the game do not have any exclusive content.  Keep this in mind when making your purchase.  They may consider updating the Steam version later, but...who knows.
All in all, it's a fantastic game.

I’m getting a little tired of the endless barrage of pixel-based titles, so the less said on this point the better.
I’ve seen a few people lauding the game’s soundtrack (which you can also purchase for a small fee), but I didn’t find it anything special. Take any lounge music track and slow it down to half speed. Done.
This is what lets the game down and sapped all my incentive to play. In the absence of a jump key or the ability to run, you’re left slowly scrolling from left to right along a completely linear path. In fact, even when moving up and down objects, the animations are painfully unhurried. Thankfully, in aside from the walking simulator elements, there are opportunities to interact with the environment. Unfortunately, these are primarily limited to two functions: chopping down grass that blocks your path, and breaking rocks that block your path.
The pace of the game is slow, and if that’s your bag, you’ll probably enjoy it. For me, I’d much prefer to run quickly by areas in which zero new gameplay is occurring, especially if backtracking previously explored areas.
Unfortunately, the leisurely, repetitive and unengaging nature of the gameplay was such that I became bored and impatient before I had the opportunity to experience much of the narrative.
Of the sections I did persevere with and play through, it looks as though the central storyline could progress somewhere interesting, pursuing the ability to connect with a spirit world.
Aside from the main narrative of the game, the dialogue with NPCs left much to be desired. The writers consciously attempted to write the NPC dialogue as humorous, but failed rather miserably and came across as trying far too hard in this respect. In fact, the strained ‘zany’ nature of the dialogue was such that I soon gave up bothering to talk to NPCs.

This game is pretty great! Talked to random people in town and they handed me weaponry, incense, and tacky clothing- and I'm not above being swayed by bribery!
In all seriousness though, the game mostly involves walking, talking, and experiencing the world. There's very little in the way of gameplay, as you generally spend most of your time moving from place to place interacting with other characters, or the environment. So if you like more passive gameplay/storytelling, this one will be worth a shot.
The writing is amazing, for while the plot hasn't sucked me in, the various things characters say more than make up for it, especially early-on. The dude that gave me the machete might've been using me to hide evidence, as he'd recently used it to murder a bunch of kids to feed to his pigs. It's delivered well though, as it's the kind of line you can easily skip over, misinterpret, or miss entirely because you were reading too fast.
The art/music/sound effects fit everything perfectly. It's gorgeous, has great atmosphere, and while it's minimalistic, it's very imaginative.
My only complaint is you use the dpad to walk, and you walk slowly. It helps push the atmospheric nature of everything, but it gets a bit frustrating after a while. Also, interacting with objects is obnoxious (ladders are hard to climb, which is nonsense).
Overall, if you like calm, story driven games, with little to no real gameplay- this one's probably worth picking up. It's fairly short though, and while it has multiple endings- it's probably better on sale.

I just nominated this game for the steam awards for the category I made up that I call The "Has a Great Personality" Award. This game.. is not a technical masterpiece. Its a graphics are 2 generation behind other current releases. Its physics are not... not from this planet.  Its gameplay is not the deepest. Most of its content is recycled, and a good chunk of it is a grind.
So why am I recommending it?
Because this game achieves something that few games do. It has a genuine charm. It is campy in all the best ways. Now some say that being campy is a negative, that it does not stand up to modern art that we collectively take seriously. But to accept and love "campiness" in media is to love the ridiculousness  flaws that make you truly love something. Not that you are looking past them, but you love  them for those flaws. And loving a piece of media for its camp says more about the consumer and last longer than any of the more generic actually (and more "objectively") good games we all play in a year.
Despite everything this game does wrong I cannot help but love it for its old B movie plot and aethestic. Being able to unite with 4 friends online as we charge an army of insects singing the EDF anthem is some of the best fun I have had in any game in years. This game always makes me smile and make me want to watch any of the campy, schlok you could see on  mystery science theater. It is glorious and you should genuinely give this game a shot, because it might just win you over even when have some shinier/smoother game waiting for you in your steam library.

This third person shooter trades next gen graphics for satisfying and large scale gameplay. Defend the earth from invading robot aliens and their armies of giant insects. Almost every level will pit you up against hundreds of enemies in fully destructible cities or dark underground caves.
The game is very accessible, with 5 vastly different difficulty levels. Each difficulty level amping up the health, damage, speed, jump height, projectile count and range of most enemies.
Approach each level a different way with your choice of class, weapon loadout and difficulty level.
: bullets and boomsticks
: flying lasers
: mechs, tanks, buffs and air strikes
: thick armour, big weapons and jet boosters
As you play a class you'll find new weapons and health upgrades along the way. There are hundreds of weapons to unlock, with increasingly ridiculous firepower. Later levels and higher difficulty levels award bigger weapons, which is a great incentive to challenge yourself.
There are many types of enemies you'll encounter in this game, both on land and in the air. Each enemy having it's own unique behaviours and attacks. Considering you can only take 2-4 weapons with you to each level, it can be quite a challenge to figure out what will be most effective to deal with all the different enemies you'll encounter in a single level.
All in all this game displays incredible variety on all fronts, whilst maintaining very basic core gameplay. Although single player makes for a decent experience, the game really shines in its multiplayer modes. I'd recommend this game to anyone and even go as far as to say it's one of my favourite games of all time.

There are two kinds of people, those who know the Earth Defense Force serie, and for them, they probably already own the game or plan of getting it anyway, and the ones who don't, and I pity you.
But let me educate you if you are hesitant of getting that game, or curious about what it's all about.
EDF is simply put, a third person shooter game which gets its inspiration from terror movies, such as "Attack of the Giant Ants/Killer bees", or more precisely, Godzilla. For the most occidental among you, think Starship Troopers.
You choose among 4 classes, a loadout of 2 to 4 weapons, and embark on a mission to kill any alien that move or doesn't in a glorious fury of destruction. Buildings explode and crumble, giant insects explode and body parts are flying everywhere, giant robots fire plasma while tanks answer in kind with all sorts of ordonances, bombers strike the field, and to put here the words of a fellow player "This game is therapeutic as f..."
Almost 100 missions, some exclusive to coop mode, 5 difficulties levels, lots and lots of different weapons ranging from comical joke weapons to absolutely devastating ones, lot of vehicules from motorbikes to giant walking robots firing lasers, all you get as rewards from battlefield drops, 4 players coop...
It's probably the only serie where you will find the game being full of bugs is a good thing.
It's sheer unadultered fun, and on higher difficulties, the game takes a strategic depth that also offers quite a lot of challenge. It's wonderfully over the top. You get to fight Godzilla in a giant robot. You get to have an army of giants robots facing an army of Godzillas in honorable melee fight.
The only reproaches I could have is the fact movement is a bit slow, helicopter controls are pretty terrible, and you need to pick up the drops falling around to reap the reward, which is a bit time consuming and tend to break the flow. But still, you WILL have fun. You will have moment where you will think and shout it's the best game ever. You will scream "NOT THE BEES!". Even the bugs of the glitch variety of the game will amuse you and make you laugh. You will see breakdancing spiders. You will see said spiders going into space after explosions.
Bottom line, like I said in the forum, you need to be an alien to hate that game. Get it. You need to. You know you want to. Soon you will know the EDF song by heart and shout along with your fellow soldiers.

Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood (henceforth referred to as AC:B) is the third title in the Assassin's Creed series. Chronologically taking place after AC2, this is a nice sequel. Admittedly the numerous graphical glitches (ground not loading, birds stretching into the sky, enemies sliding on hills) are distracting and do take you out of the moment. The story is gripping, and the addition of heavy weapons is a nice touch. However, AC:B fails in the respect of convenience: you have to buy the stores yourself in order for them to sell you things, and you often need quite a bit of money to do that. Frankly they should have not included that facet, it was the worst part of the game. The combat was much to easy, AC1 had the right idea in preventing you from using the counter move until halfway through the game, forcing you to dodge and such. Despite this, I still reccomend this game.

The electric town of Akihabara. The lights, the colors, sounds and the music that fill the city and give it the reputation of being on the fringe of modern popular culture. The arcades with their flashing screens undecipherable wall of noise, and UFO catchers packed with cute and colorful goods. The music stores blaring the latest in pop music to entice passerby's. The energy of the streets, and the mentality of a fast moving generation, wanting more but never quite having enough. Akihabara is a town meant to indulge.
And like the town, Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm knows just how to indulge. It tackles quite a hefty number of puzzle game tropes combining the toe-tapping rhythm keeping of Lumines, the logical shape matching of games like Bejeweled and Zoo Keeper, with the line-breaking color combining of games like Puyo Puyo or Tetris. Symbols are matched in pairs of four, as you would expect, but the changing of blocks is done precisely on the beat in order to keep the score multiplier going. Just like Lumines this rewards players who have a keen ear for music and a memorization of the songs being played with a much higher score and a more prestigous spot on the world leaderboards.
Classic electronic music sounds with just a touch of synthy Japanese New Wave of the 80's, which is what drew my ears. The warm tone of the keyboard, the bright and poppy bits of piano, led by a simple Karaoke kind of metronome beat. It fits the setting more than well and shows a keen knowledge of this aspect and region of popular culture from this developer. I definitely felt an authentic, albeit older generational feel from what Akihabara was trying to convey about the atmosphere of a bustling Japanese city.
I was surprised how much music there was, and of very genuine quality. Even more surprising was finding out that these were composed by the developer himself, which given the wide range and variety heard while playing was impressive to me. Considering it's indie status and incredibly low and fair price-point I was only really expecting a handful of songs, but was pleased to see the campaign continue on for a total of ten.
It's a bit busy at first, and the fact that the game is tackling so many styles in puzzling creates an atmosphere of madness at first. But as you become familiar with the shapes provided in the blocks of each distinct song, it becomes second nature, and very rewarding. Fans of Lumines who are okay with a bit more of an involved thinking process and less of a Zen-ful approach should definitely take note, because there really hasn't been anything since it to keep the style of rhythm-based puzzle solving going. Akihabara - Feel the Rhythm delivers a worthy entry in the genre and adds more than enough of its own personality and flavor to keep those within its demographic coming back for more of its great music and authentic atmosphere.

I wrote a full review that you can find here:
tl;dr:
Ignoring the ending, and the awkward humor, Qora is an interesting experience. It builds slowly, ever so carefully, in order to draw you in. Everything does end up coming together. The ending I got just seems to imply that your own story ends up being pointless. Maybe I missed something. Who knows. The ending didn’t inspire me to go back to find out.

First of all, I would like to say that this game is a lot of fun. I would definitely recommend it. There are a lot of things that they do right. Getting to play as dinosaurs is fantastic. I love how they did the raptor characters. The gyrosphere is a lot of fun. It was great playing through all the movies. The humor is very well done and in spirit with the other LEGO games. All in all, a great game. Plus they have improved a lot on some of the issues of the older games, especially with respect to camera angles and jumping puzzles.
However, I am very disappointed in the bugs that I have come across. Most have been minor, a character getting stuck somewhere, that sort of thing. But there are bugs that keep me from being able to complete 100% of the game, which is really frustrating. Especially because I was able to do everything, it just didn't give me credit for it. In the end, I have the satisfaction of knowing that I was able to complete it, but I'll never be able to get the 100% or the achievements that I'd like.
My conclusion is that LEGO Jurassic World is a fantastic game if you are not a completionist that needs the 100% to feel justified in the game. I recommend getting it and playing because it really is a lot of fun, but I recommend against hoping that it will be a completely smooth, bug-free experience.

Saints Row the Third was the first game I played in the series, and so it will always have a special place in my heart.
TLDR Review:  One of the best open-world games ever.  One of the best comedy games ever.  Slightly affected by some copy-pasting of elements.
PRO:
This has, I think, the most enjoyable driving of any game I've played.  It's not "realistic" driving or flying, but it's definitely fun to just hop in a car and drive.  The flying is pretty good and the boats aren't bad.
This game has great character and clothing customization.  I love the fact that I can play my own character.
I love the vehicle customization in this game.  I love taking a car to a show and changing the colors.
I love the variety of missions:  sniping, blowing things up, helicopter attacks, and a lot more.  Each mission offers something different.
The modding for this game really adds to the enjoyment.  Gentlemen of Steelport and Sandbox + are a must.  I'm currently playing using a save-game mod that allows me to keep all progress from the previous game, but simply resets all the missions.  It's like playing with cheats but without actually having cheats enabled (and without the corresponding block on auto-saves).  NOTE*  I only play single-player.  I'd never use these in coop.
The game is funny.  There are so many "serious" and "dramatic" games, and I really love the fact that there is a game that knows how to just be stupid, how to play everything for laughs.
CON:
There are too many copy-pasted stores.  On the down side, I could walk into different stores in SR2 and see different merchandise.  On the plus side, I don't have the problem where I walk into a store only to find that the store I want is across town.  If it's Planet Saints, chances are, it has most of what I need.
SR2 had way more places to go into.
Gangs just hang out on street corners, instead of having actual strongholds.
Pedestrians don't seem to do very much except endlessly walk around the block.
Character and vehicle customization has been reduced from SR2.
Zombies are overdone, and I'm thankful Sandbox lets me turn it off.
The beginning of the game, and a particularly dramatic death, seemed unnecessary, and in particular, Shaundi's reaction to that death, becoming a VERY different ... annoyingly different character as a result, took away some of my enjoyment of the game.  I'll take classic Shaundi, fun Shaundi, over grief-stricken-killjoy Shaundi any day.
OVERALL
Cons aside, this is still one of my favorite games ever.
SR2 had more customization and a more detailed map, but in many ways, SR2 almost seemed to have TOO MUCH space ... there was more to see, and it took longer to get around, but there wasn't necessarily more to do in that space.  SR3 is, by comparison, smaller, but it ultimately comes across as simply more compact and efficient.
This is a fun and funny game and I highly recommend it.

I backed the game during the Kickstarter campaign and I was pretty excited to play it. I played the game for almost two hours and got to an ending (there are more), and I'm quite disappointed, here's why:
NOTE: I'm posting this in the forums in case someone wants to discuss it.
I wanted to play the game but I wasn't hyped. All I was hoping for was a nice exploration game with great art, something like FEZ or Proteus where I could wander and lose myself.
The art is gorgeous and the soundtrack is great too. Seriously, that part is great and very enjoyable.
(SPOILER FREE)
The narrative is nice, feels like a collection of tiny stories told with just a bit of text.
I won't spoil the ending, but it was the only part about the narrative that I didn't like at all, in my opinion it doesn't fit the style of the game and it ruins the mood (at least it did ruin the mood for me).
There's no real gameplay in "Qora", it's just following a path and watching some cutscenes. I was expecting some real exploration but it's an extremely linear game, there are some secrets or things you can find but those lack depth.
There are some obstacles in the path(pits or rocks) but to overcome them you just have to press a key and watch an animation. First I thought it was clever, as these elements made you stop and enjoy the art, but once you have gone trough tons of them you just don't see the point in it anymore. It's highly repetitive and it's no challenge at all.
I didn't feel like I had a significant impact in the world/story and I wasn't challenged in any way. This is not an issue in games like Proteus or Gone Home, where you can go wherever you want and explore, but as I said earlier I wouldn't say this game is about exploration due to how limited you are.
I wouldn't replay the game, there's no challenge at all, I wouldn't spend another two hours going through the same stages, bored to death, just to look for a tiny secret.
The art and the music are amazing, and the game run flawless, but it feels like an animated art gallery where you have to press a button to watch the next piece of art. I've enjoyed Proteus, Gone Home and similar titles, but I had to make an effort to finish this one. Consulting a game designer would have been great. I really wanted to like "Qora", but in the end, it just didn't happen :(

Shovel Knight is a very well made platformer game made in the spirit of NES.  I was able to complete this game in a few hours over roughly 3 days time.  I usually only write reviews if a game is either very exceptional, or very terrible.  Fortunately, this game is very exceptional.  Just to briefly summarize, the game is about Shovel Knight, a hero who is trying to rescue his best friend, Shield Knight from an evil sorceress.  The game has a ton of 2d platforming action, and some of the best game control mechanics I've played since Super Mario Bros 3.  You go from area to area, defeating all of these other knights, each one specializing in a particular area.  While all that is going on, you visit a small town in between quests, so you can drop off "shanties" for the local musician to archive for you.  Speaking of music, this game features some of the best chip music in ages, and there is a lot to hear.  So as you are getting through all of the quests, you are also upgrading your armor, your shovel, and gathering new magic spells to use to get you through the areas.  They designed the levels where you have to use certain powers to proceed, introducing new challenges as the game progresses.  I don't want to spoil the ending for you, but I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who loved the NES/SNES, and enjoys a good challenging classic style 2D platformer game.  I can see myself playing this game for years to come!  Nice work, Yacht Club Games!

There are two kinds of people, those who know the Earth Defense Force serie, and for them, they probably already own the game or plan of getting it anyway, and the ones who don't, and I pity you.
But let me educate you if you are hesitant of getting that game, or curious about what it's all about.
EDF is simply put, a third person shooter game which gets its inspiration from terror movies, such as "Attack of the Giant Ants/Killer bees", or more precisely, Godzilla. For the most occidental among you, think Starship Troopers.
You choose among 4 classes, a loadout of 2 to 4 weapons, and embark on a mission to kill any alien that move or doesn't in a glorious fury of destruction. Buildings explode and crumble, giant insects explode and body parts are flying everywhere, giant robots fire plasma while tanks answer in kind with all sorts of ordonances, bombers strike the field, and to put here the words of a fellow player "This game is therapeutic as f..."
Almost 100 missions, some exclusive to coop mode, 5 difficulties levels, lots and lots of different weapons ranging from comical joke weapons to absolutely devastating ones, lot of vehicules from motorbikes to giant walking robots firing lasers, all you get as rewards from battlefield drops, 4 players coop...
It's probably the only serie where you will find the game being full of bugs is a good thing.
It's sheer unadultered fun, and on higher difficulties, the game takes a strategic depth that also offers quite a lot of challenge. It's wonderfully over the top. You get to fight Godzilla in a giant robot. You get to have an army of giants robots facing an army of Godzillas in honorable melee fight.
The only reproaches I could have is the fact movement is a bit slow, helicopter controls are pretty terrible, and you need to pick up the drops falling around to reap the reward, which is a bit time consuming and tend to break the flow. But still, you WILL have fun. You will have moment where you will think and shout it's the best game ever. You will scream "NOT THE BEES!". Even the bugs of the glitch variety of the game will amuse you and make you laugh. You will see breakdancing spiders. You will see said spiders going into space after explosions.
Bottom line, like I said in the forum, you need to be an alien to hate that game. Get it. You need to. You know you want to. Soon you will know the EDF song by heart and shout along with your fellow soldiers.

This is a great game.
Gratuitous Space Battles is not like your typical RTS fare.  Instead of manually controlling all of your units and furiously managing your economy, you design your units (space ships in this case) and define certain characteristics of how they should perform in battle (distance to maintain from enemies, formations, some AI behaviors) and then let the battles play out.  You can't control anything during the actual battles.  This game is all about planning and strategizing, and there's a lot to offer.
What I believe is the key difference that makes this game great is its emphasis on overall strategy rather than micromanaging an absurd level of detail.  Yes, a bit of micromanaging would make the battles easier, but it's your plans and strategies that will win the day rather than your ability to build structures really fast.  Prepare to think.

Saints Row the Third was the first game I played in the series, and so it will always have a special place in my heart.
TLDR Review:  One of the best open-world games ever.  One of the best comedy games ever.  Slightly affected by some copy-pasting of elements.
PRO:
This has, I think, the most enjoyable driving of any game I've played.  It's not "realistic" driving or flying, but it's definitely fun to just hop in a car and drive.  The flying is pretty good and the boats aren't bad.
This game has great character and clothing customization.  I love the fact that I can play my own character.
I love the vehicle customization in this game.  I love taking a car to a show and changing the colors.
I love the variety of missions:  sniping, blowing things up, helicopter attacks, and a lot more.  Each mission offers something different.
The modding for this game really adds to the enjoyment.  Gentlemen of Steelport and Sandbox + are a must.  I'm currently playing using a save-game mod that allows me to keep all progress from the previous game, but simply resets all the missions.  It's like playing with cheats but without actually having cheats enabled (and without the corresponding block on auto-saves).  NOTE*  I only play single-player.  I'd never use these in coop.
The game is funny.  There are so many "serious" and "dramatic" games, and I really love the fact that there is a game that knows how to just be stupid, how to play everything for laughs.
CON:
There are too many copy-pasted stores.  On the down side, I could walk into different stores in SR2 and see different merchandise.  On the plus side, I don't have the problem where I walk into a store only to find that the store I want is across town.  If it's Planet Saints, chances are, it has most of what I need.
SR2 had way more places to go into.
Gangs just hang out on street corners, instead of having actual strongholds.
Pedestrians don't seem to do very much except endlessly walk around the block.
Character and vehicle customization has been reduced from SR2.
Zombies are overdone, and I'm thankful Sandbox lets me turn it off.
The beginning of the game, and a particularly dramatic death, seemed unnecessary, and in particular, Shaundi's reaction to that death, becoming a VERY different ... annoyingly different character as a result, took away some of my enjoyment of the game.  I'll take classic Shaundi, fun Shaundi, over grief-stricken-killjoy Shaundi any day.
OVERALL
Cons aside, this is still one of my favorite games ever.
SR2 had more customization and a more detailed map, but in many ways, SR2 almost seemed to have TOO MUCH space ... there was more to see, and it took longer to get around, but there wasn't necessarily more to do in that space.  SR3 is, by comparison, smaller, but it ultimately comes across as simply more compact and efficient.

I love the immersion of this game. It has some obvious control issues, but is a great learning software.
It's not half as comprehensive as World Geography - Quiz Game by Atom Games on my Android phone, for example why is the Balearic Islands and other locations not on the map in this game? Now I haven't played that much, but I promise that I will!
So yeah it's not as comprehensive when it comes to knowledge about geography, but it still brings unique features to the PC. Like famous monuments and random facts, not to mention the unique way of interacting with the map that you can't on smartphone.
My major concern about this game is definitely the controls. There's too little customization. Too much mouse acceleration so you go too far from where you wanna go, and the scroll wheel doesn't work that effectively. You have to scroll like 3 clicks before it starts zooming in on the map.
It really needs a function so that we can learn from our mistakes. That's one of the most important things when learning, learn by your mistakes. We should be able to answer our wrong answers correctly at the the end of a quiz so that the next time we get the same question we know the answer instead of just being wrong answer. (yes I know it says the correct answer exactly when you press wrong answer, but that way you didn't choose the correct answer yourself and maybe you even missed it becuase it's fast)
I really don't like the "Learning Mode". Of course there should be a learning mode, but it's just really poorly executed. The best way of learning is by multiple choice questions and being informed of the right answer if you are wrong, not to click random countries.
There's too many easy questions on Hard mode. Like Q: Where is Cook Islands? A: Oceania. And I don't like that there's a time limit on the MCQ. Sure there should be time to calculate your score, but there's not much room for improvements when there's a time limit.

GEO Master is a game available for PC and Mac (through Steam and iTunes for the Mac version) and on mobiles/tablets under iOS and Android. The goal is to get a maximum of points by answering right at geography questions such as "what is the capital of this country" or "where is this country", etc.. Many applications exist - though this is one of the few you can find on Steam - but this one is efficient, simple and sober AND ice on the cake: it's in French too!
There are several modes (with choice of difficulty) based on a 3D globe:
As you can see, GEO Master is quite varied in terms of modes. If UNESCO challenge isn't prepared at all as the practice or the free mode are just about the countries, the rest is quite easy (well, if your memory is good). However, be warned as GEO Master isn't following any political move and is probably following something official written somewhere: Crimea is part of Ukraine - if you followed the Ukraine-Russia actuality, you know that Crimea asked to be part of Russia and is considered as such by Russia while many other countries don't recognize that - and you can find Western Sahara and Palestinians are represented. And you will be surprised to see that GEO Master is precise when it comes to many little islands in the Pacific or the Carrabeans.
I have a little problem with the game however: some mistakes can be found for the population. Indeed, Belgium is said to have 10 millions of persons when the last census is indicating 11 millions. I'll confess that living in the country that may be concerned is also an asset to sight that kind of stuff.
Anyway, the more you score, the more you're climbing in the leaderboards and leveling up. That's another little push to play the game for those liking that kind of gameplay.
Graphically, GEO Master is very good. You can even see the Moon turning around the Earth. However, I'll suspect that for aesthetics reasons, the Sun is turning around the Earth when it's the contrary in the reality. Three views are possible: satellite, flat map with somber water and flat map with clear water - which is my favorite view. The music is very relaxing and nice.
I managed to crash the game, though I'm not the only one to have the problem in the quizz mode. I don't know if it was a matter of being too speed or if I was nearing the end. Anyway, there is a bug making you stay on the same country with a question without any tie to it.
In other words, GEO Master is a good little geography game, with many possibilities (even if you can imagine something going further), for every age. Even the price of 3 bucks is very interesting. Anyway, if you want some educational game, go ahead, it's in English and for the French talkings, it's in French too!

it certainly is the most realistic fishing game as far as mechanics go. Lure/bait selection and presentation are key to having success in this game. I only have a few criticisms.
1) It's freemium, so while you certainly can fish, level up, and acquire new gear without forking out a dime, the progress is slow and the gear costs make no damn sense (why plastic bubble bobbers are the most expensive type in the game and require the highest level is beyond me, the things literally cost less than a dollar in real life). You're gonna be stuck with flimsy rods and low pound test for awhile until you build up some cash. I recognize that fishing is expensive, but if I'm going to be relegated to ultralight and light tackle for the first few levels, then rods, reels, and tackle shouldn't cost as much as a license and a fishing trip.
2) Object scaling. Fish show up as tiny little things in the water until you yank them out from 2 feet away and then suddenly they're full size. Floats stay the same size (though you can change the size from small, medium, large in options) no matter where they are on the water so good luck with spatial awareness, and lures on the end of your line might as well not even exist because you can't see them while you're waiting to cast or while retrieving (even in the clearest water).
3) Details. I crack up every time I see the shadow of my fisherman walking along trails, the sun at his back casting a long shadow through the woods.... and he's got no arms. Then he approaches the waters edge and the casting arm and its shadow suddenly materialize. Little details make or break great games.
4)Controller support. You can use a controller with this game, but there's no touch sensitivity to speak of. Tap the trigger to twitch the rod and your line goes flailing around as if you've just tried to set the hook on a lunker bass. Trying to aim can be a bit spastic, as your rod goes darting all over the place with no fine movement control.
The free lake is nice, I've already managed to hook some respectable bass and unlock a few in game achievements. For it's flaws it's still relaxing and realistic enough to pass as a great fishing game, but then I feel like the fishing genre never really evolved past the old Bassmaster games of the late 90's....

My history with the lego games stems back the first Star Wars ones. While I still nostalgicly hold those first two as my favorites, Lego Jurassic World has been my favorite once since. I had previously given up on the series after the first harry potter and batman games fell flat for me, but I am glad I came back. I can't say for certain how many of the mechanics are new to the series since this is the forst I've played to have a hub world. However I can affirm that there is a good deal of variety to the gameplay with each movie introducing different character powers along the way. The game does a good job parodying the source material, but I find myself torn between missing the charm of the mimed cutscenes the previous titles had and understanding that dialogue is what made many of the scenes in Jurassic Park so iconic. Overall, if you like the Lego games and the Jurassic Park series this is a solid purchase. If you have never played a Lego game I highly recommend starting with Star Wars because it has so many iconic characters and the most effective humor of the title I've played in the series. Also it won't seem as clunky versus going back to it after playing the more recent titles.

When they first announced this game, I was hyped to the limit, I mean two of my favourite things are coming together! Jurassic Park and Lego how epic can this be?
Well let's just say, that it's brilliant, it's easily become my 2nd  favourite Lego game of all time (JUST behind Lego Worlds) and my 2nd favourite Jurassic Park game of all time (Which is Jurassic Park Operation Genesis) *WARNING* This review contains spoilers for all 4 movies and the game!
Pros:
VERY faithful to the movies, I mean every scene is recreated (except for one but I'll go after that later) and it's so much fun to run around the islands and story mode.
The Hub worlds are brilliant, they are massive compared to all the other Lego games, and they are so big that they added teleports so you can get around faster! Plus there's a lot to do in the Hub worlds like solve puzzles with characters that you unlock in the story!
Nearly all the characters have a purpose! One of my main complaints in previous Lego games is that some characters feel like they have no use at all, I mean for an example in Lego Star Wars 2 you get R2-D2 and C-3PO who unlock special doors for certain areas, C-3PO cannot attack while R2-D2 can attack enemies and hover for a short while, HOWEVER as soon as you get either 2 characters called IG-88 and 4-LOM, they can access BOTH doors that R2 and C-3 can both use, plus attack and throw bombs, thus making R2 and C-3 useless. Here in Lego Jurassic World however, everyone has a purpose and nobody becomes useless as the game progresses. However Mr DNA and Pachycephalosaurus are kinda OP since Mr DNA makes some characters useless like John Hammond, and Pachycephalosaurus makes Triceratops useless since you can play her anytime you want and jump, while you can play as a baby Triceratops whenever, she can’t jump.
The Dinosaurs are fun to control and finding the ambers which they hide in are fantastic, Minikits also make a return and are fun to collect! Red Bricks make a return and so do Gold Bricks and trust me when I say, all are very addicting to collect.
Making your own Hybrid Dinosaurs is a lot of fun, easy and fun to control, however it’s required to get 100% in the game, so I suggest you make a Raptor with a T-Rex head, because in the game there are areas the T-Rex need to destroy some items with her roar, however she cannot fit into those areas, so if you make a custom Raptor with the T-Rex head, you can go in and destroy those objects.
This game tries to fix all the bad 2 and 3 caused! For an example in Jurassic Park 3 the T-Rex was killed by the Spinosaurus, however this time you can change it! The T-Rex now beats the s*** out of Spinosaurus and lives at the end! Another example is in Jurassic Park 2 they made the story interesting! (Seriously 2 in my eyes was just a bad movie, the ending with the T-Rex attacking the city was the only good thing) Plus they make fun of some of the movie's logic, like in Jurassic Park 2 a guy runs away from a snake while in a waterfall... while a T-Rex is waiting for him outside, and when he runs, the T-Rex comes in and looks at the other characters and give that look to say "Did he real do that?" while the others nod.
The biggest pro of this game is it's humour, since this game is more childish then serious, a lot of scary and gory scenes are replaced with very funny scenes, for an example the guy who says "Clever Girl" gets a Banana in his gun and a Raptor wear's a fruit hat! There are so many moments that made me laugh and there's so many of them! I mean I easily took 50 screenshots in my first playthrough, there are too many brilliant moments.
Cons:
Controls are very strange, I mean you don't use the mouse ONCE in your adventure, HJK are all used for Quicktime events, some vehicles use WASD while others use ADJY to drive! WHAT?
Very easy compared to most Lego games, the puzzles were easy and the bosses are easy too.
Buggy in some areas, however these aren't gamebreaking bugs, the worst ones were when you were being chased by Spinosaurus, it's supposed to disappear off-screen chasing a Parasaurolophus, however both get stuck and you end up being chased by nothing, THEN SPINOSAURUS APPEARS OUT OF NOWHERE! The only gamebreaking glitch was with Paul Kirby where he didn't use his hook for some reason, however I fixed it by restarting the level.
Remember when Rambo The Videogame used a crappy DvD to do the voiceacting? Well this game did the same, some scenes sound AWFUL while others aren't as bad, I mean the first line Ellie Sattler says in the first Jurassic Park SOUNDS SO OUT OF PLACE! Jurassic World has new lines in it (I think) however the rest of the flims/chapters use all voiceacting from the actual movies, again some sound decent, some sound good, MOST SOUND BAD!
Minikit rewards could have been better, it's just a skeleton version of the dinosaurs you can already play as, it would be cool if we got some new dinosaurs when we collect them.
Some Dinosaurs are missing, the most noticeable one is Ceratosaurus, however the scene he's in Jurassic Park 3 is gone from this game so that's possibly why. Some other missing dinosaurs are Dryosaurus, Maiasaura and Segisaurus, but even then, nearly all of them that are missing are only mentioned in the movies or hidden in brochures, except for Ceratosaurus of course.
Very weak DLC, no new areas or cool content, most of the content are just reskinned characters and cars that should have been in the game to begin with.
Overall Lego Jurassic World is a brilliant game, and any Jurassic Park fans OR Lego fans must have this game in their collections.

Jurassic Park 1: Brilliant movie, CGI and Models for the dinosaurs still hold up and the acting is brilliant, the story keeps you engaged and so many memorable moments, a must have to see, it’s tied for my favourite Jurassic Park movie.

What a truly numbing, mornonic experience packed as a game.
With Saint's Row The Third you get a very shiny, loud and colorful experience, puffed up with  cheap tricks, tasteless humor and badly written storylines that could make a case study on how not to build a game.
Outdated textures for it's time, the lighting is mediocre and the 3D models are low-poly. The moving animations are clunky and overall it feels like as if the goal wasn't on what's the best they could do but rather on what's the least they could get away with.
It goes like this: a criminal gang is taking over the city from other criminal gangs. Period.  It's not about the nature of crime or about an insight to criminal thinking or anything really that you could call multi-layered.
Another game in a seemingly endless line of games that just can't figure out money. You always have more than you need and by the end of the game your account is represented by a long line of '9''s on your in-game mobile phone. Money in this game feels like a completely random and unnecessary feature.  I personally wouldn't have felt a difference if they had no money in the game at all.
Definitely the most unsatisfying part of the whole game is combat. I can't think of a way how they could have made the shootouts more numb, plain, one-dimensional, emotionless. I couldn't care less about who, where and what I was shooting at, the experience was so zombifying. Nor did I ever have to think about ammo because I always carried a seemingly endless stash. In a fight, I gave up lifting my finger from the trigger, as it just seemed easier and faster to get it over with when I kept shooting aimlessly, pointlessly. I also seemed to have so many guns, one better than the other at killing off hordes of enemies faster than they could spawn. The developers appraently also didn't know what to do with them so they made the UZIs light people on fire and pistols seemed to have an explosion effect that made AI's blast away. I couldn't have cared less if I were using a bazooka or a pistol, they all...killed.
Your whole apartment has a customization menu trigger on it so you'll end up going to the menu quite often when you try to open the door to exit the apartment. And of course the game asks you every time if you want to exit the menu. It's a mess. Considering how customization-heavy the game is, I was surpirsed to see how few cool outfits they  actually had. The game acts as if you've got a lot of customizing options whereas  in reality it's quite poor. And it's all just gimmicks. It matters none what car you drive or if you go into battle fully armored or wearing a bathing suit, it's all the same and feels like they added it because it's trendy, but it ends up as another layer of clutter on top of this already-heavy burden.
Here's where they built the game upside down really. When you build a game you should first define what you want to do and then build the environment and the mechanics accordingly. With Saints Row The Third it feels like they built the world and mechanics first and then tried to fit some missions into it. As a result the missions feel very similar and chained to the limitations of the environment. They lack depth and inspiration. It's as if you were using the built-in assets of the sandbox which weren't designed with any particular mission or story-enhancing element in mind.
Saint's Row 3 had ONE mission, where they actually got it to work. It was a mission where the whole neighbourhood had turned into zombies, thus attacking you on sight and you were on foot. This seemed exactly the right kind of genre this kind of sanbox would have worked with. There you find yourself forsaken and overrun - the right kind of tight spot that get's the immersion going.

LEGOs and dinosaurs: somehow it's taken well over three decades for those two great childhood pastimes to join together in an interactive on-screen adventure. Life finds a way, however, and the two elements are together in a package that may not be the best LEGO-branded adventure, but one that still brings enough to entertain over the course of four fast-but-fun campaigns. The format of this puzzle-focused adventure is as old as dinosaurs -- developer TT Games has used this formula more than 20 times since 2005’s LEGO Star Wars -- but like the pre-historic creatures themselves, there's still a ton of charm.
Anything in the world that's made out of LEGO bricks that isn't one of the 100-plus playable characters can be broken into studs to be spent on bonuses or rebuilt within the environment to progress further in the world. Anyone who's uttered a line in a Jurassic Park movie can be unlocked eventually, from Ian Malcolm and that annoying kid at the raptor dig site to the dino-wrangling, motorbike-riding Owen Grady and, awesomely, Mr. DNA himself. Unlike most LEGO adventures where characters have distinct weapons or superpowers, LEGO Jurassic World's suite of skills are a little more subdued; paleontologists can dig, zoologists aren't afraid to dive into piles of dino-dung, and hunters can set off targets from afar. It's mostly well balanced, though it's weird to see the meek husband-and-wife couple who funded Jurassic Park III's expedition using a grappling hook and gymnastic moves. Also, why are the only characters with scream-based powers women? There’s been plenty of screaming men in Jurassic Park films.
Another distinguishing feature is that LEGO Jurassic World leans far less on combat than most of the previous LEGO-licensed adventures, which makes sense: the movies are mostly about humans trying to avoid dinosaurs. That makes the few fights actually meaningful -- whether it's a throwdown between rival camps in Lost World or the brutal T-rex vs spinosaurus battle in Jurassic Park III, almost every fight has some dramatic flair... unless there are compys involved. Even though the diminutive dinos only appear in the third Jurassic Park film (Edit: oops, the second one too), the species is in every chapter of LEGO Jurassic World, and they never get any less frustrating. They'll swarm in packs, immediately requiring your full attention due to their overpowered health-sapping skills, and their size and speed make them tough to hit. Sometimes there's just one pack nearby, sometimes there's two, and sometimes there's an infinite supply that won't stop attacking you until you cover up the source of the stream. Frankly, I would have just rather had a compy-free experience, since the species makes any stage it infects just a bit less enjoyable than the puzzle-solving, block-breaking norm.
LEGO Jurassic World is an all-inclusive series package, and each of the four movies is broken up into five lightning-fast stages that run two to three segments each. In the space of 30 minutes, I went from saving Lex and Tim to traversing a tree to reach a crashed jeep, to throwing flares in a T-rex's mouth during a tense car chase. Any time I started to get antsy or annoyed about a certain story or set of characters, I knew something I enjoyed would be around the corner. Sure, the gymnastic escape scene at the end of Lost World might have been a bit disappointing, but I was just one level away from seeing Academy Award nominee William H. Macy in LEGO form!
Ironically, the enjoyment I had with the people and creatures of LEGO Jurassic World didn't quite extend to the actual parks. Sure, the levels were mostly a joy, but the overworld is a bit of a mess, especially when I had to explore the islands to find the entrance to a new level. Another weird quirk; while you can play the original Jurassic Park and the newly released Jurassic World right from the start, The Lost World and Jurassic Park III can only be played after completion of the preceding movie's adaption. Fast travel is also iffy, as most of the icons on the map automatically load objectives. Since I wanted to explore the area to find new stages, I'd have to scan each icon until I found the one connected to each section's kiosk, which became so tedious that I'd usually just walk through the interconnected movie hubs to get to my destination. Much like a real theme park, you'll have fun on the attractions but dread getting there.
Jurassic World Video Review
What keeps the compy troubles and overworld woes from becoming too unbearable? That patented LEGO charm. For the first three movies, voice clips are used sparingly and sight gags help add some spice to what should be a line-by-line retellings. Instead of the cowardly investor getting eaten alive on a porta-potty, he stays in the T-Rex's mouth for a few scenes, cleaning the creature's chompers with a toilet brush. When dinosaurs need medical attention they require candy bars and ice pops instead of a tense scene of humans operating on puppets. Also, there's a bit more story being told directly in Jurassic World, so be forewarned that many of the movie's twists will be revealed along the way.
The Verdict
If you have an affinity for any of the four films recapped within, LEGO Jurassic World will be a worthwhile visit. Seeing the series' iconic moments recreated with cute figurines is a treat, and each of the four campaigns is fast-paced enough that completing the entire franchise in its brick-based form will only take roughly seven to eight hours, which is not much longer than the combined film running times (and amounts to brisk mini-campaigns of two hours or less each). Plus, you can tackle this one with a friend and run around as a raptor or Jeff Goldblum. Just beware that there are a few pests inhabiting the island and the line to the best parts of the park may be a bit tough to navigate.

While this game has good aethetics and does capture the feel of old school games it has two flaws that ultimately make it unejoyable.
1) Losing money every time you die. In a game where you need to purchase nearly every upgrade and the only way to get money is through playing the levels this means that you have to grind the lower levels if you want any upgrades because the only money you won't lose on later levels comes from beating the boss.
If the red armour prevented you losing all your money on death then this flaw would be bearable. Unfortunately it only halves the penalty.
2) Having to buy upgrades in levels. This problems is bad design if not outright trolling by the creators. On several levels you can find chests containing salesmen who will sell you a useful item for money. If you don't have enough money because you kept dying and all the money flew into difficult to get places then you won't be able to buy the upgrades. This means you cannot complete certain extra parts of the level and the level itself is more difficult. As a result good player get an easier level, bad player get a harder one. Why did anyone think this would be a good idea?
If you could find these items for free in the levels and buy them if you missed them this would solve this problem. At present if you don't have a lot of money exploration is pointless.

Resident Evil 5 has the same elements that we have seen in Resident Evil 4, but (obviously) changes were made. I'll just mention some positives, and in later paragraphs will tell what is fundementally wrong in this game.
+ If you loved RE4 gameplay, you probably like this to some extent.
+ There are more melee takedowns and you can stomp fallen enemies.
+ Graphics and animations are really good for 2009 game, and still look decent nowadays.
+ Them cinematic camera angles
+ Finding treasure and looting is always fun.
+ Boss fights here are cool, I guess...
+ Controls (PC) aren't bad in my opinion.
+
is exactly the type of villain Resident Evil needs. Probably the only character I liked in RE5
+ If you have a friend who owns RE5, absolutely play with that friend, because soon I'll explain why you have to do it.
+ A few good music tracks.
There probably are more positive things to say, but who likes positivity when it comes to this game? Negativity and complains are always fun to give. So, here we go. But first, a quick recap of RE4.
Resident Evil 4 is considered a modern classic and some people say that it's the best Resident Evil game. It completely changed Resident Evil into an action game while still having some familiar aspects. RE4 isn't flawless, but it had an amazing gunplay, good atmosphere, cheesy but fun story (didn't take itself too seriously), best video game merchant and probably has one of the only fun escort sections (Somehow Ashley didn't annoy me, except maybe screaming Leon all the time) I've ever seen in a video game. And, somehow Resident Evil 4 also has pretty interesting characters. I think almost all of them were great, despite the bad writing, but I think RE4 writing is pretty much B-movie styled game, in a good way.
It's hard to tell if Capcom got the results by pure luck or they just really had amazing talent there.
It's obvious that Capcom wanted to make a sequel and continue the now action heavy Resident Evil series. Though they thought that it was somehow a good idea to throw an AI bot to single player campaign if you don't have a co-op partner in your lobby. What I've heard is that Capcom wanted to add a co-op feature because it was trendy in that time and apparently people got mad because game takes place in Africa and a white dude shoots africans in Africa. To calm people down, Capcom added a black character called Sheva who acts as an secondary playable character if you join a lobby, but without a player, Sheva is AI controlled.
I don't know the real reason why they did this, but the AI is just AWFUL!!! Combined with confusing and weird inventory system, it's a complete chaos when playing RE5. Most of my deaths were due to Sheva making horrible mistakes and overall being a complete idiot:
- Getting stuck somewhere
- Not using proper weapons when dealing with large crowd, unless you tell her
- Using a uncombined green herb to major wounds without my consent, when I wanted to use a better health spray.
- Doesn't use her weapons properly and just wastes ammo. Resident Evil is about tactical shooting and conserving ammo to right situations, but it's almost impossible with AI being my "partner"
- Gives you the wrong ammo stack while keeping two incomplete stacks in her inventory without combining them (filling up two inventory slots....) and sometimes just gives you something when you were specfically trying to get rid off something to make inventory space and you cannot do what you originally wanted. And other times, Sheva just automatically gave the ammo back when I wanted her to keep it for a short time until I sort out my inventory.
- Not shooting when a weak spot is revealed
In one boss fight, I had to constantly command attack and cover in order to make Sheva use flamethrower at the correct time because no matter what, she always try to attack the boss unless keep shouting come on like an idiot. NEVER MAKE A BOSS FIGHT THAT IS TOO RELIANT ON AI SUPPORT!!!
And why the ♥♥♥♥ I have to spend the money on Sheva's equipment (Treasure is doubled ans split to two players but on single player you only get one), why not give the same amount of money as co-op, but instead give it all to me, so I can do the strategic upgrading myself.
Just get a friend to play RE5, and most of the issues will be fixed by doing that.
And, the inventory is the worst I ever seen in any game.
- You cannot give specific amount of ammo (in numbers), only stacks or something, I still don't know how it works
- Health spray takes the same amount of space as one weapon.
- You cannot take the item and immediately combine it if you have the full inventory as you could in RE4
- You can stack granades to five, but you cannot stack if they are different types
- YOU CANNOT GIVE WEAPONS TO OTHER PLAYERS!!! (for AI partner, yes but you have to do it in lobby)
And....there are some other problems like:
- Boring story that takes itself too seriously
- Boring and bland characters (except

- No horror elements nor creepy atmosphere (if so, it failed horribly)
- Annoying and clunky cover mechanic when dudes with guns were introduced

One of the older Total War games, this classic is still fun to play. An enjoyable blend of RTS and turn-based strategy. You start out as one of three Roman families, and proceed to conquer the known world. The world map is turn-based. On your turn you can march your armies, train more soldiers, hire mercenaries, and send out your agents to do your bidding. You can have your diplomats trade and ally with other nations, send spies to find their weaknesses, or send assassins to remove their generals and kings (or do all three!). When your army encounters an enemy army or beseiges a city, you can fight in real-time. Soldiers move in squadrons across the battlefield, flanking and being flanked in turn, breaking when morale is low, or staying to fight when the general rallies them. As you defeat nations, they are unlocked for you to play. Parthia, Britannia, and Carthage are three of them.
There are several issues with the game. Diplomacy can be rather frustrating, with enemies refusing to make peace, or demanding you become a protectorate when you are crushing them into the dust. Anachronisms abound (the entire Egyptian roster, for example). Graphics are dated, though the map view is still pretty.
Overall, though, the game is fun, and longevity is added through mods. Some like Europa Barbarorum overhaul all the races, removing anachronisms; others like Lord of the Rings change the game from the Mediterranean to Middle-earth. In the end, if you have not played it, or you enjoy history and can't get Rome II Total War to run on your computer, this is a good classic to have.
