tl;dr Absolute Drift is a lovely little game.
Controls are smooth enough to be played on any type of controller (All of my personal bests are on a keyboard, which is normally impossible to use for car games).
The points system works pretty well, although I find it has trouble if you're sliding without countersteer and/or sliding with a sharp angle.  It can also be hard to maintain a combo if you stop drifting and start drifting shortly after.
Decent car selection.  Not too many, not too few.  The cars all have a unique feel to them, and I often find myself switching cars to better take on a course.
The maps are nice.  The simplistic art style helps you really get into the zone without a bunch of distractions.  Some spots with bad clipping here and there, but you get used to them.
Admittedly, you lose interest after a while.  After beating the campaign and getting Top 8 on all of the midnight tracks, I don't have much motivation to play now.  I come on every now and then to make sure I'm still in Top 8 and try my hand at some of the mountain courses, but that's about it.  However, that doesn't at all lessen the amount of fun and joy I felt playing this game and really trying to push myself.
Overall 9/10, great game, would inertia dorifto again

So basically, playing a level works like this: You start on #9, boost yourself to #1 and switch to your car on another track which is still on #9 and like half the track behind the enemies. You boost yourself to #1 and switch back to your first car because it's back on #8 again. Sometimes you even have 3 or 4 tracks, so you basically spend the time watching your cars fall back to the last place, trying to save them somehow and hoping to get a good result.
Of course, you could say that it's the point of the game, having to deal with a bad autopilot and struggle to get a good result. The problem is: There's no skill curve. The game is solely based on luck. Sometimes you drive like a pro and only get a bronze medal because the AI ♥♥♥♥s up too much. Sometimes you drive like♥♥♥♥♥♥and you earn a gold medal because you're lucky with the AI.
A racing game purely based on luck instead of skill? No, thanks.
Maybe D!D!D! could still be enjoyable, but there are many flaws.
For instance, you can unlock cars with different stats. They are being displayed with like 30 stripes. You can't really count them and when you switch the car, you get to see an animation where all stats start at zero and count up to match the values of the car. Looks quite cool, but makes it impossible to compare the cars. As your opponents always have the same car as you, unlocking new cars loses its purpose anyway.
The GUI is terrible. The menu is always somewhere else. You enter the pause menu, it's in the middle of the screen. You end a race, the buttons are shown in the bottom right-hand corner whereas the menu is in the top left-hand corner. You NEVER look at this corner, except when the race ends. Let me tell you what, that's crap UI design. After half an hour you slowly get used to looking there, but it still feels extremly awkward.
Keyboard controls aren't remappable. The "reset" key (R) doesn't even work. Which is especially fun when you want to earn a gold medal and switch to another track only to find out that your car is heading into the wrong direction. At this point you basically lost the race already and have to restart via the pause menu because there's no way to reverse the direction of the car before the race ends. And this happens a lot. According to another review the "reset" key works, so the devs probably just forgot to implement it in the keyboard controls. Which makes this game just another case of "Devs want to sell a PC game but are too lazy to actually implement PC controls because they always have their controller plugged in." Guess what, I don't and I don't see a point in plugging my controller in for a little arcade racing game that works well with a keyboard.
If you're still interested in the game, wait for a sale. Buy it for less than 5€ or even grab it in a bundle for a dollar like I did. Definitely don't give the devs 20€ (!!!) for selling a lackadaisical arcade racing game that revolves around their lack of AI coding skills.

Drive!Drive!Drive! is a 'racing game unlike any other', the store page proudly proclaims. They're right; no other racing game will 'Drive' you insane quite like this one.
The basic idea is easy enough to understand: Try racing multiple Hot Wheels-like tracks at once, obviously driving one car at a time and switching to another lane when that car falls behind or when you need to collect crystals in the Collection events.
The problems start to add up once you realize that Drive!Drive!Drive! is constantly working against you, and I don't just mean because of the 'Intelligent Stupidity' engine. (Again, the store page's words, not mine.) When you're racing on one lane, your cars on the other lanes will slow down deliberately to create some sort of difficulty. The idea is that you switch when you see a car fall behind and race to catch back up.
Where this idea falls apart is more often than not, you'll switch to find your car stuck on another lane it's not supposed to be on, or stuck in a corner not going anywhere other than the inside of the corner it's smashing into, or just plain getting sabotaged by the other AI cars. There is a Reset Car button, but this honestly feels like a cop-out feature to me, like in playtesting these issues came up and they just said "Oh, well if they can reset whenever it's not a problem as long as we put them in front of the obstacle a little bit, right?" Well, that sometimes doesn't work right and you'll respawn only to immediately fall off course again. In one case, I just fell through the road entirely upon respawning, so that's fun.
Guess what else is broken in this game? The physics, the one thing an arcade racing game needs to get mostly right if not 100% right, and this game's physics are all sorts of wrong. Go airborne, land on your wheels, and sometimes you'll just dead stop. Yep, makes sense to me.
Try spinning another racer with your car or truck, like you'll have to do if you want to win the Arcade events, and get ready to fly into a tailspin yourself and most likely fly off course. I can't think of a single other arcade racing game where touching another car, even slightly, can completely ruin an entire race. It's just bad design, period.
Speaking of Arcade events, winning on all lanes in an Arcade event isn't even close to achieving BRONZE. You know what counts the most? Smashes. So your best bet is to pick a big truck and smash the other racers instead of trying to win. I don't know, that doesn't sound like a racing game to me. Fortunately, once you figure out how to get Bronze in the Arcade events (and GOOD LUCK getting above that, you're gonna need it, even on Normal difficulty), the other game modes are just as easy to achieve Bronze. That's all you need to do to progress in the main campaign, which is great because of how luck based these events feel at all times. Then you get to the Offensive campaign, realize all of the races there require absolute perfection, and you'll probably do what I did: stop playing entirely and get a refund.
Normally, I don't like the idea of bashing on games like this, because Drive!Drive!Drive! has some interesting ideas going for it, but I had to write this after seeing the positive reviews. As someone that was able to complete F-Zero GX's story mode on Very Hard difficulty, Drive!Drive!Drive! doesn't feel challenging in a fair, rational way. It's like the racing game equivalent of playing blackjack with a card dealer that wants you to lose, so he rigs the deck against you and occasionally punches you in the face.
I honestly feel like this is a racing game for people that hate racing games. When half of your game relies on pure luck against bad physics and insurmountable win conditions to experience
I just can't recommend it to anyone unless I actually hated them with a passion. Instead of this, I recommend playing any of the TrackMania games, probably Nations Forever if I had to pick one. At least that one's free.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers here to share my thoughts on my experience with a unique racing game called Drive!Drive!Drive! By Choice Publishing and Different Cloth. I received a copy of the game from our friends at Choice Publishing but as with all of my reviews, this has no effect on my experience.
Drive!Drive!Drive is a unique racing game that takes inspiration from classic games like Wipeout or F-Zero. It uses its own engine called the Intelligent Stupidity Engine. As you might imagine, the game gets pretty crazy due to the other racers being quite dumb. However, the game prides itself in this insanity and it does make the game much more enjoyable.
Although the game utilizes a more minimalist art style with lots of gray and lighter colors it is still quite pretty and the courses are very well designed. You’ll often see giant rocks floating in the sky or  rain/snow effects for the duration of the course. The lighting is also really good as well.
There’re multiple modes for you to choose from including arcade and, my least favorite, collection. The initial campaign has 50 courses over 10 different planets but there is also a bonus campaign that features 50 more courses with increased difficulty along with a level editor to create your own courses to share with other players.
The most unique part of this game is the way you play. Like most racing games you control one vehicle while the (rather stupid) AI controls the other vehicles.  Where this game differs, however, is that you race on multiple courses at once and to complete it, you must switch between the courses using the d-pad to take control of different vehicles. You need to time your switching well to keep your position so there is strategy involved. You can also boost to gain speed and drift around corners during a race as well. There are some courses that don’t have railings to prevent you from driving off the course so you need to be careful on harder courses.
Overall, Drive!Drive!Drive is a game that I’m surprised isn’t more popular considering how fun it is to play and how absurd the game-play is. If you enjoy fast paced racing games or are looking for something new and unique to play in the racing genre I definitely recommend it. The ability to switch between multiple courses is really cool and it’s something that’s really fun to experience.
Thanks a lot for taking the time to watch my videos and read this review folks. If you enjoyed them or found either of them helpful, I would greatly appreciate it if you could share them. Also, be sure to subscribe to my channel for future videos!
Happy gaming folks! - Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) out!

You know, over the past few months I noticed that there is a distinct decline in the number of licensed movie tie-in games. A couple of years ago, any new super hero flick was accompanied with an eponymous game with dreadful playability. I guess publishers learned a thing or two. I also think that Travelers Tales pretty much takes on any job it gets to fill in the void because they're making games of literally everything as long as it is in Lego.
So the trade is simple. No more bad movie games in exchange for Lego? Seems like a dead giveaway. The Lego games are known for their simple and addictive, but family friendly gameplay and presentation. And since they're basically all running on the same engine; easy to churn out like they're Five Nights at Freddy's. For Jurassic World TT quickly assembled a cast from the entire Jurassic Park series, built overworlds and stages and also made a few lego dinosaurs. Everything fits the mold perfectly and it works. In fact, the formula has been perfected to such a degree it becomes hard to really blame it for being completely unoriginal.
The thing that really sells lego games for me is the character roster. Sometimes over 200 characters can be collected; and the batman series and marvel entry did a good job at making it worthwhile to collect these figurines. However, Jurassic World fails to build on this because you want to play with dinosaurs, yet, you're stuck with people. It's a bit of miss. But if you're looking to play the island adventure from 1993 or 2015, you can't really go wrong with the Lego formula.

A game well summarised by a player on its forum:
"GSB is essentially a space-opera fireworks display set to music."
A delightfully entertaining indie strategy game with unique gameplay that makes it hard to pin in any particular genre.  It's definitely not RTS because you don't give any orders during combat.  The strategy of the game lies in deciding what components to fit your ships with (factoring things like cost, weight, armor, power consumption etc.), what ships your fleet will be made up of, how to spatially arrange your ships in the fleet and finally what orders to give them as they are sent to battle.  Then the player sits back and watches the lasser and missile fireworks show unfold.  There's a lot of strategic depth, but nothing by way of clickfest.
The visuals, sound effects and background music are superb.  It even has surround support so you can crank up the bass channel for those lovely explosions. :)  And it's made by a guy who knows how to choose fun over realism.

Overall the game is your typical lego game, smash everything and follow the story line and you will complete it. My main issue is with the loading times. On OSX iMac retina 27 inch computer it can take 2-3 minutes to laod a level and 4-5 minutes to just quit back to the main menu. This is not acceptable and needs to be addressed. Time to team up and face new enemies, as well as old ones, while discovering a new threat in the heart of Africa in Resident Evil 5 (or RE5 for short).
Debuting in RE5, the game introduces co-op gameplay in the main campaign, as well as the side campaigns and the arcade mode Mercenaries. This gives the player the opportunity to play alone or with a friend & this is a great game to play with a friend.
The level setup is not to small which doesn’t interfere with movement or progression. There’s a light amount of puzzles that require both players in specific places or doing specific actions, this is good, considering the fact that some games in the past had too many puzzles of such nature.
Lastly, when I was playing with my friends, the lag was non-existent. Our actions, movements & responses had no noteworthy issues. Though, this could be corrected in case others might have experienced such problems.
A reminder that if you play the main campaign by yourself, you will have an AI partner. Although I have not played the campaign alone, I’ve heard tell of a few bad things over what happens…
When playing single-player, the AI might commit itself to do a few questionable things, such examples include spinning in circles for no reason and wasting ammunition on enemies that are already dead. The ammunition problem is noticeable when playing in the higher difficulty settings and in a franchise where ammunition is hard to come by, this can lead to big problems in terms of proper progression.
RE5 was originally released on the “Games for Windows Live (GFWL for short)” services and to be honest, I’m not a fan of it. The reasons for such is that you already have the game on steam, but you need to use this service in order to play the game and having 2 different services to play one game bothers me. Not only that, but the initial setup for GFWL can take a while.
The game was migrated onto steam about 2 years ago now, so now you don’t need to register to GFWL to play RE5, but the game still requires that you install it before you can play.
Although I made my case that I’m not a fan of GFWL, I have noticed a few discussions & other reviewers saying that they prefer using GFWL because there was little or no bugs as opposed to the steam integration, where a few bugs were reported. Fair enough reason, though I haven’t encountered any bugs since playing RE5 on steam.
GFWL rambling aside, RE5 is an excellent game and it’s a game I’d easily recommend if you want to play a co-op game with a friend. This is a game I don’t think I’ll get tired of. I’ve completed the game twice with one friend and have another run going with another.

Absolute Drift was released way back in the year 2015, which really isn't that long ago when you think about it, also I'm still getting used to saying it's 2017, sometimes.
Anyway, I'd never heard of this game until I picked it up after seeing gameplay of it recently, and honestly, it's a huge shame that I didn't see it earlier, because this game is awesome.
This is the short version, if you want more detail, full review is here:

PROS V CONS
PROS
- Solid soundtrack, not too crazy, but not too calm, creates just the right tone for the laid back nature of the game and such. It seems like it may be quality over quantity however, as I've heard a few repeats that I've noticed in a single 2 hour or so session.
- The free roam level select world is a great idea, allows you to practice the handling freely and get back into it every session.
- Appears to be plenty of content with 5 worlds, each one having quite a lot of levels in each world, plus the game is heavilly focused on replaying levels and getting better scores and better times, self improvement.
- Great visual aesthetic, easy to tell what everything is, and it's incredibly nice to look at.

CONS
- Like I mentioned, I've noticed a few repeating songs on the soundtrack, but I don't really care about this, there's enough that it isn't repetitive.
- Besides super minor things, I honestly can't think of any other big 'cons' or gripes I had with the game, which is good to hear I'd imagine.
SUMMARY
It's an incredibly enjoyable game with a ton of replayable content, to speak to this point, there's a guy on the steam reviews who has 417 hours in this game, jesus.
If you're interested in a game like this, I can't really think of any competition, this game is great, if you're even moderately interested I'd say give it a go, it's only $12.

+ The gameplay is very unique. In each stage there are multiple seperate tracks that all have races going simultaneously. You must switch between cars on each track, and try to advance your position on each one to score enough points at the end. When you switch an AI will control your previous car for you, but obviously won't be as skillful as you.
+ In my opinion, the driving feels very similar to Burnout. You have a boost meter, and to refill your Boost you need to slam into other cars, drift, or make high flying jumps. It is quite enjoyable to slam into a pack of cars and watch them go flying off the track.
+ Very challenging. As you may expect, participating in ~3 races at the same time can be quite difficult and at times frustrating. You get one of your cars to first place, switch to another, and before you know it your first car has fallen behind! Although I found it to be very fun even when not doing very well.
+ Visually the game looks pretty good with a sort of minimalist cyberspace type style. I found it to be pretty interesting to see the polygon geometry of the track

Jurassic World is as one would call 'a load of fun', especially if you're into both LEGO and Dinosaurs. So I'm gonna be pasting my own review of the game.
Firstly, I present to you the good sides to this game.
PROS:
1: The maps are HUGE!! Near-endless possibilities on what you could do and in one case I managed to get a customised Indominus Rex out of a paddock and into the Main Street at Jurassic World, WITHOUT using Compy Mode.
2: You can customise your own dinosaurs!
3: I managed to get the T.Rex at Jurassic World to roar at my customised Dilophosaurus after I got it to spit at the T.Rex (Now THAT made my day that time!)
4: The classic slapstick humour is still there; with one level having Billy from JP3 kicking a Raptor in the butt in the lab, another Raptor in JP1 getting a frying pan 'round the face, and the Indominus playing a poker game with several other characters INSIDE the belly of the Mosasaurus (YES!! You can play as a Mosasaurus!! BOOYAH!!)
5: You can play up to as many as 20 Dinosaurs, from the Compy to the Gallimimus to the Triceratops, to the INSANELY MAHOOSIVE Brachiosaurus and to the T.Rex and mostly my personal favourites the Indominus Rex and the Mosasaurus!!
CONS:
1: The game itself has a load of bugs, some of which end up preventing you from progressing further into the game (This happened to me on my Xbox 360, so I got another copy off of Steam but turned out to be just as bad with the bug emerging in a level beforehand).
2: There was plenty of room for further improvement, and its a shame the producers couldn't add anything more (An example would be having the dinosaurs to have an eating contest, now that would have made up for some of the lack of fun!).
3: The entire game itself was quite short; it took me four whole days to complete LEGO Lord Of The Rings and I still had a load more gold and red bricks to go.
As a whole the game is quite good, but due to the bad glitching and relatively short timespan to complete the game it felt a bit of a disappointment. I'll be waiting for the latest patch updates but I'll still try to enjoy the game to its full potential.
I recommend the game regardless of the problems it has, so cross those fingers of yours and get this game! I guarantee you will NOT be disappointed!!

Amnesia was one of the best experiences I have ever had in PC gaming.  From beginning to end, Amnesia will grip you in an atmosphere of uneasiness, terror, and excitment.  Amnesia is one of the most mechanically simple games ever made, yet its execution is flawless.  The simple mechanic of having to hide from a shambling monster in a dark room is horrifically thrilling. This game is not limited to its horror - which ranges from simple moments of unsettling visual horror like distorted portraits and dimly lit dungeons, to the sheer terror of a disfigured monster chasing you through castle hallways.  Amnesia is centered around the gradual unraveling of a sinister plot, that while disorienting at first, expands into a story of betrayal, vengeance, morality, and redemption.

The game features an array of events in the campaign mode with different victory conditions (position-only, points-based, object collection, and time trial). Progressing through the campaign unlocks new cars with slightly different stats. In addition, there is online multiplayer and the ability to create custom layouts and share them with others. The crux of the gameplay is managing several different one-lap races on mirrored tracks simultaneously. Because the AI drivers are terrible, you must switch between races to keep all of your drivers up from in each race. Controls are typical for an arcade racing game, with boost gained from drifting, jumping, and smashing other vehicles; the game is designed for a gamepad (there is no mouse support whatsoever, even for menus). The novel concept of Drive!Drive!Drive! is enough to make it stand out as an arcade racing title.

Yesterday I was talking to my girlfriend about the time when someone decided to make a small documentary and make the world aware that the Galvão birds were in the verge of extinction. Any Brazilian knew from the first second it was a hoax, a prank to turn offenses against a soccer commentator into a trending topic on Twitter. The truth eventually came out, but one question still remains: why would anyone spend a lot of time to make a professional documentary for no other reason than fooling people with an innocent joke? And why does it sound so reasonable for any Brazilian to do so?
The answer is: zuêra (aka zoeira).
Thing is, it's impossible to translate "zuêra" properly. But after you play this hilarious game, keeping in mind that it's based on the adventures of a cartoon character that was shown on public TV for no money at all and was made by the same guy who's now basically giving this game away for free just so that you and me can have a good laugh, maybe you'll begin to understand what it means. A domestic dog blowing fire is zuêra; references to "forte gomba" are zuêra; a random appearence of Frankenstein is zuêra; flying giant babys are zuêra. And so it goes.
If you still don't get it, your last shot would be paying a visit to Brazil. Make sure you have Internet access and, most important, someone to guide you among the huge waves of zuêra.

This game is just stellar.
It takes what's familiar about Portal 2 and increases the challenge by utilising the game's mechanics in new ways. You'll end up considering cube respawns, location and timing among other things. It's a lovely way of extending your thinking outside of what you already know from the official games. The inclusion of an Advanced Mode further pushes your thinking by adding new obstacles to the same puzzles and removing too helpful elements, changing the solutions significantly.
The story is well written and executed, so much so that I'd like to consider it canon to the games. The voice acting is good all around, though my personal minor nitpick is Cave Johnson's occasional slurping and excessive throat clearing. You can hear the voice actor really flexing his throat to pull off the impression. Overall it doesn't take from the game's quality if you pay it no heed.
Far as design and gameplay goes, this Portal mod is a 10/10 in my book and I truly recommend Portal fans to give it a spin.

A very, very well designed 'mod' for Portal 2, which comprises an entirely new campign set neatly between the events of Portal and Portal 2. The chambers are extremely well designed, and are more difficult than you expect from Portal campaigns, but not so difficult as to be distracting from a compelling story. The only elements that let down this mod were the music, and the character Virgil. The first voice we hear in the game is a young Cave Johnson, It is no small feat to stand in the shadow of J.K Simmons, but the voice actor does a fantastic job emulating a young Cave. The voice of AEGIS is also on point. However the majority of the game is carried by the character of Virgil, for all intents and purposes a more likeable and less insane Wheatley. His voice actor however is a generic scandinavian man, whose amateurish delivery of cringeworthy and poorly written dialogue (or i suppose monologue given our silent protagonist), manages to ruin an otherwise perfect experience. I am aware this is a fan made mod, i am aware the 'studio' involved was unable to hire actual voice actors and pay them to be involved, however given the other great voices i simply cannot understand why they would choose such a generic, uncharacterful voice for the single most heard character in the game. My second criticism comes under Music. For a game set before Portal 2, starring a silent Olympian from the 1950s, the bizarre and often distracting soundtrack was a poor choice.
I would still recommend Portal Stories: Mel, it is a solid mod that obviously took a huge amount of work, the voice acting and music are a dissapointment, but i would still give it a 8/10, carried largely by fantastic level design and animation.

One of the least consistent and worst games I've ever had the displeasure of playing.
The devs seem cool and all, and there's not dev fishery going around, but this game is terrible. I've tried using a mouse and keyboard, I've tried a PS4 controller, an XBox One controller, and a Steam controller, on all difficulties. This game is just not consistent, and not even remotely accurate to real life handling. I understand it's an arcade game and it's not meant to be realistic, but there has to be SOME real world similarity in a game geared towards car/drift enthusiasts.
Even besides that, the scoring system is just awful. I can watch replays of everyone around my score and see some people are doing it flawlessly, and some people are just plain lucky. There are times when you are at a 90 degree angle drifting perfectly, and your combo will end and it won't detect you're drifting at all. At the same time, I find myself gaining massive combo score while going at like 10 degrees and not even trying to drift. When you crash into a wall, your combo resets, and that's normal.
However, it's absolutely inconsistent as well. I can crash head first and lose all my speed and my drift, and my combo will continue to rise, but I can just scrape a wall with the side, or my rear panels/bumper (something people TRY to do in real life, by the way) and my combo will end.
TL;DR: Game is terrible. Scoring is horribly designed, doesn't always recognize your drifts (IN A GAME THAT IS ABOUT DRIFTING) and racking up points is just down to luck unless you spend hundreds of hours learning this game. Would not recommend

This is a top down game about drifting.
It has simplistic graphics with a touch of color here and there that works perfectly for this type of game.
In free roam you have to complete challenges within the specific world in order to gain access to the next. There are 5 worlds in total which are pretty easy and don't take all that long to complete.
The real challenge lies in the events mode which you can access through free roam but they are all scattered around the different worlds so it makes more sense to just do them from the events button in the main menu instead.
The skill progression is pretty hard to begin with when doing some challenges like drifting close to poles but after a few hours practice it becomes second nature.
The Dark Souls Boss of this game is the "Complete 2 perfect lines" challenge. It took me 2 hours just to complete 2 challenges with this in it. The thing is you only get 1 chance to do it right and you need to drift at a perfect speed and angle. Many many times I completed the first one and just couldn't do the second because I didn't know the right angle, had too much or not enough speed, over drifted or just fell OF THE EDGE. Everything else in the game is pie compared to this.
There are a few different types of cars you unlock which seems to all have slightly different speeds & amounts of drift as well as some different paints & designs.
It can become a little repetitive when doing all the events because they are pretty much all the same type of thing on a different map design but it’s generally a fun and relaxed game to just chill and then almost break your keyboard when you spend an hour straight trying to do the 2nd perfect line!

Despite what the store page may say, Experience does not include a story. There's not exactly anything that shows the character is a scientific experiment, unless being able to spin your arm 360 degrees counts. You do go around killing threats, but not so much aimlessly after a while as you have to know the area to proceed. It would have been appreciated if the player could see the character escaping from a lab-like area, instead of only explaining it on the store page.
There are twenty available levels in Experience, the area changing every five levels and recycled objectives. The first level is the only different one as it does not have any objective, but is somewhat a tutorial. However, it is confusing. There are numbers on screens throughout the whole level, with seemingly no meaning behind them. It also doesn't put you on a direct path, so you can accidently fall off. The first level does teach you how to move and jump, but not everything as you find out later. The other levels include either defeating a certain amount of enemies, running away from a wall of enemies, finding the exit in the dark, and finally defeating the boss. Rinse and repeat, changing some positions here and there, and you have Experience. It would be helpful if there were health pickups you can collect throughout the whole level rather than having to have an ability. There are some instances where you can't help from being damaged due to dangerous objects being placed too low compared to your jump height, or enemies being placed in the way. Maybe if this didn't seem such as a routine, this would be seen in a different light. As other games similar to this has different level layouts and areas, with an assumed objective. The wall of enemies levels are specifically familiar, but it comes far and few between in other games. Being able to compare what Experience does to other games, it is easy to tell Experience did not use this as well as others.
Experience somewhat has a puzzle aspect as well, but it does not come off as that most of the time. It just dead ends, forced dark areas, or areas you can't get out of. It seems like bad level design, as you can't get some enemies or objects if you past the area containing them. Though it does make sense in the wall of enemies levels, as you are supposed to think fast, but not in a way Experience does. These dead ends makes it the game's fault, instead of the player, that they died. As in situations where you only have to kill enemies or find objects, it doesn't matter that you have to remember the level through deaths.
In each level, you can collect these gems, named Cristales, that comes from destroying a certain object littering each level and enemies. From this you can go to the shop to buy guns, gun upgrades, and passive and activated abilities. Though confusion also plagues this area. You can't buy a different gun unless you click a gun slot so a green line follows your cursor. The gun upgrades also have an unknown effect, as it doesn't seem it upgrades anything other than the look of the gun. Each gun does seem to have their own type of bullets, with it's own shot speed. The passive and activated abilities do not show up until you buy them, as they are hidden in the shop. I only happened to click on one of the empty boxes, buying it and showing the ability. It seems it was supposed to tell you, as it has "bought" under the description, but as it is, it is not an effective way. You have to either buy all of the abilities or pick one at random for an ability that is useful to you.
However, with the default language being Russian, it is almost impossible to know what the objective is. Even when changing the settings, it reverts back to the default after exiting. There is a work around by going into the game's save document, but no one will know to do that unless they happen to find it in the game's discussion boards. For the most part, you can guess what the objective is, such as a counter going down or the wall of enemies being able to kill you on the spot, but not on others.
There are a few bugs throughout Experience. Level five is accessible before completing level four, so you can not progress even if you beat level five during this time. You can also fall down to what would be your death, but soon turns out to not be. You are stuck walking around the bottom of the level till you exit out of it as your health wasn't fully depleted as it should of been.
I do see how Experience could have been a good game, but it feels it doesn't use this type of game design to its advantage.
Each set of levels has their own background sound, almost sounding like a remix of a one song. The boss music seems to be the same for each, but it is interesting how the rhythm of their bullets sounds differ. Almost giving each different boss characteristics. Guns also have different sound effects, but it is put back enough that it isn't annoying.
Experience has a pixelated art style, though nothing much catches the eye except the bullets and bosses. The regular enemies and objects usually do not, as most use the same basic design throughout each set of levels. The bosses, which happen to be my favorite visuals, have a unique design from others and easily dominates the screen. The bullets are bright enough to notice, but not too much that it blinds.
Most of the environments are fine, having a good mix of light and dark, but one happens to be too bright. It seems to be a snow level, but everything is white and blends together. Each enemy and platform seemed to be autofilled white, instead of creating a snow-like surface.
With the pixelated art style, Experience ran pretty smoothly. There were little peaks here and there when too many bullets were on screen due to being able to ricochet or stay on the enemy.
+ Good if you want a cheap game to play for a while
+/- No replay option when you die (instead of having to go back to level select every time)
+/- No health pickups in levels unless you have the healing ability
- Changing settings does not take effect
- Can not understand the game unless you happen to find the discussion thread showing you how to change the language
- Some instances you have to get hurt due to the jump height
- Puzzle aspect is frustrating, as it doesn't fit most of the time and makes it the game's fault you died
Experience is surely an experience when you play it, as it shows what could go wrong in designing a multi-level game. Is Experience worth buying? No, it is a very frustrating game that many probably didn't get past the first few levels. I do not recommend Experience. However, it is a good learning experience if you happen to aspire being a game developer.

Desmond's journey continues as he further relives life of his ancestor an assassin Ezio Auditore da Firenze. The story pick up right where 2nd game ended and Ezio now must find a way to stop the opposing force once again. Ezio is driven away from his home Monteriggioni vila, and travels to the Rome to stop the Templars. When he infiltrates Rome he quickly finds himself in difficult possition as the assassin brotherhood is weakened and the usual suspects refuse to help him. Ezio regains influence for assassins, rebuilds weakened assassin brotherhood and becomes the Grand Master of the brotherhood. Your quest might seem simple, to regain stolen Eden's Apple from vicious templar Cesare Borgia, but it's never that easy, especially when your enemy is a templar. You get to see city of Rome, lots of memorable locations, and immerse yourself in another incredible chapter of Ezio's life.
The gameplay doesn't seem like it was improved whole lot, like transition from first game to second, however you're given few new tools to dispose of your enemies. You now have crossbow so you can assassinate your targets 2 rooftops away quickly and silently. What I really wanted since 2nd game was carry an axe for fights, even though it's not elegant weapon for an assassin. The biggest improvement in this installment was the intern system. The intern-assassins can do your assassinations for you, that gives them experience and eventually they graduate from assassin school and become real assassins. The gameplay didn't change much from 2nd game but it's not a bad thing considering it did pretty good job improving rough angles.  The one thing that's worth mentioning is execution system, where you can go on endless kill streak after successful counter attack. This thing was so fun I couldn't stop doing it till the very end of the game. Overally gameplay is smoother version of the 2nd installment which works really well.
What I really disliked about the game was 3rd party DRM system called Uplay. There was no warning that I have to install a program besides steam in order to enjoy game I already purchased. That being said I can't see any other downsides to this game besides Uplay. If you wonder whenever you should get this game the answer would be strong yes.

Brotherhood starts off immediately where the previous game left off. When I say this, I really mean you start in the exact spot, wearing the same gear you were at the end of the previous game. The story picks up right away and continues to entice.
This game, while different in various ways, keeps the same essence of the last game. You explore Roma during the Borgia reign of the early 16th century. This allows for, like all the games, some splendid views and the ability to truly appreiciate the thought and effort put into the design of the city and surrounding areas plus the attention to detail that I have come to enjoy and appreiciate.
There is a lot to do in this game. The added Economics allows for lots of money to be made and spent in Roma. This just builds on the ability in the previous game to earn and spend money and puts that to work on a grander scale.
The added abilities, weapons, and use of the syncing percentage really shine in this game. I found myself using the crossbow alot more than I thought I would and not just out of neccesity but actual enjoyment. Leveling up you own assassins within your guild and using them in various ways allowed for more interesting encounters with enemies and missions. Having missions have an optional objectives/constraints to get a sync percentage made had me retrying missions all the time to achieve that percentage. It made the replay value, for even the first time through, appealing and challenging.
Overall, if you like the series and played the games up until this point, continue to do so. You won't be disappointed.

All that is just a long winded way of saying "its an OK game."

I see that upon release this game only costs £0.79. This makes me happy. 10/10
But for serious, this is a cute little game a definitely worth the money. Now quick disclaimer - I, having spent the majority of my childhood living in the 2000's, am not one to be prone to retro game nostalgia, despite enjoying games with similar format to games from the 80's years later.
"Tcheco in the Castle of Lucio" is a 2D platformer, in which the objective is to collect the key on each screen in order to open the door to the next. It sounds simple, but there are no respawns, and you have only one life (with multiple hitpoints). This means playing the game over and over, each time improving a little, and making it further than before, which may sound tedious and frustrating, but actually leads to a great sense of accomplishment once progress is made.
The graphics remain faithful to the NES style it attempts to replicate. The music sounds similarly authentic, and each melody is upbeat and enjoyable. The controls are pretty fluid, personally I believe working better with a controller. Fortunately this game does indeed have full controller support, although I've yet to try it with a 3rd party gamepad (only used an Xbox controller). There's no options menu as such in the game, and windowed mode plus additional resolutions would be nice.
Overall, cheap game, fun. Give it a go. 7/10

Resident Evil 5 is a fine game but that's not fine coming off the greatest.
This is the first Resident Evil game I would be willing to call uninspired. Many things that are in the game looks like they were put there because focus testers told them they liked it. It turned Resident Evil from a slow survival horror game into a fast paced action game with horror elements. It reminds me a lot of what Crystal Dynamics did with Tomb Raider: Legend. They removed or downplayed key elements of the series and replaced them with more easily digestible things. Both games even have a motorcycle chase in the desert with shooting and explosions. The difference is that they redeemed themselves a year later with Tomb Raider: Anniversary, which I still maintain is the best Tomb Raider game ever made, and Capcom just went further off the deep end after this.
The Ndesu (El Gigante) boss fight is one of the stupidest things I have ever played. You remain stationary the entire time firing a machine gun at it from close range without having to dodge anything or even take out any mobs. All you have to do is shoot at its obvious weak points and you will never get hurt. That's not fun, challenging or even particularly interesting. It's just noise. A lot of the game is like that. Despite how easy it is in the first place your partner straight up tells you where to aim when a weak point appears. The game assumes you can't figure it out for yourself before you've even started. If there's one thing I hate in video games it's when they insult my intelligence. At least give me a chance to fail before holding my hand.
One thing I liked is that they portrayed how exhausting it must be to move around in a hot climate while carrying a lot of heavy gear. The breathing and heavy footsteps portray this very well and I don't see that very often. I didn't like how your partner keeps shooting you in the back more often than not, wasting the ammo you've collected. And whenever she regroups on you she usually defaults to standing right in front of your cross hairs, obscuring your line of sight. This is a large contrast to Ashley in Resident Evil 4 who made a point to stay behind you at all times and ducking if she got in front of you.
The game also takes itself completely seriously and has no sense of humor which I thing is its biggest drawback. It just wasn't as fun to play as the previous one.

I took a look at this game, and thought "Woah, that is a high price for something that looks so dated". Sort of used to it with    $50 indie games popping up on steam almost weekly.
HOWEVER, I'd say the purchase was well worth it. This game is a gem.
This game has a metric dickload of weapons. Early on, you may unlock like 3+ weapons every level if you pick up all the weapon boxes that drop from enemies. They are pretty fun to mix and match, and there are level based variants so your favorite weapon types can often stay relevant into the endgame (barring some one-off weapons that don't have variants).
There is a quick-chat wheel to easily communicate basic messages like "Can you rescue me?", "OOOOOOOOOOOOOOOH", "EAT THIS BULLET", "EDF EDF EDF", "GRRRRRRRAAHHHHHHHHHHHH", and normal stuff like that. There are many, MANY preset messages to choose from, and a good amount of them are voiced. Some npcs nearby might even join in on the singing, screaming fun.
There is also manual text chat that you can access by pressing "t", for people that want to talk like a normal person, but even then messages like "Lets use guided missles and targeting lasers" or "help me" still have value to put in your chat wheel for easy access.
Oh, also voice chat is a thing in this game and can't be turned off unless the host explicitly chooses to or you mute your mic. Have fun hearing some random dude eating over the mic and making grunting noises that doesnt know you can hear him. You could always turn voice volume down in the menu if you hate it.
Gameplay didn't seem like it would be too exciting at first, but it gets way better. You get dropped into the game only fighting giant silver ants, but then you progress to more interesting enemies... like recolored ants.
Just kidding!
You can fight web making giant spiders, hopping spiders, the previously mentioned ants and their variants, giant flying robot drones, giant mechs with varying weapons, EVEN BIGGER MECHS that make more small mechs, energy shield generator mechs, motherships, some godzilla like thing, dropships, and some other stuff. I didnt go that far in the game yet, so there is probably more.
Wave after wave of giant insects covering buildings and marching straight for you, so you get to use all those pretty weapons you unlocked. But did I mention classes?
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There are four classes:
Ranger- Standard infantry unit that is extremely powerful in the right hands. Has access to a ridiculous variety of weapons, and has decent survivability and support potential. Rockets, shotguns, flamethrowers, assault rifles, snipers, grenades, Heal gun. When it comes to this class, you have something for every situation, but choose wisely! You can only carry two weapons as this class. Ranger is also the only class besides air raider that can drive vehicles (barring a special one that everyone can use).
Wing Diver- Can fly with the aid of a plasma-powered jetpack, with energy based weapons that draw from the same power source! Your survival depends on being able to manage your energy correctly, and know when and where to land to recharge, lest you run out of power over a group of 300 ants and get mauled to death. This class has the lowest health and armor growth of any class, so positioning is necessary. Weapons start out looking extremely weak, but the wing diver is capable of ridiculous damage at later levels, and even her default weapon "rapier" can take out a dropship within seconds if you fly in close to the hatch and fire away. Can only carry two weapons.
Fencer- RIP AND TEAR. THATS A BIG BUG, AND THAT MEANS IT HAS BIG BUG GUTS!
Carry four weapons in your loadout separated into two groupings of two. One for each arm.
You are a tank of tanks. You can use shields, extremely powerful melee weapons, rapid fire mechafists, dual chainguns, shoulder mounted giant missle launchers, rocket pods, giant tank cannon sniper rifles, etc.
Despite being a bulky mass of metal armor, you can dash around the areas really quickly with use of your weapon abilities like back and side thrusters in combination with shield reflection animation cancelling.  Shield reflection isn't just for quick transport glitches either, but can actually reflect enemy projectiles back at them provided you time it right. This is an action class for those that want to feel like an unstoppable juggernaut.
Air raider- This class excels at supporting your allies! Everybody wants one of them on their team! They can heal, increase defense of allies, increase damage potential of allies, use remote explosive guns, send out turrets, send out explosive robot beetles, call in vehicles ranging from a motorcycle with a sidecar to giant mechs. Nothing is impossible for this guy!
You also have an important role as a  spotter with your laser targeting gun. You can mark enemies to make allies able to lock on to them faster with weapons that require lock ons. Laser targeting is also REQUIRED for some fencer weapons of mass destruction, so fencers that plan on using any of their ultra powerful missle weapons better have an air raider around, else they are useless.
All in all, it is a great game that is tons of fun. Play with friends. Play with randoms online. Play solo. It is all pretty good.

The last COD's where just about "cool skins" and advanced movement and so on. For me personally these COD's were no real COD's.
The last Call of Duty titles reminded me of woodstock and some hardcore dub step festivals instead of a good game! There were little kids everywhere, wearing crazy skins.
With their childish voice they told you how many times they f***ed your whole family, especially your mother.
This has somehow disappeared in this title. But as the kids left some other downpoints appeared.
The first downpoint: The skill based matchmaking. Its not fun at all. Every game you play you have to try hard to even get a decent K/D ratio.
Every game is full of pure sweat. When you play in a "higher" skill based matchmaking elo, you tend to find a lot less games and a lot more cheaters.
This mostly results in a bad server connection because there are not many matches that fit to your "skill level".
The skill based matchmaking just kills this game!
For better players its very annoying to just play against other players of their skill level, and for new players it's useless to play against other new players because they will not get better.
Noobs facing noobs and pros facing pros is just not a solution. Nobody can get better at the game while this system is in place! And furthermore the games are not funny. Every lobby you play just feels the same.
The next major down point besides the bad connection is the fact that the hitregistration is amazingly bad! Sometimes it just feels like you play a game with a 300ms ping or more.
You can't even hit 2 out of 4 shots that were definitely ON TARGET, not just a little bit off to the side.
Thats what they call "Optimal game found!". Well, okay... I personally think that the optimal game was not found.
And another down point: The cheaters. There is nothing to say about that. There are a lot of cheaters! Especially when you play in the "higher elo" there tend to be a lot more cheaters.
In the end I want to mention the ingame COD-Points: This system has been in place since a while now. It's amazing how they manage to sell a 60-100 buck game and players still
waste a ton of money for skins. At the moment there are only skins but the better pay to win weapons will come for sure.
Another downpoint: The dumb daily rewards. Everybody tries to fulfill the challenges and therefor in every game there are so many players that trie to ram a f****ng shovel in
someones head instead of playing the objective. Or someone tries to get his sniper kills which leads to a nice campy gameplay. Sometimes you even have a team full of snipers that
all just sit in one corner waiting for the other players while hardscoping down a hallway. But there is nobody they can shoot because the other team just sits at the other
side of the map also camping. What a great system.
Final PERSONAL result: I would not rebuy the game - at the moment. They have to fix a lot of things. When they do so, the game might be close to fun again.

Amazing game.  20 hrs in one weekend, and only on level 18 of 90.  I won't go too much into the specifics right now, but I will point out few things that others might not talk about.  The short answer: If you think the game looks awesome, you'll love it.  To the average gamer the graphics are amazing, although I've seen some ultra-res pc buffs nitpick them, and the game is aesthetically beautiful.    On larger levels, shiny metal and detailed textures take a few extra seconds to load after the level starts, but they never take more than 10 seconds to load completely.  The controls are unique but not poorly designed and you will get used to them quickly.  Two things that aren't as intuitive about the controls but you will pick up after figuring them out (which is why I'm telling you):  Jumping and rolling are on the same button.  Moving straight forward or backward, or standing still and pressing the button makes you jump.  Moving sideways or diagonally and pressing it causes you to roll.  Secondly, the sortie menus are operated with the control stick/WASD keys, and the d-pad/arrow keys navigate the communications menu.  The four classes have a very surprising amount of depth to them, both in variety of gear and in base class mechanics.  The fact that the Fencer (the game's Tank class) is possibly more complicated than the Air Raider (the Specialist/Support class) should speak for itself.  The game runs extremely smoothly, and online works perfectly, with no lag or frame drops (If your connection is too bad to play, it disconnects you).  Also, SPLIT SCREEN LOCAL CO-OP AND VS!!!  And of course, the constant bombardment of dramatic psuedo-intellectual B-Movie dialogue is perfectly executed and amazing.  Actually, (this is as deep as this review will get), you could say the game itself is making fun of the people who criticize EDF for its simple nature.  The point of EDF isn't to make you feel like a selfless member of the military giving his life to save humanity in the face of an extraterrestrial threat.  You're supposed to feel like a soldier who saves the world by blowing up everything in sight with missiles and lasers while cheering and singing about the benevolent organization he works for.  Anyways...
It's definitely not necessary but might be worth it to you if you really enjoy the game.  The weapons are not overpowered/game breaking, and are unique and well balanced weapons to use.  The vehicles are just joke skins that are funny to drop in game and surprise people with, like an anime tank.  The level packs contain remixed and new levels and while they do not add new weapons, they add many more hours of mayhem and have a few levels great for grinding gear and armor.  Like I said, none of it's necessary, but if you like the game you might want to look into the DLC.  I think enjoy the game enough that I'll eventually buy the level packs and an anime tank when they go on sale.
I think I will get many years of enjoyment out of this game and although I think it should be permanently priced at $35, I definitely got more than $50 worth of fun out of it.  I think it's definitely a niche game initially, but anyone can fall in love with it if given time to experience its true scope.  Like I said, if you think the game looks awesome and you'd enjoy it, then you probalby will, but if you think it looks stupid, then try a friend's copy or do more research, only then should you count it out completely.
GLITCH: I had this problem and others had it as well.  Some Nvidia users have a problem where the game does not use their graphics card and tries to run off integrated computer graphics instead, causing bad lag.  Fix this by making sure your drivers are updated and then going to the Nvidia Control Panel and creating a folder for the game in Manage 3D Settings, create a folder for the game under Programs and set the preferred graphics processor to High-performance Nvidia processor.
I've given you all the details you might care about, but here's a rant about something that I personally find awesome that may be meaningful to few other people as well:  The scope of this game is insane, and everything is insanely detailed.  If you think the fact that a game can runs a constant 60FPS at ay resolution with literally hundreds of detailed enemies and buildings being blown up at any given moment isn't a big enough achievement on its own, the detail will amaze you.  The entire enviornment is pretty much realisticly shaped, and does not use textures to simulate depth.  In addition, while some environmental objects such as cars are a bit on the small side, and are not realistically sized to the human characters, all of the architecture is accrrately scaled.  This combined with the fact that the small details of buildings are actually modelled and not just textured in makes the world feel amazing.  Run out of fuel trying to fly up a skyscraper?  Take a rest on the ledge around one of its hundreds of windows.  One of the coolest things that happened to me was when I was playing local co-op with my brother and got blown up and flung into an apartment building, a motel-style one where the rooms are accessed from walkways on the outside.  When my brother flew onto the walkway to rescue me, we found out that we could walk to the end of the walkway and climb the stairs to the next floor, and we continued until we reaced the top floor.  While some people might not care about this, for me it's things like this that really enhance immersion and leave you with a much stringer experience.  Since the buildings in the game are made to be destroyed and not closely inspected, you wouldn't hold it against the developers if the buildings were pretty much rectangular blocks with windows and colorful billboards, but when you find that you can look through the glass doors and see the receptions and waiting rooms of small buinesses, and look at the advertisements and menus inside restauraunts, and of course, pretend you live on the top floor of an apartment and walk all the up all of the stairs on the side of the building, it's just one of the many things that make you feel that this game really has heart behind it, and was created with more in mind than just making money or being
unique enough to be memorable, like so many other games these days.  Anyways, sorry for getting cheesy there at the end, but if you've read this far you should seriously give this game a try.  It's the most fun I've had in a while.

This is definitely a worthy successor to Assassin's Creed II. It plays very similar, but there are some excellent improvements; visually and in regards to the gameplay.
All the Assassin's Creed games had one major positive aspect: They look beautiful. You feel immersed and part of the environment and getting to a high point that allows you to overlook the entire city/area is truly a 'wow' moment. As far as the gameplay is concerned, I particularly like the fact that you can actually call a horse and ride it within the confines of the city, and the new weapons you can use; particularly the crossbow. Very cool, and foremost helpful if you're free-running and have to quick eliminate guards.
Later on you get additional help once the brotherhood forms, but I won't say all too much here, because that is something that should be experienced!
The somewhat different economy system makes sense and works, as it provides you a fairly steady source of income right from the get go which definitely helps with upgrades and repairs. So far the missions are diversive, the envrionment feels lively and challenging and it's definitely a good addition to the series. Basically have, so far, never really felt bored.
As I said before, Rome certainly looks beautiful and in particular the recreation of the Colosseum is impressive. In general you have very recognizable landmarks. The entire area in which the game takes place is also huge, much bigger than you'd think when you get started. It grows very subtle, and suddenly you think, 'hold on, how did I get here?" It is true that certain areas being "unavailable" in a certain memory sequence is a little annoying at times, but I guess, since AC is a very story and narrative based franchise, despite the free roaming, it makes sense to move the story along.
The world does evolve with you though. The only other game series that ever did this to a certain extend was GTA, but not with the same kind of subtlety and style Assassin's Creed does it; that is something that was there right from the start of th series, but it certainly evolved with each subsequent game.
If you liked the Assassin's Creed series up until this point, you will not be disappointed by "Brotherhood".

Pretty cool game. You deploy a fleet and watch what happens. You give each ship or squadron generic orders ("attack frigates" or "defend cruisers") and let 'er rip. That's not the fun part.
The fun part is outfitting your ships. Each ship has so much space, so many small weapon slots, etc. You have to fit each ship in your fleet with a reactor, engines, shield generators, armor, weapons... The whole deal. You can just use the pre-generated ones, but good luck advancing in the game.
If all that appeals to you, try this game. I can certainly see why this wouldn't be for everyone. Some people don't want to have to design their fleet; they just want to play with it. Some people want to micro-manage their units. This game is for neither of those people.
[UPDATE]
Just started playing this again because I got the "Galactic Conquest" DLC. So now there's an actual campaign. I find that my favorite part of the game is designing my ships. actually buying/building them and deploying them is just what I do to test my designs.
The addition of a campaign mode is great. It's a very simple matter of conquering planet after planet, not building buildings or starbases, but just building your ships and sending them against computer-controlled, user-designed fleets.
The DLC also added a "direct control" option on the fleet deployment screen. So while you're deploying your fleet, you can decide that at some point during the battle you might want to issue direct commands to your ships. I've never used it, but I guess if you don't like the AI controlling your fleet, you might appreciate it.

For those of you who played Assassin's Creed II, you will probably like Brotherhood, as it plays pretty much the same. It starts out fun and introduces a few new features and modifications that are definitely for the better.
However, as soon as one reaches Rome, it quickly gets frustrating. Me, I stopped there after a while. Here's a few reasons why (it's basically the same reason all over, but it gets so annoying it's unbearable):
1) You see a lookout on the map and try to reach it. However, you quickly realize that you can not access it just because you see it on the map. Because "this memory is not available".
2) You want to return to a place you've been before, perhaps to get money from the bank or repair your armor? You'll notice that, other than in every other Assassin's Creed before, areas you've been to will not necessarily stay available. Suddenly these areas are "not available" anymore.
3) I feel like I'm squeezed into a relatively narrow tunnel of "available memory", with only a bit of space opening before me, while it closes again behind me. Everytime I stray form the path a little, I can't continue because "this area is not available". Like the game is trying to get me through the missions and areas in a most linear way. Not the Assassin's Creed experience I came to know and love.
4) I would like to repair a building to get a lookout point. I can reach the building. However, the building is controlled by a tower. I need to destroy the tower. However, the tower is in an area that is "not available". WTF?!?
At this point I was so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that I actually stopped playing, because I felt mucked.
Seriously, it's a great game. Gameplay-wise, it's even better than the original Assassin's Creed 2. But the way it limits the player to a rather small area really kills it for me. So much for "open world".

Achievements: All possible.  A level select exists so it's easy to collect any missed ones.
Pros/Cons:
+ Each level is totally distinct with completely different environments/puzzles.
+ The concept of the game is quite unique.
+ The puzzles are a decent challenge.
+ The platforming mechanics work pretty well.
+ There are references to other games scattered throughout.
+ Collectibles.
+ Nice graphics.
+ Each level is short and sweet.  None overstay their welcome.
+ Good length for the price (Took me ~5 hours)
- There's some signs of the game being... unpolished.  Things like cars being able to rotate without moving, your character's arms resting at their default position despite holding any of the game's tools/items.
- The physics are a little janky.  Crucial items can be accidentally flung across the level, boxes can spin wildly when you're dragging them.  Nothing was too gamebreaking, though.
- The audio settings kept resetting to default every time I started a level-- more of an annoyance than anything, really.
Overall:
Suicide Guy is so charming.  Every level had me in awe of how cool the environments were-- there was such an interesting variety.  Plus, it's so unique to have death be the end goal.  It makes you rethink puzzles entirely.  Despite the lack of polish and the unfortunate name, Suicide Guy is a wonderful, distinctive puzzle game.  It's delightfully absurd to wander dream worlds trying to wake yourself up.  I highly recommend giving it a try.

It's like Capcom mistook the RE4 criticisms as advice for RE5 and put it in a Modern Warfare campaign. "The environments were boring? How about the Call of Duty shanty towns/favelas/urban♥♥♥♥♥♥holes? The RE4 story was bad, but Leon's campy one-liners saved it. Chris has no character. Sheva is the RE equivalent of when Team Sonic designs a new hedgehog but forgets to give it personality. The plot? Excellent game! I was not precisely born in the NES era, but this game has shown me how awesome those old school gems could be.
The gameplay is excellent. The controls are tight and easy (I still don't understand what ducking is for). All the relics that you can collect mean that you can develop your own play style. Want some extra money? You can use the coin relic. Do you want to go faster or use 'dash'? Use the Propeller Dagger and enjoy its damage and platforming capabilities! Want to go full Megaman? Get the Flare Wand early in the game, craft the Conjurer's Coat armor to increase your magic, then shoot and jump like you used to in Megaman's glory days.
The soundtrack is excellent. The songs are extremely catchy, fitting and at least in my case, they made me feel emotionally attached to whatever was going on in the game. The music from the "SAVE HER" Shield Knight scenes seriously made me tear up. Propeller Knight stage's music made me feel excited and whistle along.
Shovel Knight is a challenging game. Thing started getting rough for me around the 3rd stage, but beating each boss is a seriously satisfactory feeling. I still feel really happy about beating that Plague Knight!
Overall, if you want a nice game that will have you hooked for hours, delight you with polished graphics (YES!), gameplay and music, look no further than Shovel Knight. I give this game a 10/10. I simply can't find anything wrong with it. :)

The city of Rome is massive but not as appealing as Venice or Florence, but that is realistic because Rome in that time period was mostly ruins and old houses.
The game finishes up the Borgia arc. It's not as epic as the previous one but it's still a good story
What really bugs me is the white gradient on the top of the screen otherwise the graphics improve especially the shadows.
The Score:
Gameplay: 9/10 (improves a lot, adds more fluidity)
Story: 7/10 (Good but short)
Graphics: 7/10 (The white gradient prevents from being 9)
Setting: 7/10 (Rome is realistic but too much of the same, several cities is better)
Innovation: 8/10 (several new modes are added to the game)
Overall: 7.6
If you loved AC2 buy this one but expect more of an expansion than a really fresh game.

A different take on strategy games.
Instead of having to build up your resources, army and scout for cheese, you're given a set amount of resources. You then build your fleet as you please, including ship design, ship behaviour (tell a fighter squadron to escort a cruiser) and overall strategy.
You then watch the battle unfold as your fleet tests itself against the enemy's.
Plot is unnecessary in "Gratuitous Space Battles" because that's exactly what it provides: gratuitous (as in, lots of lasers, explosions, laser-induced explosions and witty banter from the starships) space battles (battles take place in a 2D plane in space).
It also has multiplayer. If crushing your AI-led enemies has gotten too easy, feel free to go up against Admiral McNulty and the Fifth Fleet or whoever else you fancy having a battle of wits against.

Edit on January 19th (original review done in response to the first update of the 0.7.0 beta):
The devs are beginning to tweak some things and do bug fixes. This is a good sign. While I still have issues I listed below, I'm happy to see devs working on things like line physics, astronomical prices, gear balancing, and other bugs. Check out DIscussions for info.
Edit Feb 20, 2017: Short summary of game status: The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game economy is starting to feel like Cold War era dropping sad lonely rubles into a rusted coffee can to take down to buy my loaf of stale bread and 12 pieces of toilet paper every week in my holey fishing outfit I can't afford to repair.
0.7.0 Beta pre-release review (early Jan 2017):
Cons: I really enjoyed the game but the game is now being updated and features special currency ("baitcoin"...) that effectively locks the good gear behind real money. The normal game currency is becoming severely devalued to the point where 10x increased cost is the new normal. This equates to a grind to catch all the fish you need to pay down the 10x travel costs, the 10x daily access fee, the 10x daily fishing license, then make 10x a profit after that to afford all the average gear upgrades so you can then pay the next 10x travel cost, 10x daily access fee and 10x license to go to a better location suitable to your level, so that you don't sink yourself into a cash and experience hole by staying in a low-level area. Yaaay.
Avatars have been added to the game, but no way to disable them so you can't quietly fish without several others standing on top of you, nor are you able to do anything about someone using their avatar to block you. You have to move and hope they don't follow you, or leave the map and lose the enormous fees you paid to fish there. Because of the avatars, the room size has been shrunk down from 20 to 5, so the fun, social aspect of the game is currently, for me at least, not there anymore.
The game mechanics for the rod, reel and tackle have changed in such a way that lures hit the water surface like a brick, lines are so fine they're difficult to control, setting the hook on a bite will jerk the fish out of the water and send it flying way overhead.
There's also something called a pond pass which also costs real money. You can, of course, also buy baitcoin with real currency to have access to the associated perks in the game.
Current players who have shelled out over the past year+ with time, money, purchase of DLC to support development of this early access game, are in the dark about what the plan is to convert their current bank, gear, purchased content, and time invested. There's been comments but no official announcement, and the release of the beta is supposedly now only a couple of days away.
I'd have loved to shell out a monthly subscription fee for this game without all the b.o.l.l.o.c.k.s. they're adding in. Even the premiere level which you buy with real money costs additional real money for baitcoin.

Spend a few hours clearing the core game missions and learning how to build ships as well as what weapon does what, then spend hours upon hours building the perfect fleet or simply unique combat situations then linking them online for other people to try! Or maybe go try them yourself! GSB is a fleet combat sim where unlike most games you dont actualy control the ships yourself, you simply design them, place them and give them order guidelines. If your the sort of person who enjoys watching the battles in civ and rts games, likes chess, or enjoys setting up armies to then see what happens in the resulting combat, check out GSB.

Disclaimer: While I recommend the game for the concept, you do have to have a decent computer to use it. The graphics looked simple enough that I thought I'd be able to play it, but I was wrong. If you're in the same boat as me (mediochre-poor computer), I'd advise against it. Even putting it on the lowest graphics settings and turning off camera effects wasn't enough, as some aspects ought to be tweaked to make it work (i.e. lowest graphics settings shouldn't just be textures, but it ought to lower the realism of fires too and get rid of sparks). Unfortunately, I had to stop playing at about the 4th level, because my fps was simply too low to complete the puzzles.
That being said, what I did get to play was fantastic; the concept was great, and I love the way it messes with your mind a little. As gamers, we're often used to avoiding what kills us and seeking out treasure, and this game breaks that mold. I found myself breaking out of the "auto-pilot" mindset where I often find myself in other games. Hopefully I'll hear back if there's ever an update that fixes the lag issues, because I genuinely enjoyed what I got to play of this game!
