So this is going to be my second review ever. Normally I don't review games just because I don't have a lot to say about them. They are either good or bad and so that is how I would normally rate a game. However, Siege is a little bit different. I have a love-hate relationship with this game. So I am going to break down below what I think of this game after putting in over 600 hours into it.
First, lets get all the good things out of the way.
PROS
===================================================================================
1: Addictive
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game is addictive. I mean highly, addictive. From the way the main gameplay loop runs to the way the guns feel, to the noises and sounds that permeate the maps and all culminates into an awesome sensory experience. Siege gets this right, the feeling of being trapped into a small location with bullets flying by and tense fire-fights. This is why I keep coming back for that adrenaline rush-like experience.
===================================================================================
2: No pay to win (Yet...)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Around a year ago siege was in trouble. It had a declining playerbase and reviews were 'meh' at best. So UBI did a really, really smart thing. (I know, UBI and smart in one sentence whaaaaat) But they did! They made all the content whether it was DLC or base game content unlockable in game. Of course you could purchase renown (in game currency) to unlock them quicker, but the normal renown gain per match was good enough so you could get operators. Then they released the 14.99 game (That is the one I bought) and again that was a brilliant move. Not only did you get a game that had the full quality of a AAA title but at the price of an indie game. Personally this move was brilliant. So yeah all the new DLC items are free, maps, operators etc. You just have to unlock the operators and skins via in-game renown and I am ok with that.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note:  The reason 'yet' is up there is I am concerned what will happen with the alpha packs, if you are new and have no idea what I am talking about it is essentially loot crates but I am not sure what UBI is going to fully do with them...
===================================================================================
3. Teamwork
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
It's funny that I am putting this as a pro because I am the least team-oriented player around but there is something so satisfying after getting a callout about an enemy location and getting the jump on them or doing a double hot breach coordinated with your teammate. The way teamwork is so integral to this game is also why it works so well. You "can" lone-wolf it and sure you may get a few kills but you probably will leave your teammates in a 4v5 situation and be the last one left dealing with all the enemies on the objective. So teamwork is definitely a must and once you get the hang of giving those callouts and being comfortable with locations and certain spots on the maps the game will truly shine then!
====================================================================================
So you must be asking yourself by now, "So if you have all these positive things to say, why leave a negative review?" I am so glad you asked my imaginary reader. You see, about... hmm... 2 months ago we were supposed to recieve a new batch of content (which if you buy the season pass you get unlocked automatically, no need to spend renown, and get it a week early!) However, instead of that it was silence and then an announcment that they were scrapping one part of the DLC's promised and instead going with a new idea for 3 months. In comes OPERATION HEALTH.
Now I am not going to lie to you, I was one of the few people super pumped for this. Basically, the premise was that Operation Health (OH for short) was going to fix most if not all the significant bugs players were running into that were game breaking. (I.E. Invisible characters, improper bullet hit registration, incredible lag... etc etc).  Basically, UBI had become behind on major bug fixes and wanted to fix the game proper before new content. I am all on board with that. EXCEPT, that is not what happened. I am going to break it down below what has happened.
====================================================================================
OPERATION HEALTH : MAJOR CON (Currently)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So we got our first 'big' update which was one-step matchmaking or basically you click "look for game" and you can still mess about in the menus before the game starts, change loadouts etc. Yes, this was a 'feature' coming to an online shooter a year and some odd months AFTER its release. But ok, cool. I am all aboard. So update releases, breaks game even more. Here is where my main negative point comes into play. Sure they also changed up the hitboxes to allow for more realistic hits and that is FANTASTIC, I know some Blitz mains who were overjoyed in that moment. However, the hit registration got immediatly worse. Getting matched in ongoing games where the score was 0-2 is more common. More weird invisible character moments, floating and appearing characters, getting shot from angles that don't exist and more happen frequently now. I will even link a video below that shows most of the things discussed here. All of this and we lost content... It is just frustrating for a game that I genuienly like to see this happen to.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TLDR; Game is more broken than before, content delayed. Not in a better place yet.
====================================================================================
Here are just a few more cons
CONS
====================================================================================
Community kinda toxic now and Too much about Pro-League
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I am sure most of us in this community are guilty of some form of toxic behavior in a game or two but it has gotten to a point that I only experienced in LoL. Which that is saying something.
Example: I am playing a game, we are losing and there is a level... 3-ish on our team. Mind you this is in casual. So another teammate is berating him all game long about how bad he is. Finally, it comes match point. This poor level 3 who probaly has only played 1 game before gets tk'd by this guy who then tells him to just quit and blah blah blah.
Bottom line, people like this are not cool and I am seeing it more and more. It sucks being low rank and for your own teammate to do that is just crappy.
Also UBI just seems to care a little too much about the pro-league scene over the normal players. Which, don't get me wrong I totally get. It is more exposure, coverage and shows that the title is an 'E-Sport' but the normal player base is what keeps these games alive. I just want to see a little more care shown for the average player...
====================================================================================
Bottom Line: Game is fun but broken 80% of the time. Wait to get until larger bugs are fixed. UBI is still being UBI....

Fugl is a great idea, and the game is developing at a decent clip. The devs are very responsive and active on the forums, and new features seem to be added with regularity. Given these factors, I was willing to give this alpha-build title a chance.
The short of it is that if you want a game focused on flying, if you used to speed around levels as Spyro just because it was fun, if you bought Aer: Memories of Old solely for the concept of the flight mechanics -- this game is going to scratch that flying and exploration itch, and it looks pretty good in the process! Being a bird and soaring around is fun -- it's just peaceful to play. Kiting rock formations as fast as you can go and climbing high above the world to dive straight down and skirt the water is just as satisfying as cruising at low altitude to check out the local wildlife. It's the kind of game where you make your own fun out of it, but that's not bad. If you think it's going to appeal to you, you're probably right.
That said, this is an alpha build. At present, my graphics card is not supported, and I can't generate my own terrain -- which was a disappointment, I will admit. The game's install (2gb down, 11gb installed -- this will come down as optomization improves) comes with some pre-rendered terrain to explore for people like me, so I was still able to experience the mechanics -- and it was that experience that made me decided to give this a thumbs-up for the right player. Furthermore, this game has Steam Workshop integration, and the devs are going to allow players to port over their own worlds in the future, which should happily tide over sad sacks like me until the compatability is increased. There's also a bird editor, and the community is alive and well making birds in the workshop to play as.
Fugl is developing quickly, and really shaping up to be something special. It's a little bare right now, especially for me -- but if nothing else, it's just plain fun, and sometimes that's all a game needs to be, is fun to play. As the content for Fugl fills out the overall experience, I'm sure it will only improve from here.
So overall, even though this is a title in alpha, and a game that I personally had some troubles with -- even though it's a game I can't recommend for everyone because of the type of single-service experience you're getting -- I still recommend it to anyone interested, because I had fun with it in spite of its current, and soon to be rectified, shortcomings -- and I think other people might have a similar experience.
Thank you for reading.

So here is my short review regarding the game Suicide Guy.
--------------
You are playing as Suicide Guy (nameless) in self perspective and your goal is to make him wake up from his dreams. Jumping (if you can call it that way) and manipulating various objects in the various levels. Doing so was really funny and the solutions of the physical puzzles were absolutely creative. On the other hand... the controls are a little wonky at times. Which makes it kind of frustrating sometimes if you have to do a critical jump or throw e.g.
--------------
Graphics were ok to good, depending if you like the comic look. I found it to be fitting for this game. Also, I can't quite imagine this game with the dream scenario done in super realistic graphics. It would take away the fun part from the game and give it a completely new direction and feel. It would have been way too dark and maybe even be more of a horror game.
--------------
Well, you play the nameless suicide guy and are trying to wake up from your haunting dreams. End of story. It's mostly play through the 25 or so levels. Still fun though.
-------------
The sound was ok. The voice acting from the suicide guy was not fitting. It felt absolutely out of place to me. Luckily, he rarely ever talks. The music was ok. I did not find it to be spectacular, but for a puzzle game it does not necessarily has to be that way.
-------------
I would recommend you give it a try if it's on sale. It's clearly a little flawed and sometimes frustrating, but still is fun.

Arma 3 is a well developed game which follows in the wake of optimisational dumpster fires "Arma 2" and "Arma 2: Operation Arrowhead", which featured engaging tactical combat, in-depth gamemodes and squad/team controls, but unfortunately terrible optimisation, especially for higher end rigs, because logic. Arma 3 refused to make that mistake. While there are still optimisational issues, and a high CPU demand compared to the GPU demand, Arma 3 made drastic improvements to what lacked in previous games. The combat remains immersive, squad command easy and accessible, a surprisingly rich story line, and fairly-priced supportive DLC. The expansions add content that support the experience, but don't detract from it if they aren't present/DLC not owned. Arma 3 is definitely a step in the right direction for Bohemia Interactive, especially after their previous works.

This is a platforming gaming with
flair.
You are Shovel Knight, on his quest towards the Tower of Fate, to save your friend Shield Knight from danger.
But to get there, you must first brawl and dig your way through the "Order of No Quarter", a group of knights in service of the Enchantress...
I have the distinct feeling that the creator´s favourite game was Mega Man 2, the platforming action and feel of the controls mostly remind me of that game. That´s a good thing. :-)
There are also traces of Mario in there.
But fear not, the game is far from a clone, it brings enough of its own to the table, while paying homage to the classics.
Everything is tied together with an upbeat chiptune soundtrack, which I quite enjoyed.
I would say the difficulty is medium. While I mentioned Mega Man 2 earlier, this is far easier. While there are some tricky platforming sections, frustration is kept low. The boss fights range from easy (King Knight) to fairly punishing (Plague Knight!).
By gather gold and gems you can afford items and permanent upgrades to your life and magic to make things easier.
Death sets you back to the last checkpoint, which are fairly spaced out. You also lose a portion of your gold, which is left floating at the place where you fell, to recollect.
The game took me about 6-7 hours to complete. After that, there is a
mode, which has you starting with all of your gear, but increased difficulty (mostly less health pickups and more damaging enemies).
I have not completed it yet, but it is noticably harder than the first round.
There is also a number of "feats" (achievements) to be gained, and a lot of secret rooms to find.
Heartilty recommended if you like classic platformers from the NES era.
I guess the game is rather kid friendly, there is no actual violence, the Shovel Knight gives his adverseries a sound spanking, but nobody is killed.

儿子马上就要过 15 岁生日了，爸爸问他生日礼物想要什么。
儿子想了想说：“男孩子想要的东西我都有了，唯一能想到的，就是一只用塑料做的鹦鹉玩具。”
爸爸很纳闷：“塑料做的鹦鹉？真的就只要这个玩意？”
儿子点头：“恩，生日礼物我就想要塑料鹦鹉。”
爸爸虽然很不解，但还是按儿子的要求，给他买了塑料鹦鹉。可是几个星期后，有一天爸爸来到儿子房间打扫，却发现根本没有鹦鹉的踪影。当初那么想要，却这么快弄丢了，真是一桩怪事。不过爸爸也没有此多问。
转眼一年过去了，快到儿子 16 岁的生日了。
爸爸又问你呢：“儿子，今年你想要什么样的生日礼物?”
儿子想了想道：“男孩子想要的东西我都有了，唯一能想到的，就是 6 只塑料鹦鹉，装在一个精美的盒子里。”
爸爸很纳闷怎么又是这种奇怪的要求，可还是按照儿子的要求，给他买了 6 只塑料鹦鹉，还装在了一个精美的盒子里面。然而几个星期后，和去年一样，鹦鹉有从儿子的房间消失了。
儿子 17 岁生日前，爸爸又问了他同样的问题，儿子想了想，也是同样的答案：“男孩子想要的东西我都有了，唯一能想到的，就是要 28 只塑料鹦鹉装在一个巨大的箱子里。”
爸爸已经彻底的被搞糊涂了，可是毕竟是儿子的心愿，所以还是照办了。然而几个星期后，儿子房间里的鹦鹉在一次全部消失了。
儿子 18 岁生日前，爸爸决定来一点特别的惊喜。“儿子，18 岁生日我一定要送一份大礼，给你一辆轿车怎么样？”
儿子摇头：“男孩子想要的东西我都有了，唯一能想到的，就是要装满整整一屋子的塑料鹦鹉。”
爸爸发出了绝望的哀嚎：“怎么还是塑料鹦鹉！这个不行！”
儿子恳求道：“可是爸爸，我不想要汽车呀，其他的什么都不想要，就想要这个呀！”
爸爸挨不过，只好给儿子买了一整屋子的塑料鹦鹉。可是还是和以前一样，没过几个星期，儿子房间里一直鹦鹉都看不到了。
爸爸忍不住还是发问了：“儿子，你每年都要塑料鹦鹉，我都没问你为什么，这倒也罢。可是每次买了之后没多久，鹦鹉就都不见了，这是怎么回事你得告诉我吧？”
儿子坚定的看着爸爸：“请你相信我好吗，我总有一天会告诉你的，但现在还不行。”
时光飞逝，转眼要到儿子 19 岁生日了。
爸爸一脸无赖的问：“儿子，今年你也想要更多的塑料鹦鹉吧？”
儿子点点头：“是的爸爸，这次我要装满一仓库那么多。”
爸爸按照儿子的要求，买回了上万只塑料鹦鹉。可不出所料，没过几个星期这些鹦鹉又统统无影无踪了，爸爸决定蹲守在儿子的放间里，等儿子回来，解开这个迷。
可就在这时，爸爸接到了一个医院打来的电话。
“你好，你的儿子卷入了一起黑帮枪战，中弹受伤，现以生命垂危，请马上赶到医院来。”
爸爸全速赶到了医院，医生宣布儿子已经希望不大了。爸爸悲痛地来到奄奄一息的儿子床前。
“儿子，我知道现在问这个很不是时候，可是这么多年我给你买塑料鹦鹉的事情，我还是想搞清楚。为什么你想要这个？拿来做什么？”
儿子挣扎着，用微弱的声音说道：“爸爸，您能帮我实现最后一个愿望吗？”
“儿子你尽管说，爸爸什么都帮你做到”
“爸爸，我想拜托你到附近的商店里，就买一只塑料鹦鹉，送给我。”
爸爸立马去了最近的礼品店，买了一只塑料做的鹦鹉，又全力气跑回了医院，把鹦鹉送到了儿子手里。
“看，爸爸给你买回来了，现在你能告诉我了吗？爸爸真的很想知道。”
儿子把塑料鹦鹉紧紧的握在手里，用尽最后一点力气，拼命到：
“爸爸，这些年每次过生日，我都问你要塑料鹦鹉，你觉得奇怪也是理所当然的。我现在…… 必须告诉您…… 这件事情的真相了…… 其实…… 是……”
……
　……
　
　这时儿子断气死掉了。

NOTE: this is a review of the singleplayer, not the multiplayer, and I have also completed the main story and did a few of the side misssions.
This game has some good points, so I'll go over them first.
In ACB, the graphics have been slighly upgraded from ACII, so you'll still be able to run it if you have a way way weak PC, which is good, and the story for the most part is quite fluid and follows on nicely from ACII. The combat, IMO, is still great with a few added improvements.
But then, This game, to me, falls on so many levels compared to Assassins Creed II.
First, the map you play in, Rome. Rome seems to feel more empty and barren compared to Florence and Venice. In those games, you always had somewhere interesting to go, something to dominate the view, but in this game, most of the map is just open countryside with a few Roman ruins scattered around. You may get a slight sense of awe when you first see the places like the Pantheon or the Colloseum, but after a while that novelty wears off and they just become another thing to climb. It also seems to have sparce few people, making rome feel empty, which is never really good.
the ending to the story is just confusing to wrap your head around, and they just seem to throw in charecters from ACII randomly. And then the main feature of the game: the Brotherhood ability.
This ability is quite fun recruiting people and them using them to earn you money and kill guards without you having to do much. But it becomes that: getting money and killing guards; not very exciting.
So, in MY opinion, I beleive this game fell far from the greateness of ACII. I would only get it in a sale and if you want to carry on the story of Ezio.

Rome: Total War is what you play when you want to tell the Romans to go home, or vice versa.
It's the third game in the Total War series, and the first to introduce the gameplay template it still uses today. Gone are the 2D battlefield models and Risk-style campaign map from the first two games, replaced with 3D models and a strategic map you can use to finely position units and armies. Gameplay revolves around managing your territory in a turn-based strategy mode, and moving armies around the map to fight opposing armies as well as capture or defend settlements in a real time tactics mode.
This particular entry is widely regarded as a classic, and with great value to boot. It can certainly suffice for people who can't afford or run the later games in the series. Unfortunately the game is optimized to run on only one CPU core, so newer computers might run into some trouble anyway. As this is still only the third game in the series, there are some things in later titles that are lacking in this one such as resolutions above 1600x1400. Something to keep in mind, at least.
The Gold Edition comes with the Barbarian Invasion expansion that takes place during the fall of the Roman Empire, adding new factions and some new features such as hordes & religion; well worth playing after the base game. There's also a
available separately that lets you play as Alexander the Great, and it's required for some of the more popular mods to run.
The vanilla game is a good way to get the hang of things, but from the disorganized battle lines to the historical inaccuracy I wouldn't recommend playing for any extended period of time. To wit: the Greek city-states form one faction (just one) while Rome is divided into three
that each get their own faction. Egypt, meanwhile, looks like it walked out of a timewarp from 1000 BC instead of the Ptolemaic empire it was at the time of Rome's ascent.
There's a number of mods that overhaul the game to fix these issues and more, including (nominally) improved AI, which has always been a weakpoint of the TW series - with the exception of the first two games, which used Risk-style troop movement that's easier for AI to understand. Two of the most popular RTW mods include Rome Total Realism and Europa Barbarorum, the former being a general overhaul of the game and the latter being much more realism-focused to the point of near simulation.
I'd recommend this as an entry point into Total War for people on a budget. It's probably better than Rome II at any rate; even with the many improvements that game's had since its disastrous launch it's still a game about ancient warfare that uses an engine the developers intended for Napoleonic warfare.

Gorgeous meditative flyer. Lots of scenery and animals to discover, performs beautifully. Truly a joy to unwind for short sessions.
Controls are clunky, it's very difficult to take off from water or a dead stop, it's not always clear what the buttons do. Moving and controlling the camera on the ground is nigh impossible. Once in the air, flying is blissful and swooping turns and dives come second nature.
Map layout is a bit boggling. If you fly left or right from the start, you'll encounter a looping world every 15 seconds like a Hanna-Barbera cartoon background. If you fly along the intended direction, you'll traverse at least four other unique biomes including canyons, polar ice caves, and a trippy glowing shroom garden. Continue along, you'll reach an invisible barrier bordered by some kind of negative-space bizarro world.
Morphing into other animals is a little confusing at first. It's never clear exactly what triggers the transformation or reversal. Each animal has different performance and physics, from deer whose antlers will drag you into a nosedive or a bald eagle that soars effortlessly and zooms with each wingbeat. It's claimed that there are hundreds of these different creatures, I know I've seen at least dozens. The workshop and editor provides the opportunity to shape your default flyer in myriad ways.
As it stands, I doubt this is worth full price for anyone but the most avid fans of zone-out flying. Those fans have a VERY limited selection of games to enjoy, so it's a must-have title in its own niche. The developer has been readily available and verbose in interactions with the community, which tipped me over the edge into buying.
In desperate need of more features, and existing ones need to be tightened up. I'm glad to have bought in early, but only because I believe in the future of the game and developer. If you've read down this far, at least head over to the forums and see how the dev interacts with the playerbase.
Thanks for your time.

I have been a flight simulator fan since playing Flight Simulator II for the first time on my Apple II back in 1984. I’ve played dozens of flight sims across as many platforms over the years, but none of them conveys the sense of soaring that Fugl is able to deliver. But a flight sim it is not — a meditative, zen-like experience that’s really like no other is what Fugl is.
I saw early forum discussions about Fugl when it was in its very first concept phases and asked the dev team if, as a flight game fan, I could have access - alpha test, etc. This was three years ago when a simpler version of the game was being developed on iOS devices. During that time it became the most enjoyable gaming experince I had ever had. I recall mentioning in my social media discussions of the game that the experince that is Fugl was worth purchasing an iPad for. It’s a magical experience that so far I’ve put over 200 hours into, easily.
The meditative soaring, the exhilaration of “threading the needle” — diving into a craggy cave and out the other side, and the striking voxel aesthetic all come together to create a singular experience. I just can’t recommend Fugl enough.

Although definitely hosting some crippling faults, Tactical Intervention does its job in delivering fast-paced, intense action that makes you really feel like you're holding a shotgun, pulling the trigger repeatedly for your life.

Please note that this is an Early Access review, and therefore the concerns I've raised could easily be resolved in future updates.
Now this one is interesting. I *love* the voxel graphics. The flight model is passable, and the ambient sound is great.
The water effects - when turned up - are fantastic, and there's just so much wildlife. The world doesn't feel dead or empty at all.
Night-time sees lights come on until the world looks like something out of the Avatar movie.
Where this falls down, however... I honestly was under the impression that the voxel-space could be almost infinite - you should never see repetition, or at least, very little.  What I got, however, was extremely disappointing.
I would be literally flying past a landmark - an easily recognised jagged bit of rock, by a strangely shaped lake, for example - and just as I was flying past it, I could see it coming up in front of me again, and again, and again.
I was genuinely flying around the game-world every eleven seconds. I timed it. There's only so much exploring you can do when you can fly from one side of the world to the other in eleven seconds.
Now, having said that, it seemed to be only in one direction. If the repetition kicked in going East-West, it didn't seem to kick in going North-South... so it seemed to be a very long and thin world, for some reason. I don't know if it's a bug, but it's a bit of a deal-breaker for me in a game that's all about finding new things to look at.
The flying around was nice, but ultimately unsatisfying. The reason to play a game like this, for me, is to relax and tune out for a bit. I couldn't find myself doing that in this game, when compared even to something more action focused like "Superflight".
In short, it's a nice concept with some fantastic features - but it just left me feeling a bit disappointed, over all. Perhaps worth it if it's on significant sale, but I certainly couldn't recommend it for full price, at this stage of development.

Ok let's set this aside. The game could have been called a number of other, less uncomfortable names. Yes, you're spending time killing yourself but the reason is you're trying to wake up from a dream. This game is not enforcing, endorsing or encouraging suicide.
Yeah. Your character is a slob who fell asleep drinking a beer. As you began dreaming, your brain noticed the bottle dropping but you can't get out of the 'hub' until you complete a number of other dreams. Each one has you figuring out how you'll kill yourself to escape the dream, with 25 total dreams in all.
It's... imaginative. I'd argue it's good, but as a game it's not very replayable. The platforming has a weird jiggle when you climb (which you'll do often), so I doubt people will target it for speed runs. But will you have fun over the 5-6 hours you'll play? Absolutely.
The game has lots of really great references. Jurassic Park, Mario, Portal, Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥and plenty others. The graphics are well designed (although at first I though the game was an asset flip, due to wide variances in quality), and the sound/music is passable, never being annoying and never being something I could listen to outside this game.
The game has roughly 50% puzzles that have you figuring stuff out, and 50% platforming to a very obvious goal. The platforming is twitchy but not something that stops you from beating the game. The story isn't great (although being light, I don't see it as being bad). I encountered three bugs that required restarting the game due to items falling out of the level or not triggering the end.
If you like active puzzles and you don't mind everything being from a first person perspective, then you might like the game. And if you're ok with shorter games (4.9 hours under my belt) and if you're ok with a game not being perfect but still being good, you might like the game.

I have nothing but good things to say about this game. It hits all the right stylistic notes, has engaging and imaginative gameplay, deaths never feel cheap, exploration is rewarded, the difficulty curve climbs both smoothly and masterfully, the visuals are joyfully nostalgic and the music is a pitch-perfect homage.
My only minor gripe is the price point, which has always seemed just a touch too high for a game of somewhat limited size and scope. It's a fair price for the quality, but when there are massive, DLC-rich Triple A games bundles out there for the same price, it makes Shovel Knight seem like a risky bet. Had this game been $10, I'd have bought it when it came out, but for some reason that $15 price tag made me hesitate. That said, assuming you enjoy MegaMan-style sidescrolling platformers even a little, you'll absolutely get $15 of enjoyment out of it.
And, unlike many retro-style games out there, there's a very good chance that you'll actually finish Shovel Knight, rather than play it for a few hours and then move on to something more engaging.

Lets talk about the constant war being the dev Daybreak games and the community.
The dev constantly tries to fix things which are wrong with the game. But when they do there are others things like skillgap which bassicly gets reduced, this could be because of the declining playerbase and that the main playerbase are mostly veterans or already experienced players.
The community itself is extremely self centered and toxic. When you bassicly use a grenade they call you a noob so on so forth for every mechanic or weapon you use. The only thing this community wants to see is you to be in the open and bassicly with your hands in the air for a free 2 tap rather than a challenge.
Other things like gun reworks or adding new guns like the SMG have failed drasticly.
Pistols : Some are usefull like the M9 but the rest are just not worth picking up unless you have too.
AR/AK -- The AR Seems to just a gun about who can spray better and get that lucky 2 tap on the head or just about spraying people down instead of aiming and knowing where to shoot and to get headshots because of the decreased bullet drop this patch.
Shotgun -- Balanced better this patch than the last one but still has a lot of inconsistency issues.
Melee Weapon : Useless nobody ever picks them up.
Sniper : In a really good place in my opinion 1 shot headshots and 2 times the body for a fast paced game like H1Z1 is a great standing for the sniper as a gun.
Cars/ATV : I just think with the current map there are just too many cars in itself and just too few ATV's. Yes it is a fast paced game. But that doesn't mean it has to bassicly be a pug fight with 2 guys with each a copy car and an AR constantly.
The Map :  I think the map is fine in some position but some areas like the Carnaval seriously need some cleaning up or just need to be straight up removed because everything in those areas are just all over the place.
Cheating : On EU and NA East I think it is not really an issue but it seriously is an issue on NA West and Asia and Australia. Even thanks to this and the declining playerbase because of H1Z1 being from banned streaming in China. NA West and the Australian server are just not worth playing on because it takes 10-15 minutes to even fill the lobby and start the game.
Z1 : In the last tournament daybreak announced the return of fan favorite map called Z1.
This map overall has less car spawns. I think in my opinion that it will bring back some players because they loved the old map. But because of the bad mechanics and the movement/combat in its current situation, I think it will drive people of really quickly out of frustration.
In the end I could suggest it if your looking for a fast paced arcade like Battle Royale. But not in it's current state.
As of now i seriously hope both the community and Daybreak can get their hands together and come to a solution on how to get the game back on its feet just like in Pre season 3 and back in Z1.

This game is definitely a five-star achievment for the Jurassic Park franchise. Gameplay mechanics are smooth, being able to control dinosaurs and other prehistoric creatures is an amazing feature, and fighting classic dinosaur and human villains provides nostalgia to those people who have faithfully hung on to every moment of the movies. The game stays true to its source with character quotes and famous scenes from the movies done up Lego style. The ability to easily switch characters using the character wheel feature is very convenient. The dinosaurs and prehistoric creatures are very fluid in their movements and the sounds they make.
Overall, this game is great. It really harkens back to the movies we all love so much and I would recommend this title to any Jurassic Park fan or anyone who is a fan of dinosaur-based games in general. You will not be disappointed. The $39.99 that this game costs plus the about $5 in DLC added to that if you opt for it is well worth every penny of Steam wallet credit.

Fishing mechanics and all items used therein: 9/10
Environments and graphics: 8/10
Economy (with and without real money):

The new economy is, in a word, TERRIBLE. It's a grindy, unrewarding nightmare for both new and veteran players, designed deliberately to force people to buy the ridiculously overpriced Bait Coins.

As a fishing game, it's great! Easily the best title in its genre for both mechanics and graphics. I've tried many -- Euro Fishing, Ice Lakes, World of Fishing, even browser-based Flash games, and (the oldest one that I still have in my library) Rapala Pro Fishing -- and this is only one I've put more hours into than RPF.
I really liked this game when I first got a hold of it. I bought many of the DLCs, and even a few for some friends. I really wanted to support the dev team... back when things in this game were actually affordable. That said, the economy has changed a lot for the worse since I started.
The prices of all the new DLCs are overblown and appear to be nothing more than just another part of this move towards a desparate cash grab. Thankfully, some of the older (better) DLCs are still available, and they turn up in Steam's search results for "fishing planet).
But DLCs won't get you far anymore because now we have "bait coins", an avaricious idea designed to force players to shell out real money for an unlimited license -- for EACH ZONE! But even if one were to accept the model the coins built on, the prices are nonetheless exorbitant.
Well, some people might argue that most things in F2P can be attained without real money. Sure, you could (if you had nothing but free time on your hands). Unfortunately, the trip costs alone with standard currency are ludicrous. Coins aside, travel and daily fees cost an arm and a leg for new players. Even many long-time users have found themselves grinding constantly in low-level zones just to earn enough for the next trip. Never mind the licenses, which are now all temporary except for those purchased with real money. Meanwhile, a permanent license for one of the high-level zones costs as much as a new AAA title... Seriously? There is NOTHING in that zone that could possibly warrant such a price (yes, I've been to the Alaska map), and you get NOTHING else with that purchase.
Perhaps the only reason I even still hang around is that,

Hooooo boy.
Fugl.... ok.
I'm going to try and do this wonderful little game the justice it deserves. Here we go...
Why should you, or are you someone who should, buy Fugl?
I can understand why you'd be cautious. It's... unique.
If you're someone that's ever stumbled across an old game that you know people are going to think you're crazy for playing cause it looks like crap but it has this hook that's just so good, you don't care about everything else, so you sink months into it anyway; you'll not regret buying this game.
If you've ever found yourself spending more time in free-fly modes, or just zooming around in games with open levels and flying mechanics, than you ever really did playing the story; then you're going to enjoy spending time with Fugl.
If you're not heaps worried about a few bugs and crashes, or are willing to put a little time into troubleshooting; then you'll not be disappointed in the slightest.
The game had a few issues on launch, I got caught in a crash loop that required deleting / reinstalling and for a week or so, couldn't progress past the third biome. These issues have both been resolved that I can see. I didn't really care either way.
Fugl is simple. You fly around, from biome to biome, enjoying the freedom and the wonderful sound and effects the game produces when you start to gather speed. There's not really a goal that I know of, Fugl's enjoyment comes not from achieving but from simply observing and exploring. There's interactions to be had but they're not essential to the enjoyment. Also, the world itself and the interactions that do take place hint at possibilities yet uncovered, I think there's more to Fugl than first meets the eye.
You occasionally turn into other birds and sometimes animals that aren't birds. Like a monkey.
But you're still kinda a bird.... just also a monkey...
It's cool, you'll see...
The ambient noise, the noises from different animals and the environment around you, are beautiful and lend a somewhat magical quality to the world as you explore. There's so much enjoyment to be had with the simple beauty found in the world's randomised generation; things like landing and floating peacefully in a river at the bottom of a tree covered canyon, or flying with eagles around the tips of mountains, will inspire more awe than the pixelised art style suggests should be possible.
That's a point too. If you find yourself turned off by the screenshots, well, you may have trouble enjoying Fugl.
I personally feel the art style - the ever-morphing, voxel look - lends itself well to the game's style but I could understand if you're someone for which it might be a deal breaker.
The controls.... well... they work. For me they took a bit to adjust to. Once you uncover the rather obscure mechanics involved with flying and morphing into other animals, you'll have a lot of fun. Just, if you're having issues stick with it.
It's worth it.
The game also includes some editors for the world and for individual animals, allowing you to customise a perfectly multicoloured bird-monkey - just the way nature intended. These editors, however, are a tad complicated and appear to be designed for someone far smarter than myself. I admit I've done little to actually learn how they work but hey, I'm not going to subtract any points over it. It's nice they're there but it's unlikely you'll get any serious use out of them.
Ultimately, Fugl is just pretty, it captures the feelings of being free and unrestrained and gives you a world where you can be a part of something but also step away and leave behind on a whim. It's a calm game with gentle and subtle rewards for the right kind of player. If you're that kind of player, well hey, you likely know it already.
For anyone unsure, look at it this way, Fugl's an algorithmically created art piece. The generated worlds, the colours, the art style, even the very mechanics (flying, morphing, etc) are a part of that. They're all a bit unique, special and in the end, mean Fugl can stand on its own. It doesn't need to fit in with anything, it is what it is.
Will you spend years of your life perfecting and playing Fugl? No.
I think, however, you will enjoy the time you have with it and feel richer for the experience.
For the price point, I feel it's definitely worth getting it, if nothing else just to enjoy it for what it is. A work of art.
Give it a go. ;)

I don’t like the game’s title and despite what its developer states on the Store Page, it was an entirely uninspired choice, even if grim subjects such as depression or suicide aren’t depicted as being central to the plot. They are. And this is a failed attempt at dark humor which gets somewhat saved by the gameplay being more than decent and thus counterbalancing the intial absurdity. Ironically, Suicide Guy is also developer’s Chubby Pixel, finest project to date. Their previous Steam releases were leaning more towards shovelware than anything noteworthy. I’m glad that they learned at least partially, from past mistakes.
Where to begin? The nameless and nearly silent protagonist is an overweight and bearded man wearing a stained tank top while watching TV, drinking beer and literally dreaming about his next fast food meal. Homer Simpson called and wants his stereotypes back. It would have been fine and dandy, were it not for the fact that these dream sequences feel more like a reimagining of “A Nightmare on Elm Street” except that the middleman gets cut from the equation by our protagonist ending his own life each time.
A rather inappropriate topic, masked as “lighthearted fun” through the help of the large pixel graphics resembling a cartoon style of sorts. Not even Ren & Stimpy stooped so low, but let’s make an extra effort and consider the nightmare suicides as necessary to the plot. Bob has to escape his mental scars through these nasty dreams somehow and perhaps that’s his “special” way of coping with the pain. It really isn't anything coherent to discuss about here. The levels don’t connect in any way to each other. This is a case in which being random or abstract, isn’t helping at all.
Another Unity Engine 5 project. Nothing to complain about it though, since the visual style and the many pop culture references found throughout its numerous levels (24+Hub), are spot on. Sure, these stages don’t take that long to complete, yet they are working their hardest to ensure that at least stability and visual diversity are supporting Suicide Guy. No frame rate dips to report, even when running it in 4K and the absence of any UI or HUD, simplifies the capturing and future use of screenshots.
I mentioned that out hero is nearly silent since he occasionally sounds like an inarticulate Santa. I was half-expecting him to shout a “Ho-Ho-Ho!” at the end of each level only that he’s too busy killing himself to worry about that. The soundtrack is relaxing to the point of being eerie considering that the dream sequences are in fact, less subtle nightmares. Tranquility Lane from Fallout 3, comes to mind.
Perhaps the biggest saving grace in Suicide Guy’s case and apart from its interesting visuals, are the gameplay elements which ensure that you won’t get bored. One major advantage to level design which make zero sense on its own or when grouped together, is that as a content creator you’re free to go crazy with the nightmares and their topics. And crazy they went. First few levels are short and "sweet". Jumping off buildings, jumping in front of a train, you get the idea.
They don’t go into detail with a graphic depiction of violence or the aftermath, since we’re constantly reminded that these are dreams from which the protagonist does wake up. Only to find himself locked on the inside within an empty fast food joint. This functions as the game’s hub from which all subsequent 24 levels can be unlocked or replayed at any given time. The incentive to do so, comes in the form of small statues depicting the hero. Yes, what serious platformer wouldn’t feature some form of collectibles?
Discussing now about the platforming sections themselves, I was pleased to notice that they were pretty much flawless. The right amount of challenge, the occasional puzzle involving the combination of certain objects and linearity which doesn’t really bother since the rapid succession of themes, leaves little room for repetition. One moment you’re manipulating a Portal Gun imitation and the next you’re racing towards the sun in a space ship. Yes, creative ways of killing yourself. No surprise there, I guess.
If you were to judge this game just from the perspective of its gameplay, it would be a competent title indeed. With modern graphics, a cute visual style and the diversified challenge to keep most fans of the genre with they eyes glued to the screen. But then comes along, the absurdity behind this random succession of stages. Never fully explained and always ending with the player meeting his untimely demise. Why?
I’d really like to know just who thought that using suicide as a narrative thread and means of story progression, was a feasible idea. It ain’t. Some topics are better left untouched and regarded as taboo, lest you make it clear that good taste is nowhere to be found. I won’t rate the game down any lower since the gameplay didn’t waste my time. The story did and I’ll make sure to be more selective in the future.

This you don't have in Tactical Intervention because there are enemies coming at your spawn every 5 seconds! Oh, yeah, and you need to rent your weapons in this game, either with the virtual currency or with real money.

It that a racing game ? is that a relaxation game ? It's hard to tell. If you play Absolute drift like you would a normal racing game, you're soon gonna hug the walls. You need to understand how to make proper uses of theses cars that will slide at the slightest opportunity...but once you do, you get "into the zone", a zone of slow movement and perfect curves, making for a sort of zen like attitude
That "zen" aspect permeates all the game. The most obvious aspect of that is the graphic style. The game is almost pure white, keeping the touch of colors only for the elements relevant for scoring purposes. Across that white canvas, the dark marks of your tires feels like the ink on a calligraphy paper.
But the sound design is also part of the same theme. Minimalist, made only of your engine noise, and small bips and chimes sound that are there to convey are well you're doing. This is all accompanied by a muted soundtrack, that is just punchy enough to want to race, but zen enough that it's not gonna detract you from the calming aspect of the game.
All in all, it's a pleasure to get that perfect drift curve, you're instantly rewarded by a nice feeling of gliding, the "bip bip bip" indicating your growing multiplier, and a beautiful "inked" track behind you.
But the fact that the game has a soothing effect doesn't mean it's a simple one. The many challenges are there to test your drifting skills, and you will learn much by trying to finish them all. Moreover, for those who like scoring games, every track has a leaderboards, so you can enjoy yourself forever trying to beat the best scores on all tracks. It doesn't mean you have to do it, but it's there if you wish for it.
For most people though, i suspect the challenges will already provide enough content. You will find race tracks for tight cornering and frequent change of directions, arenas for a more free style approach to scoring, and finally some twisty mountain tracks where controlling your speed is key. That variety keeps the game fresh, allowing to jump from one event to the other whenever you feel like it. It took me 16h to finish them all, and I enjoyed my stay with the game

I felt like I needed to write this even though I never review games.
After playing 10 games I've got a basic idea of the gameplay. If you need to know the basics watch one of the videos.
Having to determine who is the infected whilst also preparing for the first blackout is challenging and both sides seem to be balanced. The communication needed with the team feels really fresh as a game mechanic and it is really rewarding to successfully call someone out on their deception.
The principal of this game is tremendous, the idea behind it is very fun and thrilling when it goes right. When it goes wrong however the game can be very lackluster. When there is no one in the game with mic's it can be frustrating to find the infected, down them and not have anyone communicating or willing to help / deny the claims. Without communication the game just doesn't work. If you have 5 buddies all willing to play this won't be a problem and I can guarentee the game will shine in this situation, just make sure your all not using discord instead of ingame chat while playing.
I've found no glaring in game bugs as some people suggested there would be however there is a huge bug with the game end screen. 8/10 games skipped the recap screen, kicking me to the lobby instantly. This really denied me and anyone else visual, audio or statistical feedback. The win feels hollow without a victory screen and defeats can feel confusing with no room to learn from your mistakes. The massive issue with not having a consistent feedback is you in some cases will never get to find out wether the guy you called out and killed was actually infected which tbh sucks alot.
The idea is there, and it's a great idea. The polish however is not, at all which is really disappointing as I want to like this game ALOT. The now free to play pricetag makes the game extremely playable however even if it is for a few hours to make up your own mind.
Definitely pick it up and give it a go to see if it's for you and your mates.

The question: is call of duty ww2 a good game?
The awnser is "meh".
The zombies is the same old zombies that you know and love with some new ideas thrown in to the mix. With the adjustment to a more horror style, it brings zombies to a fairly good crossroad. The lack of the ability to rebuild windows removes the easy points in the beginning, but this is the only thing that this actually removes. More zombie types only makes you have to change your in the moment decisions by running from the explosive holding zombie instead of running throught the horde before you. The easter egg is given to you by the developers. There is a notebook that will tell you how to solve the easter egg, but it can be vague at times.
The multiplayer is full of the same hackers, trolls, and twelve year olds just like the pervious call of duty titles. But with the addition of divisions and the "war" mode, this call of duty is only some what more complex. The divisions allow you to have extra perks that only that division can control. Some divisions give certain weapon types some added benefits like assault rifles get bayonets and SMGs' get suppressors. These divisions can also be leveled up to allow the unlocking of more abilities. War modes gives you several objectives to complete in order to succeed. Depending on which side your on, you will have to attack several objectives or defend these objectives from the enemy team. But be warned that the same people who played the previous call of dutys are still here.
The campain seems as if it got some attention, but still falls to the old flaws that all modern call of duty games have. The characters seem to have some personality and motives, but these characters emote. This is a slight revelation compared to the black faced character from infinity ward and the nap inducing story archs from treyarch. But this campaign still involves the terrible levels of driving a vechicle. The tank in one section is actually undrivable. It controlls so bad that you will question if the developers wanted you to give up and play multiplayer or zombies. Let me also add that this game has stealth sections. Why does every game developer that makes any game but a stealth focused game want to add stealth to a non stealth game? It only makes that level unbearable to play because they don't acuatlly understand how sealth actually works.
But in short, I give this game an eight out of ten. Points for a good zombies game and a multiplayer that isnt completely cancer. But points are removed for the shotty campaing and many bugs that still exist.
It doesn't suck.

Oh boy... I mean, I stumbled upon this title quite randomly and it hit me straight in the face, purple phallic bat style. Within the first five minutes of the game, you will be dangling off a chopper, on top of a vault you've just heisted, raining shells on a bunch of cops. Oh, and you are wearing a mask of your gangsta leader. When questioned about it (what's the point of wearing a mask of YOURSELVES), the reply goes - "ultrapostmodernism".
I am seriously glad to see that there is a development crew out there who understands that games aren't real. Even fantasy games tend to take themselves too seriously, meticulously following the limitations of the real world. But why, for Johnny Gat's sake? WHY? In virtuspace, you can literally do or become anything. I'm really jealous of the game devs, they must've had a blast.
One prerequisite of enjoying this, is obviously not taking yourself seriously either, and be able to follow, understand and accept the raunchy absurd humour. It's like a Monty Python version of GTA, with cocaine sprinkled all over it for touch. And it has everything. Yes, everything. The car and customisation part (ok, and the boobs) remind me of NFSU2, which was about as cool as a game could get for a teen. You have heists, assassinations, space aliens, tanks, more tanks, in fact all kinds of military vehicles, choppers, mutants, zombies, penthouses, jet skis, parties and pools.
One very important part of the game is the understanding of an open world - and that you are in a GAME - the mechanics for operating anything are wildly easy. You get to drive anything you can steal, at unbelievable ease - cars, bikes, helicopters, military jets, speedboats, tanks, jet skis, airplanes, you name it.
If you let it, the game will be some serious fun.

- Not historically accurate but it is CoD so who cares, you play it for fun not for historical accuracy.
- Not the best optimization but Campaign and Zombies generally never stutter. Multiplayer can sometimes.
- Balance is generally good in the game, you can use almost any weapon in the game and still get kills if you're skilled enough with it. This means you get a lot less repetitive gameplay if you use a weapon that gives you a challenge.
- No customization for the German Army in Multiplayer which sucks.
- Whilst I've barely played 2 hours of the campaign, from what I've played it has been fun.
- For some reason the game is split between Call of Duty: WW2 for campaign and then Call of Duty: WW2 - Multiplayer for Multiplayer/Zombies. It is unknown why but anyway.
Overall it is a really good game and I recommend to anyone looking for a casual shooter.
Edit: Since I have mostly played Multiplayer my hours don't show as it only shows campaign hours.

Deceit is a fun yet very troubled game. I think if the developers could fix some of the huge flaws that the game has, it would be a fantastic game. The base elements are solid and leads for some funny and interesting social interactions, Such as lying that someone drank a blood bag or lying that someone showed up as infected on the scanner. The problems however are glaring. One of my biggest gripes about this game is the lack of servers present. I play on US servers and still get constantly paired with Thai, Chinese, Russian, Indian and Brazillian people. It is to the point where at certain times I've been in lobbies where every single person speaks a different language. A language barrier removes a lot of the fun of deceiving people. Around 2/6 people on US servers don't speak english. I can only imagine how much worse this is on european servers. Not to mention the game is also filled with bugs. Pressing the interact button only works about 75% of the time on blood bags, doors won't close sometimes, and loading screens persist into the game and will not go away. Not to mention the atrocious hitboxes, when someone moves their hitbox sometimes lags behind or run ahead of the model. The game is free and you lose nothing buy downloading it, but the developers need to know that people are not happy with their neglect.

Earth Defense Force 4.1: The Shadow of New Despair, or more commonly referred to as EDF, is a third person shooter that puts you in the shoes of an unnamed soldier of the Earth Defense Force that is tasked with locating and eradicating giant insects and robots from across the globe. Your mission is simple – kill everything that moves.
You’re given four class options before starting: Ranger, Fencer, Wing Diver or Air Raider. Rangers are your typical versatile infantry class, able to equip a variety of guns, sniper rifles, or a plethora of explosives and specialty weapons. Your next option is the Air Raider, a class that has the ability to call in buffs such as shields, turrets, healing modules and heavy armor, such as tanks, helicopters and a slew of different mechanized vehicles. Your third option is the lightly-armored, agile and swift-moving Wing Diver, an all-female crew of airborne infantry that use energy weapons and jetpacks to quickly move about the battlefield. Your final option is the Fencer, EDF’s dual-wielding tank, comprised of thick armor and massive cannons at the expensive of maneuverability.
The entirety of the game will pit your class of choice and a handful of NPC AI against hordes of insects, robots, dragons and ships as you battle your way through every level. An improved feature over previous installments is the presents of your AI counterparts, which brings a greater feeling of an army, rather than just you versus the world. Some levels lack a sufficient amount at the expense of a higher difficulty, but overall the game doesn’t feel as void of human life as it once did.
There’s not much for plot aside from the simple “save the world” dynamic, set in a cheesy Japanese monster movie environment. I cannot stress this enough:
and it is meant to be. The dialog is ridiculous, over-the-top and for all accounts just plain goofy, but the game knows that and plays it up all too well. I never felt the game suffered from a lack of plot or bad dialog, as I was far too enthralled with the sheer amount of destruction I was causing in every level to really care.
While progressing through the level, you’re only real task aside from dishing out death while avoiding it yourself is pickups you get from enemies in the realm of armor and weapons. Armor drops increase your overall character’s “armor” rating, which stands in place of a traditional unit health. Weapon drops give you a random chance of finding a new or upgraded version of a weapon you might already have. However, more often-than-not, you might find yourself with two dozen of the same weapons you already own, which can be rather annoying.
This process of grinding is necessary for higher levels and increased difficulty settings, so expect to replay levels to gather extra armor and weapons so you can tackle particularly tricky levels. During my time playing I never felt that grinding was particularly time consuming, nor did it break the momentum of the game either; EDF is just too damn fun so any issues I ran into didn’t damper my enjoyment at all.


Overall, EDF is a tremendous amount of fun. It’s easy to pick up and play in short bursts, or for long marathons. If you haven’t played any of the past installments, you won’t be missing anything by picking up this title. I highly suggest it if you are even the least bit interested; give it a try. You won’t regret it.

is only the third game in the Assassin's Creed series I've yet played: I keep to the order in which the games were initially released. Ubisoft got this game, the second one featuring Ezio Auditore as the protagonist, out in March 2011, three and a halve years ago. Having played it relatively soon after the original
, I feel it natural to compare the two games to each other. This makes even more sense since the story of AC II really coninues in
: not only do the same characters appear in both games, chronologically too they follow nicely upon each other.
Brotherhood starts off splendidly, with a recapture of the final sequences of AC II which flows naturally into the new twists which the well-known story of the struggle between Assassins and Templars about world-changing artefacts takes. After the initial (short) part of the game that functions as a tutorial, I was taken straight into the city where almost all of the action takes place: Rome. The fact that there is only one major city here, compared to the two (Firenze and Venice) and the countryside of the original game, makes for a huge difference. Rome of around 1500 comes to live in
in the most fantastic imaginable way. First of all, the map is HUGE: there are 12 districts (including the Vatican and some outer area's which have a rural sense about them), and running from one side of the city to the other would cost you at least ten-fifteen minutes (happily, horses are allowed in the city and there is a well-thought-off fast-travel system). Secondly, the development team has obviously taken the utmost care in analyzing how Rome anno 1500 looked like - and that's really quite different from modern-day Rome. During the first ten (!!) hours or so in-game, I mostly just walked around, discovering the city, marvelling at all the details in the buildings and eagerly reading the information provided for almost every single church, Roman building or other landmark. During my entire playthrough, I felt like being a tourist catapulted 500 years back to a place I love so much. That's quite some accomplishment, and I would even go so far as to call Rome the main character of the game, not Ezio.
That's not only because of the painstaking detail with which the "Cità Eterna" is being depicted, but it's also due to some problems with the concept of the game. Not only is the world almost entirely accessible from the start of the game, the number of side-missions is daunting, certainly compared to the main-story missions. Since I am a curious gamer, I tried some of these, than more of those missions, mixing it all up with the main storyline. Wrong! Almost every mission gives even more options afterwards, unlocking new factions or side-story lines, and they are of course all indicated on a over-cluttered map (which I had to zoom in really close to be able to read every sign on it). After a further ten hours or so into the game, I started feeling overwhelmed: there was SO much to do, to explore, to try, and it could all be done at my own initiative. Now this open-world concept may appeal to many gamers, but I like more of a narrative element, or at least a good backbone of a main story. And this exactly where
tends to falter at times. Only by following the main story mission after mission (which I started doing after quite some time), did I refind the feeling of actually being Ezio Auditore, a feeling that had been so strong in AC II. Once I really plunged into it, the main storyline proved to be quite good, though not so compelling as the one in the previous game, and certainly much shorter (although this is more than made up for the number of side-missions and -excursions).
In all other departments than the identification with Ezio and the overdose of side-activities,
does shine, just as I had hoped for. The walking/climbing/jumping and whatever more of Ezio is so fluent, that I actually felt becoming "good" at it, but as with the other AC games, using an Xbox 360 controller really is a must. Combat has been greatly improved upon alreay in AC II, and this game even adds more possibilities, all very natural. The biggest change is the addition of the Brotherhood: a group of Assassin's I could train by giving them missions abroad, and whose help I could call for when needed. Graphically, the game still is a gem, also after a couple of years. Only musically things could have been better: the music could have used a bit more variety.
All things put together,
is a worthy successor to AC II, but it is flawed by trying to do too much, and all of that at once. It's not on the same steallr height as its predecessor, but it's still a very, very good game. Buy it if you tried and liked AC I and/or II, but I wouldn't recommend it as a first dive into the realm of the Assassins.
Gameplay: 24/30 (would have been higher with a tighter storyline)
Graphics: 18/20
Sound: 7/10
Technical: 8/10 (I don't like Uplay as an extra "shell", but that's just how it is, and otherwise it's very stable)
Longelivety: 9/10 (there is some MP which is mostly out of use, but SP alone gives you dozens of hours of gameplay)
Steam-integration: 5/10 (as with almost all other Ubisoft titles: they try to promote Uplay...)
Personal appreciation: 9/10
Overall: 80/100

Two Really Big problems for this game:
- The game itself is not hard, you just get killed by things you can't see, or if you can see them, you've literally never encountered it before and there is no indication that it will kill you.  It's more frustrating than skill intensive.
- The design seems to contradict itself.  On one hand, the game wants you to play it over and over, to have the satisfaction of upgrading your ship.  On the other hand, the game builds up each session painfully slowly, instead of throwing you right into the action.
Overall, here's what a play session looks like: slay exceedingly easy enemies for two minutes, some crazy visual effects happen for no discernable reason, run into some invisible boulder and die.  Repeat.  Not what I would call gratifying.

-The visuals are full of particle effects and filter changes, which can get a mess too often. Between those changes, you'll often lose track of what is on the screen, and what damages you or not. Most of the times, you'll die from something you didn't see. Also, it has performance issues later in the game, where particle effects are too many. I have a GTX660Ti and a 3.4GHz Quad Core... and it dropped to 5 fps at one time. That's pretty bad. But it ran mostly well on it. Still a reason to beware.
-Bugs. Well, everytime I quit the game it crashed. That's not a big deal. Everytime I tried to see the Scores (as this is mostly as arcade game), it crashed. That's a problem now. And highly diminished the game's value. If there is no one to beat, why would I play more of it, after a while? Score attack games are fueled by.. well, score. This game has it broken. There are also a lot of people who can't get the game to run.
-Dificulty Curve and balance. This is the worse part of the game. In the beginning, you're essentially running on trial and error, dying over and over until you learn how to get through certain things. But that's ok, learning the patterns and so on. But, as you progress through the game, it just gets a blurred mess in which there is no skill, and your score is mainly dependent on what you buy from the shop. And luck with the events you get. It's more of a grind-fest than struggling to get better at the game, since all you do after a while is to upgrade the ship and hope that the screen doesn't get too crumped with enemies and filters.
-All the modes are too similar to increase the game's longevity too much. There's no drive to really play them, since most don't change too much about the game. The big one being Pacifist, in which you can't shoot, only dodge.

I have to say that this game is pretty mediocore.  I realize that it's asking price is only $3 and for the amount of stages it has, 75, that's not necessarily unreasonable.  However, considering that the stages are just square rooms with a few barriers scattered around you can duck behind that doesn't offer much variety or novelty.  Plus I've frankly played games with more features and greater playability for free before, so that undermines this asking price tremendously.  If I had paid for the game, I'd ask for a refund because it's not worth paying anything for it in my opinion.
I haven't gotten past the first 25 stages and know that I won't because my interest in the game has already worn off, but I sincerely doubt that anything will drastically change from the first set of 25 stages to the last set.  If I'm wrong, nothing about what you are presented with in the game suggests otherwise, which is very poor communication and design.
The game itself plays well enough in the sense that there's no glaring problems.  The movement of your character is fluid and responsive, giving you enough control to move around the stage and dodge projectiles.  The projectiles aren't too fast to react to.  However, there's no real sense of progression in the game either.  Your character always dies in one hit and only shoots the same basic projectile - there aren't any power-ups, there's no advancement, you don't develop and grow stronger.  You beat a stage and go to the next one where there's a few more enemies or they are a bit more powerful.  With no storyline, no portrayal of events or rationale for what's going on, you have no motivation to keep going forward since your character never improves.
The game meets the basic requirements for a fair top-down perspective shooter but doesn't give you a carrot to chase after or strive for.  It actually becomes frustrating when you spawn in on a new stage, with no awareness of what it will hold, and get killed by a new, powerful foe and have to try again with nothing to help you other than trial and error, rinse and repeat until you get it attempts.  Until you learn where the enemy spawners are located and wipe them out early.
If the developer could greatly expand upon this first draft of a game I think they have the basic capabilities to make a competent game.  Otherwise though, I'd avoid this for something more developed and fleshed out.

I have purchased Fugl as soon as I got wind of it's early access release. Sadly, my 3 years old laptop sporting an AMD card had firmly refused to run it. I've sent an email to the dev and got response the next day. Within 3 weeks, they managed to get the game to work on my card, and I've been flapping my boxy wings happily ever since.
Now that's what I call customer support.
Fugl's main draw is pretty clear at first glance. When GPUs became mainstream, this kind of voxel aesthetic has fallen out of favor. Which is a shame, because voxel graphics has much the same charm as pixel art do. A lot is left to the imagination with enough to stimulate your brain to make it work.
For more than a decade I longed to walk the pixelated deserts of Outcast, and now Fugl's world is about the only place where you can get a piece of that experience. In my opinion that alone is worth the asking price.
One thing to keep in mind though: Fugl is not a game. There are no goals, no fail-states, no good old shootin' and killin'. So if you are looking for gameplay and mechanical challenge, this is not it. As of now, Fugl is solely about the power fantasy of being able to fly.
But if you are willing to spend some quality time with your own imagination, you are going love this birdie very much.
As for me, I can't wait to see how it's will grow and expand during it's tenure in early access.
I dig it.

I don't know how this game has such high reviews.
Honestly, I think it's because it's cheap, so kids, who don't know what quality is, can easily convince their mom and/or pop let them get this game (granted they don't say the super edgy name)
Let's start with the name.
It's...really dumb. Obviously this is an incredibly minor and pedantic point to bring up, but wow. I feel like that name should be a PLACEHOLDER for a better name. It's just so...dumb.
Moving on.
Graphics: Alright, graphically, game is very cute. I adore cartoony looks in games, and this is no exception. Very pretty, and the lighting I also enjoyed.
Audio: No. It's so bad. Defeningly loud, and poorly compressed. Also the voice acting is just the same 3 grunts depending on what you're doing. Very boring in that regard. Also, the music in the "Mario" level is...ech. I hate music meant to emulate something, but clearly isn't that because copywrite laws. Also, there's this strange, VERY loud jingle when you load into a level.
Story: Eh. It's passable. You're a fat old guy, your beer is falling because you passed out, and now you need to wake up before the bottle hits the ground. To wake up, you have to go into several "sub-dreams" and kill yourself. It works, and that's the minumum I ask for in a game.
Gameplay: In short, Buggy, not fun, boring.
In slightly longer, First person platforming isn't good. It's just not. Combine that with very finicky climbing (Hope you like bouncing on ledges you're trying to climb up!) and it's even worse.
The puzzles, which I'll admit, I could only stomach through about 6, were oh so boring. Insulting even. Yes, they were early levels, but you have to engage me, or I'm not going to want to continue. I play puzzle games to be challenged, not to be pandered to.
One level involved climbing to ladders so as to click on two diferent objects, then I had to climb a long, boring spiral staircase, push a button, then go back to the main room.
That's it.
Invigorating stuff, isn't it?
Conclusion: Feels like something I'd find for free on gamejolt, that I would play for about as long as I did before getting bored with it. Only this time I feel insulted knowing I gave them money. Thank god for refund policy! Would not recomend purchasing, even on sale.

Released several years after the original Portal 2 game this mod sports some tremendously great levels! There are overall five chapters and they include several levels (or test chambers). Some more than the other. As the title implies our protagonist is called Mel and - similarly to Chell - she is facing an A.I. as the antagonist of the game.

This is what you are. An innovator. Mel is an Olympian, to be specific. But astronauts and war heroes are also welcome in the '50s where this game takes place. You'll just love to hold the '50s version of the Portal gun in your hands, believe me! The initial part of the story is similar to the train journey experienced in the first two (but mainly the first) Half Life games: you go through a tunnel seeing various rooms and you understand you are underneath a huge building complex. All the way you are greeted (and treated) by the then CEO of Aperture Science. The dialogue and voice acting are great!

So, your task is to get into an elevator and begin a kind of test that you'll eventually never get to see. You wake up and while Virgil (your A.I. companion) impersonates Johnson's voice later on he reveals this was a trick and you've been in some hibernation and several years have passed. Your job is now crystal-clear: there's a new A.I. to eliminate!

Pretty much everything returns from Portal 2; the mechanics remain the same but the particle field now has a red-coloured version that can disintegrate the player. Also, the mobster-looking turrets are fun (and deadly) to look at. Funny thing is that after playing the first two games and checking their test chambers in an advanced version I thought this mod would have a moderate difficulty for me. I had to realise I needed to look up the solution occasionally for a couple of levels. Not only that but once I finished the story mode I realised you can replay all of it with more difficult chambers!

And know Mel, too! It is not just for Portal fans but even for those who haven't played the... erm... Portal genre, I guess. There are a few nods here and there - references to the original game and, naturally, a handful of secret achievements. I believe this is a great example what a great studio can achieve if it tries hard! The cake may be a lie, but this mod is not!

Deceit is a fun yet very troubled game. I think if the developers could fix some of the huge flaws that the game has, it would be a fantastic game. The base elements are solid and leads for some funny and interesting social interactions, Such as lying that someone drank a blood bag or lying that someone showed up as infected on the scanner. The problems however are glaring. One of my biggest gripes about this game is the lack of servers present. I play on US servers and still get constantly paired with Thai, Chinese, Russian, Indian and Brazillian people. It is to the point where at certain times I've been in lobbies where every single person speaks a different language. A language barrier removes a lot of the fun of deceiving people. Around 2/6 people on US servers don't speak english. I can only imagine how much worse this is on european servers. Not to mention the game is also filled with bugs. Pressing the interact button only works about 75% of the time on blood bags, doors won't close sometimes, and loading screens persist into the game and will not go away. Not to mention the atrocious hitboxes, when someone moves their hitbox sometimes lags behind or run ahead of the model. The game is free and you lose nothing buy downloading it, but the developers need to know that people are not happy with their neglect.

Arma 3 is definitely a step in the right direction for Bohemia Interactive, especially after their previous works.

I felt for a while that the LEGO games were losing their way. They were focusing on huge hubs and tiresome fetch quests. LEGO Batman 2 had a bit of that, but it also still had hundreds of environment puzzles. The environment puzzles stopped sharp with that game, however. LEGO Marvel Superheroes, LEGO Lord of the Rings, and LEGO The Hobbit were having none of that. So I really didn't enjoy those games. I was coming to the conclusion that I'd simply lost my love for the LEGO franchise.
It turns out those games were just really soulless cash-ins. When the LEGO Movie video game came along, I saw hints of the TT Games I loved from back around the time of LEGO Pirates of the Caribbean, and LEGO Harry Potter Years 1-4. It was representative of the golden years of the LEGO games, it opted for a number of small hubs, rather than one big one, andit had a lot of fun little puzzles and secrets.
LEGO Jurassic World follows this trend. Except it takes another step back toward when the LEGO games were actually good. I think that there are two teams working at TT Games (not including TT Fusion). One of the teams is making cheap cash-ins with giant world hubs and soulless grind quests; The other is making
which have none of that and are more similar to the halcyon days of TT Games LEGO efforts.
Not only that, but they allow you to play as dinosaurs so often! They've made some mistakes with the dinos, but it's still not as galling as in the awful Idiocracy-fuelled affair that is Jurassic World.
So... it's good. It's not that it's good because it's Jurassic Whatever, either. It's good because it's more of a return to form after one too many really bad LEGO games. If you thought that the LEGO games were at their height around the time of LEGO Pirates of the Caribbean and Harry Potter Years 1-4, then this one is for you. It'll make you smile.
