This game is amazing if you have a time machine.
I started playing TF2 around 2009 on a friend's account, mained medic, and thoroughly enjoyed what was something of a growing phenomenon with a revolutionary take on the FPS genre with class-based combat and some brilliant character design. In the better part of a decade, I've racked up over 2k hours across that and my current account learning the intricacies of just about every class and loadout, an amount of time out of my life only exceeded by my most favourite mmorpgs.
Unfortunately, all good things must come to an end, especially when a chronically inattentive development team starts struggling to remain relevant.
There are a number of gripes I could address regarding this game over the years, although for the most part I've taken the quirks of the Source Engine in its various incarnations in stride. However, in July 2016, Valve very suddenly launched a notorious update known as Meet Your Match, and as far as I am concerned, that was the beginning of the end of Team Fortress 2.
I will confess to a bias in that I absolutely despise matchmaking systems in online games, especially shooters. I do not enjoy having a server thousands of miles away force me to wait a completely nebulous amount of time while it decides what I get to play and whom I get to play it with. I have begrudgingly tolerated this method since it was popularised in 2004 by Halo 2, and now in recent years this insidious parasite on gaming has wormed its way, permanently it seems, into PC gaming. I was born in the 20th century. I got to watch gaming evolve from a couple sprites on a screen to the goliath that it is today. I got to watch as PC gaming went from the choice of gamers who wanted control over what they played, a choice that allowed games to be the free and glorious enterprise of the gestalt consciousnesses of gaming communities, to just another industry.
I know this methodology is here to stay, and I won't fight it. But that does not mean that I haven't grown weary of being at the mercy of pet projects by developers who, in their infinite confirmation bias, have concocted formulae to line up arbitrary numerical statistics into a glorified spreadsheet that merely appears logical, and then implemented them in a way that strips yet another dwindling layer of players' control of their gameplay experiences. I am weary of how developers continue to insist this is about "fairness" instead of maintaining total proprietary control over every single aspect of gameplay (indeed, this is exactly why it was so swiftly implemented on console games in the mid-2000s in the first place). But of course, how are those oh so profitable children on reddit and youtube going to know the difference when they don't know the first thing about statistics or probability? The profit margins, it would seem to any corporate board of directors, are secure.
But I digress.
To understand what a massive paradigm shift that update was, one must first understand what preceded it. Originally, as was the case with most online PC shooters before ~2012, the game servers were community-run, and joining a game was as simple as firing up the infinitely recognisable Valve server browser and double-clicking. Valve supplemented this with their own rotating servers, and a "Quickplay" system that could automatically select a server for players to join based on game mode. A unique aspect of this system was that community servers that met a small set of elegibility requirements were seamlessly blended in with the Valve public servers. I will not pretend that this system didn't have issues; a number of servers made it notorious for any number of abuses to generate ad revenue. However, the fundamental system itself represented a beautiful symbiosis that perfectly suited the very much free-for-all community-driven game that TF2 is.
And now, almost a year and a half later, I still honestly can't understand
they would annihilate that.
The addition of the new matchmaking system did two very important things. Firstly, it converted all Valve public servers to the matchmaking system, permanently removing a significant proportion of servers supporting the game's core gameplay from the server browser. Secondly, it pushed community servers by the wayside, stagnating to fend for themselves in a now very much disregarded format. This was not helped by the fact that the wait times were near-infinite and there were a number of clunky UI issues surrounding the system, assuming it didn't crash outright for the nth time. Valve, in their usual level of responsiveness, proceeded to address these at an utterly glacial pace. Following Meet Your Match, player activity plummeted, and it still hasn't really recovered, and now there are only a fraction of the number of community servers there once were. I remember in 2016 when many, most perhaps half-jokingly, declared that Overwatch by Blizzard was going to kill Team Fortress 2. Blizzard can't compare to Valve, because if anything ended up "killing" TF2, it was its own development team, or lack thereof.
TF2 today and TF2 two years ago are like night and day. Instead of being able to hop into quickplay or explore uncommon or even new maps in the server browser, you now have two options.  You can use the matchmaking system, where you'll end up waiting utterly ghastly amounts of time if you elect to play on something other than the half dozen GoldBowlFort maps we've all been playing for years, where a distressing amount of time the match is hideously unbalanced because one team is short by 3-4 players for the entire game. Alternatively, you can get into a community server that's inevitably an incomprehensible niçoise of broken mechanics and obnoxious mods populated by young children. The matchmaking system is effectively nothing more than a much slower version of quickplay, albeit offering xp points, which, as far as I can tell, are just a participation trophy. It could be removed tomorrow and one would not be able to tell the difference.
I am certainly not ungrateful for the recent Jungle Inferno update. Indeed, the combination of a pile of new maps and equipment, coupled with some sorely-needed UI changes and a revamped contract system, has been a breath of fresh air after a year of total chaos. That being said, a year to provide those changes, and new content that was ultimately the product of whatever is left of this development team's policy of adding new content by hurling darts at a wall of player mods, is hardly responsive, even by Valve standards. The fact that the fundamental implementation of the new contract system comes with an unsurprising price tag also hilariously misses the mark as to why that general style of gameplay is popular and retains players. Indeed, the sheer amount of hype that has arisen from Jungle Inferno is quite telling in that it shows how starved this game is for attention from its own development. Nonetheless, it fares as adequate atonement for what's happened to player activity, at least for now.
The main thing that I, personally, need to get off my chest is as follows, as vulgar as it might be.
Screw you Valve. You've taken a game that revolutionised and even codified an entire genre of video games and propelled you to untold wealth and  reduced it to a technically-alive carcass festering on life support through modernised trendwhoring. Instead of continuing to expand upon the fundamental platform of gameplay and community engagement that originally defined this game, you dumped an absurd amount of time and effort fixing a problem
. You've taken modern trends in gaming, with their endless proprietary control hidden behind the slick veneer of infinitely-replicated media presence, and halfheartedly forced it upon a game that could never fit that format. I want to play Team Fortress 2, not a screenshot of it stuck behind a matchmaking timer.

Having played this game for more than 1,000 hours now I can say that if you ever find Rainbow Six Siege on sale either on Uplay or Steam I would definitely recommmend picking this one up. The gameplay takes a more realistic approach compared to some of your other modern military shooters. One thing that I personally think that keeps the game fresh is the destructability of most of the walls you'll find in the game. The gadgets for the operators, some being more unrealistic than others (I'm talking about you echo), you'll find have a rock, papers, scissors kind of effect to the gameplay which compliments the game very well. The purchasable content within the game is relatively fair with the only thing being completely unpurchasable with renown (currency you get overtime) is some of the cosmetics for the operators or weapons. Even the two operators they release every so often can be purchased with renown after the one week period of their launch. Some things the game struggles with is unfrequent updates and less-than-stellar servers. Some things like bugs for the game don't get patched in hotfixes until it has already affected a majority of the community which is bad especially because they are trying to establish the game as a competitve shooter which can't be done without reliable and stable builds of the game. The other complaint being the servers which everyone I have talked to while playing this game have experienced. Its been known on all platforms that at launch on new updates that the servers struggle to stay up and eventually get taken down to say the least, can be frustrating, especially in the middle of a ranked match which has happened to me three times. The worst part about it is that it's counted as a loss. Thank god they have finally taken their health of the game seriously with the launch of Operation Health although some of ancient bugs in the game still linger. One last thing that I should address is the community. One thing that bothers me is the toxic community. Things like teamkilling and trolling still presists in the game and it gets even worse on free weekends on steam and uplay. Even though this can be at rarity just one experience of this for someone who just bought the game can set a bad impression and can result that player just quitting altogether. Overall, the game is worth your purchase if you can deal with some of the small things with the game that needs to be ironed out. If you do decide to pick it up, have fun and siege on!

This game has so much in store. Such a beautiful game, I have to say.
...No, it's not. That was a joke. The world is massive. Like, the size of... well, It's big. The play area and wildlife is vast, and free to explore free from any objective.
The world you fly in is perfect, huge, but sadly it does have a border. It would be phenominal if it were to be removed, but I don't think it really
to be. The shape of the land gives way for many, and I mean many opertunities to do stunts through tunnels while flying at the speed of sound, or take a relaxing glide over mountaintops. From the glowing mushrooms and fungus of the "Strange" biome, as I call it, to the arctic ridges of the polar biome and farther past down to the sandy dunes and green river valleys of the desert, there's a lot in store. Each biome is vastly unique, and there's an unbelievable amount of new biomes coming along the way if the Developers stay true.
The wildlife is, from what I've heard, very diverse; But from what I've
, this massive array of different creatures seems to be rather hard to find. I may have come across several different kinds without knowing, however. I do know there's a lot, though - Even from the few I've seen, I counted maybe... thirty? I don't know. That includes sharks and fish, butterflies, deer, bears, and other birds. Lots of stuff to morph into, that's for sure.
If you're looking for a game with story, this isn't for you; But a questless adventure can be beautiful in so many ways. The sheer freedom of not having to give some reindeer a long-lost mushroom is great. You can do whatever you want, wherever you want, whenever you what, however you want, and with the only reason being "Because I wanted to."
For instance, I just straight up spent ten minutes ramming into trees for fun. I tried over and over again, each time trying to- wait. Waaait a minute. I'm not trying to do
! Because I don't have to. Let's go try to play chicken with a bald eagle. Play tag with penguins? Sure. I mean, they won't tag back, but sure. Flat out dive into a lake to see if you can swim? Go for it. Float circles around a polar bear? Nothing's stopping you.
I think I've made my point.
The mechanics are a bit on the wonky side. Controls are rather hard to get used to, and the avatar editor definately needs some work on a user-friendly interface. Flying top speed can be really dangerous for someone new to the whole idea, so take it slow. Although I can't force you into anything, so I guess have fun ramming your head into trees every two seconds. Curving and turning can also be slightly frustrating, but adapting comes with time. The flight controls may or may not need some work, but the avatar editor takes the bait.
The avatar creation screen is really... confusing. I got used to it through maybe fourty-five minutes of expirementing. It's a bit too long, if you ask me; That definately needs a change. Maybe not right now, but once the game gets waaay more popular, then I think then would be high time to change it. The general sense of things is OK, but it just looks sloppily put together, and some things I can't even figure out yet. Maybe in time, that'll come. Some explanation on things would be nice as well, as it took me a while to figure out what exactly everything does. I got the gist now, but it took me a great long while, and the "color" section doesn't really seem to... you know,
anything. Maybe it does for a few birds, but it sure doesn't for the falcon.
Yeah, that's right. Direct compliments to the developers, probably the coolest dudes I know. They listen, they have plans, and they know what they're doing from the looks of what they already have. They're incredibly helpful, and usually respond pretty darn fast to whatever bug report, question, or suggest you have in mind. Granted they don't have much on their plate in the way of community to destract them from the game and/or your complaints or whatever, but what little's there is fantastic.
All in all, it's worth it. Now for the delicious Pros Vs. Cons:
...Just, get the game. It is much more worth it than some may think.
Oh yeah, and it's only $10. That's pretty cheap.
(No, I'm not writing a great review just because I got it for free. Nobody told me to, either. This is my honest, totally opinionated and 100% true review)

Shovel Knight is the perfect amalgamation of many beloved and classic NES games. It carefully borrows elements of popular 8-bit titles and repurposes them in a unique and refreshing way. Duck Tales-type downward thrusts, Castlevania-esque subweapons, and Mega Man-style bosses are only some of the heavy influences prevalent in this game. It was an ambitious concept for a LEGO game. You didn't have that wide a variety of characters so most of the characters are just fillers.  At first it looked like any other lego game, but it took me a while to really appreciate it. It's not one of the best open world's in a lego game, but those who are fans of the franchise will definitely have a great time venturing through parts of the park that they never could imagine. The story mode is decent, and goes a lot more smoother than most lego games.
If I could make one complaint, it would be that the open world aspect limits you to not exploring a lot of the island, and it was disappointing how much of the island each movie didn't take up. I also thought it would be better if the open world had more random dinosaurs along the paddocks. It would've been cool if instead of having so many easy gold bricks, that you could have many little puzzles to solve in each paddock while trying to avoid spawned dinosaurs and making gold bricks seem more valuable. If you failed the puzzle it'd be like being smashed (eaten) by a dinosaur. It would make the game seem more of what you're supposed to be: a survivor.
Nonetheless, if you're a fan of the franchise you should get this game, and even if you're not I bet you'll become one if you play.

PROS AND CONS FIRST. THEN AN IN DEPTH REVIEW.
PROS:
-Contains the story of all 4 Jurassic Park movies, basing the story of the films plot
-Original voice audio (taken from the movies too)
-Game looks great with graphics turned up
-Supports Most gamepads which really helps
-LEGO! NUFF SAID
-THE THEME MUSIC AHHH SO MUCH FEELS

Cons:
-Not really any freedom to explore, game is set on a path to stick to the plot
-A few bugs and glitches
-Game audio sounds like it was pulled directly from movies, with background sounds still included
-UI is sometimes confusing about who can do what/when
-The price is sooooo good it should be illegal (this is a con because on steam its $40NZD but Console $110)
REVIEW: I was so excited when Steam notified me the game had finished downloading. I booted it up and sat at the menu screen for a while taking in the funny antics in Jurassic World playing behind the Menu Screen (and listening to the amazing music and Dr. Malcoms laugh from the first movie. Harr huh huh harrrr harrr. Eventually I adjusted the games settings to max (get a good 87fps with VSYNC OFF (see profile for specs) and began a new game. It starts off at the dig site from the first film where we first meet Dr. Grant and then a helicopter takes you to choose between Jurassic Park and Jurassic World. Jurassic Park's two sequels will be unlocked after the first games story is complete. Playing through the story follows the movies plot and looks beautiful while doing it. Various characters and dinosaurs YES DINOSAURS can be unlocked for you to take control of, each with their various uses. A few minor glitches and texture pop ins here and there but this is a strong game that actually released without being broken. I will continue this review as I finish each movie. Of course one of horror gaming's modern classics, I don't think I need to say much about this one. All I will say is that I am very glad to have played it when I did, trying to avoid as many videos and spoilers about the game as possible. It helped me get into the game much more having not been exposed to so many memes about the Servant Grunt (mostly PewDiePie-related I'm sure), videos on the more highly derivative custom stories, and so on. If you yourself are still someone lucky enough to know little about the game and are interested in checking it out, please, by all means, do so!
I did take a swipe there at custom stories but actually one of the best things about this game is the custom story community. The Frictional forums are a mostly friendly lot while still unafraid of offering criticism to the various people offering up their custom stories (and there are some now-overdone cliches that run through the lesser stories they, and anyone else with sense would have low tolerance for - read up on teleporting naked guy jumpscares to see what I mean). It's a good place to get feedback and also help on how to use the game's editors for models, levels, textures and so on for making custom stories. ModDB is also a good place to go to look for the better stories (from what I've seen of the most highly rated stories their user base has pretty good standards). It's great since once you're done with the main game there's a solid variety of other stuff, some full conversions, some games almost as long if not longer than the actual game itself, you'll get a good amount of hours from booting up this game. While not nearly as robust as say the Half-Life 2 / Source mod scene (then again what is?) this is up there. If you want to make your own stories you can download a lot of custom-created stuff to use for a custom story, including a flashlight to replace the lantern if you're putting your game in a modern setting, plus the importing of a ton of textures and models from the Penumbra games, and recently Frictional offering A Machine for Pigs stuff to import too, currently in testing stage.
Oh yeah and this version includes the extra side story Justine, which many of you may know, so that's a nice bonus too. I'm not personally fond of Justine, due to some annoying puzzles and the fact that there's no save function at all (it isn't a long game, no, but it's easy enough to die a few places and starting the whole thing all over is aggravating). It does though have its own unique music and creatures which are really good and creepy, AND, dun dun dun, can be used for your own custom story as well (though I haven't actually yet found the files that contain these, I'll have to ask around).
Follows the usually formula for Lego games, but the humor and easter eggs were worth the play through.

Really Big Sky is a fantastic twin-stick shooter. As most games from the arcade era, it doesn't have much of a plot. You simply have your spaceship, and must fly through space killing aliens who want to take your planets. And there's tons of them. It doesn't really have a story mode, you don't get to "win" the game; it's all about surpassing your best score. And I must say this game is great at it. You'll find yourself playing again and again, improving not only your skills, but also your ship as well.
So, to talk about gameplay, as I said, it's a twin-stick shooter. That means you can move your ship in any direction across the screen (although it's always heading right), and you can also move your aim wherever you please. The ship has two forms: the "shooting" form, in which it automatically shoots wherever you're point, and the drill form, which is used to pass through planets and asteroids that you might find in your path. There's a lot of different enemy ships, ranging from small ones, to huge ships that act as bosses; and there's also random events that add an extra difficulty during their duration. You also collect stars after killing enemies, that can be used later on to upgrade your ship. The game also offers a multiplayer co-op mode, for up to four players, but it only works locally, meaning you'd need to have at least three extra controllers around, for your friends.
This game also includes lots of gamemodes. Most of them play out largely the same, being more (or less) difficult, but there's some that put a new spin in the game, like the Retro mode, that plays out like early shooters from the 80s or 90s, with powerups, lives and all that, or the Pacifist mode, in which you can't shoot at all.
The art style is pretty nice; full of vibrant colours and some really good effects. Entering a wormhole is a pretty cool visual experience. And the design of the different enemies (and of your own ship) is great, with some looking like what you'd expect from a space shooter, and some with pretty unique designs.
One more thing I should talk about is the soundtrack. Oh, what an amazing soundtrack this game has. I think it'd still be a pretty good game without it, but the soundtrack makes it an excellent game. The music, while being somewhat "loud", so to speak, still manages to be relaxing in a special sense. It really fits the tone of this game. And then there's the narration; as there's a narrator who talks during your gameplay, giving you advice and things like that. Now, don't worry, he isn't talking the whole time, he just shows up here and there, and whoever voiced him did a great job.
Well, I think that's enough for my review of Really Big Sky. I really recommend this game, and if you get it, I hope you get to enjoy it as much as I did.

It's kind of hard to accurately express the feeling of Fugl, it is exactly as it describes itself. You play as a bird like creature that morphs fluidly between colours and shapes and you explore an ever morphing world of colour and shapes. The majesty is that it doesn't try to be more than that but it so perfectly captures the feeling of instinctive flight that you just want to go forever. If you've ever played something like Minecraft and rather than engage in building you set out and just explored what the engine would generate, Fugl is that but far more visually stimulating.
So here's the ugly bit, the game is still very much in early access - if your computer isn't at least a bit of beast there's no chance of the game running well. Temporarily there's a mode where the game pre-generates an environment to fly in if your computer isn't up to snuff but the developers are hoping to reduce the system requirements.
There's also more content expected to be added so it's hard to say what the final form of the game will take precisely but put simply, if your computer can run it and you want an unforgettable game of pure experience, Fugl is here right now and you should buy it immediately.

Gratuitous Space Battles is exactly what it says on the box. You're having big, messy, fun space battles. Your reasons for waging such battles are wafer-thin in-story, but that doesn't matter. The game makes up for it with smooth graphics, a nice and simple ship creation system, and a quirky sort of charm in a lot of the text. Everything from descriptions to ship names to in-battle transmissions often have a sense of deliberate silliness woven into it, making the game that much more amusing as you read through the transmissions in battle. One thing that might throw people about this game is that it's a creation/programming game rather than a proper real time tactical game. Your control of your ships is gone the moment you start the fight. Only your orders and the way you built your ships matters then. If you can accept watching battles without directly intervening yourself, this is a fun little game for spending some time being amused. Besides...they do put on a good show...

Space, the final frontier. It is large void, which is largely unexciting, except for the occasional contact with a third-kind.
Unsurprisingly, games based on space settings are hyper-efficient in capturing the unexciting parts of space, either forcing players to explore large areas, or to establish themselves on planetary systems for hours on end, before finally getting to the more exciting parts.
Gratuitous Space Battles (GSB) threw out these nonsense, with no empire building, no resource hunting and no aimless exploring. Instead, GSB throw players right into the fray of combat. Even though battles are auto-resolved, with players able to zoom in and out of the autoplay actions, players can test out their hands on ship design and battle instructions to refine their strategy further, in hope of eliminating the opposing force, while using the least amount of resources (money) given.
Not a AAA title, GSB still manage to give a new breathe of air in removing the boring bits of space.

Gratuitous Space Battles is a very complicated tactics game. It allows you to create your own ships and set commands for them and ,instead of you having to manage all your ships, you just get to sit back and enjoy your fleet blasting your opponents into intergalatic space dust. The game is extremely addictive because it makes you strive to create the unstoppable fleet, and once you get there you always realize that you could do something else to make it even more amazing. Small tweaks can change entire battles. Adding or taking away ships or weapons can mean life or death. If you spent more money on shields you could last longer but you might have a cheaper engine. These things have to be accounted for when playing.
Pros: Addictive gameplay, endless amounts of customization,  online battles, wonderful graphics, and countless other features.
Cons: Price (its pretty expensive for what it is), online could be better, High learning curve.
Great game, for very little money, do yourself a favour and buy this game but be prepared to lose 100s of hours of your life

If you like the lego games, you'll likely enjoy Lego Jurassic World.  It doesn't change the formula in the slightest.  This has its upsides and its downsides because of it.
Pros:
Classic Lego gameplay.  You break stuff, you collect studs, you build things, you solve rudementary puzzles, it's all the classic lego games, just with a jurassic park skin.
Stories are handled rather well.  They (mostly) keep true to the stories, they're presented in a fun way, it's well done.
Classic Lego humor is back.  Lego Marvel was lacking a lot of the classic lego slapstick, this has brought it back.  Characters do silly things, there are plenty of visual gags to laugh at.
You get to play as dinosaurs (some of them, see cons for an explaination)
Cons:
Let's get the big one out of the way, it's glitchy.  This is the glitchiest Lego game I've ever played.  There are puzzles that require raptors to jump on certain things.  I believe there are 5 times you have to do this in the story.  Of the 5 times I tried it, 4 had the raptors getting stuck in midair.  Waiting about 30 seconds finished the animation and I thankfully didn't have to restart any of the levels, but I was dreading each time I'd have to do the raptor jump to progress the game.  I've also had issues with characters getting stuck on objects, compies not being able to get out of tubes, animations glitching out.  It's a glitchy game.  I personally didn't have any gamebreaking glitches, but the ones I experienced certainly had the potential to be gamebreaking.
The voice acting.  This is a problem I've had with every lego game since they started with it in Lego Lord of the Rings.  I don't like the voice acting in lego games to begin with, it works much better in games like Lego Star Wars where the stories are told purely visually.  Lego Jurassic World is the worst of the worst when it comes to voice acting.  Like in the lord of the rings, they decided to use clips of audio taken directly from the movies.  I'm not sure if they were aware of this while making hte game, but sound quality in movies from the 1990s wasn't exactly very good.  It's even more apparent when there are background npcs that have freshly recorded lines form the 2010s.  The difference is instantly noticable, and it's really really badly done.
Strangly anti-death.  In a video game series full of comedic violence and cartoonish death scenes, it's strange to see the lego games go so anti-death with Jurassic Park.  No one dies in the game.  All the people that get eaten don't actually die.  They either get tickled by raptors, or if they do get eaten by a T-Rex, they are vomited out by the end, totally unharmed.  It's very unusually that they'd be this anti-death with such a death filled movie in a series of games that has never been shy about death.  Very strange.
Honestly, it's kind of boring.  The other lego games typically had action based characters, Jedi, Super heroes, Indiana Jones, Magic.  Characters that get into combat based situations, that have special powers, interesting things like this.  Jurassic Park consists of people running away and screaming.  Aside from the main characters, no one is really memorable.  There are a ton of characters to unlock, and only about 15 that you'll actually know.  The unique and cool "powers" these characters have consist of screaming to break glass, but only sometimes, and that's really about it.  All of the other powers have already been explored in other lego games, girls jump higher (which makes no sense but whatever), kids can climb in ducts, people with guns can shoot things, ect.
Lego Jurassic World may well be the first lego game that I have no interest in 100%ing.  I've beaten the story and it's honestly too boring to bother getting the minikits, gold bricks, red bricks and unlocking the other characters.  The level structure, not to mention the hub world, are so either dull or poorly made that I just don't want to bother.

I purchased this during the Summer Monster Sale 2015 for $30 ($10 less than retail of $40).  With the savings, picked up all 3 DLCs that were out at the time.
Game is decent, only 2 hours in and gameplay is fairly fluid.  Standard LEGO abilities and breakables.  Gold bricks, red bricks and mini kits are here too.
My only complaint is tried to run this on 2 different computers with 3D monitors.  The scenes look amazing with the very high detailed textures.  Almost all LEGO games work very well in 3D.  This one is questionable as I've tried several video options in the clunky menus and cannot get the game to run without screen turning blank for 1 second, followed by 3 seconds normal play, then blank for 1 second, 3 seconds normal play.  I can forgive this if it occured on 1 pc not being hi-spec'd enough to handle DX11.  Nearly unforgiveable on 2 different machines with 2 different monitors.  I can only play it in non-3D on one machine as I am unable to turn off 3D on the other.  Frustrating.  Switching from DX11 to DX9 requires a full exit of program, which I can understand.  But this error occurs on either version at high end and low end settings.  Have never experienced this on any other LEGO game ever.  Hopefully will get patched, but not holding my breath.
One cool new feature is you are able to play as the dinosaurs in certain areas.  That's neat.
There's a lot, and I mean a lot, of cutscenes with dialog from the films.  A few standard LEGO humor animations thrown in.  First high priced LEGO game I've bought.  Normally, I never pay more than $20 for a $30 game.  Since this covers all 4 films, I think I can forgive.  More play time...we'll see.  Still on first film.

The concept of the game is very simple: shoot stuff that's shooting back at you.  Some of it is mobile, some is not; some is better armored than you are, and some fire in different patterns.  Your little destroyer is generally a little faster than everything else, and there are walla you can (and must) use to your advantage.
Think of it as a slightly more colorful throwback to the old Atari2600 game style.  Only basic strategies are needed - but you HAVE to use them well.
Still, 1.5 hours after I'd started playing this, my mouse finger was locked in pain, trying to keep firing as much and as accurately possible.  No, this bullet-hell game wont win awards, but I found it strangely compelling.
I really wish there were achievments, because I think that'd make it MORE compelling.  Also, a way to customize your playlist would be nice.  It's easy enough to mute the music and play your own, but havcing everything contained in a single package would make it feel more slick.  Finally, a small number of powerups, or maybe a secondary weapon/ability would rule.
I'll recommend this because it's simple, inexpensive and appeals to my "retro sensibilities" - and it's surprisingly fun.

Drifting has always existed as a sort of accessory sport to traditional racing. Flashy and dangerous, drifting — the act of taking a corner so as to lose control of the back wheels and cause the car to turn sideways — prizes style and precision over speed and vehicular power. Though organized events such as the US’s Formula D series exist they are still searching for a large audience, and outside of Japan drifting remains largely a novelty, something to spice up action movies and arcade racers but rarely thought of as a legitimate sport itself.
Absolute Drift (2015) feels in large part an attempt to move away from drifting as spectacle, giving you a car and a road and letting you figure out the rest. The presentation is stripped down to blunt polygonal buildings and red highlights to tell you where to go, with your car itself a nondescript toy-sized vehicle only visible by its bright paint job and lengthy tire tracks.
When placed next to the gleeful excess of Need for Speed or the cartoony impossibility of Mario Kart, Absolute Drift singular focus is clean and consolidated. Drifting is the literal name of the game, so drift away to your heart’s content, careening through rectangular roads that only further emphasize the exacting grace of your curve.
In a 1995 interview on Jeremy Clarkson’s Motorworld, drifting progenitor and legend Keiichi “Drift King” Tsuchiya says that one of the reasons he began drifting was to entertain the crowd during racing events. It was almost always assured he would win, so drifting became a way to put excitement back into a race where the outcome was no longer the reason to watch. This ideology is a key component to drifting’s popularity in media and as a spectator event. Watching cars go fast is fun, but watching cars go fast and take turns in ways that seem to defy the laws of physics is exhilarating.
One of Absolute Drift’s earliest contradictions is in its reliance on traditional events and score attacks as means of creating a sense of progression. Absolute Drift’s prevailing methodology is that drifting is itself reward enough, and that the problem with the way drifting is used in other media is that it has become deluded by the obsessive adoration paid to it by movies like The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006). Drifting should be about the screech of your tires and the smoke of your skid marks, Absolute Drift seems to say as it positions drifting in an almost religious context (the game itself opens with a Shinto deity welcoming you into a sort of drift heaven).
And yet here the game is asking you to do a donut around this building, or jump your car over this gap. The problem with Absolute Drift’s attempt at drifting solidarity is not that it doesn’t stick to that goal, but that it never could. As Zach Kotzer writes for Kill Screen, “drifting is not an absolute; it is a means to an end.” Absolute Drift needs its leaderboards and its car stunts because drifting in isolation just isn’t that interesting. Just as Tsuchiya incorporated drifting into his racing to spice up his corners, racing games have utilized drifting for the similar purpose of making themselves more interesting to play and watch.
When you strip everything but drifting away from these games, sliding through corners begins to dull rather than excite. Absolute Drift may see drifting as an elevated form of racing, but there is a reason the sport has only ever garnered a niche audience. There are only so many ways you can drift the same turn before it starts to feel routine. This is a problem for games with far more robust handling systems than Absolute Drift can manage (your toy car feels like a boat cruising through a bowl of ice cream), which only exacerbates the problem as what is drifting but the precise understanding and control of a car’s grip and power.
Absolute Drift’s devotion to a singular idea is compelling in its focus and clean production. Its sparse world is as easy on the eyes as the trance soundtrack is on the ears, and there is some fun to be had navigating these large sandboxes populated with fighter jets and Ferris Wheels. But that fun is akin to setting up a ramp and watching a Hot Wheels car fly down it, popping off the ground and begging you to do it again. Eventually you grow tired of this simple task and long for something more involving. But your toy is still just a Hot Wheels car, and this is still just a drifting game.

After all this playing, the final verdict is simply that this game isn't nearly as good or properly balanced like EDF 2017 was. At first it is fun, but if you're a completionist this IS NOT the game for you unless you have the patience to grind several hundred hours of tedious maps because you've played each one 14 times over just to unlock the limits (not including the times you've died.) GRIND.
In the late game, the weapon drops for the levels you're on that can actually make use of them become so rare that you'll be playing the same level repeatedly, winning by the skin of your teeth, and not getting anything new. The rare time we did get new things, the weapons proved to be novelties and nearly useless. GRIND.
For whatever reason they decided that giving you 1 armor point per pickup was too much... except now you have FOUR classes that all get these pickups separately. The strongest class will only get 1 armour point per TWO pickups. GRIND.
The Weapon and Armor limits in multiplayer are simply pointless other than to make you waste more of your life than you wanted to on this game. I got a level 50 weapon, I want to use it. Oh, but hey, you can unlock the weapon and armor limit if you beat 70% of the game.. meaning you have to play and WIN 1372 maps (98 levels, 4 classes, 3.5 difficulties.) GRIND.
This game is the absolute epitome of tedium, and it really pains me to not like this game because 2017 was close to my heart, but the grinding in this is just too much. The first game was perfectly balanced, and took about 70 hours to complete all difficulties. You had to grind once in awhile, but it wasn't to the point of being ridiculous like this one is.
The only thing that would redeem this for me is modding support with a weapon editor and map editor.. and possibly a random mission generator that would slowly ramp up the difficult with each completed mission.
Oh, but then you wouldn't be able to sell your map packs for $10 a pop? You got enough money out of me for your $50 B game ($50 for a B game... cripes.) and all I did was waste so much of my life for a game that was more often frustrating than entertaining.
Please note: THIS IS NOT AN MMORPG. Take all this grinding elsewhere and get it out of my EDF.

Set between 1499-1509 Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood takes place immediately after the plot of Assassin's Creed II, featuring the 16th-century Assassin Ezio Auditore da Firenze in Italy and on his quest to restore the Assassin order, and destroy his enemies: the Borgia family.
Intersecting with these historical events are the modern day activities of series protagonist Desmond Miles, who relives his ancestor Ezio's memories to find a way to fight against the Assassins' enemies, the Templars, and to also prevent the 2012 apocalypse.
Assassin's Creed Brotherhood introduces rectruabile Assassins to the game. Ezio can now recruit new members to the Assassin Order by destroying any of the twelve "Borgia towers" around Rome where the papal troops are stationed, then by rescuing disgruntled citizens in their districts from the harassing guards.
There are new enemy archetypes in addition to those that were seen in AC II such as the horsemen, arquebusiers, the papal guards and others. Horses now also have a much larger role in AC Brotherhood, not only used as a means of transport, but also as a component of different acrobatic sequences and also so much more advanced combat as well, allowing ranged weapons to be used while riding them.
Assassin's Creed Brotherhood is also the first game in the whole Assassin's Creed Franchise to feature multiplayer which consists of three game modes, Free for All, Co-Op and Team. This game is just full of amazing detail in every aspect; The story, Graphics, ambiance, environment, sound and much more.
I really recommend this for the mere fact that it's just always fun to play, and there is just so much things that you can do in the game. I absolutely cannot recommend this game to you enough it really is just absolutely outstanding. So once again I highly recommend that you get this game because I'm sure you won't regret it. I am definitely without even a single doubt 100% sure that Assassin's Creed Brotherhood will not disappoint you!.

Nothing in the media has terrified me more than this game has. Its absolutely brilliant, immersive experience will make you cringe with fear, yet peak your curiosity enough to bravely carry on. Stephen King claims the word "Alone" as the most awful word in the English language, and that is exactly what you feel here. You are alone (at least, not until near the end), shrouded by a mysterious atmosphere, with escape seemingly impossible. There are no cheap thrills; rather, your deepest fears slowly creep into your brain and then suddenly explode with horror. This is why many have refused to play this game thoroughly, or have to take breaks.  It truly does bring out the coward inside of you, going places you never want to go to. My only gripe would be the explanations provided to an otherwise outstanding story. Curiosity is the game's main driving force, and the more answers it provides, the less scary it becomes. While some questions remain, I would prefer to interpret the conclusion myself rather than have the endings leave many questions resolved. But regardless, this is without a doubt the scariest game ever made. If you're not faint of heart, I highly recommend it.

This game is a direct continuation of AC2 and improves upon the gameplay in many ways. There are new gadgets (crossbow, poison darts, parachute to name a few) that make Ezio's arsenal finally feel complete (I'm not sure why it took so long to get the crossbow though, Altair had one in the intro movie for the first game). The ability to call assassin's is great fun and actually makes you feel like part of the brotherhood instead of just a lone wolf. In many ways Ezio is just completely overpowered (which isn't necessarily a bad thing) so when I see a group of guards it's a question of how do I want to kill them as opposed to what is the most effective way to kill them since all the methods are effective. The Leonardo missions are also fun (Ezio gets to drive a tank in one).
That said, this game feels like it really should have been an expansion pack for AC2 instead of a sequel. There isn't much to the story and what is there is drawn out longer than it should have been. Ideally the best placement for this game would have been right before the final act of AC2 so Ezio builds up to finally confronting his arch rival. The bad guy in this game just doesn't seem all that exciting after fist-fighting the pope at the end of AC2.
The world is also MUCH smaller. You're stuck in one city the entire game with no countryside either.
That said, the game was still a lot of fun and is easily recommended. As with all older games, wait to pick it up on sale.

Assassin's Creed II was, for all intents and purposes, the game the original wanted to be but fell short of, do to a variety of reasons perhaps most largely its own incredible ambition. With the sequel, Ubisoft managed to monumentally improve virtually every aspect of the series, giving us a tightly wound narrative, a charismatic lead, and refined mechanics that came together for one of the best games of the last few years.
Following up this achievement is Brotherhood, arriving barely a year after the first and on the surface seeming little more than a retread of what we already saw, and an easy cash grab before a full fledged sequel can be made. In some ways this is accurate, as Brotherhood in many ways is incredibly similar to its predecessors, but to call it anything less than an entire new experience would be a disservice, as for how short a time it had in the oven it's just as large and engrossing as the games that came before it, while also adding an assortment of excellent new mechanics that push the game forward even when it occasionally stumbles in the wake of critical acclaim.
Being a direct sequel, Brotherhood picks up mere moments after the end of II, with the surprising (arguably convoluted) events that transpired still fresh in Ezio's mind though it would appear he has finally arrived at a moment of peace after all his struggles. Of course nothing good ever lasts long, and it doesn't take long for his enemies to catch up with him, kill yet more of what little family he has left, and send Italy tumbling into chaos, leaving you to pick up the pieces (though for once you aren't alone).
After the fantastic birth to assassin story of II, Brotherhood's more traditional tail of revenge mixed with some incomprehensible supernatural elements never quite manages to achieve the same level of intrigue and pacing. Though perfectly solid and enough to drive the experience, aside from the first and last few hours it meanders through much of its plot, spiraling off into dozens of disconnected tangents that feel more like side missions than an overarching narrative which left me feeling rather disengaged with everything that was happening. By the end I had lost the investment I previously had in these characters, and simply wanted it all to wrap up in a way that somehow made it all pull together, which again it unfortunately failed to. This isn't to say that Brotherhood isn't entertaining, or that the story is terrible, but it lacked the sense of urgency and tightness that exuded from every moment of II and came off a tad rushed.
Thankfully, Brotherhood plays incredibly well, taking everything that worked with II and adding in enough fresh elements and interesting mission types to be just as engaging. The most readily apparent change is that of the scenery, moving away from Venice and into the sprawling city of Rome. It's a far larger environment, that feels more alive than ever thanks in part to the expanded town building system which now encompasses the whole of the city, allowing you to renovate shops and tunnels to provide income, more areas to purchase items, and fast travel across the map. It also makes it easier to feel invested in the city as you see it build up around you with each new renovation. It's a huge world to explore, yet every inch of it is packed with an enormous amount of things to do, leaving little idle space and a never ending stream of missions the vast majority of which are surprisingly fleshed out and enjoyable.
As the name implies, Brotherhood no longer sees you fighting alone but instead building up an army of assassins which you can then send on contracts and call in when you need aid. It's a tad underdeveloped in its current state, but it nonetheless greatly changes how you can approach an encounter, as often times calling in assassins which can pop out of anywhere is far less risky than attempting to get close to a target yourself. They also work as convenient distractions, and add a layer to encounters that feels especially needed when the combat is still trapped in a fairly dull design that despite numerous cool kill animations never became very fun and was best avoided whenever possible.
Other minor tweaks in takedowns, platforming, and general movement add some noticeable refinement to the series core gameplay, though there are still moments when the camera will freak out or the free running system will send you jumping randomly completely in the wrong direction. Animations in particular continue to stick out to me as incredibly well done, with Ezio in particular moving with as much grace and fluidity as you'd expect from an assassin. Lastly Jasper Kyd's original score is utterly gorgeous and sets the mode strikingly well at every moment, as if his music is deeply tied into the world and speaking to you as you traverse it.
Despite its narrative shortcomings, Assassin's Creed Brotherhood is by no means the sloppily churned out annualized rubbish it very well could be, instead a brilliant successor to what I would consider an utter masterpiece, and a remarkably well crafted game on its own measures. If you've yet to touch the series this certainly isn't the place to jump in, but if you were left wanting more after II, Brotherhood will certainly satisfy and then some.

Absolute Drift is not a standard racing game, it's heavily focused on the handling mechanics of a drift car with a steep learning curve. Previous experience with racing titles and real life knowledge of how drifting should work will definitively help to get over the first approach to controls.
Don't even bother using a keyboard, this game is best played with a controller that has analog input for throttle control, a xbox 360 controller is just fine.
In addition, I strongly suggest to try manual transmission and disabling the assisted steering in order to gain direct control to the car.
Thematically the game is full of reference. From the iconic "Initial D" manga to the Japanese drifting car culture in general.
Overall the game aesthetic is minimalistic and beautiful, with an awesome soundtrack to complete the well polished package.
The only complain I have is the "white buildings on white roads" which can cause confusion, but admittedly I'm playing on an awful monitor so your experience may vary.
I strongly suggest this title to every car enthusiast. Just the turbo whistle when you lift of is enough to justify the purchase.

What if you fall asleep while your beer is falling on the ground? You would try your best to wake up and grab it on time! One way to wake up from an unwanted dream is "killing yourself"... but this is no easy task, if you continue falling from one dream to another, and maybe a mysterious force is keeping you locked up in these multiple, fantasy worlds.
This is the idea of Suicide Guy, basically a first person platform/graphical adventure with multiple levels, each one with a specific way to put an end to your own "dreamlife". Some of these are more easy to understand, but others will require all of your insight and creative thinking to grasp the "logic" of absurd and funny dream environments.
Controls are easy and the game can be played in any language (only some written sentences in english and figures showing how to play). Best feature of the game is its narrative context, which allows for the inclusion of potentially illimited levels and environments; most of the fun for the player comes from wanting to know what kind of situation will show up next!

Loading Screen Simulator is a fantastic game but how can such a simple concept have such a large impact on my life and the gaming industry as a whole.
Lets start with basic gameplay, You left-click the earn money button! But why is this so important?
By earning money you are able to purchase upgrades to load your (*SPOILERS*) faster, it what makes the game progress. With this mechanic the game publishes a political viewpoint in the world of technology and gaming as a whole. Imagine earning the money you earn in real life (per week) and imagine earning this much money within a minute of clicking. Ruslan uses this to show how long it truly takes to load (*SPOILERS*) nowadays.
The money is used to purchase upgrades for your pc whilst loading. One of these is upgrades is a retro pong style game. Except with a twist: the game is VVVEEEERRRYYY slow, like the loading screen the game is based around, and has no score system. But why is this so important? The lack of score once again takes a political viewpoint on the gaming industry and how games nowadays feel like they have NO reward for playing them. Take ARK Survival Evolved for example. When you get all the good dinosaurs and have the largest base in the game, you receive no sense of achievement or meaning in your 1000+ hours of game time. Or the recent Call of Duty games thats story does not leave you satisfied after doing what sociopathic soldiers do. What was the point? Ruslan's use of humour and design clearly highlights the problems with current games. The speed of the game also presents how slow the gaming industry is currently progressing in quality.
However, this masterpiece also takes a stand against high end businesses like EA, Microsoft and Apple. Once you begin loading and tapping that earn money button with sheer joy and determination with your playable characters newly bought pc, then game demands you spend YOUR money on upgrading software and getting more features through purchase (I'm looking at you EA) Ruslan shows his view in a comedic way whilst sticking to the classic clicker game mechanics and design. One of these points is shown in the web explorer upgrade, after paying $300 on a simple browser you expect it to load much faster then your current browser (which is loading (*SPOILERS*)throughout the entirety of the game) But it still takes 10 MINUTES to load a simple image of our lord and saviour (*SPOILERS XD*) This level of deep game design cannot be seen in other titles (apart from undertale, The Last Guardian etc) and really seperates Loading Screen Simulator from the rubbish at the top end of the video game spectrum)
Another incredibly amazing feature in this game is the media player upgrade. The fact that you have to pay for music presents a negative view towards subscription fees (or premium) for services like Spotify and Crunchyroll (except Crunchyroll makes sense..) Not to mention that you get royalty-free music from your purchase making you ask yourself.. What was the point of that?
Yet behind the Lemon by Kevin MacLeod is the console feature. One that promotes coding at your free will but instead asks you questions with one set answer. Finally after showing the dystopian government that you can answer all of their questions you are finally asked for the name of your overlord "Ruslan" This brave move makes you aware that the government controls everything froom the shadows they... oh god they'r*Sounds of struggle followed by gunfire*
3 Months later
"Guy's i escaped from the camp." *heavy panting is heard* "I should be able to finish this review before i am found again.."
Now is the time to talk about the "Helper" game mechanic. The Helper's job is to give you advice on how to make your loading screen progress faster. It is useless. It's like Nardole in doctor who, it is just there for comic relief. Yet it has a purpose. It tells you to spend money, infact enforces it "Upgrade your OS" presenting the problem of over-advertisement and commercialism. If you are a pretentious snob who thinks video games are supposed to be pieces of art, full of cutscenes, cinematics that rival Kwaiden and a plot that attempts to rival Citezen Kane, go away. This game might be too fun to be good. Go play another walking simulator.
For normal people who play video games for entertainment this is one of the best video games to come out in at least the last decade. Earth Defense Force 2025 (A.K.A 4.1) is an unpretentious, pure, and wonderfully absurd third person shooter that pits the EDF against an evil alien threat hell-bent on conquering earth with an army of giant insects and building-sized alien robots. It's a game that combines Starship Troopers, classic Toho films, with a dash of  a (more or less)Power Rangers vibe. From it's gameplay to it's gleefully cheesy dialouge EDF never once forgets that it's a entertainment product first and foremost.
EDF if you have never played it before, is about fighting large waves of enemies using a vast array of destructive weapons, in a fully destructible 3D envoirnment. Essentially the closest you can get to a modern 3D equivalent of Robotron 2084. And there are a lot of weapons. Different character classes can carry a different number into battle, for example a Ranger can carry two weapons, and you choose them before starting a mission. Weapons range from assault rifles, to missile launchers, even rocket launchers that can annihillate an entire city block with one shot.  The game has 4 character classes each with it's own strengths.
-The Ranger- He is your generic soldier whom is mostly unremarkable, but the most well balanced class. He has decent move speed, and a dodge roll. He has access to the more conventional weapons and is the best class to start playing the game at until you unlock better missions for armor/weapon farming for the other classes.
-The Wing diver- She is the most mobile but the least armored. She can fly around the battlefield and rain death from above. Unfortuanately the Wing Diver has a an energy meter that decreases as she flies, and this meter is also used to reload many of her weapons
-The Fencer-Initially starts out near useless because of his starting weapons and abnoxiously slow move speed. He needs to utilize jump jets to get around at an acceptable level. The trade off? He can get some of the most powerful weapons in the game. He also has the quickest armor gain.
Air Raider- A support oriented class, not as good in direct combat, but he is the only one who can call in vehicles.
A lot of missions have minor updates and there are a couple of new missions. They added the Kaiju and "Walking Fortresses" from 2017. A few new vehicles as well, and a mech.
There's only two issues witht the game I have.
1.Most weapons are blatantly better than others.
2.Unlike in 2017 you can NOT use vehicles unless you are a Air Raider, or are playing co-op and have an Air raider to request vehicles. It would have been nice if they could have added pre-placed unpiloted vehicles in single player to use if you are playing as a Ranger, and there is only one mission that I know of where you can pilot a vehicle. And that one be one of the several new missions, there is one that you get to use the new mech.
Easily recomennded to anyone who enjoys japanese monster movies, cheesy movies in general, fast paced arcade action, and games that are fun above all else.

This is the best EDF game to date.  I have played the majority of the EDF games on the consoles including EDF 4.1 on the PS4 and they all suffer from slowdown... horrible slowdown.  This version of the game does not!  I cannot even begin to explain the joy of seeing a franchise actually reach its' potential on the PC over consoles.
Anywho, The gameplay is as it looks in the screenshots, aliens and bugs controlled by aliens are attacking and you and up to three others must deploy to stop them!
The only flaws are:
- The lobby system is kind of a mess
- alien attacks can clip thru buildings to hit you (A major pain when dealing with large spiders)
- weapons do not scale down - meaning if you have a lvl 90 explode all things gun and you go back to a easy lvl that caps weapons at 5, you have to switch to a different weapon between lvl 0-5.
- no quick way to disable voice chat.  If you restrict chat it does turn off voice chat but also disables keyboard inputs. Outside of that you have to select the player in the lobby and mute their mic (steam auto enables mics for games with no disable feature)
- A big flaw of the game is no joining on the fly, new players have to wait until the game returns to lobby for a repeat or next level.  They can set items/chat however, they cannot join in.  So sometimes you will see a bunch of people join and quit as you go thru a match.
Should you own this game?
If you love B movie cheese and sifi goodness then YES.  They have rounded out the character classes in this version and you can now summon tanks, aircraft, mechs, bombing runs, arty strikes .... it can turn the game into a Micheal Bay wet dream of explosions!!!! and depending on your system, all in glorious 60FPS+.

This entry was  vast improvement over Assassin's Creed 2 for me.  I'm not even sure if I can put my finger on why that is either.  Perhaps less flag/feather gathering.  I'm a bit of a completionist so that drove me insane in AC2.  Though admittedly I didn't gather everything in this entry either.  For those without AC experience, there are flags and other items to "collect" scattered around the game.  Some are in hard to reach places or locked areas that open up as you progress.  For the most part I enjoyed the "jumping puzzle" and added challenge of figuring out how to get to them.  Some may not...for some reason in AC2 I was at my wit's end due to the size of the game and high number/variety of items. The feeling of "missing something" was constantly there and it became tedious trying to figure out what I may have overlooked.
One of the bigger changes in Brotherhood in regard to missions, was that every single one had an added challenge in order for you to get 100% synchronization for a memory.  At first, I found this extremely frustrating especially since I hadn't mastered some of the combat mechanics (like kill streaks, though once I figured that out it, my game changed dramatically).  But eventually I ended up finding that the missions were a lot more fun with the added challenge.  Granted, there were times I was cursing how clumsy I was with the controls. This did eliminate some freedom in how you decided to complete a mission.  That was my biggest lament over this feature...but for me, it wasn't a terrible thing.
The acrobatics in this installment are as you'd expect them.  Perhaps it was my imagination, but it felt more responsive than the previous games and  traversing the rooftops felt more fluid than ever.  As much as I'd expect to get tired of it, just jumping from rooftop to rooftop, is a good time.
It's no wonder flabby gamers everywhere love the AC series because it lets you become the ultimate acrobatic badass as you hang from a ledge by one hand flashing your 12 pack abs to the ladies below. Those courtesans may sleep with everyone else in the game, but let's face it, they all want you (Ezio).
I have to give props to the music in the game.  The perfect track always started when you were jumping through ruins, fighting 20 guards or racing the clock.  It always felt right.
I liked the storyline this time around.  I had to recap what happened in AC2 before I played Brotherhood. But I'll be starting Revelations knowing exactly what happened in Brotherhood. No shortage of intrigue and I have to give the writers credit, I love the whole premise of visiting a time period hundreds of years ago while progressing a sci fi story in the present/future. I've avoided horror games, by and large, because things like horror movies scare the bejesus out of me, and I end up squealing and running from the room like a little girl.   My problem is that I am *there*.  Not, sat in the cinema "there", but standing in the room with the people on screen *THERE*.  so when Freddy Krueger turns up, I take it all a little personally.
So, when I was at a games show and someone suggested I play Amnesia, I said "no thanks" and left it at that.  Scroll forward a year or two, and Amnesia was  in a sale on Steam, so I snaffled it up with a bunch of other games.
A little while later, I thought "what the hell", downloaded it, and proceeded to spend the next 6+ hours sweating profusely, and shaking (but not in a good way).
Amnesia's primary mechanic of "hide in the corner, and don't look at the monsters" bypassed my frontal lobe, and jabbed a gigantic needle into that primitive part of my brain that said "by the way, there's a sabre-toothed tiger right behind you, and since all that snowing started he's been getting a bit hungry, and is sniffing you out."
The environments are down-right pants-wettingly scary, and the monsters (if you can call them that!?) are worryingly effective.  There was one bit of the game where I just paralysed. I didn't WANT to go forwards.  Every time I took a step out of the flickering light down the corridor, the hairs stood up on the back of my neck, and I had to run back into the light.
So, what is it about this game that evokes this reaction? Well, primarily it's because you're almost helpless.  You can run, hide and creep around.   There is a LOT of bad unexplained stuff happening, and (as with all good horror games), it's happening in the old abandoned lunatic asylum, built on friday the 13th 1913 on the old indian cemetary by a thrice-cursed 13th son of a vicar who was defrocked for unspeakable acts of naughtiness.
Running away isn't an option.  It's time to descend into the old abandoned mines, and unravel the reason why nobody ever came out of the asylum.  You're not going to like the answer. muahaha.
Oh yes, atomsphere is DRIPPING from this game. And don't adjust your gamma.  Keep it low. Keep it dark.. because THAT is how this game is played.  If you can see the evil coming, where's the fun?

Warning, there may be spoilers ahead, so if you wish to not have anything about the game or the new film spoiled, please do not continue reading, and catch up on the game and the film. AS IT IS A GREAT FILM.
Jurassic Wolrd has been a long awaited film for many fans of the original Jurassic Park films, and was worth the wait as it is one of the best sequels and films out there. Lego Jurassic World on the other hand, while lives up to what they advertised, is more or less the same deal. The game itself is a pretty terrific and terrifying expierence, play as your favorite characters from the four films and explore the sections of the island from the same films, such as Isla Srona (Site B), the first park, and the newest, Jurassic World, and even explore them as the dinosaurs themselves. The storys have all been retold in the from of legos and all the inappropriate parts removed aside from an obvious refference in the form of one of the achievments, it is regardless an overall excellent way to bring children into the franchise and to let them see the movies in a much friendlier and funnier form. There are several parts with the story mode of the game that some will have issues with not because they're different from the film, but because as all PC Lego games go, there is a bug instead of a dino in the way of getting past some parts. This can usually be resolved by changing the resolution to a different setting,and that may require for you to reboot the game, which can be tedious if the first one doesn't work. But besides that, story and freeplay modes for the story selections are excellent, and the exploration of the levels themselves along with the detailing is amazing, inquiring both dinos and humans to work together to unlock mini-kits and gold bricks. Speaking of freeplay, or in this instance now free rome, you basically have the entire island to explore. Only thing wrong with exploration is the inability to explore it all, as you're made to explore only on designated paths and open areas, say the Indominus Rex Paddock for example, you get to go in and explore the living qaurters of the Indominus first hand and even be able to spawn one in just for a little added scare, but you can't explore the inside of the viewing area, where in the film it is a important part of the first scene. And there are so many others like this that could've been a great addition to the game and make the free rome more fun. As for the set path part, it takes away the free rome just a bit, but is understandable for finding parts of the story, and making it feel like you really are in a jungle with dinosaurs. Which sadly are not able to outside their designated spawning areas (you can't leave the Indominus Rex Paddock with the Indom as it can't fit/not coded or soemthing to) and you hardley see any outside of the character selection (seee any on the open roads, in the pens that they're suppposed to be in). Instead, you have to spawn them in, or find them lying on the ground as part of the Sick Dinos Gold Bricks. It really takes away from the whole Island being inhabited by dinosaurs feel and mkaes the game not really live up to it's name. Now this is not to say you can't be a Raptor in a crowd of people, as there are several dinos that can be used in the game outside of the spawning areas that can be selected from the character roaster. Now some instances may be understandable, as you can play as a Brachiosaurus, which is the BIGGEST dinosaur in the game and it is absolutly huge and would probably be unable to traverse most of the parks, but something like the T-Rex would be smaller and easy and fun to play as in front of the Visitor Center. But that is just a nitpick and a personal opinion. Now as for the gameplay and side-quests, they are very smooth, although I played all of it with a controller, so the opinion there is somewhat bias. Regardless, controls are smooth and favorable, while the quests are more or less what you expect from a Lego game. Now there a few that will not appear on the map, even if you've discovered the map location, and you will have to search for them manually. While a bit tedious, you should still be able to get them in the end. Now as the menu, which is odd for a review, I know, but in the menu there is an event and time  thing that depects when a certain thing will be. THis sadly does not happen in the game and would've been a nice implement for some more gold bricks like with Lego Batman 3 with the added DLC's. And on a final note, there is no automatic day and night cycle, it either switches to either dependant upon the story, or when you teleport to a map location. Now do I recommend this game? Yes. But I will say that it needs a lot of work done on it as constant bugs and glitches may prohibit some from being able to play the game. Maybe wait a bit till it goes on sale or if you are keeping up with the forums, look for a decrease in bug reports. Thanks for reading, and have a great day/night.

This game is probably one of the best tactical shooters I have ever played! I put this game way over CSGO. CSGO compared to this is pretty bland even though it as well is quite a good tactical shooter. The community on this game is pretty good, but not everyone is nice and you may run into a few jerks who act like they know everything about the game yet they are only level 25 and can barely aim to save their life. I will say that latency plays a role in this game, so if you don't have the best internet and you seem to lag a lot in other games I would suggest staying away from this. The best thing about the game is probably the amount of people you can play as and the replay value. There are 30 operators to choose from at the moment and each have a different ability to help beat the other team. As for replay value you see that my hours continue to grow as this review stays here which means I continue to enjoy the game after countless hours of gameplay. I ALSO wanted to add what the difference between the starter addition and the normal additon was.
STARTER EDITION:
2 Operators are instantly unlocked for you(random), 600 R6 credits are given to you to purchase anything you want(This is the ingame purchaseable currency and you will most likely buy an operator with it), Operators cost more money than in the regular additon and the game becomes more grindy. (With the steam summer sale going on right now I simply suggest picking up the normal version since you can not upgrade to it once you purchase the starter edition).
NORMAL VERSION:
Probably the better investment in the long run. You don't get 2 free random operators and 600 R6 credits, but everything is way easier to unlock and less of a grind. Yes there is year 1 and 2 characters to unlock, but as long as you play the game regularly you can get those quite quickly.
Overall, I would HIGHLY recommend this game and if you have friends to play with it makes the game a lot more fun.

This is not the kind of game you will be playing for the story, the characters or the environments.
This is the kind of game you will be playing for the thrill of facing overwhelming hordes of insects and gunning them down with a massive variety of weapons.
During the times where it feels like a literal wave of insects is about to overwhelm you, as they climb across buildings and charge towards you in massive groups, EDF is at its best. It is in these moments where you will experience a rush of adrenaline and feel a strange mix of desperation and euphoria as you work to fight off enemies in their hundreds. Never have I played a game like this where all of the most common individual adversaries are at least ten times bigger than the player character. It is that mix of scale and sheer enemy numbers that contribute to the unique feeling mentioned earlier.
However.
This is not the kind of game for you if you do not enjoy constant grinding.
This is not the kind of game for you if you want balanced classes.
This is not the kind of game for you if you care about detailed levels or passable AI.
In addition, while the PC port is acceptable, one detail I do not understand is how or why menus can only be navigated with the keyboard alone. There is no mouse support until you load in to an actual level.
This is the kind of game where you zone out and blast hordes of insects, and while that certainly has its moments of euphoria in the most intense engagements, everything else begins to feel like a chore as you work hard towards that next big moment.
To address the common retort to any criticism of this game, no, playing for hours up to "Mission 26" or "Mission 28" or wherever the community commonly states it becomes amazing at, is not a valid defence.
I do see the appeal of this game, and priced less I would certainly recommend it to others with some choice warnings to heed. However, at the current price, this will be a no from me.

This is due to a mixture of enjoyably eye-rolling NPC banter, and mission scenes/commentary that would be right at home in a budget alien invasion movie. The shadow of new despair, yet most EDF soldiers appear to be overly content and upbeat, often discussing meals and marriages on the battlefield.
The gameplay is pretty simple - mainly made up of you shooting things, or calling in things that will assist you in your bid to shoot things, and/or helping others in their struggle to shoot various things. The result? Explosions, pretty lasers, crumblings buildings, and flying bodies are all a common sight here - so you'll likely be finding yourself reviving people a lot, or in need of some medical attention yourself. Especially on the harder difficulties, which can genuinely be a challenge, many of the most sedate-seeming missions are a bullet-hell environment on Hardest/Inferno difficulties. Generally more enemies with higher health is a bad way to increase difficulty, but it works in EDF. The enemy behaviours do change slighty, they become more aggressive and dangerous, but you can also make yourself expontially more dangerous too through the equpping of unlocked weapons (and blood doping too).
The game is separated into Online and Singleplayer modes - with singleplayer mode offering split-screen co-op. There are 4 very unique classes to play as, with separate pools of collectible weapons and armour (health). To level up your classes, you pickup armour/weapon drop boxes in-game (red/green drops). Higher difficulties and later missions generally tend to give better weapon loot. There are 4 difficulties to play as, and progress is tracked independantly for each of the 4 classes, and missions progress is also kept separate from online and singleplayer modes - however armour and weapon loot is shared between the 2 modes.
There is a large range of weapons/equipment to obtain - these will help you shoot things and increase the enjoyability of shooting those things. It also makes for some collecting to be done - and if you want to 100% the missions, you need to play each one 16 times! Yes that sounds like a chore, but the beauty of the game isn't in chores, but in it's gameplay - which is fun in singleplayer, and exactly 3 times more fun in multiplayer. Although in singleplayer you can player the easier difficultyies without a weapon level limit, making for some really brutal insect fumigation.
Improvement areas do exist with EDF4.1, despite all my positive feedback. My personal annoyances mainly revolve around the ranger's general lack of movement options - the fastest way to move being to roll at 45-degree angels, and yes this means literally looking away from where you want to move. I tell a lie, actually you could launch yourself into the sky with a high-powered sniper rifle, so there's that.. All my other personal annoyances are tied into the UI, being general UI layout/limitations and some UI related bugs. The gameplay is largely robust though which is good, i've only ran into 2 gameplay bugs that required us to restart the mission. Unlike some games, you don't have to linger in the menus for long.
