TL;DR: Visually stunning and a load of fun to fly. Intuitive once you have a grasp of the controls. If you have a problem with diamonds in the rough, don't buy this game just yet. Otherwise, it's definitely worth your $$, especially if you're into flying and like infinite worlds.
More detail:
Epic: The terrain generation works like a treat. Smooth and fast, even when you're rocketing along at max speed (which feels like podracing XD ). With the right settings, you get a lot of fun caves and passages to fly through, and with a few minutes of practice, you can even navigate them decently.
Great: Good variety of 'bird' models and full shift/partial shift stages. Personally had some fun with the flying bear type.
Needs work: -XBox 360 Controller input was super, super twitchy.
-Mouse input lags pretty hard.
-Most of the birds fly really fast and barely glide, which makes it difficult to be precise in tight spots. I'd prefer if flight were less hectic and visibility a little better as a trade off. It's supposed to be meditative, after all.
-Flapping mechanics are primitive at the moment, and landing is weird.
-Also, the unpredictable shift mechanic is irritating sometimes. Would be better if you only changed shape on command and when targeting a viable creature/plant/whatever.
Summary: It's very much an early access game, but one that (glitches, bugs and crashes aside for now) could develop from an amazing concept to something truly spectacular. I will definitely keep coming back to this, because it's great if you just want to unplug for a bit and fly.

Ok so this is my second review after Lego Batman 3.  I've played almost all the lego games on multiple platforms but Lego Jurassic World, Pirates of the Caribbean and Batman 2 & 3 were played on my computer with my wired xbox controller.  My review is based on 100% completion of the game and achievements.  I have previously 100% all three Lego Batmans, Pirates of the Carribbean, Lego Movie, and the first Lego Indiana Jones.  With all that said let's get into the meat of this.
The length it took me to finish this game reminds me of some of the earlier Lego games.  Forty hours compared to how long it took me to do Lego Batman 3 and Lego Marvel really isn't much.  I didn't run into some of the same game stopping glitches that others have but that doesn't mean that my game experience was entirely glitch free unfortunately.  There were two very prevalent glitches I ran into.  The first was when a character went to jump a fence quite a few times the character would instead fall through the island and into the abyss never to be seen again.  This usually lead to me having to restart the level, checkpoint or free play depending on what I was doing.  The second one was in one of the bonus levels in Jurassic World.  For whatever reason the dinosaur would just not appear on screen and you couldn't see what you were doing. Sometimes it would magically appear but most of time it wouldn't.  If anyone else is having this problem I waited to do the level until I got the attract studs brick and one of the stud multipliers.  Doesn't really matter if you can see the dinosaur when you have those.  I also had a problem with characters and dinosaurs disappearing and reappearing or just magically ending up in the abyss.  In Gyroscope Valley my character in the gyroscope suddenly disappeared and ended up in the abyss.  I had to start the level over again from the last checkpoint only to be surprised to find that the game hadn't saved my last checkpoint and I had to start over again.  For once it would be nice if Lego would put out a game that didn't have so many glitches.
So why do I still recommend this game?  Well despite some annoying aspects (above named glitches and a very repetitive storyline gameplay) I still had fun with the game mostly for two reasons... the dinosaurs and Mr. DNA.  Yes Mr. DNA is your guide in this game and is also a playable character later on.  He's one you'll want to buy right away because he can hack, acess igen terminals, dig in dino poop (yes characters dig in dino poop), hit targets, track and do the genius equations.  Very valuable especially in free play.  Most dinosaurs are fun to control and can all be customized.  The only one I wasn't fond of was the brachio.  It was big and hard to manuver.  The apo can do what the brachio can and is much smaller.  There are certain things you can't do in free roam/play without the proper dinosaur.   You either need to find the dinosaur's corresponding amber in the levels or customize a dinosaur, only you can't customize a dinosaur with that ability unless you find the dinosaur that has it in the levels first. The biggies are the poison shooting dinosaur and the t. rex from Jurassic Park, the compy from Lost World, either the brachio or the apo, there are a lot of dinos for cracked objects but the one I found worked best was the pachy and the indominous and the swimming dinosaur for parts in Jurassic World.  Some of the other dinosaurs are unnecessary for anything but fun to play around with.
Now as I said above the gameplay is rather repetitive.  Each movie is pretty much set up the same way with quite a few chase sequences.  It was cool at first but got kinda annoying by Jurassic World.  The one kinda cool thing is they actually use dialogue from the movies in the cut scenes.  I'll admit I couldn't always understand what was being said, the movies were shot twenty years ago, but it was still kinda cool hearing Jeff Goldblum's voice coming out of this little lego character.  While the gameplay wasn't always to my liking the story was a fun lego twist on the original.
A few things to note: There are terminals with a blue circle and an I inside spread all over each of the four hubs.  Make sure you stop at each one of these because not all the gold bricks, red bricks, workers in peril will show up on your map unless you do and you'll be flying blind until you get detectors.  Also there is an area in Jurassic Park III where you have to cross in order to get a collectible.  Make sure you have the destroy all objects brick shut off if it's on becuase when you go to jump on the barrels to get across it'll destroy the barrels and you'll end up in the water.  If you forget there is a way to get the barrels back should you make this mistake.  Go to one of the terminals I told you about and use the map to go to another location.  Once there go back to the map and pick to go back to the location.  It will ask if you want to go back at night or day.  Pick the opposite of what it was when you destroyed the barrels.  When you go back the barrels will magically reappear.  Finding the terminals are really important cause it allows to move from place to place and park to park easier so make sure you stop at them all.
The only other comment that I can make on the game are these:
- The graphics are gorgeous.  Best out of all the Lego games.
- The vechicles are slowly becoming easier to control with each game.  Some of the races weren't as bad in this game if you found the right vechicle (Note: buy the gyroscope as soon as it becomes available.  You will need it for some of the hub stuff.)
- While the vechicles are easier to control there was a boat that was absolutely awful.  I had to do that race like twenty times before I got it.  The race with the swimming dinosaur was also a bit tedious.  Lego still needs to work on controlling things in water a bit.
- The little bit of flying was better than previous games but still needs some work
- There was one red brick called compy mode that you can't get without the swimming dinosaur.  It was the last red brick I got when I was already done with the game.  I wish I'd gotten it earlier because it shrunk people to compy size and they started moving really fast.  It was kinda cute.  There was another brick that made everyone talk like they were on helium.  That was kinda cute for awhile too.
While I do recommend the game I also recommend waiting for an update and the price drop as well.  Paying $30 on steam instead of $60 on my PS4 made some of the glitches a little more bearable.  Hopefully there'll be an update soon.  Unto Lego Avengers.

The game has a few interesting ideas for the bullet-hell/twin-stick shooter genre-hybrid, but it lacks focus and struggles to follow it's own rules resulting in a highly unsatisfying experience.
Here was my experience.
First thing that struck me was the obnoxiously flashy menu screen.  I mean, the bloom rendered the menus unreadable!  But perhaps it is my monitor that isn't perfectly calibrated that is causing the issue.  I can try to look past that.  So let me change the resolution so I can enjoy it in full-screen... wait a minute.  Why is there an unsatisfying selection of screen  resolutions?   The game just reeks laziness now.  If your monitor resolution isn't the top 4 most common resolutions, gg to full-screen experience.
I still decided to give the game a shot.  I tried the tutorial, but it left me feeling very confused about many things.  Why add in the drilling ability?  The spinning ability?  When would I use each one?  What are you talking about "hoops in the nebula"?  Perhaps if I play a few levels I will come to understand... Nope.  After playing a few levels, I didn't even understand how I died most of the time nor understand what I should have done to stay alive.  Maybe the fun is in figuring all this out?  But first I got to use my points to level up.
What should I level up?  What does each of these do?  The description doesn't clarify most of the time nor can I see how the leveling affects my ship.  The leveling process is so unsatisfying, I don't even care what I level up as I often feel no sense of progress.  Also, why are there two play/back commands in the level up menu?  Such lazy menu design.
After playing and dying so many times, I decide to refer to the library archive in hopes of reading up on the enemies I faced.  "Know thy enemy" right?   Well, it would make a lot more sense if they actually placed images of the enemies so I know what they are talking about instead of focusing on trying to be funny.  For the record, their attempt at humor was so invasive, there was nothing funny about it.
I keep playing hoping I get over that hump to where I can start to have fun, but the more I play, the more I realize how rotten the game is.  Due to randomly generated  levels, each playthrough is unique, but it's also not satisfying because the difficulty feels very artificial and removes the feeling of progress.  Also, by adding shields that absorb damage in a bullet-hell game, it removes the threat bullets have at all.  I'll bet it was introduced because when things get too intense, all the flashy effects makes it impossible to tell what the hell is going on.  So rather than toning down the effects, they removed the core of what made bullet-hell bullet-hell.  It doesn't stop there though.  What makes difficult games fun?  Because the game lays out rules, and defeats you while following those rules.  And the simpler the rules, the better.  As such, when you die, you know exactly why you died and that reason was you.  The game didn't cheap-shot you.  Due to all the elements added to a supposedly simple genre, many times it's not clear why you died, and it breaks it's rules quite often, removing any fun from the challenge.
So in conclusion, the game ebbs feebly with nice ideas and flashy effects, but the game lacks much needed focus for the experience to be satisfying.  Avoid this game if you can.

From EDF 2017 to now, the game has only improved. However, as where I liked EDF 2017 for the 360 I have to say...
THIS GAME IS WORTH ITS PRICE.
That is something I rarely say, so hear me out.
Pros:
CONTENT! There is a lot to do, especially if you are looking for 100% and even if you aren't there are so many missions and difficulties to do and the anticipation of new weapons can easily keep you going and make harder levels worthwhile.
ENEMIES! There is a good amount of variety in the enemy types. To even throwing in some Mutant enemies on Inferno difficulty, This makes the game a blast to play, but at the same time, the start is limited in enemy types to help the player get into the game.
DIFFICULTY! The Difficulty is handled VERY WELL in this game. Some levels are against massive hordes while some are against special targets or bosses. On each difficulty setting, the enemies' health and damage scale really nicely as to give you a good margin of error on normal and easy, but to punish you for getting hit on the harder difficulties.
COOP! This is a big thing I like. Playing with others. If a game can have an amazing single-player game, then if they can do it right, they can have a far superior Multiplayer experience. EDF 4.1 NAILED IT! You can bring your friends in to help you clear the game in a multiplayer lobby. And it runs really well! There are also items that work well in conjunction with one another for much more of an advantage against the waves of enemies!
CONS:
UNSTABLE! This is really the only bad thing I have to say about it. Sometimes in multiplayer lobbies, when loading a mission the game will get stuck on connecting with the other players, dropping everyone out of the lobby. Probably just a small coding oversight but it can get annoying. Even if it doesn't happen all that often.
_______________
All in all, EDF 4.1 stays true to the series, a run&gun third person shooter with a lot of variety of weapons for dispatching HUNDREDS of enemies in a very well done atmosphere that gives a sense of urgency!

I'll start this by saying that when it comes to video games, I'm a very transient person. Typically I'm the person that'll play a game for a couple dozen hours, drop it, and typically not pick it back up. A few games that have managed to hook me in the past/present were/are Counter Strike:Source, Diablo 2, Path of Exile, World of Tanks, Dragon's Dogma, Warframe (Pre-Pushover DE), Dungeon Siege 2, KOTOR, SWAT 4... And a couple more I can't remember.
Long story short, it's very rare that a game grabs me and keeps me in, and I've played many hundreds of games over the years. Many very good games, too. Many games that claimed great replayability.
But this one hits all the right notes in all the right ways, and I can firmly say is WORTH the hefty price tag.
---------------
Now, let's get into an actual review. There are 4 classes for you to choose from: Ranger, Wing Diver, Air Raider, and Fencer. I'll say that Wing Diver is my least favorite class to play... But it's still a blast to play Wing Diver. Each class in this game has its niche and play style, and such a varied arsenal that you just want to play each class just to see what they can get.
----- Classes -----
Ranger is your standard foot-soldier type class, with a very variable arsenal, their weapon classes as such: Assault Rifles, Shotguns, Sniper Rifles, Rocket Launchers, Missile Launchers, Grenade Launchers, and other miscellaneous weapons/tools. This would including healing tools, flamethrowers, and other weapons that don't quite fit into the other categories.
Ranger's specific attributes entail that he can jump, roll (through light obstacles), has the 2nd-place armor scaling, has two weapon slots, can pilot vehicles, and has the fastest normal recovery time to get up off the ground after being knocked down.
-----
Wing Diver is the class I know the least about, but I still know enough to give a decent overview.
Wing Diver has a flight-frame that runs on a power-pack that'll allow you to fly around at a good clip for a decent bit of time, however, a good deal of their weapons draw from the very same power pool, so one has to be mindful of their energy consumption. Their arsenal's theme is very high-tech weaponry, such as laser, electronic, and mind-guided missiles.
Wing Divers have access to the following in their arsenal: Short-Range lasers, Mid-Range lasers, Mid-Range Electric, Particle Cannons, Sniping Weapons, Other Ranged Attacks (Such as plasma-bombers and grenades,) Homing Weapons, and other Special Weapons that don't fit in the rest. This class has weapons that can cover just about any range, but I'd say they're more-so specialized for Close Quarters and are proficient up to mid range, however they have powerful tools for long range as well.
Their specific attributes are that they can fly, have the least armor scaling of the 4 classes, can use a bit of power to burn their thrusters and recover from a ragdoll knockup/knockdown, has two weapon slots, can NOT pilot vehicles, and probably some other stuff I don't know.
-----
Air Raider, my personal favorite class, is the support class of this game. While he doesn't have much in the way of direct-attack, (being limited to "Limpet Guns" which are basically remote-trigger grenade launchers,) He has access to a powerful arsenal of air/sea support and vehicles to draw from.
Air Raider's arsenal goes as such: Guidance Equipment (Such as laser-designators for homing weapons,) Calling for Support, Support Equipment (Such as buffs, heals, and power-rechargers for Wing Divers,) Limpet Guns, Stationary Weapons (Such as C4, Sentry Guns, Claymores, AA Mines, etc,) and other Special Weapons such as razor-wire launchers, decoys, and electromagnetic shield systems.
They also have an equipment slot for a vehicle of choice, which can range from tanks, to AFVs, to SPGs, to Helicopters, to Hard-Suits, to a giant rock'em-sock'em robot.
Air-Raider's particular attributes are that they can pilot vehicles, have 3rd-place armor-scaling, and have laser-designator tools that grant/assist functionality of the other classes homing weapons.
-----
Fencer has a super-heavy exo-suit which allows them to use heavy-weaponry, and at that, dual-wield them. It's also the most technical/skill demanding class of the game, having many mechanics and caveats.
Their arsenal goes as such: CQB Striking weapons (Hammers, Swords, etc,) CQB Piercing weapons (Spears, auto-spears, etc,) Shields, Automatic Artillery, Artillery, and Missile Launchers.
While they have the least weapon categories, don't let that fool you. What goes under "Auto Arty/Arty" is a very diverse cast of weaponry, such as autocannons, gatling guns, heavy machine guns, cannon-shot, mortars, etc. Missile Launchers, while some of them are personally usable, the heavier ones are crew-served, requiring an Air Raider to designate targets to grant them functionality.
Fencer is the only class that has access to shields, which are what makes them able to be tanky. Shields come in different flavors, such as ones that are focused on re-directing ranged attacks, focused on giving you wide-angle protection, focused on high damage-reduction, etc.
Fencer's particular attributes are that they can carry two sets of two weapons, can bull-doze through obstacles, and have a very tricky to master ability to use the thrusters some weapons grant them to recover from knockdowns.
Something important to bare in mind about Fencers, is that due to the heavy-weight of their ranged weaponry, they are very unweildy and have slow, dragged out aiming. Dual weilding ranged weapons amplifies this effect, making it very difficult to use them proficiently, but still very possible with practice.
----- Gameplay -----
I'll say that I'm only on mission 47 of the standard online campaign, but it's to my understanding that, DLC not-withstanding, there are... I believe 90+ missions, with 5 different difficulties, so there's PLENTY of game time and replayability to be had.
This is a Third-Person shooter game, with an arcade-y feel, and a big focus on co-op gameplay, supporting sessions of up to 4 players, with a solo-mode as well. Enemy health scales with the amount of players ingame.
Let me tell you, that the difficulties aren't just what you'd expect them to be. You actually need to come prepared with a respectable arsenal from the lower difficulties first. The higher the difficulty, the more health your enemies have, the more deadly their attacks (Both in damage dealt, and in functionality,) and the faster they are. This game does difficulty very well, and doesn't just give them more and more HP... It adds a progressively more challenging gameplay that requires you to be prepared, both as a player with skills and logistics, and with your classes' weaponry.
The missions you play in vary, from wide-open mountains and/or fields, to cityscape, to underground tunnels and caves. It's to be noted that Air Raider's Support doesn't work underground, and only particular vehicles can be called in.
This game has a way of really imersing you into the atmosphere; from the battle-banter of your NPC allies (A+ for having NPCs under your command singing along with you and responding to your emotes,) commander, and mission handler on the comms; really making you feel tiny as you behold your gigantic enemies, in the hundreds and hundreds that you're tasked with eradicating in each and every mission; and the way the lighting plays with the underground environments is something I have never seen in any other game before... It's both beautiful and distressing at the same time.
---------------
I could go into details about some other junk that doesn't really matter, such as graphics, sound, controls, yadda yadda, but I'll simply say that this game does it all RIGHT. It hits all the right notes, and the controls perform exactly as you'd expect them to.
All said and done, this game gets a resounding 10/10 from me.

Do you like the idea of a game where you don't have to think too much, but just get to blast away at hordes of huge enemies with anything from lasers to explosive plasma blasts to lightning guns?
Where you can wreck the environment, causing more explosions and turning more skyscrapers into rubble than a Michael Bay movie?
Then this game is for you.
The basics of the games is this: Earth is being invaded by giant insects, arachnoids, alien spaceships, giant robots and more. Are these things connected? Who cares? Just let HQ worry about that while you mop up the enemy forces to the sound of your fellow soldiers singing songs about the EDF.
Graphics are not exactly top notch, but I suppose that's the tradeoff for having such huge scale battles. There's a city map, for example, with skyscrapers tall enough to make me want to avoid the edge just because the height makes my self-preservation reflexes kick in XD
There are 4 classes to play and 5 difficulties. Normal starts off relatively easy, but ramps up quite a bit during the midgame missions. It's what I played through the entire game at, though I did have to go back to some earlier missions on higher difficulties to get the weapon drops I needed to overcome certain levels.
It took me about 24 hours to go through all the missions on Normal difficulty (not counting DLC missions) with the flying Wing Diver class, which was a ton of fun. I expect I'll try one of the other classes soon to see how they play.
I also spent something like 2 hours in multiplayer with a friend. The multiplayer lobby system is a bit clunky, but once you're in a game together it seems to work just fine.
Music is overall fine, though it seemed a bit uneven in volume depending on where you were in relation to the action (could be someting with my system, I guess). The voice acting feels just cheesy enough to fit in a game like this. The ragdolling can be quite hilarious depending on what weapons are used, but seeing a ~8 meters tall robot flying off in 4 different direction after an airstrike hardly ever gets old :)
TLDR: It's like an 80s/90s B-movie - the game. Starship Troopers meets Independence Day, only turned up to 11.

I had been waiting for this game to come out for months, and it's finally here. But would it live up to what I hoped?
In a word, yes.
It's not perfect by any means. The background music is a bit too quiet at times, especially further from the radio, and I don't want to carry it around with me all over the level. Is the game fun? Definitely. Sometimes you have to get damn creative to complete the levels. Do I regret taking the time to play it? Pfft, no. Definitely worth my time. Would I spend $5 on it? Arma 3 is a military simulation game. I'd describe it to the layman as "like classic Battlefield (with the vehicles and the big maps), but on a much, much larger scale and instead of feeling arcadey the focus is on relative realism".
The base game is full of content both single player and multiplayer, but the game's pièce de résistance is the ridiculously large modding community. Examples of popular mods include the AltisLife RPG mode, the Battle Royale hunger games style survival mode, IFA3 Lite which is a WW2 conversion, The Unsung which is a vietnam conversion, Exile (Arma 3's version of DayZ), Wasteland (DayZ without the annoying zombies) and there are also tons of custom missions and maps available which have been made by the community.
The game comes with an excellent map editor to allow players to make their own missions and the free Zeus DLC lets a player build and control a mission for their friends on the fly.
There are communities dedicated to military realism, if that's your thing, and there are also communities dedicated to more arcadey game modes with a ton of action, too.
On the one hand, you can be as in depth and detailed with your missions as you can possibly imagine. On the other hand, there is a lot to learn which can be daunting for a beginner. Generally, throwing yourself in head first and learning as you go is the best approach.
Arma 3 is a game with so much content that it's easy to get totally lost in it and more content is being produced all the time. If you're interested in a true military action game then it simply has no equal.

Though I am not usually the biggest fan of platformer games, Shovel Knight managed to surprise me.  I purchased it after having heard the rave reviews and I must say that I was not disappointed.
The game at its basest level almost reminded me of the classic Megaman games, though, instead of an arm cannon you use a shovel to defeat your enemies.  That same shovel is also used as a pogo stick to bounce off of the environment as well as your enemies, and is a tool that the game requires you to master especially toward the end when timing and control are all that stands between you and a gruesome death.
The map phase of the game takes place on a map that is reminiscent of Mario Bros. 3, with levels, towns to purchase items from, and adventure locations sprinkled across it.  Each of the levels that you play has a theme based around the boss, and each of these these levels unlocks an ability similar to those that that particular boss has.  By the end of the game you're capable of swapping between a large supply of tools acquired from previously defeated enemies, some of which are dangerous weapons, others are invaluable tools.  Combine this aspect with the ability to purchase health and mana upgrades, a variety of items, and armor and weapons, and you've got a significant amount of lite-RPG added into the formula.
The story is rather light in the game (as you might expect) though it does convey the sense of urgency that Shovel Knight has in rescuing his love, Shield Knight, from the clutches of evil.  As far as action-platformers go, I was pleased with the story and it kept me entertained.
I would definitely recommend this game to any one particularly enjoys action-platformers with a touch of RPG, and would suggest the game to anyone else who has an open enough mind.  Just be prepared to scream obscenities at your computer screen for half an hour until you finally experience the sweet taste of victory.

I have been eyeing fugl for a long time, and today I finally got to play it. Here is my experience so far. I played the game with an XBOX ONE controller via USB cable.
REALLY GOOD!
- Really beautiful music when it plays.
- Really relaxing sounds, especially the sound of waves and the wind blowing.
- Vibrant colors painting a beautiful world.
- Lots of fish and creatues that are fun to spot.
- Interesting highlights making you want to see what might be there.
- Performance. I have an an i5-2500K CPU (3.3 ghz) and a gtx 970 GPU. Everything was butter smooth all the time.
- A joy to find new biomes.
- Playing as different creatures are fun. Ducks are fast, but hard to control when flying slow, butterflies pretty much the opposite.
COULD BE BETTER...
- You do not play 1st or 3rd person, but in "bird♥♥♥♥♥quot; perspective. Simply said, I feel the camera is way too close to the bird. I'd prefer the camera a bit further away. And I would absolutely ADORE first person perspective.
- It's currently a bit hard to land and take off. I'd prefer it to be easier. Also the bird flaps lake crazy when taking off. Would prefer a more slow, but powerfull flapping.
- You "become" the birds and creatures you get close to for a short time, before turning back into your start bird. It is kind of cool sometimes, other times kind of irritating. I do not find it serene to become a flying monkey all the time. A skill to target and transform into the creates you see when YOU want to would be better (my opinion).
- No reward for exploration. I don't expect much, but certain areas/spots should give a reward when you reach them. It could some interesting creatures to observe, a special view, some music you don't otherwise get to hear, a new ability, a piece of lore, , a nice little animation or scene, a mini game, or whatever.
- More variation in the terrain generation. When you fly fast, things seem very similar. Points of interest, like an extra special create, a castle, and such would be nice.
- Bird walking and sound animation. Right now you just hover in silence when you move on ground.
IN SORE NEED OF IMPROVEMENT
- Bugs. I often experienced the immidate surroundings around me disappearing. I could see things in the distance, but they would disaapear when I get close.
- Crashes. I experienced it twice now.
- A jump button. Srsly, I really missed that while on ground.
- An introduction to the controls. You get a 5 second overview of the controls before the screen disappears. I'd like that to stay for a bit longer. Also, there was no mention that you can control the power of flaps by the amount of pressure you apply on the shoulder buttons.
- The camera got stuck a couple of times.
All in all, I would recommend getting this game, especially it costing next to nothing. Gameplay wise it has some way to go, and control/camera wise it could use a lot of improvement in my opinion. But seeing this is an early access game , I am in no doubt that this will all improve over time.
I hope you and the developer(s) will find this review helpful. I can't wait to make this my go-to chill game after a long day of work, when it becomes a bit less frustrating to control your bird  ;)
Best regards from Denmark.
P.S. Please please PLEEEEEASE add first person perspective! :D

The thing which made Counter Strike great was that it had fun gameplay and it didn't start it's life as an E-Sport so it was built and designed as a game, RS6S is the opposite in the fact that it feels like it was built to be an E-Sport and the game comes second, the problem with that is although RS6S is turning into a decent E-Sport it isn't filling in all the slots as a great game.
Gameplay is good, feels relatively comfortable minus the occasional match where peeker's advantage takes over, and it feel's well put together in terms of the dynamics of the gameplay.
But beyond some good gameplay there's not much in this overall, generally speaking I found ranked to be completely broken, from playing against Gold's as a Bronze rank to vice versa, and the high likelihood is that you will never get to the point where you feel like ranked is working.
Then we move onto unlocking characters, it takes the same approach as the League of Legends formula x 2, the only problem being that they lock up the game for their playerbase bar either the hardcore or the spenders.
You see when you get passed the games initial characters it makes it exponentially harder to get the newer characters, and the only real way to get serious points to unlock those characters is to play ranked and win, except you aren't going to win many matches.
It sounds great on paper as a business idea, but completely breaks any traction you can potentially gain from trying to be an E-Sport, you see the biggest watchers of an E-Sport are usually the players.
If you have a small player base then trying to gain traction with an E-Sport type game is going to be very hard, and even harder when a simpler more refined experience (i.e. CSGO) is around the corner and doesn't throw hurdles in the way for just playing the game.
The good thing is that lately RS6S has been uping it's ideas with recent updates, so hopefully we will see some more faces appear making this good game great.
I really do hope that one day RS6S does bite the bullet and go F2P because in it's current situation it's never going to gain the traction it requires to become a true E-Sport, and even though the starter edition is a step in the right direction it still makes me wonder if the RS6S devs actually know where they are going with the game.

Welcome to Jurassic Park! The long-awaited sequel has arrived, and with it the entire collection of movies in the form of LEGO. The Developers at TellTale games have on many levels outdone themselves once again, and they've managed to migrate an extremely violent and unforgiving movie franchise into a fun filled adventure appropriate for kids of any age.
It tells the story of Jurrasic Park, The Lost World, Jurassic Park III and Jurrasic World. Having not seen the latest movie myself, this game has introduced much of the story and inspired interest to go and see it. There's a range of minifigs to play as, including dinosaurs and the larger dinosaurs, which all feature unique skills. Much of these skills are featured in existing LEGO games, but there are some new ones such as the Velociraptor's special move.
There's not much to say other than it's a part of the LEGO world, in which all of the original movie assets were used and available - we got to hear much from Dr. Hammond who the real actor is sadly not with us anymore. The sounds of the Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus are amazing in that they match the movies assets and were enjoyable and believable.
The maps are captivating and interesting, but the puzzles didn't present themselves like a challenge as they did in LEGO Marvel or at all - however the games are not targeted at middle-age men...
The game for many people has been riddled with bugs, however I only experienced one bug where I had to restart the level. As for technical issues, it seems that the game was rushed towards the end with woeful DX11 support which should have been either mandatory or not available as once you start a game, your save game will become corrupt if you change - and the game is pretty poor in DX11 mode without locked fullscreen resolutions - so my experience was purely 720p streamed to my Laptop, With this said, it didn't present as a problem to me - but it would have been nice...
If you enjoy LEGO games, this is a must. The game is supurb though lacking some technical refinement of which I hope does not come back for their next release. It's plentiful of comedy, almost violence free, plenty of replayability for those completionists. Overall the fun factor is here, which matches LEGO Batman 2 and Marvel - it is one of their best.

This is a fun twin stick shooter. There is a fairly major seizure warning to be aware of, lots of flashing lights and effects on screen. There's also some entertaining voice-acting in a British accent which comments on some events.
For those that don't know what that means, it's a shooter where one stick (or WASD) controls movement, while the other stick (or your mouse) control the direction your weapons shoot in. This isn't a standard bullet hell game where you have a tiny hitbox and one hit will destroy you, you have a shield and two alternate modes for your ship that can (or must be used) to protect you from enemies and the environment. There's only four bosses, but the enemies appear in a wide variety of patterns and it's easy to pick up and play for a little while.
If you like stacking massive high scores while trying to keep your little ship alive, this is a great game. If you like your shoot-em-ups to be orderly and have no unpredictable elements, this may feel like a frustratingly different experience.
I like it, and there's lots of developer's commentary included in the in-game Library that really shows the love and dedication the creators have for the genre and games in general.

"pretty" "artsy" visuals aside, Really Big Sky is basically a game that fills in a checklist of how NOT to design a shmup.
The visuals are simply "crazy" and not in the good, Crimzon Clover sort of way. All of the post-processing effects that do not interact well with each other at all make it hard to see what's going on, and the lack of level design and spongy enemies make playing Really Big Sky a confusing and ultimately pointless experience. (The worst offender is the "retro" mode, which only looks retro if 60's acid trip raves are what you consider to be "retro" in videogames.)
Additionally, the gameplay is not at all noteworthy or creative. The only unique mechanic in this horizontally-scrolling twin-stick shooter is the "drill" option, which allows you to drill through certain objects and collect items. Although this could be fun, the game doesn't do much with it, largely due to the lazy procedural generation and simplistic obstacles, which leads me to my next point, the game is laughably easy - you can take many hits before biting it, and all of the enemies and bosses have extremely simple attack patterns that pretty much everyone has seen before. you may ask "so how does the game introduce challenge over time?" and the answer to this is that it instantly kills you by some kind of hazard or enemy that enters at speeds that you could not reasonably react to, and since the game is randomised it's not as though you can reliably memorise them. Needless to say, this is incredibly lazy game design that any arcade game worth its weight in quarters could not get away with.
This isn't even mentioning the obnoxious narration that goes on throughout the game (which at least when I played it, you could not disable). Hearing a sterotypical british guy say "oohhhhh you♥♥♥♥♥quot; every second time you die is cute the first couple of times you hear it, but quickly becomes grating.
Really Big Sky is a game filled with unnecessary additions weighing down the otherwise simplistic and boring gameplay, that tries to excuse this fact by shoving in post-processing effects and obnoxious narration to try and be "artistic". Even worse and even more overrated than Sine Mora. Avoid.

Where to start with this game...
Well, it comes straight off the heels of AC2, not missing a beat. It's expansive, has a TON of collectibles of all kinds, a massive map that's genuinely interesting and fun to explore, not to mention a handful of additional areas outside of Rome. Rome is a spawling, living, breathing city that really comes to life with purpose and function, both helping and hindering you depending on how careful you are. The social stealth is still in strong and the extent to which you can customize your appearance is also nice.
The new features in the climbing and combat are welcome, making things more fluid and tactical. I liked the 'boss battles' that don't repeat themselves or rely on simply being strong enough, instead weave story into their encounters. The story, by the way, is fantastic. The voices, both in english and Italian are also amazing. Characters are great, lovable, amusing, visuals hold up well... etc. The pluses go on.
That being said... I did have a few small critiques. Not that they affect my rating, but you may have trouble associating which way is "forward" during some fixed-camera sequences, as well as some inconsistent behaviour by the AI and engine in general, such as guards detecting you immediately when they normally don't, or even glitching to appear out of thin air. It wasn't often enough to ruin my experience, but it's not a perfect game because of these, and the sometimes frustrating requirements for 100% completion.
All in all, a fantastic title and well worth playing AC2 for, I look forward to playing Revelations greatly. Highly recommended.

Though I am not usually the biggest fan of platformer games, Shovel Knight managed to surprise me.  I purchased it after having heard the rave reviews and I must say that I was not disappointed.
The game at its basest level almost reminded me of the classic Megaman games, though, instead of an arm cannon you use a shovel to defeat your enemies.  That same shovel is also used as a pogo stick to bounce off of the environment as well as your enemies, and is a tool that the game requires you to master especially toward the end when timing and control are all that stands between you and a gruesome death.
The map phase of the game takes place on a map that is reminiscent of Mario Bros. 3, with levels, towns to purchase items from, and adventure locations sprinkled across it.  Each of the levels that you play has a theme based around the boss, and each of these these levels unlocks an ability similar to those that that particular boss has.  By the end of the game you're capable of swapping between a large supply of tools acquired from previously defeated enemies, some of which are dangerous weapons, others are invaluable tools.  Combine this aspect with the ability to purchase health and mana upgrades, a variety of items, and armor and weapons, and you've got a significant amount of lite-RPG added into the formula.
The story is rather light in the game (as you might expect) though it does convey the sense of urgency that Shovel Knight has in rescuing his love, Shield Knight, from the clutches of evil.  As far as action-platformers go, I was pleased with the story and it kept me entertained.
I would definitely recommend this game to any one particularly enjoys action-platformers with a touch of RPG, and would suggest the game to anyone else who has an open enough mind.  Just be prepared to scream obscenities at your computer screen for half an hour until you finally experience the sweet taste of victory.

Brotherhood picks up where 2 left off. You continue following Desmond and he continues reliving Ezio's life. The game made a few improvements over 2, although not as big of a jump as it was from 1. The entire story takes place in Roma and only a few of the mechanics are changed. There are a few new weapons, a few new moves, a few new ways to get around buildings, and a few new vehicles. Before you can use shops, you're going to have to rennovate them yourself which cost money but increases the value of the city. I found the economy to be much more steady in this game than the previous game.
One of the most satisfying parts of this game was destroying the Borgia's towers. In every area, before you can rennovate shops and buy buildings, you have to eliminate the Borgia's influence. To do this, you need to assassinate a leader near their tower and then set the tower on fire. What makes this so satisfying is because this is completely open. You don't have to "start" the side quest like you have to with others. You can just go there, sneak in, and kill the leader however you want. If you are discovered, some leaders will come fight you while others will hide in the tower (forcing you to wait until the next dusk/dawn for them to return).
Also, about halfway through the game (maybe a little earlier) you can begin recruiting people to the brotherhood. When you rescue a citizen, they start training to become assassins. You can send them on missions to increase their level and upgrade their weapons and armor or you can use them to fight for you. Sometimes it's not worth getting your hands dirty so just lock onto your target, hit the appropriate key and your recruits will jump out of the shadows and assassinate for you. If you have enough recruits, you can also arrow storm which will eliminate a group of guards.
The only thing I didn't like about this game was Uplay. It's not so much that I don't like signing up for Uplay or that I feel annoyed my game is forever attached to my Uplay account (after all, that's basically the same as Steam). But what frustrated me was that Uplay would open every time I exited the game. If you are using Big Picture mode and a controller, this is problematic mainly because you can't close the window with a controller; you need to grab your mouse. I got around this by setting up a Pinnacle Game Profile to run when Uplay runs so that through a few button presses, I can control the mouse and close the window. Despite this annoyance, I would recommend this to anyone who likes stealth/open world games only if they've finished Assassin's Creed 2.

EDF is a game that takes its story and characters and puts them off to the side for the sake of dropping you right in and letting you have fun in your bug blasting, building toppling mayhem simulator.
The story feels like a very intentionally crafted Sci-Fi b-movie you'd find on at 11pm on a Wednesday night which works perfectly since the story really only exists to offer up some reactions to "Oh no, there's spiders now!"
The playstyle is incredibly arcadey and really shines once you start piling up your hoard of weapons. You'll start off with basic stuff like rifles and rocket launchers that feel really tame, but by the end that rifle will shoot in a V shape with bouncing bullets reflecting all over a small tunnel that turns into a tornado of ant death while your friend is summoning the not-Megazord to punch not-Godzilla in the mouth.
The only real negative I can give this game is that as a single player experience it feels somewhat lacking. The gameplay doesn't change in any way, the missions don't gain or lose anything nor do you (unless you're playing the Fencer class that has a few weapons that require an Air Raider present), but the game just feels -right- as a co-op experience. The satisfaction of coordinating your efforts to land that PERFECT hit on a group of enemies just feels so rewarding that going back to playing solo almost feels dull by comparison.
Ideally, get a few friends together, kick back and enjoy the ride that EDF has to offer. If you can't talk your friends into it, jump into a game online and go nuts. It's a game worth picking up even at full price, you'll get more time out of your money than many other games will give you.

Even after 10 years, TF2's core gameplay still shines incredibly bright.
Its weapons are extremely satisfying to use, and Its mechanics have a lot of subtle depth.
Matches are always fast paced and exciting, thanks to its strong focus on skill-based movement and sense of speed.
Healing ramp-up and excellent map design create a push-pull dynamic that allows player decision-making to become noticeable.
Each of its nine classes fill a distinct design space with little overlap on both a visual and mechanical level. This allows you to focus on how to respond to each threat, rather than figuring out what the threat is.
Even the medic has balls of steel. In most games, healing roles are cowering wimps who hide in corners all day. Not here. Bold skillful plays are heavily rewarded.
Counters don’t really exist, any class can outplay and outskill any other. 1v1 dm skill clearly separates good players from great ones.
Team play is important, but TF2 is flexible enough to give strong players the chance to shine by going nuts and killing everyone. Having an awful team does not mean the fun stops.
Stuns do not exist, because they are not fun to play against in first person games.
You can edit any of the maps or create your own with its extensive editor. Make small tweaks to your favorites or go beyond and design all new game modes.
Whether you use its community for a fun social space to meet great friendos, or its development tools to create something new, or its depth and high skill ceiling to continually improve yourself, TF2 truly has something to offer to everyone for many more years to come. Please enjoy this fantastic game.

It's wild, colorful, disorienting, and hard to tell what's happening half the time. It's also dirt cheap when on sale and plenty of fun despite its drawbacks.
Also, there is an option to turn that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ narrator off. You know, the one that insults you whenever you die. I don't know why the developers felt the need to include him, but the voicing just makes the game seem pretentious.
Here's the breakdown: It's a solid twin stick bullet-hell(ish) shooter with great music and wild colors that is often on sale for next to nothing. Hell, I got it for free in a promotion. Movement and shooting is slick and simple, the drilling mechanic (where you have to sacrifice the ability to shoot in order to drill through oncoming solid objects) is interesting and well-executed, though the game would be just as good without it, and the music is great.
The only downsides are the narrator and the fact that it's easy to lose track of what's going on. One minute you're blasting away at a boss, when suddenly all the colors invert without any indication as to what triggered it, nor does it seem to change the gameplay at all. Other times your projectiles (and those of your enemies) will travel agonizingly slowly, or blindingly fast, with no indication of what triggered this change. Sometimes you get a big laserbeam that lasts for a few seconds and obliterates everything, again with no indication of what triggered it. The screen is often packed with so much activity that it's hard to tell who's an enemy or what they do, and the best strategy becomes "fire wildly and hope for the best".
But whatever. Psychedelic color schemes, boopin' music, and the ability to pick it up and play for 10-20 minutes at a time make it worth whatever pocket change you spend on it.

If you've beaten Portal 2 and want some more, then get this.  Right now.
Be aware, that you do not need Portal 2 installed to play, but you do need to own it.
I got stuck  and struggled far more often than I would have liked.  I think some of the puzzles are more difficult than Portal 2, and may take some more time to accomplish.  I started using quick-save extensively, and I remapped it further away from quickload so I wouldn't press the wrong one by mistake.
Over all the quality is good.  It's not quite on the same level as Portal 2, but it's close enough to be very impressive for a small team that released their product for free.  A few puzzles might not have been quite as polished, or maybe they used some mechanics that were kind "fiddly"(that's the best word I can think of for it)?  That left me pretty frustrated some of the time, but I found that frequently I was simply making a mistake.  Either I had forgotten some critical bit of information (that I probably used successfully in a previous puzzle), or I was overthinking it, or just going down the wrong path.
I suspect that a bigger QA team probably would have made for a smoother gameplay experience. Again, for a small team releasing their product for free the quality was excellent.  The writing and voice acting were not as good as Portal 2, but still pretty good.
The time I spent on the game was well worth it, and the price is unbeatable.  I suspect that if I had played this right after playing Portal 2, instead of years later, that I would have struggled considerably less.
So, it might have been beneficial to play through Portal 2 again, first, before playing this.

I'm writing this as someone who has played every single major Lego game from Lego Star Wars 1 on the PS2 all the way up to Lego Jurassic World. LJW is by far and away the best and most well made Lego game of all time. It is eminently kid friendly in its controls. Even more so than previous games. For the first time I can say that even children as young as single digits will probably not get frustrated and will more than likely be able to complete the entire game to 100% completion with little to no help from anyone else. Some of the races are a bit finiky and more than one will require repetition to get them just right but they are all still way more forgiving of mistakes than any previous game. The audio taken from the movies is a bit off at times but that's to be expected given that the movies are a fair bit old by this point and it's no worse than either the Lego Hobit or Lego Lord of the Rings. I think in terms of sheer fun and playability, Lego Jurassic World may very well be my all time favorite Lego game beating out Lego Batman 2, Lego Harry Potter 2, and Lego Batman 3 for the title (those were my top three favorites previously). This is a wonderful game to add to your collection and well worth the cost of even full price ($40 if I remember correctly).
One thing of note, if you find yourself missing a gold brick or two at the very end, walk around the Jurassic Park map with the gold brick detector on. I ran across a couple bricks that weren't indicated by the map point menus but did pop up with the detector. Aside from that and the occasional glitch that were easily gotten rid of by restarting the level (and they haven't come up again since) the game is perfect. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!

Simply one of the best game I have ever played. This might not be the most popular game out there, but the fact that it has been out for around 10 years and is still holding solid 50k players, is pretty impressive. The developers of this game always strove to make the game as balanced as possible. Even after 10 years, they still tend to update their game and I am really thankful for that. So for those who say that Valve doesn't care, you're wrong. And no, this game is NOT pay to win. There are no "overpowered" weapons or anything of the sort. All of the weapons were made in a way to balance everything. The game has nine playable characters. Together they are split into 3 catagories: Attack, Defense and Support. Some people might rant about one class being more overpowered than the other and they may be true. All of the classes were made to be a counter to something. Although the game does have some bugs, it is still enjoyable in its own way. Apart from that, there are multiple gamemodes available for everyone to play. For starters, there is a gamemode named "casual". That is the gamemode where both newcomers and experienced players tend to go to. It is really good to warm you up and just to have fun in general. If you really want to get into the competitive scene, you should try out "etf2l" or "faceit" since the "competitive" option is really broken. Apart from casual and competitive, there are also "community" servers. They include all different varieties of gamemodes. From deathrun, to slender. From hide & seek to prop hunt and so on. There are also some game mechanics that take skill to master. For example: rocket/sticky/sentry jumping, sniper aim, mobility, movement, ect. You've got plenty of servers available for you to practice any of those things.
Obviously this game is for free, so it never hurts to try it out. I can say for a fact that once you really get into it, it starts to get addicting.

Arma 3 is a military simulation game. I'd describe it to the layman as "like classic Battlefield (with the vehicles and the big maps), but on a much, much larger scale and instead of feeling arcadey the focus is on relative realism".
The base game is full of content both single player and multiplayer, but the game's pièce de résistance is the ridiculously large modding community. Examples of popular mods include the AltisLife RPG mode, the Battle Royale hunger games style survival mode, IFA3 Lite which is a WW2 conversion, The Unsung which is a vietnam conversion, Exile (Arma 3's version of DayZ), Wasteland (DayZ without the annoying zombies) and there are also tons of custom missions and maps available which have been made by the community.
The game comes with an excellent map editor to allow players to make their own missions and the free Zeus DLC lets a player build and control a mission for their friends on the fly.
There are communities dedicated to military realism, if that's your thing, and there are also communities dedicated to more arcadey game modes with a ton of action, too.
On the one hand, you can be as in depth and detailed with your missions as you can possibly imagine. On the other hand, there is a lot to learn which can be daunting for a beginner. Generally, throwing yourself in head first and learning as you go is the best approach.
Arma 3 is a game with so much content that it's easy to get totally lost in it and more content is being produced all the time. If you're interested in a true military action game then it simply has no equal.

The shoot 'em up has been seeing a resurgence lately in the land of indies. As technology has blossomed, so too has the love of flashy lights and cool explosions. Really Big Sky lives for the ridiculous and the flashy, with spinning psychedelic dinosaur heads and gorgeous 80's inspired everything to really keep the mesmerization of those watching all of that stuff explode in colorful, saturated bursts.
Whomever the art designer was, they must've really liked the most recent Star Trek films because my god is everything glare-y and saturated. Most of the time, it's gorgeous watching the chaos unfold on screen, but sometimes the overwhelming brightness of explosions or attacks and the sheer information overload can disorient and end an impressive run without even knowing what exactly killed you. It can be frustrating, but it's hard not to love a game so charmingly bombastic.
There is a lot of inspired ideas implemented into this little indie title, and more than enough to keep someone engaged to see everything it has to offer. Randomized encounters and an increasing difficulty, along with permanent upgrades and so forth adds further to the fun, even if it is fairly easy to max everything out quickly. The speed in which things are unlocked can be fairly cathartic, and wiping out swarms of T-Rex skulls is never not satisfying, but you will see just about everything before too long.
It's fun, it's wildly stupid, and it's fairly cheap and on sale often. Are there better games? Yes. Of course there are. But as a schmup, there are few so willing to embrace the insane, I can't help but love this one.  Drilling planets at an insane speed is also one of the coolest things ever. Definitely looking forward to whatever else this studio releases.

This title expands to what Assassin's Creed II so great, but also takes a small step back. And that step back is for the better. ACII wanted to make everything bigger and better. They made a lot of things better as opposed to AC1, but some of the cities and locations felt very empty. In this title (which in my opinion should be could Assassin's Creed III: Brotherhood) the entire adventure takes place in Rome. It is gigantic and very well detailed. It looks way better then Assassin's Creed II and there are some subtle improvements to the gameplay of ACII.
The Story is not as good as the last two games in the series. The ending is great and leaves you guessing. Ezio is now becoming a Master Assassin and thus recruits new Assassin's. You can call these brothers in arms into battle whenever you wish. Yes, it's a cheap and overpowered way to get yourself out of a tough fight, but I love the way these Assassin's come out of hiding places just like Altaïr or Ezio would. You bond with a lot of characters and I love that.
In other words, did you play the wonderful Assassin's Creed II and you want to know the next chapter in the story? Brotherhood is a very safe purchase. Fun, beautiful and exciting! Love it.

Shovel Knight, in short, is a fantastically crafted game. It's level design is great and, for the most part, fair; its settings and levels are wonderfully creative and as beautiful as 8-bits can portray; it's soundtrack is good, but can be slightly ear-grating at times due solely to it's 8-bit synth; and the colorful characters and NPCs in the game set the world of Shovel Knight to life in ways older games wish they could have done. Do I suggest the game? Of course! But here's all of my thoughts in a convenient list:
PROS:
Great soundtrack.
Charming, likable characters and NPCs.
Colorful and creative settings.
Plague Knight.
Fluid and highly responsive controls.
Good level design.
Lots of goodies and collectibles to obtain.
Water level that is actually fun.
Free extensive DLC to come in the future (Playable Plague Knight and Spectre Knight, and possibly more).
Butt Mode.
CONS:
1: Highly demanding achievements such as:
Don't die ever (this one in particular can go screw itself).
Don't get hit ever (screw this one too).
Don't die via bottomless pits.
Don't collect relics.
Beat the game in 1 hour and 30 minutes.
And 2: Archaic level and gameplay designs such as:
damage knockback.
instant death spikes (which, like in Mega Man, are EVERYWHERE).
Certain levels extensively plagued with ice physics and bottomless pits.
If I had to rate Shovel Knight, I would give it a solid 9/10. It's a fantastically crafted game from start to finish, but some design choices truly (and negatively) set it back into the retro era of gaming.
All hail the Troupple King! The King of Fruit and Fish! Long may his stem grow!

Alright, I want to start off by saying I am by no means good at this game.  I usually only play casual instead of ranked because I feel that I cannot meet the expectations and skill level of players in ranked.  That said, if you plan on purchasing this game:
1) Play with friends.  If you don't have any, make some.  It is more enjoyable and less frustrating to play with people you are familiar with.  Otherwise, if you're bad at the game like me, playing solo, and miss an entire mag of shots point-blank, some teammates will not take kindly to that and just rage quit your match leaving you and whoever decided to stay with you to finish the match against a full team of 5.  But, if you have a group of friends, they are more likely to tolerate terrible aim/stupid decisions.
2) Please, please, PLEASE communicate with your teammates whether it be by voice or typing it out.  Too many times I've gotten into matches where my teammates don't say anything to one another.  Simple callouts like sounds of a window breaking in a room for example, help A TON.
3) Optional (but VERY highly recommended): get a decent headset/headphones and microphone.  You will appreciate being able to hear quieter sounds (i.e. footsteps) with a good set of headphones, and your teammates will definitely appreciate good mic quality and the ability to understand what you are trying to say to them (so long as it's relevant to the match   :P).
Finally, I'm going to go ahead and recommend this game in spite of my solo experiences because I've had such a blast (pun not intended) playing with my friends.

Darkest of days has is a game with many strengths and weaknesses, but its a game youd probably want to pick up any way. first lets look at some of the strengths
1. Gameplay: the gameplay is great. the guns each have an authentic feel and there are reasons to like/dislike either the futureistic or past weapons meaning that even when you do get a chance to try out some of the futuristic guns the older weapons never feel useless in comparison. its a well balanced game
2. though pradicatlbe as hell the games stroy is actually great. i really enjoyed the few charaters you interact with and dexter is a very good and actually useful A.I follower. i liked the varity of, though similar looking, very definitive and induvidual time periods. Being in pompii was a nice surprise for me being a keen fan of classical history
3. its creative. its never been done before. and even though it has alot of issues its something that id personally like to see more of, if they ever devalop a sequal id very much enjoy it i also liked how open the levles were and how for the post part you could approach an event how you chose
Cons:
1. its very buggy an performance on my i7-7700 and GTX 1070 (with 16gb of ddr4) was medicore at best. physics were off and it stuttared alot. how ever it will run on almost anything now days so its nothing to complain about.
2. Though the game engine is some what powerful with sometimes hundreds of objects and people on screen at once and well textured and high quality weapons the textures of the landscape were in all honesty crap. though alot of the nature looked okay
3. its short and ends out out of nowhere. though i liked the fact that it set up for a sequal but we are now 8 years down the line and the story still has no conclusion so eh the ending is meh, and it only lasted me about 7 hours and i died a fair bit.
To conclude its probably not worth the price tag but i really enjoyed it even though it has alot of flaws.

I didn't expect a stellar storyline, but the idea of using weapons from different time periods was really interesting to me, so I gave it a "shot" (pun intended).
Unfortunately, this game is ... terrible. From the tutorial mission to the "final showdown", it was a pretty bland and stale experience. And a short-lived one at that. The story is dumb, the characters are uninteresting, the acting sucks, the action sucks, the weapons suck...
And there's a cliffhanger/let's-set-up-expectations-for-a-sequel "ending". I'm not going to spoil it, but just to say, it's marvelously absurd and I would actually be curious to see if and how they could pull off such a sequel.
It's not all bad though. I had fun at times, even though the story made little sense. Darkest of Days is the video game equivalent to an unironically mediocre B-movie. If this was one of the devs' first games, I give them a kudos for the ambitious premise, and actually look forward to finding out what projects they went onto next... but this one was definitely a 'practice ball'.

It is rare to see games with the effect of time traveling in them, when I found out about Darkest of Days and how you get to "time travel" in it, I was totally into getting it, and I did and it is awesome.
The game follows the story of a man named Alexander Morris, a soldier in General Custer's army. The game begins with the Battle of Little Big Horn (or Custer's Last Stand) going down in the dumps when all of the sudden Morris is injured and rescued by a man in futuristic armor who appears out of a bubble like portal. In the game you are assigned to "Protect and Preserve History as it is" by traveling through time into events and famous battles of World War 1, World War 2 and the American Civil War, rescuing certain individuals that play a key role in history.
The shooter and story aspect of this game is awesome, because you get to use different weapons from the American Civil War, WW1, and WW2. The graphics of this game...not the best and you can tell there are some glitches in it, it is like the producers of this game wanted to make it quickly, and the ending is a cliff hanger (hence the four star rating). But all in all Darkest of Days is an action filled first person shooter that is exciting and fun to play. It is long and can be difficult if you are not careful but I like the time traveling, Characters, Story, and weapons in it. (Just a side note, there is a lot of swearing and cussing in this game just to give you a heads up).
But Darkest of Days is a fun game and it is great to see a game with time traveling in it, I would recommend this for any time traveling/shooter fan. :)

I nominated this game for The "Test of Time" award because it deserves it. Absolutely deserves it.

PREREQUISITES
(1) A friend or two or three
(2) A healthy sense of humour and taste for the absurd
(3) A juvenile appreciation of titanic explosions, godzilla-scale destruction and B-movies
EDF is one of the most entrancing yet mystifying series in all of video games. A mechanical analysis of the game would center around its most prominent 'flaws':
- 80 missions with no coherent context, featuring similar city-scape sandboxes and nonsensical underground burrows
- Glitchy physics where giant bugs are propelled across the sky by your explosive weapons
- Hundreds of unlockable weapons and vehicles, many of which are broken to the point of being useless
- Voice tracks of screaming soldiers and moronic scientists that have no correlation to what's happening on screen
An analysis of systems and function would pronounce this game a dismal failure, and leave it there.
But only someone with no joy in their soul could miss the forrest for the trees and misdiagnose this game as anything other than a spectacular success. Every glitchy giant ant that you propel into the stratosphere is cause for mad giggling. Every weapon unlock is a thrilling lottery - you might find an orbital ion cannon painter that vaporises swarms of bugs, or you might be gifted a hilariously useless assault rifle that sprays two lines in a horizontal V pattern. Your vehicle unlock could be a colossal megazord mech that punches the freak out of elastic Michelin man alien robots, or it could be a motorbike with a side-car featuring the worst turning of anything ever coded. But in the spirit of mad experimentation, you'll jump into it anyway with your friends, and barrel into swarms of hopping tarantulas, cackling like maniacs.
Somehow you'll survive, with the city you've been entrusted to save now just flattened rubble. All civilians massacred. Your commanders over radio will declare your mission an unqualified triumph, and you will be whisked off to your next mission. Alien orb motherships loom ominously in the sky, dropships spew streams of ants, moronic attack drone swarms bumble and richochet off buildings as they attempt to strafe you with lazer globs. But you will hang your head high, knowing that you have nothing to fear. You are the EDF - the finest Earth has to offer against the alien menace. And you will emerge victorious.

I grew with my family in Alamogordo New Mexico which was close to where Atomic bombs used to be tested in the 50's and 60's.  There were a few movies based on the nuclear fallout that caused mutations in insects - ants in particular.
As a kid growing up near the place where these A-bomb tests took place, my parents would sometimes tell me as we were driving through the desert that those hills were where those giant ants came from and that the would come and get me if I wasn't a good boy.  I remember cowering in fear in the rear seat, peeking over the door ever so slightly hoping that I wouldn't see a silhouette of an ant in the distance.  To this day, I have a fear of giant ants and also Colonel Sanders, but that is a story for a different review.
Earth Defense Force is about taking my childhood fears and dropping my own A-bomb or whatever I choose to use in my arsenal of collectable weapons to wipe out those hauting memories of giant ants, spiders or whatever else my parents might have conjured up to keep me in check.  While you're at it, take out half of Tokyo pretending you're a small scale WMD or just a walking Godzilla who uses guns and rocket launchers.
I'm a good boy mommy, I really am.  Don't let those giant ants get me...
Oh and there are tons of missions and different classes to interact and play as, something about an action shooter game in there as well.

Assassin's Creed Brotherhood is a fun game, just as good as its prequels. It is filled with many Assassin's Creed II functionalities, but maintains a fresh new take on the franchise.
Continuing the open world aspect (thank goodness), you play as Ezio once again, this time exploring Rome, of which was a brief setting in II that you could not roam. Now all the city is yours to do whatever you wish. The adventure never fails, letting you climb on vertially anything, until you get to the top and see Rome in all its glory. The setting is amazingly beautiful.
The voice acting is terrific, and it's awesome seeing Ezio age from the beginning of II to the events of Brotherhood. The combat is the same as well, allowing you to stealthily hide in crowds or hack and slash through guards as you please. Because pleasure is guaranteed in this game.
A fun new feature in brotherhood sticks with the title: you can now recruit other assassins to help you in the game. You can have them eliminate foes for you, or send them on missions to make money for you and strengthen the asssassin's abilities. The story is magnificent as well, keeping you on your toes the whole time.
For any action-adventure lover or fellow Brotherhood members, this is the perfect game for you. But, keep in mind, this is not the first game. I advise you to play Assassin's Creed I and II first. Assassin's Creed I CAN be skipped, but I do not recommend it. Play them all. "Nothing is true, everything is permitted."

Upsides include everything else, including the soundtrack, the oh-so-british silly voice acting, the infinitely replayable gameplay, the ease at which you can just load this up for a quick blast when you're short on time, the simple controls, the wonderful array of enemies and bosses to fight and learn how to beat, the drill/vortex mechanic, and the range of different playmodes to increase (or decrease in one case) your challenge. This helps keep the game wonderfully fresh. Bored of the normal mode? Try pacifism mode! Or Boss Rush! or HELL, or Nightmare! or Retro for that Atari-esque feel complete with eyebleedy colour clash!
There is literally no reason not to give this a try. It's a blast!

At long last, I know what it would be like to go into War tomorrow if I were Robert Downey JR. As I watched dozens of German WW1 troops spawn in, arms upraised, and drop onto a hill before charging our position, I manned the automatic gun. Streams of brilliant gunfire shot wildly, yet shocking accurately onto my foes, but there was no way to stem the tide! The huns breached the trenches and began firing at the fleeing men around me... Yet to a man, every German troop was looking straight at me! They shot with unnerving pin point precision, but never tore they eyes from me.
This, my friends, is the Robert Downey JR war simulator. Enemies spew over the mud and blood, but despite aiming their guns at enemies, they all stare right at you in slack mouthed awe! I could almost hear the Germans whispering: "Schauen Sie, Hände! Das ist Robert Downey JR! Nicht schießen, schauen Sie nur." as they elbowed their friends in the ribs softly, not interrupting their gunfire as they smiled at me.
Okay, okay, so there's more to this game then that... Here's some things to like:
I got to kill toga clad civilians fleeing the Mt Vesuvius eruption with a flame thrower. That was a big'ol plus. I turned the tide of the American Civil War by introducing them to the automatic weapon. The game didn't give me a tumor of any kind, so that's pretty cool.
Here are some things that weren't great:
"Mother"'s voice actor sounds like she's reading the news and weather. The levels, despite SEEMING to be large, open maps are, in reality, a series of straight lines with knee high fences keeping you from moving around enemy positions. The programming is a bit lack luster... For example, you can star reloading one weapon and switch to using another while it continues to reload on its own. This includes powder rifles that require powder, wadding, bullet and sabot all to be pounded down with a loading pole while your... Um... Other set of arms shoots your pistol? Stairs are sometimes only surmountable by jumping up them, which doesn't sound too bad, but when you're running backwards up them as you shoot at suicidal enemies that charge towards you and you suddenly stop in the open, letting round after round puncture your precious organs... Then you'll long for the days when stairs could be programmed correctly. Don't worry, though, your enemies have the same problem. Sadly, their solution is to phase halfway through the stairs themselves with only the tops of their heads showing and shower you in gunfire while they remain mostly unharmed by all but the luckiest attacks.
In short, while being a time traveling Robert Downey JR, shooting Roman legionnaires with a machine gun SOUNDS awesome, you could instead take the $20 US asking price for this game, buy Iron Man and 300 on blu-ray, record footage from each and splice them together and watch that instead.

Shovel Knight is quite different from many platformers in many senses. To begin the idea of using the shovel is interesting because it allows for more unique puzzles/treasures. Another interesting part of the game is the ability to press down to bounce on top of enemies with your shovel. The extent to which this can be used to grant you bonus treasures, defeat bosses, and even get more power ups makes it more than a gimmick, but turns it into a very important mechanic to learn and master.
Furthermore, the game has some of the most creative bosses and stages of any game. Each stage has its own mechanics that you must be able to pick up on the fly. Normally I would not like this, but you are usually given one stage where you can practice using the mechanic before having to use it to complete a screen.
Overall I highly recommend Shovel Knight.

I've forever been envious of people playing this game... And now it's finally on steam. It is everything I had hoped and more, with the co-op feature I hadn't known about. Co-op works flawlessly, overlooking a bug that slows down the game while in equipment select (but is easily fixed by backing out of the room and reentering after a long play session) and there are no issues with unnatural lag or desync.
Highly recommended for playing with a partner or a group of friends up to 4 players, the reason following: Air Raider and Fencer classes in particular I feel benefit the most from playing with friends, having the most extreme strengths and weaknesses that are best rounded out with a friend than the other classes. The Wing Divers seem to be the strongest class to solo the game with, and so at first one might think you should go and do that, I feel like you miss most of the experience of the game while in the air; Coop'ing with friends as a Wing Diver actually leads to a uniquely fun situation where you get to be the shining savior for your friends on the ground as they struggling with the stages in the way they were intended.
In all cases, playing alone or playing with friends, I recommend playing on Hard difficulty for your first run. It is highly challenging, but is completely possible and the struggle is worth it.
