With amazing graphics and a wide selection of characters to play as, LEGO Jurassic World has everything that a LEGO game is based on. Added into that is the open world setting of the game, a newer aspect to be added to such a game. They also added in the ability to play as dinosuars that you encounter in the game, as well as custom create your own dinos. This is a completely new experience available because there is not really a point in the movies where you get to ride on the dinos. Thanks to that we are given the ability to play as characters as big as a bus and use them for heavy lifting of sorts (although it is more akin to demolition). The fact that the dinos draw attention to themselves and encourage playing as them is not enough to stop you from playing as the human charaters though. The clever use of tools, like the tasers, in the puzzles helps to keep them interesting, in addition to some characters having multiple aspects to capitalise on (your first high jumper is Dr. Ellie Sattler, she is also a paleobiologist in her abilities, and she can help the ancient plants grow or search for clues in dino poop). The vehicle use is not like it was in older games either. When You get into a vehicle you do not get to just move by use of a joystick, you actually operate by normal standards, you have to hold "A" to go forward and "B" to go in reverse. While this can get annoying there are many times where you can get stuck in a corner and backing out works better than slightly turning while moving forward.
LEGO has also kept their normal humor in the cutscenes, giving random objects to the characters, but they have moved on from primarily doing this with bananas (what sort of carnivorous dinosuar would attempt to kill someone just to get a banana). To replace bananas in this game they have sausage. It does not have the same comedic value as a banana does, but that does not make it any worse. While LEGO used out of place objects to create the comedy we have all laughed at in their games, they have gone from completely out of place to based on the situation (a sausage has no place in the first scene of Jurassic Park, but it provides a good reason for the Velociraptor to attempt to escape and eat someone).
The biggest dissapointment this game had to offer, however, was not a change in how the game functioned compared to previous games, but how they changed the cutscenes from how they were in the movies to make them more kid friendly. Everyone remembers the scene at the begining of Jurassic Park when John Hammond opened the bottle of champagne that was being saved. In the game it is replaced with a less "adult" drink. While I support the games being kid friendly, I do not support the way they changed cutscenes to allowfor it.
Overall I would highly reccomend this game and I say that it is totally worth whatever you drop on buying it.

This game is very enjoyable as a classic First Person Shoot, similar to many WW2 era shooters created in the early 20-00s. It takes place across history mostly in WW1 and the Civil war, however there are missions which go to similar eras such as the Eastern front of WW2 or the battle of Little Big Horn. The game is rediculously well balanced for fun, in any situation you are equally valuable as the allied troops, acting like a decicive shock force during skirmishes, and like a sharp shooter during large battles. The game occasionally brings up gimmicks such as characters who need to survive a battle or futuristic weaponry. Also, I am reminded of Crysis from time to time because of the way the game handles new and unexpected enemies. If you happen to enjoy fighting aliens or enemy supersoldiers in Crysis, then make sure to take a shotgun and shoot enemy time travelrs in the face! The playtime should be about 20 hours, however despite being incredibly linear and filled with invisible walls, it is still very fun to replay.

Sure some of the movies may have been garbage, but this game kind of blends the games into a really really good mixed cake of tasty dinosaur rompage...plus theres quite a few minigames where you rampage around as a T-rex...how is that not cool?

Zelda
Mario
Mega Man
Castlevania
You basically run around through different levels collecting a variety of items (power-ups, coins, hidden music sheets) and fight a boss at the end of each level. Shovel Knight is quite different from many platformers in many senses. To begin the idea of using the shovel is interesting because it allows for more unique puzzles/treasures. Another interesting part of the game is the ability to press down to bounce on top of enemies with your shovel. The extent to which this can be used to grant you bonus treasures, defeat bosses, and even get more power ups makes it more than a gimmick, but turns it into a very important mechanic to learn and master.
Furthermore, the game has some of the most creative bosses and stages of any game. Each stage has its own mechanics that you must be able to pick up on the fly. Normally I would not like this, but you are usually given one stage where you can practice using the mechanic before having to use it to complete a screen.
Overall I highly recommend Shovel Knight.

How would you improve Resident Evil 4? Brilliantly paced, densely packed with new kinds of fun; next-gen a few years early -- it’s hard to put your finger somewhere on its taut execution and say: “Fix this.”

Some may complain about the input model, others roll their eyes at the archaic inventory management. Why can’t you move and aim at the same time? What’s with the key-lock puzzles and weak spots? Capcom wasn’t listening. Capcom was tuning the combat.

Gunplay turns into a kind of dialogue-tree, where shooting different body parts prompts disarmament and various stagger-animations that enable melee attacks dealing massive damage in a wide arc in front of the avatar. Weapons don’t just deal damage, but manipulate state.

Lone enemies are played like puppets: Head shots triggers knock-back stagger, pop one in the leg to trigger knock-down stagger. The puppets telegraph their attacks for seconds before committing, lending ample opportunity to shoot a flailing arm, cancel the attack and disarm the subject. Even if you miss, dodging is mostly a question of not standing still. The symmetry of power is decidedly in your favour. Unfortunately it doesn’t scale.

There are too many puppets to master, their threads tangled together now, over-eager twitches and twirls just jumbling them more. Favourable stagger animations cancel into useless ones, aim foiled by a scythe signalled three seconds ago but ignored -- just like the broken bottle -- in favour of the chainsaw.

Resident Evil 5’s core loop is pure survival horror, compressed to panic: The mob gathers, you control it, sharp-shooting limbs and stomping faces. The mob surges, and you get tactical, kick down a ladder, defenestrate some fools, looking for some time to reload. The mob swarms you, no weapons loaded and your finger slips so you fail to quick-reload your magnum in the merciless real-time inventory. Chainsaw meets neck.

Co-operative play adds combo melee attacks, real-time item trading, area-of-effect healing and defibrillation pads. The few but strictly enforced chores keeps co-op players from floating apart, while the weapon composition in both campaign and Mercenaries mode (which refines the combat experience to its surreal, exploitative peak) gently lends crowd-control roles and duties. It’s not flawless, but brilliant.

The greatest niggle is representational. The crowds you control are angry Africans, some of whom chuck spears. Others wear great wooden tribal masks that double as shields. A Mugabe-look-alike rouses a slavering mob with a loudhailer. It’s neither tactful nor very tasteful, but it is effective, schlocky horror from a culture that does not appear to observe Black History Month.

The story’s motif is exploitation, human experiments perpetrated on the disadvantaged by a shadowy conglomerate of capital interests. But arch-villain Albert Wesker -- former policeman and blond beast who always wears sunglasses -- literally turns into Nazi-Satan. Offensive? Problematic? Dumb fun?

The safari-themed bonus costumes blurs the line further. Is it tone-deaf or satirical? Self-referential or just gauche? Remember, this is a game that reads its own title out loud in a spooky voice with reverb. Resident Evil. Five.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is by far the most horror-survival game of the year. It will scare you, and for good reason. The game first opens up in a nice story, which leads your main character to have Amnesia, hence the name, so your goal is to remember what happened and figure it out.
Amnesia is a horror-survival game, but there are no weapons, so your only way to survive is hide from the monsters in the game and not to die. Sounds easy, but it isn't. Monsters will appear and give chase at you if seen. You have inventory and items at your disposal and many puzzles to solve throughout the game. Not every area will be easy and will take some time to mentally figure out the puzzles.
The visuals are top notch, a very beautifully stunning 3D world to explore. Everything is done so well, from the books to rooms even to places you don't even need to go visit have all these visual details done to them. Lighting effects, shadows, enviromental effects etc.
Not only is the visuals good, the audio is spooky too. The game has haunting audio effects and every narrative story is voice acted well. There is a haunting over tone and the game is best played with headphones so you can hear where the monsters are coming and everything.
The game is best played at night with headphones to really scare you, and the game is LONG, many levels and areas to explore, puzzles to solve, this game is well worth the purchase.

This game is probably one of the best tactical shooters I have ever played! I put this game way over CSGO. CSGO compared to this is pretty bland even though it as well is quite a good tactical shooter. The community on this game is pretty good, but not everyone is nice and you may run into a few jerks who act like they know everything about the game yet they are only level 25 and can barely aim to save their life. I will say that latency plays a role in this game, so if you don't have the best internet and you seem to lag a lot in other games I would suggest staying away from this. The best thing about the game is probably the amount of people you can play as and the replay value. There are 30 operators to choose from at the moment and each have a different ability to help beat the other team. As for replay value you see that my hours continue to grow as this review stays here which means I continue to enjoy the game after countless hours of gameplay. I ALSO wanted to add what the difference between the starter addition and the normal additon was.
STARTER EDITION:
2 Operators are instantly unlocked for you(random), 600 R6 credits are given to you to purchase anything you want(This is the ingame purchaseable currency and you will most likely buy an operator with it), Operators cost more money than in the regular additon and the game becomes more grindy. (With the steam summer sale going on right now I simply suggest picking up the normal version since you can not upgrade to it once you purchase the starter edition).
NORMAL VERSION:
Probably the better investment in the long run. You don't get 2 free random operators and 600 R6 credits, but everything is way easier to unlock and less of a grind. Yes there is year 1 and 2 characters to unlock, but as long as you play the game regularly you can get those quite quickly.
Overall, I would HIGHLY recommend this game and if you have friends to play with it makes the game a lot more fun.

There are a couple things to know about this game before I go into pros and cons that could be either depending on whatever.
-This game is HARD and i have raged quite a lot
-This is not something that is played in 20 minute sittings. Each level is long and difficult and if you exit while on a level, you'll start again at the beginning next time you log on
Now for some pros and cons: (disclaimer i haven't gotten through the entire game yet. These are some of my first impressions)
Pros:
-entertaining
-full controler support (GREAT FOR PLATFORMERS!)
-storyline
-soundtrack
-complexity of armor, weapons, magic and health systems (very well balanced)
-Charming style with visuals and soundtrack (great animations)
-Intricate Platforming with many different mechanics
-A good death penalty (you drop some gold in the form of bags based on how much total gold you have, you then procede from a  checkpoint and you can reclaim the gold if you don't die first in which case the bags will disappear and new bags will be dropped)
Cons:
-Unforgiving at times
-a steep learning curve when new things are introduced (i.e. Platforming mechanics)
-Casual play isn't as easy as levels have to be done in one sitting and the game itself is extremely difficuly
-Spikes kill you in one hit (What the heck is up with that?)
Overall I recommend this game. It is a solid 9/10

At the start, I hated the game, because it takes so long to make it to a level that you can actually catch some "real fish", like Pike and Muskie, instead of constantly sunfish, Crappie and Bluegill. But once you've made it up to higher levels and upgraded your tackle, the game is fantastic and very fun. The only times I hate, is when the makers of the game do upgrades or add a new map, sometimes it screws up things on other maps and the way your lures work, and sometimes you won't get any fish on lakes that you regularly get tons of fish. Also, it seems like it's the same favored people catching the biggest fish on every map, or the same people getting Unique fish on every map, when I'm using the exact gear and bait, and fishing in the same place as them. Other than these issues, the game is great and the graphics really make you feel like your fishing outside -- the water glistens, the birds are chirping, the weather changes while you're standing there from sunny to partly cloudy to cloudy to rain - and the fish change their eating times in these conditions too. If you love fishing, be very patient at the start and you will love the game.

Aesthetic wise - this game is rather gorgeous. The graphics are polished to a mirror sheen, the control scheme and mechanics have been even more tightly refined from Resident Evil 4, and the level design flows quite nicely. The PC port is even exceptionally optimized. However, with all of this in mind, it still (in my book) falls short of capturing that survival horror experience fans have grown to appreciate from previous games in the series.
Resident Evil 5 is heavily dependant on action-based gameplay, but that is not to say it cannot capture moments of survival horror in particular scenarios. I feel like the most tension was in the inital playthrough before any upgrades are obtained - ammo is scarce, there are limited opportunities to heal, and the outcome is still unpredictable - much like the original games of the series. The game demands multiple (and I stress MULTIPLE) playthroughs in order to achieve 100%. By this time, the player is equipped with a full blown arsenal of weapons that rival a Next Generation Special Forces Team, and the whole aspect of "surviving" is consequently thrown out the window - outside of the 1-hit kill damage ratio of Professional Mode.
On my first playthrough (many years ago on the PS3) the storyline was captivating enough for me to want to see it through. Unfortunately, it becomes less interesting as the player's priority shifts from the narrative to farming money, gathering treasures, and acquiring new weapons - only to play the same events over and over just to repeat the process. The game does offer many additional documents of storyline to attempt to immerse you in the lore, but these are easily ignored because they are outside of the gameplay and do not really add any weight to what you are doing.
The game was clearly designed for a co-op experience - that much is painfully clear. Contextual actions are almost always co-cop based, and will require teamwork in order to advance. This is actually a great theme - when you have somebody to play with. As a single player experience, it feels like an entirely different game. The AI is among the worst I have EVER seen in any game (veteran solo players typically will use the AI as an additional "item box" - removing all weapons because of how wasteful they are with ammo, or how ridiculously stupid their actions become when they are equipped properly). To attempt to solo the game on higher tier difficulties is basically suicide because of these reasons. Professional Mode is literally IMPOSSIBLE without 2 human players.
All in all, I would still recommend this game, especially if you've got a buddy to play with. Even with all of the many faults, I still had a blast on my first few playthroughs. I've met a lot of cool people during my time with the game as well, so that is always a plus. Unless Resident Evil is your favorite series, expect to run out of gas sooner than later though.

While the only common thing in Resident Evil 5 and its predecessors is the title, it is hard to argue that it is a fun third-person action shooter with a solid campaign and one of the most beloved time-attack game modes in the series.
Upon its release, Resident Evil 5 was a dividing game. It is undeniable that it completely lost any connection with its roots by going the full-fledged co-op third-person shooter way with zero horror elements, but it does a damn great job at it.
Co-op is an operative word, because both the hordes of common enemies and the bosses need teamwork. It also means that solo players have to deal with a mandatory AI partner, who is the bane of existence for some, or an unkillable aimbot for others.
Strangely, the gameplay feels balanced entirely for New Game+. This means that new players may not enjoy it as much until they beat it once—especially if they bought the DLCs, because those remain locked until the campaign’s completion.
Just like in RE4, the level design is linear, where the African shantytowns, the old half-abandoned laboratory complex, or the tanker ship fit the game’s theme like a glove, but the swampland and the underground caves feel like some rejected levels from Uncharted. (Especially with such ridiculous elements like an
solar laser built from stone.)
The serious levels design (well, sans those middle parts) got some serious writing as well. The adventures of returning protagonist Chris Redfield, as he teams up with a local agent to stop an intentional biohazard outbreak in Africa are played straight, including some competent translation (for a change) and voice acting. While this puts RE5 even further away from its sibling titles, the entire package somehow clicks together as a great action game, which happens to bear the name of a franchise associated with survival horror games.

Darkest of days is a game worthy for history fans. There's one problem: it's too short. The game has a huge potential, but it has bugs and often crash especially graphics as well. The plot is trying to be cool, but feels like a Sci-Fi B movie at best. The ending was like weak to say. I must address the pro and cons of the game.
Pro: the actual historical weapons are accurate. Imagine reloading a rifle musket is long and tedious. If you planned to use it in close range, use its range since its rifling barrel gives huge advantage. I recommend use the rifle musket in long range. WWI weapons are authentic to say which its very impressive that the developers understood the weapons of the time. What's great to experience some of historical moments in Civil War to WWI, but I will not spoil it.
Con: the story felt weak, graphical issues, and wasted potential. They could done a better job explaining, but they assume time travel as if it was Back to the Future. I would like to see Time Travel fit with Multiverse theory where altered timeline interact with original time. This is like as if it was a Terminator's version done badly. The graphics are another problem; if you don't have Nvida, don't buy this game. But if you have Nvida even a good one, it will crash for no good reason. My laptop can run Attila total war without any problems, but this game will continuous crash. The AI is the worse and sometime use an aiming bot as if out of nowhere.
The AI are like brain dead and always focus on you instead of other enemies. The game is flawed in the content and the ending is a sequel bait which they were about to make a franchise out of it.
Conclusion: I do enjoy the game. Not perfect, but I would play it once and awhile. This game is a guilty pleasure and might do a Let's Play series. My rating on this game based on enjoyment, criticism, and idea is 5/10. It has flaws which many will not enjoy, graphical issues, weak spiked difficulty AI, and weak story. However, I like this potential idea where I wish some one will remake this game or a better than first one sequel, historical events, and using historical firearms.

Despite the praise this game has receieved from critics and my love for old platformers like Megaman, I ultimately did not enjoy Shovel Knight.  The aesthetic is great and the music and charm are exceptional.  However there are a lot of problems I could not look past.  Powers are almost all worthless except for the invincibility and fireball, which takes most of the charm out of collecting new skills.  New equipment is similar with few shovel or armor set upgrades, most of which are not useful either.  There is a lot of enemy variety, but they do negligible amounts of damage until NG+ mode, and this is further lessened by the fact that you always have 2 chalices for full life refills.  The levels are varied in style but are plagued by frustrating spike/instant death sections which make up large portions of each stage and many boss battles.  Finally, there is little replayability since all the upgrades can be collected in one playthrough of the short story mode.  In all, I enjoyed the charm of the game but just could not look past many of the frustrations of the skills, equipment upgrades, and level designs.

After the macabre event that led to the annihilation of Raccoon city, Chris Redfield former S.T.A.R.S. member and one of the survivors of the first disaster in Arklay mansion (Resident Evil), enlists as an agent in an Anti-bio-organic Weapon Organization known as the Bio-terrorism Security Assessment Alliance (B.S.A.A), a paramilitary worldwide organization with the prime objective to advert bio-organic weapons from spreading through the world and from being used for diabolical and amoral means. This Organization hauls the world in search of Umbrella, to vitiate all its canker plans and abhorrent monstrosities. Umbrella is a gigantic conglomerate and a major international player in a number of markets; including pharmaceuticals, medical, top-secret operations tampering with genetic engineering and biological weaponry. The company before the public has always been able to maintain its benevolent corporate image, due to the dumbing down of the masses through cosmetics, consumer and food products.
Chris Redfield is sent to Africa to a region called Kijuju after receiving a tip that an underground weapons dealer will be making a huge deal that could be related with biological weapons in that African Region. Chris as always worried for the safety of the world, ends up meeting with his new partner to end the possible outbreak of a virus, a nightmare that he certainly does not want to relive once again. After Chris Redfield and Sheva Alomar (a local agent from the B.S.A.A) meet, they learn through a contact Informant about a strange Doomsday project known as Uroboros being set in motion and the necessity to locate a man called Ricardo Irving, being the only lead to the project.
Sheva Alomar helps Chris Redfield with his assignment and together they will fight hordes of people infected with parasites that will sometimes mutate into full blown parasitical monstrosity form.
Along their journey they will confront familiar faces linked to Cris Redfield’s past, including one well known arch-nemesis called Albert Wesker. Will Chris and Sheva be able to stop one of the most heinous plots in gaming history?
The game mechanics in Resident evil 5, specially the action combat system run from a over the shoulder view, in order for you to shoot an enemy you have to sever your movement for a steady aim. Resident evil 5 might appear to have slow movement at first glance but after some gameplay, players get used to it due to the action oriented and staggering plot.
Regarding the co-op experience, you can play with a friend or A.I. (Artificial Intelligence) companion. Sheva’s AI competence utilizes her skill set to a degree with fire arms that makes her the perfect candidate as a support role in a way that enhances the player’s experience. The grafting of a second character adds more depth to the game and encounters with the infected. Having an ally by your side will grandly encourage the need for teamwork, to help you deal and take down with ease overpowered enemies and bosses. Having a partner will ensure extra protection, someone who will be watching your back at all time, it will also bring some anxiety to the game pressuring both characters to be co-dependent on each other for support, leading to better survival outcome. With two characters on the field, the task of covering larger areas becomes easier, keeping in mind that all enemies can attack you from any point. The hordes of infected feel like a balanced equation with the right amount appearing at the right time to attack you. All environments altogether have managed to capture an idyllic equilibrium, from the brightest light from the African savanna's to the obscure underground dimmed facilities.
The motion of many infected can outsmart you especially in big numbers, some are faster, others can simply overpower you with their raw strength.
Resident Evil 5 provides an online Co-op experience along with a split screen view that will certainly deepen and enliven the players experience, in addition boost the fun factor overall.
Resident Evil 5 presents us with stunning visuals, which are much more refined than its predecessors, delivering a tastier and sharper higher resolution. The vast array of environments have been worked to such detail, that you can find yourself in humongous, open wide places always on the move from several enemies which are scattered through the environment. The games cut-scenes are simply nifty and tip-top in its quality, luring the player into the story in a way that you sympathize straight away with the protagonists in game. The character animation, facial expressions, voice acting and soundtrack amplifies and imparts a great deal of realism to the gameplay which was designed not to disappoint, supplying the player with a precise visual in which objects and enemies seem to breach the digital world, creating exceptional depth to the gameplay.
After a complete walkthrough in Resident Evil 5 you will still have loads of tasks to do in order to receive extras, bonuses, collectables, trophies, costumes, infinite ammo, etc. Starting the game for the first time you will have at your disposal three levels of Difficulty (Amateur, Normal and Veteran). Later on, after completing Veteran, you will unlock the Professional difficulty, which presents its self as a very devilish, challenging feat by concocting the most lethal combination to create the most powerful enemies (all enemies have increased health, higher resistance, more attack power, higher A.I., faster attack speed and movement speed). After completing the game you also unlock the Mercenaries mode where you can try to eliminate as many enemies possible in a time limit, you can do this alone or with a friend.
Resident Evil 5 is able to stand out from many games out there. It is Capcom’s best selling game of all time with 7.2 million units sold, until this date. It offers an electrifying story line, fluid and satisfying gameplay, with fewer words I can only describe it as a unique pearl in a vast sea of games.

Brotherhood is Assassin's Creed at its best. It takes what's best from AC2 and makes it even better, while changing the mission structure to be more open-world than previous games. I love the ability to call assassins at any time during the game. There's only one city to explore, but Rome is absolutely big and varied, and full of things to do. It's a great and geographically varied setting, ranging from rural areas to densely populated city areas. There's also some additional levels outside the city (Leonardo's war machines missions) and some nice surprises along the way. The secret locations from AC2 also make a return as fantastically designed Lairs of Romulus - these are some great platforming levels and completing them is a real pleasure.
Brotherhood has a great cast of characters and the overall story is interesting. My only gripe is lack of character development for side characters later in the game - Claudia, Maria and Leonardo all suffer from this, leaving their stories a bit incomplete. What's great about Brotherhood is also the modern day bit of the story. It's fantastic - and you actually get to do things as Desmond.
This Assassin's Creed outing has also introduced multiplayer for the first time in the series. Keep in mind that unfortunately multiplayer is mostly dead, as the player base moved to newer games in the series.

The game for short:
+ explores two eras that have been left behind in the gaming industry (US civil war and World War One)
+ gun upgrade system related to ingame performance (and guns change visually to some upgrades)
+ good maps (very open; much happens in multiple areas and sidepaths which allows for some replayability, ...)
+ NPC's use languages according to nationality (German NPC soldiers in ww1 speak german most of the time, ...)
+ graphics were good for their time
- story leaves you with quite a cliffhanger yet no sequel can be expected
- characters are sometimes dull
- NPC's, like in many other games, spam 'battle cries'
- even though NPC's use the language according to their nationality the translations and voices themselves are frankly poorly made (german NPC soldiers in ww1 sometimes speak like some english dude tried to speak german or something that isn't even german, ...)
- AI is sometimes not all that intelligent
- logical errors (you change history yet people from the future somehow still remember how history was supposed to go down, ...)
- only story- and some kind of skirmish-mode
---------------------------------------------
Das Spiel in Kürze:
+ Erkundet zwei Ären welche von der Spieleindustrie vernachlässigt werden (den US Bürgerkrieg und den Ersten Weltkrieg)
+ Waffenupgradesystem verbunden mit der Performance des Spielers (ebenfalls verändern sich die Waffen nach einigen Upgrades visuell)
+ Gute Karten (sehr offen, vieles passiert in mehreren Arealen und Alternativrouten was etwas Wiederspielwert gibt, ...)
+ NPC's benutzen die Sprache ihres Landes (Deutsche NPC im Ersten Weltkrieg reden meistens Deutsch, ...)
+ Graphik war gut für ihre Zeit
- Die Geschichte lässt einen mit einem Cliffhanger zurück und es kann kein zweiter Teil erwartet werden
- Charaktere sind manchmal langweilig

I have never thought a game about drifting would be interested, I am not a fan of racing games at all. Absolute Drift was a random choice from my library and I absolutely loved it.
In the game you have to do some drifting tasks by driving a car. Sounds simple, but mastering the car takes hours.
Performing the tasks seems to be easy at the beginning. But with increasing difficulty, it becomes bloody difficult in the end. Honestly speaking, getting the last achievement 'Complete all event challenges in the game.' is a masochistic task.
Still, despite of repeating some stages again and again (in some cases for few hours) the game is not boring at all. There was a little irritation, of course, but somehow the failures were motivational to keep playing.
Absolute Drift has a minimalistic graphic. Tracks are plain white with some red addons. The driving car looks like a toy among a white bricls jungle. But this game does not need anything more - instead of distracting colours and complicated environment it gives an opportunity to focus on tasks.
Another thing is the soundtrack. It suits perfectly. Actually, despite of my dislike of the music genre used in the game, I enjoyed the songs which brings a proper ambience.
After all those hours spent with Absolute Drift I can recommend it to everyone.

This game is gorgeous to look at with its very vibrant colors and randomized galaxies. If you are simply just a fan of recolored deep-space phenomenon, you will be hooked easily.
Whenever you find yourself inside a worm-hole, the game shifts into a 3D plane, letting you travel down the space-pipe of many deep colors. However, I do find that sometimes it gets difficult focusing on staying centered due to how dark it can get.
There are also many moments where the colors shift and go negative or very dark, leading to their own obstacles. Due to their frequency after a while, I never really felt obstructed by them except for when the screen is very dark and I can't see an enemy that absorbs shots (however, bullets and asteroids are contrasted so avoiding them is fine).
There is even a semi-rare event where floating dinosaur fossil heads breath bullets and fire at you while the background goes black and the screen goes blurrier while everything slows down and an air siren plays.
Enemy design is top-notch, even referencing classic arcade games and styles. This is very hard to explain in text, but just looking at screenshots should clarify.
Bosses all feel adequately boss-like (even impressively so in one regard), although it may feel a bit stupid fighting a giant orb with a shield around it if it never gets to the point it can drop suns on the screen.
The worst part of the visual design is just the shape of your ship, even tho it's perfectly acceptable as is. It just gets overshadowed by how intense the rest of the game is.
Techno, a relaxed (and younger) British narrator, and modern mixed with retro beeps and boops come together for a very calming yet engaging experience. There is an option to disable the narrator, and playing the game without audio doesn't take anything from the game; which I say is a good thing due to not everyone being fond of techno and narrators. However, I am, so the sound gets a pass.
Also when you kill the enemy based off of Vector graphics, it dies in a satisfying old-school 'boop'.

Have you ever wanted to level an entire city to kill one spider?
Have you ever wanted to Low Orbit Ion Canon a nest of ants?
Have you ever wanted to be part of an godly chorus singing to the glory of Earth Defense Force whilst pummeling giant robots in their giant robot balls with your giant robot fists?
- If you have answered 'Yes' to any of the above then this is the game for you.
Earth Defense force pits you as one of four classes against waves of giant bugs, aliens or sometimes both. There is a story loosely tied in that you learn about as you progress through the game levels - all through some 'so bad its good',  B movie tier of dialogue. Though it is just background fluff that serves as an attempt to justify why you are on a certain level fighting the giant enemies that you find yourself fighting.
Each of the four classes do feel inherently different and do serve individual roles.
Ranger - This is probably the easiest class to start out with and the most balanced. The Ranger has access to a decent variety of weapons and levels up health at a reasonable rate. They have good mobility and have access to a a dodge roll.
Wing Diver - The Wing Diver is a more specialised class with access to flight. Her weapons are quite powerful and share a power source with the jetpack - meaning its important that you keep an eye on your power levels whilst flying and shooting lest you end up falling into a crowd of creepy crawlies. Her health is the lowest of the classes and it levels up the slowest.
Air Raider - The Air Raider is a semi support role and requires a little more skill to play. As an air raider, your main weapon is the vast array of vehicles you have access to. These range from rail gun tanks, to helicopter to huge Pacific Rim style mechs. In order to call these vehicles in, your team needs to build up kills. You can support this by dropping health, shields and turrets. The air raider also has access to laser designators that is used in conjunction with some of the Fencer's heavier missile systems. Once you and your team build up enough kills, you can call in your chosen vehicle and switch from support to reigning in utter destruction as a 500ft mech. His health and health leveling are fairly high.
Fencer - The Fencer is the slowest and heaviest of all the classes and tends to occupy a support from range role and and direct attack role depending on the load outs. Fencers have two main weapon set ups, one being a melee based set up with various spikes or fists or hammers as well as a shield which allows you to reflect ranged attack back at an enemy. These load outs also give you access to the jump packs which allow you to boost upwards or dodge sideways. The second load out style gives you access to huge artillery canons and missile launchers. These weapons tend to be the hardest hitting and have a lengthy delay in their reload times and times between firing. Some of your missile launchers can only be used in combination with the Air Raider's laser designator. The Fencer has the most health and has the quickest health gains of the four classes.
The game can be played solo or co-op and from what I have played seems more suited to co-op play. You can revive downed allies although this requires a portion of your health to do so.  The game contains a loot system - weapon boxes grant you weapons (either new or duplicates) and the armour boxes grant you additional health/armour for your character - both requiring that you successfully complete the misusing at hand before granting these things. If you die, you loose it all, which can be quite frustrating and lead to you having to farm weapons and more so armour before you are able to progress in the story.
The port itself could be described as 'clunky'. The menus are clunky to navigate and can be a little tricky to get used to navigating with mouse and keyboard. This is one of the rare times where i've actually preferred to use a controller over the keyboard and mouse both in menu and in game.
All in, this game is a lot of fun with friends. Don't take it too seriously and you are in for a great time.

Earth Defense Force is dumb. Earth Defense Force is fun. I'd even go so far as to say Earth Defense Force is dumb fun.
Harkening back to the days of cheesy science fiction movies like Starship Troopers or the kind you'd see on MST3K, in Earth Defense Force 4.1: The Shadow of New Despair you're a single soldier tasked with eliminating droves of giant insects, towering robots, dragons for some reason, and... Godzilla? Taking a kitchen sink approach to enemy design, there's really no rhyme or reason to what you're shooting at, but honestly who cares? If it's big and dumb and can be lumped into the general “sci fi” genre it's fair game.
There's a loose story about aliens attacking Earth, and you're humanity's last hope because you have a rocket launcher. Despite the mission briefings before starting a level (it's usually the “biggest threat you've yet faced”) and battlefield chatter, most missions have the exact same objective: kill everything. Kill the monsters by any means necessary, even if that results in entire cities being razed to the ground.
Turn your brain off and keep your finger on the trigger; this is essentially an old school arcade game. Hundreds of enemies will mindlessly swarm your position, and you're doing your best at crowd control as they assault from the ground, sky, and the sides of buildings you haven't destroyed yet. The scale of the battles are truly impressive. At first glance the graphics are bland and outdated, PS2-era quality. However, once the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan you appreciate the trade off; massive environments and enemies, decent explosions and effects, almost fully destructible structures... and it all runs buttery smooth.
The old school nature of the game bleeds through to the presentation as well. Menus have little personality, they are just there to get the job done. Select what you want to do from a list of options and be on your way. After a few missions it's easy to see how the overall game has been structured: the developers made a sandbox, then populated different sections with enemies to create the scenarios that make up the missions. There's nothing wrong with this approach, it just once again feels decidedly PS2, almost simulation game design. Truth be told I think any other method would fundamentally break the game and rob it of it's charm.
Despite the simplistic nature, a few niggling issues I found got in the way of achieving complete arcade zen. There's a grind to be endured: weapons and armor upgrades (that increase your maximum health pool) are dropped from defeated enemies in the form of physical loot boxes. The weapons are RNG, so if you want better/specific ones it can become a time sink. Some people may enjoy playing the same stages over and over to “level up”, but I find it slows down the otherwise frantic vibe the game is going for. The same type of issue is a result of having to walk over to boxes to collect them; after fighting through an army of bugs and robots with heavy metal blaring to get your blood pumping, it's quite the mood killer having to march through those barren, massive levels to collect loot while keeping the last enemy alive. It just seems like an unnecessary slog. Why not just award XP or credits for kills? There's also a fair amount of enemy types that enjoy slowing/stunning/tripping you, and that's always annoying.
Don't be fooled by the low budget dressing Earth Defense Force wraps itself in. Between discovering "the truth" of Subject 16 ( similar to AC II) and discovering what happened to Ezio's love, Christina, not to mention, taking down the Borgia's - yes, even Lucretia makes an appearance here, the scope of this game is LEGEN....wait for it....DARY!

Continuing my revisiting of the Assassin's Creed franchise, here comes AC: Brotherhood! Having previously played this game on the PS3 when it launched back in 2010, I can say it was a fun revisit! Gameplay speaking, this Assassin's Creed "2.5" adds more mechanics for playability, you can recruit assassins to join the Assassins' cause.
Brotherhood continues the trilogy story of Ezio Auditore da Firenze and now focus solely on Rome. The city is big, really big to explore. Although, even if it is quite big, I much preferred the different locations in AC2 than "only being in Rome". There is a tons of collectibles in this game... too many for my taste. 101 Borgia Flags does unlock you the Borgia Cape, which sets the notoriety permanently at none. Same effects occurs if you completely rebuild Rome with renovations, you unlock the Auditore Cape. I had the Auditore Cape on my PlayStation 3 playthrough and it was satisfactory to go on a rampage without being chased by guards all the time. But you're more than likely to unlock that cape quite late in the game which makes it almost pointless.
PROS:
+Strong narrative, both in the present with Desmond Miles and in the Animus, Ezio Auditore da Firenze.
+Graphically improved compared to AC2 albeit contains visual glitches at times.
+Soundtrack is excellent and again, composed by Jesper Kyd.
+Same as AC2, the voice acting is solid.
+Improved combat system.
+More weapons and you can now carry heavy weapons.
+Recruiting and using assassins on targets.
+Multiplayer ain't my forté in the AC franchise, but it is very original nonetheless.
+Ability to replay missions.
+High replay value.
CONS:
-Uplay DRM.
-Horrendous WASD keyboard + mouse scheme. Play this game with a gamepad! (I played Brotherhood with the Xbox One controller and it worked without any issues).
-AC: Brotherhood feels like a big filler and not a proper sequel or expansion.
-Silly timer on pretty much every assassination missions. Very irritating!
-Some stupid requirements during missions like to not be seen or it causes desynchronisation.
-Draw distance in this game seems broken at times, especially when you see guards appearing right in front of you, i.e.
-Rome pretty much looks like the same anywhere you go in Italy.
-Steep learning curve for the Multiplayer mode.
-The cliffhanger ending is very irritating.
-Too many collectibles... however, once seen in Eagle Vision, it sticks on your map for later acquisition.
-Annoying "Full synchronisation" on missions / side-missions that don't do anything except unlock Trophies (PS3) or Achievements.
OVERALL:
Brotherhood ain't perfect for sure. But if you loved previous AC games, you'll enjoy this game very much. If you're a newcomer in the AC franchise, you could love this game a lot as well but you're gonna feel lost in the story. My best advice, you better play the previous games or at least, get informed by reading / watching wikia and videos online or you're gonna feel completely off the track!
This game adds a few great mechanics which is always welcomed. Although, I felt this game to be more of a filler than a sequel / expansion. It is a good filler that is well paced... right until the very end scene which leaves you in a cliffhanger!
RECOMMENDATION:
Yes, I highly recommend this game for anyone loving this playstyle. The story is very interesting and you feel quite engaged with it as much as the past and the future events. My favorite AC game so far is still AC2 but Brotherhood continues on the same premise so you won't feel lost when playing it.
RATING:
8.0 / 10
And now, going to revisit AC: Revelations...

LEGO Jurassic World an amazing and casual game that should appeal to kids and adults alike. If you've ever played a LEGO game before, then you know what you're in for; destroying every rock and bush to get studs (the in-game currency), classic and corny LEGO humor, and simple yet fun puzzles and platforming. While it reuses the same LEGO formula that almost all LEGO video games use, it is still a fresh experience following all three Jurassic Park films and Jurassic World.
The soundtrack really does take you back, using music and voice acting directly from the films. The voice acting doesn't get too annoying for the most part, but you can clearly tell that they ripped lines directly from the films and can oftentimes hear static and background noise throughout the dialogue.
As mentioned previously, the game follows the classic LEGO video game formula; simple platforming and puzzles, as well as the standard LEGO humor in the mix. The game, like many other classic LEGO titles, offers a lot of unlockables and replayability options. There are tons of things to discover within this game, including 100% Stud Bars, Gold Bricks, Minikits, and a host of characters, vehicles, and dinosaurs to unlock. Yes, you can play as the dinosaurs within the game, which is what impressed me the most throughout my playtime and it was a blast to play as them.
• Some people have claimed to have encountered game-breaking or game-stalling glitches, but I have yet to encounter any of these glitches during my playthrough, and I'm assuming they've been patched.
• The voice acting is directly ripped from the Jurassic films and is extremely noticable with static and background noise during the dialogue between characters.
• If you are playing with a mouse and keyboard rather than a controller... then the controls can take some getting used to. The mouse is never touched in this game and the default controls are rather confusing. By default, JUMP was bound to the 'J' key rather than the standard 'SPACE BAR'. You'll probably have to customize the controls when playing with a keyboard, but you should be fine once you get used to it.

Plants vs. Zombies is such a great game I don't know where to start.
The game is a classic. One of the best in its genre. I remember when I first saw it at my friends house and I knew it would be a great game. Many years have passed and I still have fun playing it now.
It has a good variety of game modes such as:
Adventure - where you play through the story with Crazy Dave and your plants by your side vs. The mastermind Zomboss and his zombies that want to eat your brain. There are 50 levels. But it can never bore you cause in every level you get a diffrent plant with diffrent gameplay. There are 5 diffrent maps : Day, Night, Pool, Fog and Roof with each having diffrent gameplay and mechanism from the others. Every new level you get introduced to a new zombie with its tricky special ability. But fear not you have your plants that can counter his ability, soo as long as you make a good combination you can clear every level easily. If you do not know what plant does what you can click on the Almanac to see all the plants and zombies, plus amusing "facts" and quotes.
If you are not satisfied with your plants power you can go to Crazy Daves shop and buy seeds for more powerful plants. You can also buy many more useful stuff for in-game currency (It is a EA game without micro-transactions).
It has amazing music and sounds. Plus it has a music video in the end when you defeat the zombies.
While playing adventure you can unlock your garden where you can plant plants for decorations or make them first class and sell them to Crazy Dave for coins.
Mini-Games - personaly my favourite part of the game. It has a lot of variety in gameplay and its very creative. Explaining every mini-game would take me too long to do soo go and play them for yourself cause its totaly worth it.
Puzzle - also a great aspect od the game where you can vase break. Oh and you can also play as the zombies and invade other homes for their brain the fun never ends.
If you are an Achievement hunter this game is for you as it has 21 incredible achievements to unlock from the easies to the hardest but everything is worth it as this is an incredibly fun game.
Overall this game is a fun game and you can always play it if you are bored and dont know what to play cause it has Infinite replayability: the game is never the same experience twice!

Most of you have most likely heard of Assassin's Creed so I won't bore you with details about the series as a whole. Assassin's Creed Brotherhood is the third installment to the series leaving off where Assassin's Creed 2 left off. The game feels very much like the second in many ways but the most notable is that the main character is still the assassin named Ezio, honestly most of the time I think of this more as an expansion pack instead of a standalone. Even with that being said many new features were brought into the game, most of these changes are still in the most recent release Black Flag.
The game takes the gameplay of the second and enhances upon it, for example now you can equip the hidden gun with the sword or the dagger with throwing knives. Combat is far less time consuming with the introduction of the kill streaks, although this is useful it takes much of the difficulty out of the game. This is also the game that introduces assassin recruits, although it feels less refined than revalations they are still a very welcome addition to the game. Also the game adds some replayablity by allowing you to revisit missions unlike the second game, it even goes as far as to give you a reason to go back with extra objectives in a mission to accomplish what is known as "full sync". Full synchronization is nice for those who are completionists and want more out of the game but sometimes they get frustrating. Last but not least the controls are still a little touchy at times you may jump the completely wrong way, this can get very annoying especially when you jump off cliffs.
Sorry about the rambling there, honestly this may not be mechanically my favorite of the series but it is still one of my favorites from the series. The game introduces many mechanics that would later be some of my favorite aspects to the series after they were refined. This game definitely has my approval for anyone thinking of purchasing.

I didnt expect much from this game, thought it was just another take on the whole open world formula that made Grand Theft Auto Successful. Finishing the game I really enjoyed it.
Graphics wise the game looks dated since it released in 2011 but it does have moments where it looks pretty. I particularly enjoy it when the sun is setting and during the night, where the city lights glow bright. It does look decent on lower graphics for those with less powerful PC's
The story is very enjoyable indeed. GTA takes a more realistic and grim gangster approach where as this game takes the mayhem, chaos and awesomeness of the GTA series and multiplys it to 11. I will not go into detail but the story is more than just a bunch of gangsters taking over the Steelport. There's gang wars, military battles, Space , zombies and a whole lot of other ideas which make this awesome masterpiece. There is plenty of content. According to the game I have only completed 67 - 69% which inculdes the story and a few side missions as well as owning some areas of the map. Ive spent about 30 hours in total playing the campaign at a casual pace. What's great is you do not need to own the second and/or first game to know whats going on in the story ( or at least thats what I think). There were a few filler missions that I found a grind however the main story didnt feel too bad.
The gameplay feels awesome. In a nutshell its all about how badass your main character is. While we are on the topic of character let me talk about the main character for a bit. The main character ( which others refer to as The Boss) is how you want him/her to look, When you start the game you are allowed to create a character you wish. The character customization is pretty good for the most part. You can choose gender, build, race ( although it is limited) , how your character sounds ( limited as well), eye colour and so on. The clothing customization is also pretty expansive. My issue with the customisation is that it is limited to whatever the devs have put into the game. I would have loved to see custom colour options ( and maybe a lot more clothes or clothing styles). Back the gameplay. the gunfighting is standard Third person shooting. The game does not use a cover system per say , as I spent most of my time shooting enemies in the open. There are quite a few weapon options, and each weapon can be leveled up. There are some wacky weapons but a few of them are DLC ( which I got from a bundle with the game), maybe one or two of them. My favourite weapon being an 'interesting shaped' purple object is part of the vanilla game for everyone to 'bash'. The driving feels standard open world although the trucks feel clunky. The flying was also wierd ( for me) at first but I quickly adjusted. I had played the game on normal and didnt find it very challenging at all ( this could differ) and the only reason I died was due to a silly mistake done by me, or the level was full of AI. The AI in this game is kind of rubbish. Enemies are ususally easy to kill and do little damage, they are only able to kill you due to the large amount of enemies in the missions ( however this could be different if I bumped the difficulty up). There is a decent selection of enemy varitey although one particular type of enemy does feel very bullet spongy and requires a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of headshots to kill. The gameplay overall feels good, especially taking into consideration the explosions and pure chaos you could create.
I did mention before that there was DLC. There are a few bits of DLC that you can purchase but they do not take away from the game as modern games like to do. They are just cosmetics and new weapons you can purchase as well as a few side missions, but nothing from the base story is taken and put into DLC.
To conclude ITS ♥♥♥♥ING AWESOME. :D

The game features an asymmetrical structure whereby the teams are not always balanced in their ability choices.The Counter Terrorism Units (CTUs) available for play include the FBI Hostage Rescue Team, the British SAS, German GSG-9, Russian Spetsnaz and French GIGN, each of which has four operators per unit. Players also have access to a "Recruit" operator who can choose from a more flexible assortment of equipment at the expense of having no unique gadget. Players pick an operator from any unit before a round starts, and are not allowed to change operators during a round. An in-game shop allows players to purchase operators using the in-game currency, "Renown", which is earned at the end of matches from actions performed in-game. The different gameplay modes award renown at different rates, with ranked matches offering the largest renown multiplier potential per match. Renown can also be affected with the addition of "boosters" which give the player a 100% increase in all renown earned for 24 hours (real time not play time). Renown can also be purchased using real-world currency. Renown can be used to purchase weapon customization options, which allow players to put attachments such as silencers and scopes on their weapons.

Before I begin, there are mild spoilers about the various settings you visit in this game, if that bothers you don't read this review.
What can I say about Darkest of Days? It has been quite some time since I've last played this title and sadly, I may never get a chance to play it again (more on why exactly later). My regret at not being able to play again and my recommendation should be enough to indicate that I enjoyed this, but let me tell you why.
Darkest of Days is not a AAA title, it lacks polish and was clearly not developed with a large budget. It reminds me of a girl that you find enchanting and even sexy despite a plain apperance, because she has that certain "something" you like in the opposite sex, she has quirks in all the right ways, that allow you to overlook or even like any flaws she has. Darkest of Days was that sort of game for me. It has bugs, it's actually kind of ugly (even when it came out), the premise of the story is amazing, but the execution isn't very good. The main character is a faceless man rescued from certain death from the scene of Custer's last stand, whisked away time agents and put under the wing of the forgettable and strange Dexter. You are then thrown in various historical periods to prevent changes to the timeline, it follows a somewhat predictable but not entirely boring temporal civil war-like paradigm.
So far it sounds like I hate this game, but I don't, as I've said I like it. Why? I'm a history buff. The sheer gratitious pleasure of wielding a futuristic automatic weapon against American Civil War era soldiers, Roman Legionaries, and World War 1 era German soldiers was enough to sell me on the game alone. While the environments and situations are not as varied as you would think based on what I just said, it was enough to keep me interested and wanting to see what happens next. This novelty of concept alone was enough to make me like this game, if someone ever picks up this concept and does it better I may never want to play another first person shooter again. Also everything felt well done enough to not distract significantly from my enjoyment of the theme. By far the best segments of the game are the beginning sequences in the American Civil War and the end which takes place in the ancient world.
Should you buy this? Well, that depends. Remember how I mentioned I can't play this anymore? Well, when I built my new PC I decided to go with an AMD GPU, Darkest of Days does not function without an NVIDIA GPU and to my knowledge (and last I checked) there is no work around for this and the development house that created this game no longer exists so a solution is unlikely ever to be forthcoming. The other factor you have to consider is: does anything I mentioned to you sound like it would be as interesting to you as it was to me? Remember, this isn't your Call of Duty or Battlefield. It's a somewhat mediocre offering from a small studio that collapsed. What it does have is an interesting concept, it has little else going for it. If you like the concept and you can actually run it, I suggest this highly as a short diversion. If not, stay away.

As a gamer, I've never been too keen on the big-name modern games.  I want to enjoy them, but they often come off as bland, uninspired, and lacking a distinct charm that I crave.  Hell, it took me until Team Fortress 2 to even own an FPS title.
So yeah, I'm a fan of the classics, and it saddens me that younger gamers seldom get a taste of what gaming was like back in the day.  Leave it to Shovel Knight to set the record straight.
Right from the first notes of the intro stage theme, I knew that this was gonna be FUN.  And I was exactly right.  It was FUN.  The distinct charm that I crave.  FUN.
Poetic language aside, I love just about everything in this game.  The gameplay is simple to understand yet hard to master.  The presentation is quirky and colorful (the main character wields a shovel, for Mew's sake). and everything from the 8-bit graphics to the kickass chiptune soundtrack reeks of retro charm.
Speaking of retro, the gameplay reflects this quite well.  As stated before, it's simple and draws inspiration from several sources, yet it still feels like its own entity.  After all, it's still a game made in 2014, and the achievement system and upgrade shops serve as a reminder to this.
Of course, a game isn't retro without challenge, and it's sadly the one point that I find slightly lacking.  That's not because there is no challenge; it just feels like the wrong kind of challenge at times.  I can tolerate challenge via level design and game progression, and Shovel Knight does that well.  However, I still can't get over certain factors that feel rather cheap at times.  Enemy placement is ungodly annoying, especially in the later levels, and design choices like the blackout segments from the Lich Yard never cease to infuriate me.  Even then, all you're doing is losing money upon death, but if you die repeatedly, get ready to grind gold and backtrack to get what you want.
But I can overlook this.  Because really, if that's all I have to complain about, then Shovel Knight is truly worthy of the acclaim it's received.  Mainstream developers, take notes.  Because indie companies are on the rise, and if this game is any indication, they're doing your job better than you are at the moment.

This game has no substance. It's its biggest flaw, and a major one. It has about... I don't know, a combined total of about 15 minutes' worth of content, randomized infinitely to pad out the gameplay. Different game modes add little to the variety.
The music is good, - really good sometimes, even; I really appreciated Mike Smith's contributions to the soundtrack, - and the graphics are... well, flashy and sometimes the colorful chaos is enjoyable to watch, I'll give it that. However, it turns out it was a _terrible_ idea on Boss Baddie's part not to try and make enemy bullets and other hazards extra visible and perhaps unaffected by all the graphical distortion effects going on and particle effects flying by, obscuring your vision. As the game's difficulty increases and the screen becomes cluttered with all sorts of randomized junk, it becomes nigh-impossible to tell what's going on, and what hurts you and what doesn't - and it is entirely the game developers' fault.
The feeling of being utterly confused is fun for a while, but gets old rather quick, like Mister Pineapple's comments heard throughout the game. (He has about 20-30 lines he says from time to time, those can be turned off once they get repetitive.)
There are numerous other shortcomings that I'm not going to discuss in detail, because while a bit annoying, they can be overlooked and the game can still be enjoyed to an extent in spite of them. (resolution locked at 720p, restricted aiming with the mouse, game rules are not explained clearly enough, the library only provides vague descriptions instead of pictures of objects in the game, often making it even harder to figure out what exactly it describes, expo mode in the options, game always crashing upon exiting)
I don't think you can get more than about 6-7 hours of entertainment out of the game, and that's really stretching it. Unless maybe you have some friends to play the game with - I asked a friend to play with me, but I showed a gameplay video to him and he refused, turned off by the chaos on the screen. Your Mileage May Vary, I'm pretty sure Boss Baddie stated at some point that their game was designed primarily for co-op with up to 3 others and should be played on a machine with a good sound system, with the bass turned up a couple notches.
I mean, all in all Really Big Sky is kinda okay, definitely playable to a degree, a solid 4/10 if I had to grade it on a scale, but I'd say forget the game and just buy the rather awesome soundtrack if you can get it somewhere (and then turn up the bass), or risk getting RBS if your friends are willing to give it a shot as well.

The story is very enjoyable indeed. GTA takes a more realistic and grim gangster approach where as this game takes the mayhem, chaos and awesomeness of the GTA series and multiplys it to 11. I will not go into detail but the story is more than just a bunch of gangsters taking over the Steelport. There's gang wars, military battles, Space , zombies and a whole lot of other ideas which make this awesome masterpiece. There is plenty of content. According to the game I have only completed 67 - 69% which inculdes the story and a few side missions as well as owning some areas of the map. The gameplay feels awesome. In a nutshell its all about how badass your main character is. While we are on the topic of character let me talk about the main character for a bit. The main character ( which others refer to as The Boss) is how you want him/her to look, When you start the game you are allowed to create a character you wish. The character customization is pretty good for the most part. You can choose gender, build, race ( although it is limited) , how your character sounds ( limited as well), eye colour and so on. The clothing customization is also pretty expansive. My issue with the customisation is that it is limited to whatever the devs have put into the game. I would have loved to see custom colour options ( and maybe a lot more clothes or clothing styles). Back the gameplay. the gunfighting is standard Third person shooting. The game does not use a cover system per say , as I spent most of my time shooting enemies in the open. There are quite a few weapon options, and each weapon can be leveled up. There are some wacky weapons but a few of them are DLC ( which I got from a bundle with the game), maybe one or two of them. My favourite weapon being an 'interesting shaped' purple object is part of the vanilla game for everyone to 'bash'. The driving feels standard open world although the trucks feel clunky. The flying was also wierd ( for me) at first but I quickly adjusted. I had played the game on normal and didnt find it very challenging at all ( this could differ) and the only reason I died was due to a silly mistake done by me, or the level was full of AI. The AI in this game is kind of rubbish. Enemies are ususally easy to kill and do little damage, they are only able to kill you due to the large amount of enemies in the missions ( however this could be different if I bumped the difficulty up). There is a decent selection of enemy varitey although one particular type of enemy does feel very bullet spongy and requires a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of headshots to kill. The gameplay overall feels good, especially taking into consideration the explosions and pure chaos you could create.
I did mention before that there was DLC. There are a few bits of DLC that you can purchase but they do not take away from the game as modern games like to do. They are just cosmetics and new weapons you can purchase as well as a few side missions, but nothing from the base story is taken and put into DLC.
To conclude ITS ♥♥♥♥ING AWESOME. :D

Review in a few:
+Visuals
+Soundtrack
+Steam Controller
+Mad Drifts
+Leaderboard asyncronous multiplayer.
-No story
Absolute Drift is a game about a man with a family to save from the Yakuza and the only bid they’ll take on their lives is if you beat their leader in a drift-off, so you play a montage of training until the final battle scene like every kung fu movie.  Wait that’s not right…  So there’s no backstory.  You’re just a car with mad drifts.
It’s a very simple concept, drift as much as you can, chain together drifts, and get points.  The more points you get, the higher your score, the farther up the leaderboards you go.  There’s a large open-world area where you can complete challenges like drifting around certain objects, performing jumps, and collecting spinning plus-signs.  It’s sectioned off into areas, and you must complete objectives in each area before advancing to the next one resulting in solid progression as your personal skill improves.
There are dedicated tracks with leaderboards (as mentioned earlier) that allow you to compete against others asynchronously, which are placed around the open world map for you to find.  If exploration is less your thing however, you can find the tracks on the main menu as well and jump right in.  These tracks can have one of two types: open areas with trick spots, and race tracks that record both your time and your drifts.
The controls are easy to pick up, tough to master -- Or maybe I just suck.  It’s definitely not a game to play keyboard only, as feathering drifts is nigh impossible, so a controller of some form is a must.  It also has some really nice feedback on how good your drift is through rumble, which translates well onto a steam controller.
Graphics wise, it’s visually pleasing.  It’s very easy to tell what is where and what’s important, and there is never enough on screen to get busy.  With a pleasantly good looking drift line showing your mad skills, you can watch your past as you tear up the present.
Overall it’s an enjoyable game and worth picking up on sale for a few hours of fun.  It’s not going to keep you gripped for a dozen hours, but it’s better than your average movie with a lower admittance fee.

There are a few technical hiccups on PC (I originally played through it on console). I'll list them below.
In certain chapters there were game breaking bugs that halted progress. The boss at the end of chapter 5-2 was invincible. We threw everything short of an atomic bomb at him, and he wouldnt go down. Me and my friend had to reload with a Rocket Launcher to progress, so at least that's an option. Another section in chapter 6-1 when sheva/chris get's stuck in a cage, there was a bug that prevented an enemy from spawning and an item being dropped. We had to reload several times before we just lucked out that the enemy spawned and the item dropped. That was really annoying.
Last but not least during entry into certain chapters at the end sometimes me or my partners health would just be depleted for no good reason.
Despite the bugs, me and my partner perservered. Luckily we didn't start experiencing the bugs until later on in the playthrough, but some of them are borderline game breaking in my opinion so they have to be mentioned. I would pick it up on sale because despite the bugs I still had a blast. I look at this game as strictly a co-op game so have a friend if you can play with you because the AI is as dumb as a stump. Anyone who can appreciate 2D platforming games should play this; it nails every single aspect of its design.
- Every gameplay mechanic is taught actively and without exposition, in a subtle but smart way. You don't have to read anything, you'll learn everything you need to know just by playing. Every single room in the game is engaging without being cheap.
- The soundtrack manages to be BOTH atmospheric and memorable, with songs that both fit the theme of the level and feature catchy melodies - every single one. No game has done this so consistently before in my experience.
- Every boss and NPC has a unique design. The color palette is bright and vibrant but not sore on the eyes. Each villager feels like a real person. The bosses are fun to fight against; they overwhelm you at first but you pick up on their patterns and beat them in a satisfying way.
- It uses the Souls series death system: you lose money if you die unless you can make it back to the spot where you died on your next try. In my opinion more games should implement this as it's a great balance between punishing failure and rewarding consistency.
- It doesn't overstay its welcome. It's a short and satisfying game you can complete in a weekend.

I recommend this game highly. It is a great game for those interested in an FPS that goes to different points in history.
Well, if you have an older Nvidia graphics card anyway. Running a GTX 970 the Physx features of this game wouldnt work, even with legacy drivers installed (fog, leaves, weapon smoke and other particles) - without these the game just isnt as good IMO. Therefore, i had to play on an old 9600GT to get PhysX working. Worse; It wouldnt run on my Radeon card at all.
EDIT: Tested on Windows 10 Tech Preview 64bit. Its not the OS that's causing the issue for some people. You just need an older GPU
Technical problems aside, the actual game:
PROS:
- Fantastic idea - Travelling back to various periods including WW1 and the Civil war. These arent exactly common in other games and it was a refreshing change, and on the whole they did it well. They actually explain the time tavel part of it too, and the plot involves 2 opposing groups fighting to either preserve or change history.
- Good levels - who doesnt want to form up in rank against the confederates at Antietam, or break out of a WW2 concentration camp?
- Reload animation minigame - get it right and it speeds up the reload, get it wrong and it jams and takes longer. Great mechanic.
- Weapon upgrade system
- Fairly good voice acting, and chatter from other sodiers on the battlefield
- Slight choice to pick the mission you want to do next
- Feeling like a badass when you are wrecking Romans and Confederates with future weaponry
CONS:
- Maps arent as open as they appear, invisible walls and linear design
- occassionally getting stuck to surfaces
- A few turret sections that are only ok
- you can bypass the necessity for reloading by switching to secondary and using it, by the time you go back to your primary weapon it has reloaded itself. This takes away from the feel of the game, especially in the civil war with muskets that should take a while to reload.
- The ending leaves the game open a bit for a sequel thats likely never coming.
In conclusion though, the negatives don't outweigh the positives for me and I think if you have an older nvidia card this game is definitely worth a shot. If you can get it working with PhysX the graphics hold up surprisingly well, and the game has a great concept and its a hell of a lot of fun.

An ok sequel to RE4, but another step further from survival horror. The people who made this game were obviously influenced by popular movies and other games. The first 40 minute are inspired by Black Hawk Down. Wesker is now Neo from the Matrix. There's a turret/car chase level that feels right out of the original Uncharted.
+ The game looks fantastic for an 8 years old title. Especially the first half set in Africa, the later stages are a bit bland.
+ Very nice selection of guns.
+ Fewer QTEs than RE4, there is nothing obnoxious like the Leon/ Krauser knife fight from RE4.
- Chris is now The Hulk. His upper arms are bigger than his head. He even gets to punch a giant boulder out of his way(!!). What were they thinking? He looked fine in Code Veronica and the RE remake.
- The majinis use the same animations as RE4's ganados. Lazy.
- Forced co-op with a terrible partner AI (if you play solo). You have 2 options for the AI: Cover or attack. Cover means Sheva will stay close to you and use her pistol only. Attack means she'll use the strongest available weapon, wander away from you and get killed because you can't save her in time. Some AI customization would have been nice (stay close, engage long distance first, use shotgun at close range, etc)
- Too many gimmicky boss battles, some of which are extremely tedious because there is only one way to win and trying anything else is just wasting ammunition. I like having options when fighting bosses.
- The music is absolutely forgettable. A far cry from RE4 and the classic RE trilogy.

I have to get one thing off my chest right off the bat.  There is a lot of hate for this game because it seems like a mobile port and Steam PC gamers are highly sensitive to preserving the state of PC gaming, and not allowing it to slowly degrade to the completely unskilled, lowest-common-denominator experience that console and mobile is known for.
Know that Loot Hero DX is definitely in the unskilled, lowest-common-denominator category.
However, the game works as expected on PC, and having played the mobile version while slowly waiting to die, I can say they did an excellent port with gamepad controls, graphical/mechanic upgrades, etc.
The game is as simple as can be.  Run left/right and as you head right you hit progressively more difficult monsters.  Gather gold, upgrade skills, lather rinse repeat.  Only the graphics change, not the core game or anything else really.
Adults will be bored quickly unless this is your kind of thing, but I got this for my GF's son who is 9 and he loves the crud out of it.  He won't stop playing my phone version, so now he has the PC (we play on the TV on Steam Link) and that's great.  So if you know what you're getting up front, and you know that it it simple as heck.  It is worth the minimal price tag.
I'm giving a thumbs up on the basis that what it does, it does well.  Not my cup of tea, but there is a place in the gaming world for games like this.
