This game is a very, fun game. However, There are a couple of major problems with it.
1) The audio. The voices are god awful, they, quite literally, sould like someone was in a rush and put a mic in front of a T.V. with the movie playing. In one instance, Malcom started speaking, and you could hear water running in the background. When he stopped speaking, the water noises stopped. This was at a point during LW while looking for Sarah. You can hear the mic buzzing, or the T.V. buzzing, when certain characters talk, expecially Malcom and Hammond.
2) The game has a couple of major bugs. Now, I have only experienced one of them, and upon searching it up I found that other players have the same problem. The game would crash in Jurassic Park, during the T-Rex car chase, seconds after the car does a jump under the branch, and the T-Rex has to go around it.
As for small issues that I can deal with:
1) No mouse support. At all. Period. You can't even use your mouse in the menus.
2) Only local Co-Op. I get it, that's what Lego games do, but it's such a pain for me, since I have this on PC, not a console.
3) The massive menu maps. It's fun exploring and all, but having to run all the way around places to get to the 1 place you're looking for is a huge pain.
4) No real explination on what you're doing, with the exception of Mr. DNA, except you have to figure out how to get his hint to pop up. (You have to hit a button, with no button clues, rather than just walking up to him. I had no idea that he was even a hint when I first got into the game.)
However, I'm sure some of these thigns will be fixed, expecially the crashing bugs, which is why I'm recommending this game. It's very fun, but needs some work.

This is easily my favorite PC multiplayer game. I've been playing it since the first alpha stages and it's been fun watching the game continue to evolve and grow, especially since the changes the devs have made were pretty much always fully thought out.
Teamwork is key in this game, even if you go 10 and 2 your team can still completely fail to communicate and cost you matches. This game has an ability to be both slow and fast paced. The destruction and variation in operators keeps things fresh. Even though the learning curve is a bit steep, playing this game with friends is extremely fun.
The graphics and sound design are great, and the gun play is almost perfect (hit boxes keep getting tweaked, making for some interesting changes). The community is still alive and well and the dev team still cares.
I've got almost 300 hours on this game and it still isn't getting old. That may not sound like a lot, but considering I've had the game since it came out in 2015 and I can't play all day every day, that should give you a good idea about how much this game draws you in and makes you want to keep playing, long after you've unlocked everything (which doesn't take all that long).
This was the first game in a long time that really got my heart going (in a non fearful/jumpscare sort of way), and it still does so as close games play their way out.
I highly recommend buying this game if you're looking for a teamwork based ,multiplayer shooter with great mechanics and a good community.

Lego Jurrasic Park is exactly what you would expect from any Lego game established before it. Quick to pick up on, and easily suitable for both casual and more devoted gamers. The team behind the environment design as well graphics certainly push it a step further than previous titles in the Lego Games lineup.
The humor is spot on and had myself, a man in the quarter of his life so far, giggling like an idiot. The game content and replayability proves out with many collectables, unlockables, characters and hidden easter eggs even the most hard core of completionists will find satisfying. It is also a fresh step back onto the film series some of us have grown up on, and others not even aware of. ( Lord help the fools who watch the Lost World. )
There are minor complaints to be made. The original dialogue is taken from the film, and unfortunately that translate to a poor audio recording that seems so low in quality that it can seem a little distracting once in awhile. It is especially noticable when fresh voice actors and actresses have made new lines for this game which by all means sound fresh and crisp. There are minor glitches with AI or the environment and not every puzzle or path is intuitively developed for a straightforward experience. Lastly, there are minor slow downs and hang ups now and again but on rare account.
All in all the pros certainly outweigh the cons  and I could not recommend this game enough. If not for the fact it is riding on the back of a great gaming legacy, but also that they made Jeff Goldblum a scary man you would not want to sit next to on a helicopter ride. You know, like real life.

If you've ever played any of the previous Lego games, this one will not disappoint.
I'm only about halfway through the main storyline, and 20% completion overall. There's so much to do! There are probably close to a hundred different characters, a dozen dinosaurs, and two dozen vehicles to unlock. Spanning all four Jurassic Park films, this game offers hours upon hours of replay value. It's a steal for $30. Lego games are typically a phenomenal value.
The game blends the rich lore of the Jurassic Park films, with the humor and style of the Lego sets. This game is kid friendly, but plenty of great fun for adults, too. If adult fans of the series are looking for a game to play with their children, this is a wise choice. There are a lot of pop culture references scattered about the game, including ET and Jaws, two of Universal's other successful licenses.
Gameplay is what you'd expect from Lego, drop in/drop out co-op with intuitive level design and a multitude of ways to achieve goals. Side goals will earn you extra mini-kits.
The voice acting is pretty solid, in some parts it sounds as though the original VHS tapes were used for the sound bites, but most of the time it's great. Some of the characters sound as though the actors who originally portrayed them returned to re-read their lines (Like in Alien: Isolation) but I'm not sure. As far as I know, however, Jurassic World's cast lent their voice talents to this.
While this game is pretty standard fare for a Lego-fied IP (Hobbit, Star Wars, Batman) it is notably improved in its graphics, and some of the game mechanics are smoother as well. The improved character selection and open world gameplay are a big step up from Lego Star Wars 3, the last Lego game I played.  The game runs smoothly at 1080p, well into the 90+FPS range.
The levels are well-made, and while some gamers report a plethora of glitches, I can gladly say I have yet to experience any. As with any Lego game, an Xbox controller is a MUST. This game is an incredible value, filled with tons of fun for the entire family. If you like Jurassic Park, you won't want to pass this up.

Enjoying the BR genre and coming from PUBG after putting about 500 hours into that game, I thought I would try H1Z1. On Sale for $5, nothing to lose right?
Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing god was I wrong.
The controls, after this game has been out for almost 2 years is laughable at best. The UI is appauling and the whole Inventory System feels more like a sandbox survival rather than a BR.
Performance? Sure. Runs alright on my rig. Why? It looks like a game from 5-7 years ago and even with the settings up high it just doesn't look right. Can't use Early access as an excuse after this long of being out.
My first match? 6 People. Six. And I killed 3-4 of them to secure a win. There is virtually no variety in weapons or loot, you can't choose where you drop as it just boots you out somewhere random, there is no ADS so otherwise you have a Rifle or you are stick with a hip fire.
I guess I should focus my ranting down a little more.
- Game will start with less than 10 people even though boasting a what, 150 player server?
- movement Mechanics are no better than a game in the late 2000's
- No Vaulting, climbing or otherwise tactical mechanics.
- Gunplay is not only severely unrealistic but not even the good sort of realistic.
- Lacking Variety in gun, no attachments exist and wont exist if the devs stick to their words.
- The last 2 kills of the match involved Myself and another player jumping around in a circle with shotguns, myself having shot him 5 times before needing to pull out another gun to finish him off.
What I am trying to get at is this game is arcady, in the wrong style. Has been in Early Access for almost 2 years and has nothing to show for it, and has devs that seem more content in giving you a CS:GO style market, while having a lousy game to go with it.
If you are looking at the reviews now because the game's on sale. Don't be cheap, give it a Miss and go play PUBG. Millions of players per day, a Much better movement system/mechanic, more guns, more variety, and a dev team who are working on making their game better.
It's a classic, what's not to love?

Played RE 5 for the first time in 2015, 2016. I beat it only a few days ago with a friend. My playtime is roughly how long it took us for one playthrough. The graphics don't look bad for being older. The game ran smoothely on both my older system and my newer setup. I never tried to play it alone, and it ran fine for my friend as well. There were a few moments that the game got repetitive. It's not a bad game, but definitely not what I would consider to be Resident Evil. Storywise, you'll read bits of journals as you progress which can be quite tedious and lengthy at times. Overall I enjoyed RE 5. It was mostly pure arcade fun.
Aside from everything else, I would like to point out that RE 5 on Steam (not sure if it does this on consoles) has one major flaw that I noticed. My friend was the host for the majorty of the time and I was the one invited into the party. Because of this, sometimes a glitch would occur at the end of missions where the game did not think I completed the full mission. One way to tell is that it would not reward me a letter grade on how well I did upon mission completion, thus also not giving me an achievement for beating it. So if you are a completionist this will be a nuisance because you'll have to play many missions again (more than you ordinarily would). Also due to this, when we beat the game my friend was able to unlock several things but I was not. I can see this being annoying for many people. Several of the things you can unlock are for playing through the game again such as infinite ammo, new costumes, etc. but since I don't plan on replaying the game I didn't care much.

In an industry where everyone's battling to have the best graphics and the most "immersive" gameplay, the games that really shine are the ones that ignore all this and instead go for something a lot less modern.  Shovel Knight is a prime example of this past inspireed approach and is a fantastic lesson to AAA developers that hyper realistic nose hairs don't necessarily create a superior game and that sometimes it doesn't hurt to look back at the huge legacy of games that have preceeded yours.
Shovel Knight is both intelligently and challengingly designed, requiring you to conquer it with skill, brainpower and a lot of shovelling. It's difficult in the same way that many of the classics were, but with some minor tweaks to make it more fair to the player. Each level introduces new obstacles and enemies that can't simply be beaten by bringing out the biggest gun in your inventory, but instead actually require you to think about the situation. This adds to the sense of accomplishment when you complete each level, as not only are you a skillful platformerer(?) but are also rather good at utilising that brain thing that you have.
The beautiful pixelated presentation, excellent 8-bit influenced music and witty dialogue is the icing on the cake, giving you a retro experience like no other, combining the genius creativity and core gameplay of the classics, with the more modern sensibilities developers have learnt from retrospect, all of it accomplished without a single polygon. To say Shovel Knight is a good game would be a massive understatement and with more content on the way, Shovel Knight is only going to get better.

It there's one thing that practically all horror games don't do right it's making you feel vulnerable. Thankfully, Amnesia makes you feel as vulnerable as a scared little girl. There is no offense, only defense. You will never feel powerful, but that's the point of Amnesia. While most games give the player a power fantasy fuelled by testosterone and nigh invulnerability, Amnesia exists to emasculate and scare the player.
It's not a game that's challenging due to skill requirements, but a game that's challenging due to its constant reminder of what we're not. We don't take up the mantle of the bald space marine or the tough-as-nails survivalist or the calm problem solver. It's a wonderful game because it forces the player out of the power fantasy comfort zone that they're used to.
Play it with the lights off and the volume high. It's a wonderful game.

I was skeptical at first, but Shovel Knight is truly an amazing game and it DOES live up to the hype. The platforming can seem overwhelming at first but it quickly begins to make sense. The satisfaction of beating a level or even just reaching a checkpoint is phenomenal. Instead of losing lives when you die you drop flying bags of money that can be picked up when you make it back to where you were. This idea was genius and fits perfectly with the intense platforming that will result in many deaths.  Every detail in the game amazed me and the quality of the story was far beyond my expectation. If you take into consideration how much of your time is spent on retries from deaths then you realize that shovel knight is sadly a short game. If I had to give this game a rating it would be a 9.5/10. In the way of DLC you can get the amazing soundtrack for around $10, which I highly recommend, and a free DLC storyline following the adventure of one of shovel knight's bosses, Plague knight, will be released soon.

I completely appreciate the effort that was put into this game, but for me it will always feel "less-than".
Though I like that the modders of this game chose to set the story to when Aperature was in it's golden age, they really did a bad job of setting themselves up to be crtiqued in this light. Modders: you don't have JK Simmons to perform your script as Cave Johnson--that is acceptable and understandable. HOWEVER the script they wrote for his character is so clumsily written. What I mean is, the dialogue feels completely unnatural. If you're trying to allude to the face that Cave Johnson is lying, you only need one line that establishes an obvious cover-up. Repeatedly saying OVER, AND OVER, "Here in my 1950's computer, in my 1950's folder, because it's the 1950's," is insulting to your player. I would argue that even as talented of an actor as JK Simmons would have a hard time performing the dialogue and actually making it sound good and natural. It's just super awkward.
My second big criticism is with the opening. We ride a train car for so long that even the dialogue of Cave Johnson's greetings ends before we reach the station platform. Then! It is only to walk to an elevator that we ride for a very, very long time. And to cap it all off: this loooooong ride on the elevator and train is TO BE PUT IN A CHRYOGENIC SLEEP. This is the such a slow-paced beginning, that by the time I got to the part where I actually get to, oh you know, PLAY I was done. You lost me. I didn't care anymore.
Either set something relevant up to the user during these long opening sequences, or just skip to the character waking up from a chryogenic sleep. Instead of referencing Half-Life/Half-Life 2, just go right to the Portal throwback. I'm not even sure if I'm going to keep this in my library anymore.

Originally EDF 2025 for the X-Box 360, then EDF 4.1 for the PS4, EDF 4.1: Shadow of New Despair is a port of a remaster of an already excellent game.  The 4.1 update includes several fantastic additions, from excellent class gameplay tweaks, to more weapons, to more missions, to more enemies, better lighting, etc. etc. etc.
To put it simply, Earth Defense Force 4.1 is a B-Movie that you play.  While it doesn't include Bruce Campbell (waiting on that DLC, Sandlot), it DOES include big, fake-looking bugs and robots, as well as hilariously bad voice acting (don't worry, it doesn't get annoying quickly), and more explosions than Michael Bay's wet dreams.
However, the smarmy B-movie charm isn't the main draw:  that would be the incredibly tight gameplay.  The series has been fine-tuning itself over the years, and while the ill-fated American-made Insect Armageddon may have flopped, it did introduce to the series class-based gameplay (although earlier versions did have two playable characters) and teammate reviving (I wish sprinting would've made its way over, too).  Each class has a very different set of weapons and moves very differently from one another, so even if you play through all 90+ Missions on all 5 Difficulty settings with a single class, you've only completed 20% of the game.
Apparently, there are some problems with certain processors and troubles with cheating, but I have not encountered either of these.
If you don't care about story or presentation or set pieces (basically everything that's killing video games today), then EDF is the game for you.

"Amnesia: The Dark Descent" is a survival horror game. This is by far one of the scariest games have ever played... definitely trumps over a lot of the other "horror"/ survival horror games out there. I actually played it at night with no lights on and headphones...it really enhanced the eerie atmosphere.
Anyways, you play as Daniel, a man who awakens in a castle with no memory of who or where he is. As you play through the game, you can uncover fragments of information from books, notes, etc, to piece together what is going on, which makes the game feel similar to the original "Metroid Prime" style of story-telling: plenty of backstory and history which you must uncover by exploration.
One of the unique features of the game is the sanity mechanic, where the more time you spend in dark areas without light, the more delirious you can become. The more delirious you are, the harder it is to see and hear clearly as well as increasing your likelihood to run into enemies. Become too delirious and you may fall unconscious, allowing enemies who find you in this state to kill you instantly. You will also become more delirious as your health bar drops. The game will randomly attempt to scare you in order to make you delirious, so managing your sanity is important.
Moreover, there are no weapons in this game, so you cannot fight off enemies. You can only run from them, attempt to block doors with objects (although enemies can tear down doors and break objects) and hide. This is a cliched mechanic, but it works well the sanity mechanic, as you can hide in darkness to avoid enemies, but you will become more delirious by doing so.
Replayability is high as there are several difficulty settings, a free DLC and numerous player created mods to play through.
Overall, this is definitely a survival horror game worth picking up.

Shovel Knight is a retro-style action platformer that was heavily inspired by classic NES titles such as Mega Man, Castlevania, The Legend of Zelda and DuckTales.
You play as Shovel Knight, a knight named after his signature weapon. He's a former adventurer who had been roaming the land alongside his friend Shield Knight for years. One day both came across the mysterious Tower of Fate. While Shovel Knight and Shield Knight were exploring the tower something awakened and all of a sudden all hell broke loose. At some point Shovel Knight passed out. When he woke up his friend was gone and the tower was sealed. Devastated, Shovel Knight gave up the life of adventure and started living in solitude. One day a mysterious order of knights appears out of nowhere and start ravaging the land while the Tower of Fate opens up again. It is time to dish out some shovel justice.
Shovel Knight stays very true to the games that inspired it. It looks and feels like an NES game. Actually the developers deliberately tried to keep it as close as possible to the original NES aesthetics. There are some features in Shovel Knight that the NES would not have been able to handle. The developers stated that they were working under the assumption that the NES would still be supported today so while still being an 8-bit system the cartridges would have vastly improved chip sets.
Shovel Knight's gameplay is a mix of platforming and combat. Shovel Knight can simply strike enemies with his shovel but is also able to jump up and perform a downward strike to deal damage to enemies and bounce off of them. This is a necessary move at some points in the game since there is no double jump. He can also use his shovel to dig out piles of dirt or some walls to find treasure, opening up a way or reveal secret passages. It is possible to reflect enemies' ranged attacks via shovel strikes with the right timing. Shovel Knight has three resources: health, magic and gold. In normal mode getting hit reduces Shovel Knight's health by half a point while in new game plus mode one hit equals one full point of health lost. Touching spikes always results in a death. Magic is drained whenever an artifact is used. There are several artifacts hidden throughout the level. While you can replay almost every level as often as you like those artifacts can only be purchased at a hidden vendor the first time you visit the respective level. If the level is completed without the artifact having been found that artifact can be purchased at the vendor in town. Gold is used for buying artifacts as well as upgrades or sidegrades. Shovel Knight can upgrade his shovel as well as his health and magic pool as well as buy alternative armor sets that often have one particular benefit while carrying one disadvantage that other armor does not have.
The artifact system is very reminiscient of the one in the Zelda games. Shovel Knight can have one artifact at a time selected. The selected artifact can be changed anytime by bringing up the inventory. There is a wide variety of artifacts and while most of them have an offensive use some are primarily used for defensive or utility purposes. There is for example a fire staff, a locket that makes you invincible for a few seconds, a fishing rod that can be used to catch treasure, health pickups or collectibles and a dagger that enables mid-air dashes. While artifacts make the game a whole lot easier they are not required to beat the game. It is entirely possible to complete the game using only the shovel if you are skilled enough.
Shovel Knight starts you out on a world map from where you enter the first level. While the game is mostly linear and all boss levels need to be completed to get to the final level you can often pick the order in which you tackle the boss levels. There are also some optional bonus levels that only serve the purpose of collecting treasure. There are two towns that can be visited when you feel like spending your gold. Also, there are some enemy encounters that don't occur within a level but on the world map. Aside from the optional treasure levels and the world map encounters you can revisit any level as often as you like.
Every boss has a specific theme with his level reflecting that. For example there's King Knight, a knight who is not actually a king but nonetheless dresses like one and resides in a pompous castle which is also not his. Or there's Treasure Knight who wears an old-fashioned diver's suit and can attack by shooting an anchor chain at you. His lair is in a flooded shipwreck. Every level has some specific mechanics which are unique to that level, keeping the game fresh.
Compared to many other games Shovel Knight is quite tough. It is however not overly hard nor is it unfair. The controls are very tight and responsive and with all of the enemies it comes down to the player knowing their patterns and behaviour. Every level has a bunch of checkpoints from which you can restart after you die. Since there is no life system you can retry as much as you want, but you drop a part of your gold every time you die. Luckily this gold can be reaquired if you make it to the point where you died. Checkpoints can actually destroyed for bonus gold, so be careful around them. You don't want to destroy a checkpoint by accident. However, if you accidentally destroyed a checkpoint or just lost too much gold you can always leave the level and enter it again. If you leave the level without having beaten it everything is reset to the point before you entered it.
The graphics and music of Shovel Knight do very well within the developer's self-imposed confines. The graphics are colourful and show great attention to detail. The music does a good job in conveying the respective level's atmosphere. All of the ingame music can be found as music sheets and given to the bard in town. Aside from paying you in treasure the bard will then play any of those songs for you if you ask him.
Shovel Knight is still to be expanded content-wise. While what you get when you buy it is already a full game the developers are currently working on an expansion campaign in which you play as the boss Plague Knight. There will be several more content updates in the future. Since they were promised due to the game's kickstarter campaign reaching its stretch goals all of those will be completely free which is awesome.
In summary, the developers have done a great job at Shovel Knight and the game delivers everything they originally strived for. If you are fond of platformers and/or retro games you should give Shovel Knight a try.

I've been playing this game for years, but only now do I take the time to review it.
TL;DR: I'm saying the same thing everyone else is saying. It's really fun, and the best game in the franchise (and probably always will be, thanks to EA..)
I've been playing this game for quite some time, as I previously mentioned. I've purchased it several times from the Popcap website, because every time you delete it or want to play on a new computer, as far as I knew at the time, you have to re-buy it. Not only that, but I also own this game on my Nintendo DS as well as the Xbox. And I've beaten it countless times. Luckily, I eventually bought it on Steam, where I can install it on as many computers as I want without having to worry about losing the game.
After buying the game so many times, do I feel like I wasted any money? No. Not a single cent. Sure, the game is easy. Really easy. And it gets really repetitive. But.. it's
. I just fought Dr. Zomboss for the millionth time, and I still had
.
Why is that? Well, a few things for me:
1) the AMAZING soundtrack
2) the fact that every 5 levels you get to play a mini-game of some sort to break up the monotony
3) The variety of areas, plants, and zombies that you will have to encounter
4) the amount of hidden things in this game, which (unless you look it up online) you may be still discovering new things for years
So, yes the game has problems. It gets boring eventually, even for me. And, as I previously mentioned, it's so easy for me now - I don't know if it was designed to be playable for everyone, or if it's because I've beaten it so many times. But the campaign offers virtually no challenge any more, and I feel like Crazy Dave just taking up seed slots is artificial difficulty.
But, despite all that, it's charming and fun enough for me to have gotten all my money's worth. I've played so many hours of this game total, over all platforms... I really wish there would be a good sequel that wasn't riddled with microtransactions and like literally almost impossible difficulty (which spikes at a certain point), but that'll never happen. I hate EA.
Regardless, this game as a standalone is a great piece of entertainment, and I'd reccomend anyone, no matter how old you are, to play this game at least once. At least try the demo or something.

Shovel Knight is without a doubt 1 of the best 2D platformers I have ever played. You could even say that I really dig it *cue laugh track*.
You can really see all the dedication and effort that was put into making this game. The Controls are great, The soundtrack is great. The Level desing is great. Even the characters have a lot of charm and personality to them, even though they don't exactly have a lot of depth to them. Shovel knight is also full of humor and all kinds of references, and both of tose have been done extremely well. I laughed out loud a couple of times while playing this game.
The levels are also quite varied and they are full of all kinds of little secrets to find. And then the boss fights, oh those boss fights. Each of them has their own theme(just like the levels they are in), and all of them are simply fun and quite challenging to fight against. Speaking of challenge, the game starts out quite easy, but the difficulty ramps up quite quickly, yet the game never felt unfair. If you die, you only have yourself to blame. You can always try to blame the game but you are only lying to yourself if you do that you silly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The game did have a few flaws though. Some of the items you can get are EXTREMELY overpowered compared to others. Also, it is a bit silly that you can tank a huge hit from a boss no problem, yet a spike scratching your ankle is an instant kill. The game is also a lil short, but I didn't really mind it that much because the level of quality remained high from beginning to end. If they make another Shovel knight game, I really hope they would make a co-op mode of some kind, where the other player could play as the Shield Knight. If that  ends up happening, they better send me a million dollars for creating this idea.
Edit: Well it seem that I got what I asked for. Plague of shadows update was released, and it dramatically increased the amount of content in the game by adding a challenge mode and a completely new character who has his own campaign. With the Plague of shadows, Shovel knight reinforces it's status as 1 of my favorite indie games of all time. Keep up the good work Yacht club!

The current market is (arguably over-)saturated with "8-bit style" games attempting to ride the wave of nostalgia of gamers longing for their childhood games again, and generally the only real similarity of these games to the Mega Mans and Castlevanias is the 8-bit art. Shovel Knight, however, absolutely nails it. Every aspect of the game is not just a homage to classic 80s platformers, but a faithful recreation of the style of gameplay. Platforming segments that are hard until you figure them out, varieties of enemies styled for the level in which they appear, interesting and engaging boss fights, it's all there. Obviously there are plenty of other nods to ye olde video games, such as "____ Knight" bosses in the vein of Mega Man, Castlevania-like subweapons, and the ability to drop down on enemies from above to kill them. Shovel Knight is in every way a love letter to the "classic" games, and it's done so much better than every other game that claims the same.

If you like Super Mario and Castlevania, do not hesitate buying this game!

Got this game back when it was still alpha, for very cheap. Knowing it was alpha, and browsing the forums, the game was a very fun experience. There were contests, and a bunch of good spirited discussion, etc. I definitely had my moneys worth of enjoyment from this game.
Sadly, devs started delaying new updates, kept cutting out parts of the game that were promised, and eventually "settled" that the game was finished in the current state, which let me tell you, is not even close to what it should be.
From that point the game left its "alpha status", apparently went through a very short beta period, and it released here on Steam (I only have little time with the game here on steam, because I played a lot of the standalone version). Like it was a full game or something...
The rest is history now, but in case you don't know, it goes something like this: The general public in steam find that the game is really lackluster for a full game, and complain. Devs promise to improve, despite insisting that the game is complete. At some point one of the devs simply disappears without warning. After some time, the guy reappears, saying that he had problems and he couldn't deal with the pressure the players put on him, or something of the sort... and promises to try and get back on the game again. Never heard of him since then...
The game as it stands still has a ton of balance issues, incomplete features, and despite that I really enjoyed my time with the game, I doubt anyone can really enjoy it as it is today. The promise of future improvements and the community is what made the game fun, other than that I admit that it was pretty mediocre.
I advise that noone buys this game, if anything to keep their moral integrity and not fund half-baked abandoned projects.
If you still wanna buy it, at least be aware of what it is.

Resident Evil 5 is an action blockbuster that has you play as Chris "McTestosterone" Redfield, after becoming a Gears of War character and training to the point he can
, Chris travels to Africa in the hope of finding his missing partner Jill Valentine. With the help of his new partner Sheva Alomar, they journey throughout West Africa murdering every inhabitant in their line of sight and constantly screaming each others name when wanting to open a door in hopes of finding Chris' partner and stopping the demon lord who wants to saturate the world with black tentacles.
They encounter many things such as:
- Axe man and Megaphone man
- black tentacle monster #1
- Chainsaw guy from Resident Evil 4
- a large bat
- tribal people with spears
- a tentacle monster fish with a man's face
- black tentacle monster #2
- cigar chomping Gatling Gun dude
- A larger black tentacle monster
- A Demon Lord
- and Demon Lord with black tentacle arm
Essentially Resident Evil 5 is a 3rd person action game that tries very hard to take itself seriously and at times I lost interest with what was happening story wise and focused more on the "shoot everything that moves" aspect. If you are a fan of Resident Evil 4, you'll feel a bit at home with this as it shares the same style of gameplay with the exception of removing the grid based inventory from 4, for a simpler inventory system like on the first set of Resident Evil games with the add of a Dpad quick equip, allowing to change weapons without entertaining your inventory.
Resident Evil 5 also offers  co-op play in the campaign and Mercenaries mode.
The second player can join via local or online and takes control of Sheva (in mercenaries it's whatever merc they desire) The only real difference to them is that instead of punching things, Sheva just roundhouse kicks or flash kicks stunned enemies as well as having different call outs.
One thing i found lacking was Chris' personality, on 4 we had Leon's bombastic cheeky humor and would make a wise crack at the situation. On 5 however, we are given Chris who essentially mimics a western AAA action hero who's motives are to save his partner and beat up the demon lord, it isn't all that bad as they clearly make fun of the whole roid'd Chris in the final sequence of the game.
I'd also like to add the voice acting at times isn't terribly great however it is saved by Ricardo Irving's comic book style of villain dialogue (no joke, despite the wackiness that was in 4, Irving feels like a character ripped right out of Viewtiful Joe) and D.C Douglas doing a fantastic job with the Demon Lord.
If you looking for another taste of Resident Evil, before it turned into the mess that was 6, this will fill that nourishment beflre they hand you food poisoning. I highly recommend playing with friend as it actually makes the experience much better, it's like playing Resident Evil 4 but with someone else, and who isn't the brain dead Sheva AI with the only purpose is to be a walking inventory.
My final thoughts are eight boulder punches out of CHRIIISSSSSSSSSSSSS!

The current market is (arguably over-)saturated with "8-bit style" games attempting to ride the wave of nostalgia of gamers longing for their childhood games again, and generally the only real similarity of these games to the Mega Mans and Castlevanias is the 8-bit art. Shovel Knight, however, absolutely nails it. Every aspect of the game is not just a homage to classic 80s platformers, but a faithful recreation of the style of gameplay. Platforming segments that are hard until you figure them out, varieties of enemies styled for the level in which they appear, interesting and engaging boss fights, it's all there. Obviously there are plenty of other nods to ye olde video games, such as "____ Knight" bosses in the vein of Mega Man, Castlevania-like subweapons, and the ability to drop down on enemies from above to kill them. Shovel Knight is in every way a love letter to the "classic" games, and it's done so much better than every other game that claims the same.

If you like Super Mario and Castlevania, do not hesitate buying this game!

Right off the bat,
is an amazing 2D platformer game, and easily one of my favorite recent games. The game has a strong reminiscence of early Nintendo games, a lot like
,
, and
, while producing it's very own unique storyline and gameplay.
Playing as the titular protagonist 'Shovel Knight' as he goes on a quest to rescue his beloved Shield Knight, you progress through many different stages of the game, all ranging from plains, to a volcano, underwater, in the air, and more; the levels are very detailed with hard boss battles and plenty of secrets. The game overall gets progressively hard and I cannot express how many times I would get frustrated over my deaths. You're able to purchase useful relics, armor and weapon upgrades, have the ability to use magic, and find collectible music sheets; there's also random boss encounters and side stages where you can do different tasks.
I totaled myself up with 12 hours lonesome on this indie game, and enjoyed everything about it. Even though the game came out in 2014 and has retro-styled graphics, I thoroughly loved playing it and is a great example of how these retro games can still be dominant over others. From the cliché, yet original, storyline and characters, to a wide range of useful trinkets, the game is a must-play whether or not you've ever played old-school Nintendo games, or retro games in general.

Absolute Drift: Zen Edition
Arcade Driving
Funselektor Labs Inc.
Funselektor Labs Inc.
is an arcade driving game developed and published by Funselektor Labs Inc.
The game uses an isometric camera, giving it an instant old-school feel. The use of white and red in the maps helps you relax, while also highlighting challenges and important items.
The game is all about one thing: drifting. After having played some tutorials that help you understand the controls, you can play either Free Roam (where there are challenges to complete and objects to collect) or Events (which are maps where you have to complete certain tasks, like drifting for over 10 seconds or spinning into a circle for 3 seconds).
The controls are deceptively easy, but the more you play the more you understand how deep and sensitive they are. Mastering the art of drifting sure ain't easy. So, I think that playing with a controller is mandatory, because when I tried playing with the keyboard it was almost impossible to complete even a single task.
The Free Roam mode is very fun and relaxing, while the Events are damn hard and challenging (especially if you still can't drift that well), but thankfully only a couple of tracks were really frustrating.
The soundtrack by C41 and Nyte is incredibly relaxing, and listening to it while exploring playing Free Roam immerses you into the driving quite a lot. And, for once, the sound effects of the car aren't annoying.
Even though the game itself will take you around three hours to complete, you can unlock new cars and paint jobs, and you can try improving your high-scores and completing all the tasks.
Overall, if you are a fan of driving games but don't want the pressure of actually taking part in races, definitely play
: it is relaxing and it has some of the deepest drifting mechanics I have played.

Pretty colors, great graphics, however, both these things are the game's downfall.
Once you start upgrading your ship and surviving longer than a minute or two your screen becomes chalk full of pretty effects that cover up bullets and warp your screen so you have no idea what is going on because you can't see anything. The more upgrades you get, the more visuals erode your vision.
Random stuff will happen, such as your bullets moving too slow to actually hit bosses, your screen will go "negative" but everything is nearly the same color which prevents you from seeing further, or giant laser beams will shoot across the screen without warning of where it's going to hit. So when you think you have a good streak going, prepare to be dissapointed from randomness stopping you.
Also there's these nifty little forcefield pods that prevents your bullets from going through the field to destroy the pod. Sometimes these will clutter up your screen moving extremely slowly, or stand still during boss fights. The only way to destroy them is to use a spinning sphere around your ship to destroy them. So you get really close without touching them, stand there for 2 seconds, to wait for the sphere to come around to destroy them. In the middle of the boss fight this is very impractical. During some of those random screen effects, you're unable to see the forcefields at all. In addition, there are "hard forcefield" enemies that kill you on impact as well. These as well you can't see when you're in some of those screen effects.
Visuals 9/10, so pretty, but obscuring.
Gameplay 5/10, visuals too obscuring.
Music 7/10, menus have extremely loud music, ingame has repeating decent music.
Sounds 10/10, very well done, plenty of non-grainy sounds.

Pros:

- Great humour as always

- Honestly can get a bit suspenseful and exciting at times

This game is perhaps the highest-quality, most entertaining, and overall polished fan project existing today. Although extremely difficult in a few spots (And lacking any sort of tutorial design that would help it stand on its own without having previously played Portal 2), I was enamored from start to finish.
I was not expecting such detailed environments, nor the high quality of the new models; They looked just as good as all the original game assets! I felt like I was back in a story-driven Aperture, not merely a few puzzles flimsily stitched together.
A complaint that I have is how inconsistently Virgil would help the player with hints; There were some times I could have really used a nudge in the right direction, and other times that I would have really rather he not say anything at all, especially in the endgame. However, this may come down to personal experience, as all players approach these puzzles in different ways. Secondly, I wish that I could have been the one to press the shutdown button on A.E.G.I.S., rather than it being a cutscene.
These complaints are minor at best, however. I truly enjoyed the game all the way through, and am stunned that it didn't have a price tag attached, like the similar project "Aperture Tag". The work that Prism put in, despite building on Valve's foundation, deserves compensation. I wish Prism the very best in their future endeavors, and will be watching for their new content.
As a side note, I liked the effects in Mel's portal gun better than the original Valve version. I always thought that the gun was lacking more prominent moving parts and energy effects.

ZEN EDITION UPDATE:
I gave another try to Absolute Drift after the Zen Edition update this week. Being able to play it with the controller definitely makes it less bad to play. However, I don't feel the drive model has been changed. It still needs improvements in my opinion to be enjoyable.
Using analog controls definitely does the difference. But it's still a real pain to just enjoy the game drifting. I know the game is more focused towards highscorers and achieving perfection through repetition, but my expectations were that I would be able to just drift smoothly easily, even if not in an efficient way. Or at least doing it in the easy mode.
After the 2 hours I've spent on the update, it turns out I had a way better time in hard mode than in easy mode. I still had to be fully attentive to not mess up, as hitting a wall always breaks the rythm of the track, as well as ending up in a spin. Recovering from a spin is a hassle, you can't quickly go reverse-turn-forward using the car's inertia (and same for the other way around).
Regarding controls, having multiple layout for controllers is better, but still, none of them suited me. I would have prefered to have the option to set the handbrake as LT. I personally can't handle acceleration + handbrake with the same hand. So I ended up only using acceleration and rarely brake/reverse. And you still can't change the settings while racing or free-roaming. And you can't reset the settings either.
So eventhough this update has brought improvements to the game, it hasn't done so for it's core gameplay. I've personally enjoyed it a bit more, but I would still not recommend it unless you are a highscrorer, love repeting something unnecessarily hard to master and cramped hands after 1-2h of gameplay.

ORIGINAL VERSION:
I started playing that game because I heard some good about it, feeled like my jam and I had it in an humble bundle. Once I started the game and started playing it in free roam, I really wanted to like it. The art style is good, the music is great and I like the concept.
But after a few tracks and missions I realized the drive model wasn't up to par with the rest of the game. I played the whole game in easy. I tried different sensitivity settings but not much because it's really a hassle to change it: you have to EXIT TO MENU to go to settings, you can't even change it while playing!! I also had to play with keyboard because of the problem with my Xbox One controller. I went to the forum topic in the community hub and followed the different tips to make it work but none of it did the trick. It's the first time I see a game do that bad with a standard controller.
I forced myself to go through the 5 worlds in free roam to try and get better. I did a bit, especially with The Missile and Das Whip, which are way easier to control than the previous cars in my opinion. I also felt quite good playing the mountain drift tracks, which only appear starting with world 4! And after getting to world 3 I stopped doing the driftkhana tracks which were just pointless and not enjoyable at all to me.
Wanted to like it, loved the looks, loved the sounds, hated the driving model which is the key part in this game ><. I was so tensed during the game to not mess up my driving that my arm now hurts after only 1.5h of continuous play. So if you like to master broken games, go for it. If you don't, go look for another one.

There's a quaint simplicity about Really Big Sky: twin-stick shooter, drill through planets/asteroids and you can funnel points you earn during runs into improving certain attributes and powers. Levels are randomly generated (as far as I can tell) and defeating bosses and certain enemies requires some thought but isn't an obnoxious puzzle. Additionally you can unlock more modes that are essentially the base game but with extra parameters, greater difficulty or alternate milestones! On the surface it's all really good and the graphics are decent.
It was about an hour into the game that I realised I hadn't the faintest idea of what I was doing: obviously I was shooting ships and (trying) to dodge their attacks but then I would be sucked into a vortex? Or perhaps the colours would invert or suddenly blur? Did I unlock something? Am I more powerful? Does this enemy have a shield? No wait, that shield apparently damages me but another one didn't? I put a bunch of points into some random stats but I don't think they've done anything?
Really Big Sky's gameplay is completely incoherent and this is not helped by the scorchingly bright and blurry visuals. The "library" doesn't help remove the obfuscation surrounding the gameplay mechanics but is full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ed smug descriptions, which on reflection should have been expected from the atrocious voiceovers heard during the game. Some of the stats are incredibly obvious and very necessary, but a lot of the laser related upgrades often seem to have little effect, or at least their impact is not conveyed effectively.
I got this game for free so technically I got my money's worth, but it's really difficult to recommend this game over pretty much any other scrolling shoot 'em up or bullet hell games on Steam. Admittedly the genre is not "my jam" but Ikaruga is good so maybe start there instead?

This is a retro 2D platformer. it is based around the platforming games of around the SNES era, I believe, and it is difficult, very difficult. however, people see it as being more than a bit too difficult, saying they couldn't get past the first two of 'The Order Of No Quarter', and I say that they are massive wimps.
the game looks and sounds exceptionally pleasing. the retro graphics are done well and the animations are beutifully fluid. the soundtrack isn't anything to sneeze at either. I myself have only been playing it for around 4 hours upon making this review, but all of the music that I have heard thus far have found a snug spot in my memory and intend to remain there.
As the name of the game may suggest, your weapon is a shovel... really. pressing the attack button swings your shovel about 1-1.5 blocks directly in front of you. pressing down while in the air points your shovel downwards, landing on an enemy like this deals an un-modified hit as though you were on the ground, and bounces you higher.
Secrets are riddled throughout each stage, not too many, but just enough. for those who pay little attention, secrets will completely pass by them, paying enough attention and having the skill to get to it is rewarding, you may get a piece of the soundtrack, chest or jewels.
the games difficulty is, well, difficult. DIFFICULT, not unfair. everything is out to kill you, meandering about will get you hit in succession, and kill you. having the skill to traverse through a segment of the stage unscathed is satisfying.
each boss is different, both in comparing to each other and to themselves in different times of facing them. a boss does have a set of abilities they can use, true, but the order they do them in is randomised, meaning you have to be prepared, just seeing a boss do a set of attacks in one order and remembering that order is worthless.
everynow and then when you defeat an area a roaming icon appears. these icons move every time you enter and exit a stage or village. these can be mini bosses or extra stages. these mini bosses are just as memorable as the main bosses, but not much easier.
and that concludes my review of Shovel Knight, and I heartily recommend it to everybody vaguely interested in it. for those wondering if they would actually enjoy it because they are no good at video games, I am sub-par at video games, and I am good at this game, and enjoy it

Loot Hero DX is a decent little timekiller from Varagtp, the same crew who gave us Tap Heroes and Plantera. Of the three, I'd say this one is my favorite. The whole premise is fairly casual: go straight, lance whatever's in your way. As your body count builds, you get money to upgrade your attack power, crit chance, movement speed, and defense, which you repeat ad infinitum until you can kill the dragon terrorizing the land.
Then you do it again. And again. And again. As things get gradually harder. That's about it.
I liked the look of the individual monsters and other art, and the visuals feel like a fair amount of love were put in them. Screenshots don't really do them justice; I was legitimately concerned that things looked a little muddy before I sat down and played. And there's something to be said for how fun it is once you reach ridiculous levels of speed and are just tearing through levels like nobody's business. Eventually, the cost of upgrading caps out (and keep going after all the little icons above a stat are full, by the way), which makes the grind a bit more straightforward since you're paying the same for every given boost each time.
One caveat I should point out is that to utilize your speed upgrades, you need to stop at an upgrade inn and tap Up on the d-pad to increase your speed. I didn't notice this for a while, and it seemed an odd choice. I imagine some players might get motion sickness or have trouble stopping to upgrade at super-high speeds, so I understand the decision.
Loot Hero DX is fluff, but okay fluff, and not bad for burning a little stress by whooping piles of monsters. And it's pretty easy to full-chievo, if that's your thing. Gets a thumbs up from me.

It’s not everyday that I think about this. But every once in a while, when I do, it puts a really stupid looking grin on my face. Don’t get me wrong. I love this part of the game. In fact, it’s probably the only part that sticks out for me. It feels like the part that the whole game is leading up to.
I hate 40% of this game. I love the remaining 60%.
Well, maybe the split is a little more odd. Let’s say 35-65.
There will be no spoilers, don’t worry.
In Resident Evil 5, you play as Chris Redfield, a 30-something BSAA (Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance. I know, right?) agent who’s seen some♥♥♥♥♥♥ In 2006, Chris and Jill tried to apprehend Albert Wesker, the cool-guy antagonist. Jill gets rekt, and Chris denies that she died. Over the course of three years, Chris becomes obsessed with finding the truth and becomes the biggest cool guy in the BSAA.
Following a lead, Chris heads to the “Kijuju Autonomous Zone” in Africa to investigate some B.O.W (Bio Organic Weapon) stuff. Sheva Alomar, who works for the BSAA’s West Africa branch partners up with Chris to meet up with Alpha Team, who were supposed to intercept said B.O.Ws. But seeming as they were side characters in a Resident Evil game, they all died. And – wouldn’t you know it – everyone in town is infected by ZE PLAGAS 2: Electric Boogaloo, which are the better version of the parasites you see in Resident Evil 4. Tasked with essentially finishing Alpha Team’s job, it’s up to Chris and Sheva to follow through and complete their mission.
Resident Evil 5 is a third-person action shooter, through and through. You’re given nine inventory spaces and a wide array of weapons to fight their ways through streets, swamps, the wild and even a damn boat. By beating enemies, you can upgrade your weapons of choice to better fit your needs.
This, in my opinion, is one of RE 5’s biggest strengths. The way guns feel and fire in this game just feels right to me. And there are quite a few guns to choose from, which is pretty awesome. On top of that,  by fully upgrading certain weapons, you can unlock ‘super’ versions of those weapons that you can fully upgrade as well. And the upgrades make a difference. The first pistol you get in the game can hold 100 rounds if you put the time and nairas into it. Once you fully upgrade it, you can buy a way cooler version with a three round burst. This is just one example, the other possibilities are pretty cool. The game starts throwing enemies at you that can prove to be pretty hard to beat, so it becomes pretty clear that upgrading weapons can really help. The game also has a little treasure system where certain enemies can drop jewelry, precious stones and the like that can give you an extra boost to your moolah. The enemy variety is fairly wide, although it becomes apparent that there are archetypes in every area’s enemies. You’ve got the big dudes that practically eat your ammo, the dudes that will one-shot you in a big, slow, telegraphed attack and the normal baddies that throw themselves at you only to get shot in the face. Something that keeps it fresh is the whole parasite thing. More often than not, you’ll shoot a dude’s head off to find a very sharp and flailing parasite worm thing coming out of his neck. These guys can prove to be a problem in mob situations and make gunfights a little more tense, which is something I appreciate.
Something I DON’T appreciate, however, are the boss fights. This is the 35% I was speaking of. Don’t get me wrong, the boss designs are pretty cool, but the methods to beat them can get pretty boring pretty fast. The first boss enemy in the game has a pretty smart way of killing it, but everything past it becomes more and more facetious to defeat. Boss battles become slow and droning puzzle fights that don’t feel as satisfying that a boss fight in, say, Rogue Legacy or Bloodborne would. I found myself hating the game after each session JUST because of the bullcrap I had to pull to kill tentacle monster #2. By throwing these bosses at you, the game makes you feel like all the ammo gathering and green/red herb farming was JUST for the boss.
What made this game fun for me was the online co-op. The game gets a lot more fun with a friend. Not only is it nice to have a human partner rather than a slightly-less-than-half-brained-AI partner, but it’s pretty funny to screw with each other a long the way. Plus, your partner can carry over their items from their own playthroughs and upgrade weapons the way they see fit. This is easier than having to deal with managing BOTH Chris and Sheva’s inventories and weapons, like in single player mode. I’d recommend teaming up with someone you know, though. I’d say that public matchmaking can be a little risky, but no one really plays this game anymore.
The game takes you through some decent settings, some of them forgettable. This game is linear, so you might miss some things here and there. Although this isn’t really a big deal, some of the levels you play through can look pretty drab. I can really only remember chapters 1 through 3 as gray and brown. There was a lot of gray and brown. This is a pretty grim game, so it’s not as bad as you think. However, I don’t think it would’ve hurt to make some more vibrant areas in the game. These vibrant areas come up later, but the second half of a game isn’t going to keep a brand new player playing.
Resident Evil 4 players wouldn’t really like some of Resident Evil 5’s characters. They’re somewhat flat, and speak mostly in reactions and observations. Chris has depth, because he’s a veteran of the RE series, and for the most part has some pretty memorable stuff in this game. Sheva, being in the RE universe for the first time in RE 5, isn’t really all that interesting. That may be because she’s new, though. Wesker, in my honest opinion, is my favourite character in this game just because he’s such a villain in this game. Like, unforgivably so. He’s condescending and cocky all game, and his voice actor did a pretty serviceable job conveying that attitude. RE 5’s story is serviceable too, and adds a pretty big point to the Resident Evil universe’s story line. I’ll let you find out what that big point is.
I didn’t like the soundtrack. It might sound uppity of me, but I really like to focus on the music I’m hearing when I’m playing a game. It’s nice to have music to accentuate the mood and the action that’s happening in the game. Most of the music in Resident Evil 5 isn’t really memorable, except for a few ‘enemy encounter’ loops here and there. To be fair, that’s what most OSTs of this genre, and what every OST past Resident Evil 3, are like. So one could argue that it wouldn’t be fair to pick on the soundtrack. But I like being picky.
Is Resident Evil 5 a great game? Well, Mr. Example Question, I wouldn’t say it’s great. I’d say it’s pretty good, and it would be better if it didn’t have annoying boss battles in it. Would I recommend it? To those who want to play a pretty good third person shooter with some exciting moments through out the game, totally. To those who want another great Resident Evil game like RE 4 or 2, maybe not. To the latter group, go into Resident Evil 5 with a lot of patience, and you’ll enjoy it more.

I’m usually not much a fan of driving games these days. I used to play them a lot more when I was younger but at some point I just stopped having fun facing the same challenges again and again in every driving game. But I did enjoy drifting mechanics from time to time and since I got this game in a Humble Bundle, I decided to check it out.
Unfortunately, I can’t really say I was having a great time with it. The first problem I had with the game were the controls. Giving cars realistic physical properties is difficult and more importantly, difficult for the player to control. Which is why most driving games focus on fun, arcadey feeling driving that doesn’t challenge the player too much with real world physics.
unfortunately goes a completely different route, eschewing physical car mechanics as well as typical tightly controlled driving of other games. Your car is almost always drifting. You can barely drive in a straight line and then enter a curve without the car breaking out at the back. This is also explained by the extremely wide turning radius that you drive while trying your best not to break out.
Then again, drifting is the main attraction of this game so it makes somewhat sense for your car to be easily turned sideways. The problem is that the controls feel extremely floaty. Acceleration is slow as if your car weighs twice as much as a real car. And I sort of suspect that may be the case, since the easiest way to get a physics engine to behave this erratic is by increasing the mass of an object and then increasing the torque of the motor providing it with energy.
This leads to very hard to learn drifting mechanics that can lead to much frustration. And I know some people will inevitably like it this way, if the scores on the leaderboards are anything to go by. But I just found it annoying. And this leads me to my next complaint: The camera. The game utilizes a bird’s-eye perspective which means when you’re driving towards the camera the controls are reversed and foreshortening makes it difficult to make out where you are in relation to the borders of the tracks. I would’ve much preferred a typical racing game camera hovering behind the car or at least one that follows the rotation of your car.
But all of that could be forgiven if the game had actual content. Unfortunately, it doesn’t. There are plenty of levels there. But drifting around them is the only thing you do. There are no challenges beyond comparing your score to the global leaderboards. Coupled with the very minimalist aesthetic, that makes this game look extremely empty. If I didn’t know better, I’d assume it was still in early access. Which it very well might be, since the developers are adding new features with the upcoming Zen edition. And honestly, to me there isn’t much incentive to doing something very limited over and over again.
The devs also highlight car customization and free-roaming areas as features and these are just not enough. You get to paint your car in a few different colors and that’s it. Free-roam is just an empty overworld filled with “challenges” which boil down to “drift between these two objects”, “donut around an object”, “collect 5 items in this part of the map” and “jump over an object with a ramp”. And those last two highlight how little there actually is to do in a game that is only about drifting.
Honestly, if this weren’t part of a Humble Bundle that contained games I was interested in more, I probably would’ve stayed away from this game. There’s just not much there to enjoy here for me. But I do have to wonder if the price of $12 is justifiable, even though I paid nowhere near as much. Because the aesthetic is – like the developers’ previous game
– deliberately minimalist and only features low-poly objects with basically no textures applied to them. And I can’t believe that it took that much effort to create the gameplay, since most engines nowadays feature basic driving mechanics as prefabs.
If you’re into games with a very narrow focus and can deal with the repetition or if you’re the type that has to be competitive 100% of the time, you’ll find something to enjoy in
. But I honestly couldn’t recommend it to anybody else, since it’s just too light on content to be anything substantial.

Resident Evil...5!
Resident Evil returns with yet another entry into the survival horror genre. This time, you are placed in the shoes of Chris Redfield who is partnered up with Sheva Alomar to get rid of a terrorist threat in Africa, as sanctioned by the Bioterriorism Security Assessment Alliance (BSAA).
Story: The story thrusts the player into Kijuju, a fictional region of Africa. It starts slowly but becomes interesting soon after you have a first encounter with Ricardo Irving, who is attempting to sell a bio-organic weapon (BOW) on the black market. Through a series of events, Chris sees a picture of what appears to be Jill Valentine (an old partner of his) and is determined to track her down and eventually, have a showdown with an old foe, Albert Wesker. Throughout the game, we see Chris and Sheva develop a strong friendship with each other through the fights they have to go through and the words they speak to each other. However, some of the dialogue between them is often corny and silly. The crux of the story is Chris seeing Jill in his new partner Sheva.
Graphics: The MT Framework graphics engine Capcom used for this game still holds up well today, with textures being crisp and colours saturated. The environments are well detailed from a single leaf, puddles of water to the dirt on the ground. For a game that was released in 2009, it can still compete graphically with some games released even today.
Sound: From the screams of infected African people to the roar of a mighty monster, each sound effect is chilling and done to great effect. They are also quite distinct from each other, so it is easy to tell what enemy you are facing just by hearing the sound they make. The voice acting of the different characters were also pretty good I thought. Typically, Resident Evil games have awful and cringy voice acting but I found that in this game, Chris Redfield's voice in particular was great as was the villainous voice of Albert Wesker. Props to Capcom for improving the voice acting for this title in the franchise.
Gameplay: In short, the gameplay is fantastic and very fun. Capcom has improved the way the inventory system works, by making it easily accessible through the press of the 'e' button and allowing for the player to switch out weapons in real-time. The side effect of this, is that it increases the tension of the game as enemies can still damage you as you are managing your inventory, though I believe the game is better for it. Moving your character around feels smooth and intuitive, although you cannot shoot while you are moving. I believe that this was a deliberate design decision from Capcom as to retain the horror element of the game. The gameplay is at its best when you are playing with a friend through online co-op. I've spent many hours playing through the campaign with a friend online and I have to say, it has been one of the best and most fun gaming experiences I've had. Resident Evil 5 is truly something special when you are playing with another person.
Overall, Resident Evil 5 is an excellent survival horror action game. Although it is vastly different from its predecessors such as Resident Evil 1-3, it is a great game in its own right and deserves to be in any gamer's collection.

This is a retro 2D platformer. it is based around the platforming games of around the SNES era, I believe, and it is difficult, very difficult. however, people see it as being more than a bit too difficult, saying they couldn't get past the first two of 'The Order Of No Quarter', and I say that they are massive wimps.
the game looks and sounds exceptionally pleasing. the retro graphics are done well and the animations are beutifully fluid. the soundtrack isn't anything to sneeze at either. I myself have only been playing it for around 4 hours upon making this review, but all of the music that I have heard thus far have found a snug spot in my memory and intend to remain there.
As the name of the game may suggest, your weapon is a shovel... really. pressing the attack button swings your shovel about 1-1.5 blocks directly in front of you. pressing down while in the air points your shovel downwards, landing on an enemy like this deals an un-modified hit as though you were on the ground, and bounces you higher.
Secrets are riddled throughout each stage, not too many, but just enough. for those who pay little attention, secrets will completely pass by them, paying enough attention and having the skill to get to it is rewarding, you may get a piece of the soundtrack, chest or jewels.
the games difficulty is, well, difficult. DIFFICULT, not unfair. everything is out to kill you, meandering about will get you hit in succession, and kill you. having the skill to traverse through a segment of the stage unscathed is satisfying.
each boss is different, both in comparing to each other and to themselves in different times of facing them. a boss does have a set of abilities they can use, true, but the order they do them in is randomised, meaning you have to be prepared, just seeing a boss do a set of attacks in one order and remembering that order is worthless.
everynow and then when you defeat an area a roaming icon appears. these icons move every time you enter and exit a stage or village. these can be mini bosses or extra stages. these mini bosses are just as memorable as the main bosses, but not much easier.
and that concludes my review of Shovel Knight, and I heartily recommend it to everybody vaguely interested in it. for those wondering if they would actually enjoy it because they are no good at video games, I am sub-par at video games, and I am good at this game, and enjoy it

Shovel Knight is a gem.
It is an action-platformer wearing the armor of an 8-bit NES game, but at it's heart it plays like a brilliant modern platformer.
I personally did not like the graphical style when I saw screenshots of the game, but as soon as I started playing it I thought that with all the animations and unique settings, it looked good. The 8-bit music is great and suits perfectly the game.
Now that the style is out of the way, I will focus on the flesh of the game:
The Shovel Knight has to battle through 8 levels and their associated boss before being able to tackle the final levels and the final boss. A few other levels or boss fights exist on the world map, which is presented in a style reminiscent of Super Mario Bros 3. Unlike Super Mario Bros 3 there is only one world map to explore, so the game might appear short (around 8-10h), but each level is long and received so much care and is so unique that Shovel Knight is really a tight experience that doesn't overstay this welcome or feels like a repetitive grind.
I started this section with the description of the levels on purpose, because each level is actually very unique and has its own gameplay quirks and its own visual style and its own original boss fight. This is really where the game shines, in its variety of situations associated with an excellent level design.
The Shovel Knight is able to perform a drop-down attack with his shovel, which will be at the center of the gameplay. Some harder sections require to navigate through screens only with drop-down attacks. Some platforms can only be activated with a drop-down attack on a switch. Some secret places can be accessed through a drop-down attack then rebound on an enemy.
The combat features a lot of different enemies with their own visual style and attacks. Unlike recent Rayman or old Mario games where enemies feel more like a moving obstacle rather than a dangerous threat, Shovel Knight requires more subtlety and fighting skills.
A secondary attack which can be equipped with a wide range of magic powers helps deal damages or evade them.
The only real controversial point about the game is that a player loses money upon dying. The money can be retrieved on the location of death, but it can sometimes be impossible to retrieve. The good thing is that there is an incentive not to die even though there are no finite "lives" and that it creates mini-challenges, the bad thing is that some levels can squeeze their fortune out of the player and will make it harder on already struggling players.
Overall, Shovel Knight is a polished game full of personality made by talented developers, it offers a tight and satisfyingly challenging experience, and shines through its perfect gameplay and excellent level design. An easy recommendation for anyone looking for a good action-platformer.

I know that some may feel hesitant about picking up a title like this based on the way it looks coupled with the price it is asking but I'd recommend watching some gameplay videos of it on Youtube to help get the idea of what it really is offering.

I really want to like this game: it has really neat pixel graphics, lots of critters to kill, keeps stats, and has achievements and trading cards. But, the reality is that the gameplay gets boring after the first three minutes. Even the added concept of releasing miners to collect gold for you after every successful run through all levels fails, because it's just accelerating a timer event...it doesn't add to the gameplay at all.
In the end, all you do is collect enough treasure and XP to buff your character, who kills the baddies by -- literally -- running into them. There is no learning tactics for combat or developing strategies by buffing your character a specific way. You just level up your stats evenly as you collect loot, enough that you don't watch your health bar go down much at all while you're running back and forth, grind away until you start taking damage as you continue through the levels, and then rinse and repeat. Gameplay does not change on any levels, nor do you treat any of the creatures differently...you just run through them.
I did play long enough to get 100% achievements (and collect all trading cards), which is easy except for the final one of leveling up to level 100. That's a long grind, but I basically did it while in boring, listen-in virtual meetings for work since the game requires little to no brain power and I had almost zero chance of being distracted enough to get into trouble.  :D
TLDR; this game is a left-mouse-button simulator, and it succeeds in that regard. Where it does not succeed is in being interesting or, consequently, fun. Only bother if you're an achievement hunter looking for an easy 100% or a hardcore card collector, and even in that case you should look to get it as part of a bundle or epic sale.

As Spinal Tap said, there’s a thin line between clever and stupid.
It is not clear which side of the line Earth Defense Force falls, or whether it deftly straddles the line before falling on it’s head. EDF has the beating, unconvincing latex and ketchup heart of a B movie, and every component of the game is below par. The graphics would have been primitive ten years ago, and the animation truly needs to be seen to believed – a jumbled mess of spazzy death animations and clipping errors, assuming the enemies get that far and don’t just vibrate repeatedly against a poorly rendered tree for the whole battle. To the game’s credit, nearly every structure in the game can be destroyed, and the buildings fall apart with all the force, dynamism and realism of a Styrofoam jenga tower.
And yet, it all works. The extraordinary level of jank on display is entirely in keeping with its B-movie inspirations. The terrible voice acting is absolutely spot on in both languages – every actor sounds like they’re reading their lines for the first time with a mixture of confusion and disbelief, and every line has only the most tangential relation to the last. It sounds like a conversation between two concussion victims, and it is glorious.
The game itself has been described as Dynasty Warriors with giant insects, and that’s a pretty on point comparison. Whatever the mission claims to be, you have one objective – kill all the red blobs on the radar. There is a surprisingly excellent variety in enemies, even with the inevitable palette swaps, and despite the jank the controls are responsive and tight. The four classes have admirable variety as well, from the nimble jetpack enabled wingdiver (taking to the air sans breastplate and trousers, ostensibly to reduce weight) to the vehicle summoning support class air raider. There’s a huge variety of weapons available to each class as well, and in co-op building a balanced team is key to survival.
Whether or not I can recommend EDF to you will depend on your circumstances. As a single player, EDF is enjoyable but repetitive and lonely, and the difficulty is very uneven with some enemies being a breeze for one class whilst being a nightmare for others. It’s obviously built for co-op, and this is where it’s manic gameplay shines – getting one shot by a superlaser 90% through a mission is annoying but hilarious when a friend can drive over and revive you, but utterly infuriating in single player. The class based gameplay and ridiculous excess are at their best when enjoyed with inebriated friends, a playable Mystery Science Theatre where the enjoyment comes both because of and in spite of its budget and limitations.
Unfortunately on the PC version at least, the game is plagued by cheating, and cheating players can permanently screw up your save file. The cheating is so ubiquitous that I cannot recommend playing with randoms if this is your only multiplayer avenue. With a friend or three and a suitable level of intoxication/brain damage however, the game is a blast and absolutely worth the surprisingly hefty outlay – but this is not a situation that everyone is lucky enough to be in.
