Good story, but very poorly implemented. As early as the normandy beach scene you see artillery fall around you, but no change to the terrain. Bad company 1 on the 360... 9 years ago... in 2008, had destructable environments... but apparently COD can't figure that out.
Once on the coast, you'll watch half a german batallion run at you with no regard for tactics. They seem mindless. In a later mission, after you clear an area and kill a tank, you'll watch enemies come out of nowhere, bearing down on you, firing full auto. When you know they'd run out of ammo after 3s, and they're still firing... after 6s... 7s, 8s.. No staggered fire, just full auto continuously. It's not dramatic, it's annoying. Don't insult your audience's intelligence. They're walking in the open too after you just obliterated all their friends. They'd be afraid or smart enough to advance cautiously.
Watching a mechanically actuated flak gun move as fast as you can turn your mouse is also just wrong... even modern guns don't turn that fast. Albeit much faster than a flak would turn with a hand crank.
At one point I was half way down the stairs after I saw a tank; leaving a sniper tower... and the cutscene put me back atop the tower on the completely opposite side of where I was, falling off the side. And the number of times my legs should have been blown off by nearby explosions.. You get thrown in the air at one point, but apparently take no damage besides a mild headache. Shrapnel from artillery would chew you to shreads too, but apparently you're superman.
Flying a plane with your mouse is also brutal, developers should try hawx or ace combat; use W or S for pitch and make movement flow. The controls don't feel natural. The tank should have completely independent controls for turret and body too. I shouldn't continuously have to force the body to turn to keep straight while shooting sideways. The body will always try to turn towards your mouse and it's extremely frustrating. Maybe it's fixed in consoles. If so, the issue lies with lack of consideration, thought, or time for the PC port controls, but I suspect the development team had either too little time, or no idea what they were doing. Controls in the last COD game (infinite warfare) were very well done, but that was a different team. The vehicle sequences in gernal, all of them, were garbage.. if you're going the same speed as another car and they're shooting at you, every shot would connect. And migrating hilly terrain that would clear impact or flip a car at very high speeds is ridiculous. Vehicles in this game are terrible.
The hero moments were irritating too. Countless times, you'll be dragging a friendly, but he'll die behind cover because it wasn't one particular piece of cover. And it's the same voice actor over and over..The same one line, "i owe you my life Daniels blah blah blah." By the end of the game you want to shoot the idiot for being so incopetent. I started ignoring the hero moments because it annoyed me so much.
The game also tries to paint Pierson in a poor light. I can't forgive his drinking, but at the same time I can understand the incredible responsilbility he feels and undestand his harshness. He's best suited to lead the mission given the other options I see. In battle he's collected and gives orders quickly, even if they're borderline suicidal e.g. calling close air support danger close. It was the right call. You don't coddle men in war. You break, they break.
The AI is horriffic. Having two friendlies shoot at distance enemies when they're in arms reach of hostiles is bad coding. The AI hasn't been changed in a decade. I really feel like it's the same bots from COD 2 in the early 2000s. The engine is alright, but still dated. The PC version should also have way better graphics than the console. And if this is the case, I feel bad for the console gamers because this isn't enough given what hardware is on the market.
I want to like this game, it returned to WW2, but so much is wrong with it and it really bothers me. I will give credit for the cinematics and voice acting. Those are well done. And you feel bad for your jewish-american friend Zeussman; and of course Paul.  Redd/Daniel's wife was hideous, if everyone says she's pretty, make her pretty.. The stealth was a nice addition, but it's poorly implemented. You can walk within peripheral vision of hostiles. You can't drag bodies behind cover. An alerted enemy counts as  blown even if you kill him before he shouts or shoots. Glad it's there, but it seems like an after thought. The knife kills magically changes the enemies skin texture to a generic bloodied look. No transition or animation. It looks cheap.
Don't waste your money until it's $30 or cheaper. DLC really should be free. Not sure if the devs or corporate is to blame. Maybe if the developers had a longer production cycle, then the game would be longer and done better. I'd like at least 10 hours of campaign, maybe 20. But I probably got closer to 6. A specialist should have been brought in for the vehicles, someone from a racing game or flying game, something. The linear approach to missions is also painful. It feels forced when you're constantly surrounded by rock barriers, thick brush, full closets, etc. Guess it's my fault that I keep buying this garbage. Take a page from ghost recon wildlands. More open = better. Never cared for the multi-player so I do feel ripped off considering what I paid. And COD mp is the plague regardless. Hopefully nazi zombies gives it some extra life. That was the primary reason I got the game.

Absolute Drift is a challenging racing game that is all about sliding, drifting, and hitting walls. Do you have what it takes to become the so-called drifting master?
The game is all about drifting. You control one of several vehicles as you drift your way through dozens of missions spread throughout several different connected "worlds". Missions include doing doughnuts around various objects, jumping large gaps, collecting hard-to-find objects, and performing various drifting feats near, through, or around various obstacles. You must complete all missions in a given world to progress. Beyond world-specific missions, there are various event tracks found in each world. Some event tracks cater specifically to drifting, while others are more specific to maneuvering through winding mountain trails or racking up lots of points by performing various tricks. Event tracks are completely optional in completing the game, though they are necessary in earning all of the achievements.
There are a handful of different vehicles to collect. Each vehicle handles slightly differently, and each one can sport a unique paint job. Steering assistance, handling difficulty, and tranmission types can be set from the settings menu. I suggest trying each vehicle to find the one that best suits your play style. I also suggest playing with a controller for the best experience.
The game is fairly short. I finished all of the missions and became a drifting master in about 2 hours. That being said, there is a lot of replay value here, and there are several achievements to earn. I spent several more hours earning all of the achievements.
Absolute Drift is a fun, challenging racing game that gets better the more you play it. Drifting controls can be a bit tedious, but with patience and a willingness to learn, it becomes easier and more rewarding. I recommend buying this game if you are interested in different, challenging racing games.

This game has serious interface flaws which need to be addressed before I would call it enjoyable, as well as many other issues:
-Huge pixelated text that covers the screen and is near impossible to read.
-Imposed rendering cap of 720p for no apperent reason, with incredibly awkward and unweildy settings.
-Primary button used for multiple things at once means that you can skip important information or navigate away from what youwant to while trying to do other things - like shoot.
-Overused effects domination the already low-res display and make it hard to tell what is going on.
-Sluggish controls. (Not really too bad, and would not be a problem if the above were not true.)
-Good music! But you can listen to it for only a very short amount of time.
-Unintiutive design.
*The tutorial is ambiguous.
*You often cannot tell whether you are supposed into fly into a thing of avoid it until you try.
*You have an arbitrary limit of how many 'special drill attacks' you can use, which is at no point brought to your attention,
*and this limit is represented by a completely unrelated text character near the top of the screen.
*Mashing the primary button brings you back to the title screen, not back to the game, after death.
*Respawn text is often ambiguous and changes ever time you see it.
*Generally unclear, hard to read, and confusing interface. Even if it is shiney, shiney does not a good interface make.
Another big issue is illusion of speed, which plagues a lot of games. The background makes it look like you a re traveling incredibly fast, while the things you can encounter move by you much more slowely relative to it. Effects and other shiney things also do not accurately depict speed, so is leads to a confusing gameplay environment where you'd be better off assuming you were not moving, and that things where moving past you at different rates.
Good things about the game? Like I said good music, and fancy effects, but these are used so poorly I cannot claim that they count positively. Under other circumstances they might be selling points, but under these they are merely things which are not terrible.

First of all, I'm one of those people who wasn't in age to play the NES era, I always found it overrated by people who think that this was the golden era of gaming because they had full nostalgia glasses most of the time. I'm still a fan of games like castlevania, megaman or the mario series, but most of the other games are not very good and hasn't aged well in my opinion.
Saying this, I love shovel knight, is a game that made a good mix of 8 bit gameplay with modern gameplay. This is a game where difficulty is skill related and not unfair like some games from the NES era. The levels are well designed, with tons of secrets locations that require some strategy to reach. Also the shovel mechanics are remniscent to the duck tales series, which is great since makes the plataforming very funny.
Graphics are great, isn't like most indie games where one has the feel that they used nes sprites for laziness or skill rather than artistic direction. The animations are superb and do a good job on telling the emoions of some characters. I's true, Shovel Knight pulls things that couldn't be used on a real NES, but still, is a game that feels close to those game from the final years of the console.
Music is also good, nothing to write home about but makes his job well. The writing is also well done, it has a great sense of humour and the story gets an emotional ending that will make you want for more.
In conclusion, shovel knight is one of he best games that I had played this last year, is a proof that kickstarter games could work when you put realistic goals, and is a test that you can make 8 bit games this day that doesn't feel lke lazy jobs and that could get the status of timeless clasic,

I do recommend Shovel Knight; it has no flaws worth mentioning and can captivate your attention easily.

There's a plethora of games with "retro-style" graphics or "retro-style" sound and music, but few have the polish, the class, and full-out loving attention to detail that Shovel Knight has in... well, in spades. In almost every way it feels like a game that could have been made by Capcom during the height of the NES era, from the catchy, sparkling music to the crisp colorful graphics to the ridiculously tight gameplay that is exactly the RIGHT kind of difficulty: difficulty that forces you to learn how to play the game better. If you beat Shovel Knight, you will be Good at Shovel Knight, at the very least, because it takes no less than your best; it's not overbearingly punishing, but if you don't learn enemy patterns, trap patterns, the way protectiles move, the way YOU move, etc and learn it quickly you won't get very far. This is the kind of difficulty we need. This is the kind of retro game we need. Shovel Knight is a true winner.

it certainly is the most realistic fishing game as far as mechanics go. Lure/bait selection and presentation are key to having success in this game. I only have a few criticisms.
1) It's freemium, so while you certainly can fish, level up, and acquire new gear without forking out a dime, the progress is slow and the gear costs make no damn sense (why plastic bubble bobbers are the most expensive type in the game and require the highest level is beyond me, the things literally cost less than a dollar in real life). You're gonna be stuck with flimsy rods and low pound test for awhile until you build up some cash. I recognize that fishing is expensive, but if I'm going to be relegated to ultralight and light tackle for the first few levels, then rods, reels, and tackle shouldn't cost as much as a license and a fishing trip.
2) Object scaling. Fish show up as tiny little things in the water until you yank them out from 2 feet away and then suddenly they're full size. Floats stay the same size (though you can change the size from small, medium, large in options) no matter where they are on the water so good luck with spatial awareness, and lures on the end of your line might as well not even exist because you can't see them while you're waiting to cast or while retrieving (even in the clearest water).
3) Details. I crack up every time I see the shadow of my fisherman walking along trails, the sun at his back casting a long shadow through the woods.... and he's got no arms. Then he approaches the waters edge and the casting arm and its shadow suddenly materialize. Little details make or break great games.
4)Controller support. You can use a controller with this game, but there's no touch sensitivity to speak of. Tap the trigger to twitch the rod and your line goes flailing around as if you've just tried to set the hook on a lunker bass. Trying to aim can be a bit spastic, as your rod goes darting all over the place with no fine movement control.
The free lake is nice, I've already managed to hook some respectable bass and unlock a few in game achievements. For it's flaws it's still relaxing and realistic enough to pass as a great fishing game, but then I feel like the fishing genre never really evolved past the old Bassmaster games of the late 90's....

Solid game.
It has the usual marks of a Resident Evil game. Zombies, tank controls, cheesy over the top♥♥♥♥♥♥
My only issue with this game are the Quick Time Events, which are the absolute worst of any game I've ever seen.
The default keys are really inconvenient and you have to reset your key bindings to work around them. The cutscenes and actions also tend to switch up between the 4 keys you need to use to perform an action, so you can't just cheese through them.
The problem with that is that almost all of the game's QTE against highly dangerous enemies tend to have a repetitive or slow element and a really fast one that's impossible to react to fast enough unless you happen to have your finger over one of the right keys. If not, you'll fail the QTE 80% of the time and usually die instantly or take massive HP loss.
These usually appear on the screen for a fraction of a second, and pretty much 90% of my deaths while playing were due to quick time events. Incidentally, they're also the only time I ever rage quit the game.
Never had a problem with any other game, but I guess it's because they leave people 1-2 seconds to input a predictable command, not 0.5 of a second to see which one of the random 4 keys it is and act on it.
That and the port isn't incredibly good and I had a lot of issues installing the game because of GFWL, but other than that, it's a solid game.

I genuinely wish I could give a neutral review for this one. The game is not bad. In fact, it is very good at what it does.
Absolute Drift is a minimalist drifting game, in which you're a white (can change) car, in a white world, with white objects everywhere. Except for a few things. Orange colored objects are destroyable and/or important. Each "world" also seems to have another flavor color splashed in periodically. (i.e. Yellow in world 2, Blue in world 3, etc.) And each "world" you unlock by completing various "missions" (such as doing donuts, spins, drifting between obstacles, etc.). There are no time limits as far as I can tell, and it's just a very open-world (on a table top), relaxed, easy going drifting game with no rules, no conflict, and no consequences.
All of that, it does EXTREMELY well.
However, it is not FUN. At least not to me. I'm playing on an XBox controller, and I also tried it out on my keyboard. There's five controls. Gas/Accelerate, Brake/Reverse, Steering, and E-Brake. You can also remove automatic transmission and have another shift up/down pair of buttons available. But I found the shifting on this tedious, and without shifting the game is repetitive. You can learn to do all you can do within the first ten seconds of playing. Spinning only works in reverse as far as I can tell, and "donuts" are just, basically, a slow lazy drift. When you are told to donut something, you can get 10%, crash, and get 10% more, crash, and repeat until complete. I've played plenty of other racing games with drifting components, and a few other drifting-centered games. This one, you have significantly less control over your vehicle. And the way the game calculates a "drift" you can literally drive straight up to your obstacle and slam on your brakes and succeed in just about any of the "missions". There is no incentive I can tell to do well (other than placing higher in the global rankings), and no punishments if you just crash into a wall over and over until you succeed.
To feel successful, one must suceed. To succeed, there must be a chance of failure. To avoid failure, one must learn. Learning is caused by either positive or negative reinforcement, or some combination. This game has none. Perhaps I just suck at this game, but I didn't find it fun.
TL;DR: If you want a laid-back drifting game with no clear rules, where you can just drive around a pristine environment to your hearts content, this is for you. Otherwise, look elsewhere.

Where to start? Rainbow Six Siege is a fantastic team shooter with a large, and ever growing cast of operators with their own unique loadouts and skills. Set on highly destructable maps, that combined make most matches compelling and different each time you queue up. Featuring multiple game modes, and even a co-op "terrorist hunt" mode that simulates online play.
While having many positives the game has many faults, as most do, like absolutely awful matchmaking, unfinished imbalanced ranking system, latency, and more. There isn't even a server browser! You literally have to manually go into a file and change a notepad file to choose which server you want to play on! Unbelievable! On top of that the game is riddled with an immense amount of micro-transaction content - which some, if not most, are obtainable through large amounts of in-game currency. Granted, these are all cosmetic, so it isn't anything to be too worried about, but, as they say, "buyers beware"!
Where this game shines, as I remarked before, is it's operator selection, and highly destructable maps. You have a selection of a couple dozen operators to choose from, each having unique skills that can work off or counter other players operators. This makes operator choice crucial in each match you play. Some are better for breaching walls or windows,  jamming electronics, entry denial, and much more. However, these operators each have a set loadout and you can only customize within that loadout, so whatever weapons, or gadgets they have, you are stuck with. This is extremely limiting, while not necessarily a fault, it leaves a lot of room to be desired.
The maps are very satisfying to play on! You are able to enter through windows, doors, walls, ceilings, roofs, and if you can believe it more! You can shoot through these as well, making for an equally compelling experience whether defending or attacking. Admittedly, some aren't as open as you would think. Some areas combined with certain game modes can be very one-sided. This is where operator choice, communication, and player skill comes into play, a well put together team can still beat the strongest defense - or attack. So, this is a blessing and a curse.
Rainbow Six Siege is one of my personal favorite shooters in recent memory. I would highly recommend it to anyone wanting a tactical team shooter experience. This game offers a "Starter Edition" - which is just as advertised, a starter. Not something I would recommend not upgrading to the full version at a later date. It gives you a miniscule amount of operators to start with, and a gigantic cost to any you want to buy. I would always recommend getting the full version instead.

In conclusion, the game is an absolutely mindless joke not providing enough mechanics to justify its price tag. It does serve as a distraction though.

Resident Evil...5!
Resident Evil returns with yet another entry into the survival horror genre. This time, you are placed in the shoes of Chris Redfield who is partnered up with Sheva Alomar to get rid of a terrorist threat in Africa, as sanctioned by the Bioterriorism Security Assessment Alliance (BSAA).
Story: The story thrusts the player into Kijuju, a fictional region of Africa. It starts slowly but becomes interesting soon after you have a first encounter with Ricardo Irving, who is attempting to sell a bio-organic weapon (BOW) on the black market. Through a series of events, Chris sees a picture of what appears to be Jill Valentine (an old partner of his) and is determined to track her down and eventually, have a showdown with an old foe, Albert Wesker. Throughout the game, we see Chris and Sheva develop a strong friendship with each other through the fights they have to go through and the words they speak to each other. However, some of the dialogue between them is often corny and silly. The crux of the story is Chris seeing Jill in his new partner Sheva.
Graphics: The MT Framework graphics engine Capcom used for this game still holds up well today, with textures being crisp and colours saturated. The environments are well detailed from a single leaf, puddles of water to the dirt on the ground. For a game that was released in 2009, it can still compete graphically with some games released even today.
Sound: From the screams of infected African people to the roar of a mighty monster, each sound effect is chilling and done to great effect. They are also quite distinct from each other, so it is easy to tell what enemy you are facing just by hearing the sound they make. The voice acting of the different characters were also pretty good I thought. Typically, Resident Evil games have awful and cringy voice acting but I found that in this game, Chris Redfield's voice in particular was great as was the villainous voice of Albert Wesker. Props to Capcom for improving the voice acting for this title in the franchise.
Gameplay: In short, the gameplay is fantastic and very fun. Capcom has improved the way the inventory system works, by making it easily accessible through the press of the 'e' button and allowing for the player to switch out weapons in real-time. The side effect of this, is that it increases the tension of the game as enemies can still damage you as you are managing your inventory, though I believe the game is better for it. Moving your character around feels smooth and intuitive, although you cannot shoot while you are moving. I believe that this was a deliberate design decision from Capcom as to retain the horror element of the game. The gameplay is at its best when you are playing with a friend through online co-op. I've spent many hours playing through the campaign with a friend online and I have to say, it has been one of the best and most fun gaming experiences I've had. Resident Evil 5 is truly something special when you are playing with another person.
Overall, Resident Evil 5 is an excellent survival horror action game. Although it is vastly different from its predecessors such as Resident Evil 1-3, it is a great game in its own right and deserves to be in any gamer's collection.

Here is how to describe it. An indie casual shooter, where your goal is to survive the longer possible while travelling at faster and slower speed in the endless space with your ship, while tons of random things may happen (from sudden endless battalions of ships, to floating jurassic bones that can shoot from their mouth).
The controls are pretty simple, though the game lacks of a tutorial to explain what your ship can do (become a drill to enter inside asteroids or planets and other kind of stuff, move at extremely fast speed to create a super-lethal ring of fire around your ship, channel a limit break of your ship while you collect shiny thinghies, or charge your projectiles just to make them bigger). The options don't allow most of these controls to be changed, but their key bindings are pretty good and not really needed to be changed.
There are also upgrades you can buy after every death you score, but careful that by buying them you make the next tries more difficult than your previous. Also, it may happen that you won't know what are you upgrading at first, but by playing again and again the game you will understand their use.
I don't really think there's a local coop in, but the singleplayer is good enough thanks to it's replayability to make this game a good choice for bored people.
No other game out there like it, entertaining and tilting at the same time.

Loot Hero DX is a mobile-to-PC port that isn't free but also has no in-game purchases. The premise is simple: move right, defeat a boss in the end, move to the next level. Your character auto-attacks enemies on the way and you use your gold to purchase upgrades. Between each "wave" of enemies there's a house/building where you recover your HP and can buy upgrades. Once the game is finished, you free a miner who will generate gold passively for you and move on to the next difficulty. This goes on endlessly - there is no limit to how far you can go on the game as there's always the next difficulty level.
At first, the game is quite fun as you start out slow and progress through, buying upgrades, making your character stronger, faster and more resilient. However, further on as you've already finished the game a few times, the game loses a lot of its value and becomes a grindfest. The levels are the same over and over so there isn't anything new to work for too, so it's just replaying the same game over and over. Eventually you'll have reached max speed for your character and as you continue to upgrade your character, you'll find yourself finishing entire levels in less than 5 seconds, until you hit a difficulty barrier which then forces you to grind for a while to buy more upgrades, then continue to push through.
And specially, if you're looking to get all achievements in the game, prepare for a lot - a LOT - of grinding.
Overall, fun game but loses its value very quickly.

This game features 3 level types: A-to-B mountain tracks, freestyle drift courses, and 3-lap race tracks. The free roam map has additional missions you can perform only once, such as donut around a light pole, drift between buildings, jump over a river, etc.
I was pretty terrible with the drift controls for most of the game, but finally seemed to start figuring it out near the end. (The controls work just fine; I am just not very good at drifting.) Despite repeatedly crashing into walls, I really enjoyed playing this game. I enjoyed the game even more once I finally figured out how to drive and drift. I particularly loved driving around the map in free roam and discovering new missions to complete. The minimalistic art style and varied environments provides for a beautiful game that keeps you coming back for more.
Pros
+ Beautiful minimalistic art style
+ Many missions to complete
+ Large soundtrack with ability to skip tracks whenever you want
+ Ramps! Launch your car into the air and spin out of control
+ Customizable car body and paint jobs
+ Controller support
Cons
- Not much replayability once you've completed all free-roam missions
- Difficult learning curve for controls
- Only three types of levels gives feeling of repeating the same thing over and over

Shovel Knight is perhaps one of the most original independant platformers of 2014 which makes an attempt to emulate a traditional NES game. Not only this, it plays simplistically yet very fluent very similar to popular titles from that era. But I'm getting ahead of myself, let's talk about this masterpiece.
Gameplay 9/10: The game is simplistic enough that even very young gamers can have fun with and -eventually- beat, while having more complex mechanics like the relics you find and use throughout the game, though not manditory, they make your life a lot easier. Unfortunately, said items can be exploited at best and make the game easy as pie, which personally, I think games should never be easy throughout the entirity of the session unless theres a clear difficulty setting (hint, there isn't).
But there's a lot more positives than negatives, you can simply slash at things or you can jump down with your shovel and impale your rivals from above, and even deflect most projectiles with your shovel, making swords feel obsolete to the glorious weapon that is the shovel. This makes the first weapon you have one of your most reliable. This ontop of you capable of upgrading both your armor and shovel makes it that much more sweet to wreck your enemies with.
Soundtrack 10/10: I hate giving things a perfect score, I really do, but there's always something to improve, but honestly, there is not a single song in this game I dislike. The best thing about the game is probably the soundtrack itself, which gives Touhou (a game series that heavily relies on soundtrack) a run for its money. Funnily enough, the whole soundtrack can fit in a Kirby's Adventure NES Cartridge.
Graphics 9/10: The devs for the game have made the graphics and visuals replicate almost exactly like an NES game. Emphasis on -Almost-, since there are quite a few colours utilized in this game that the NES can not support (Example Polar Knight's cape's beige colour). These colours also make the sprite work not just good, but too good for NES standards, and it's honestly noticeable in a fair amount of areas within the game. I only take off one point because of this reason alone, while the majority of the game does look genuine to the NES format.
Story 7/10: The story is your generic knight saves a damsel in distress (Despite the damsel being a knight herself), which is cliche'd beyond belief and the situation itself isnt really taken into parody, which is really the only way this could work without it being a Mario game. What makes the story good is the subtle comedy, a good example being the name of the antagonist group "Order of No Quarter" makes it that much better. The Story's also greater with its ending and final battle, which to be fair, won't be spoiling for those readers.
Overall, this game's an NES platformer in 2014 on the PC, what more can I say? It's amazing for retro gamers along with the mechanics being great and the controls as fluent as ever. The subtle comedy is a fresh relief from all the adventuring you're doing. Not to mention the glorious soundtrack this game has will have you hooked on 8-bit music for a long time.

Before you read any further: this game has been abandoned. Any flaws, problems or glitches will not be fixed.
Towns might have been the first Early Access game I've ever bought and it made me skeptical and wary of all future Early Access titles. It has a great premise that is executed poorly and although you might have a bit of fun with it for a few hours, there is little here to recommend an indepth playthrough.
I don't mind isometric, retroish graphics but these are, more often than not, absolutely annoying to look at. Towns has gone for a sort of Populus/Simcity kind of look, all graphical tilesets and while I think some of it works, particularly outside of the Town in the woods and forest, it often just looks totally ugly. There's no definition or clear sense of layering; what lies in front of things and behind other things can be really hard to tell. When you do have a Town, it all runs together and looks like someone who just found out they can download Final Fantasy sprites and has mashed them all together. Certain textures really grate on the eyes, particularly the water texture which you see a lot of.
Controlling this game isn't much better as the inteface is awful.  I've played a lot of games with clunky interfaces and struggled my way through them but this might be one of the worst. Absolutely nothing about it works properly; you'll probably have to hit every key on the keyboard to figure out what does what and even then, attempting to divine the systems that control anything in this game is like trying to scry the future or turn lead into gold.
Towns had a lot of potential for growth (with a bad launch, but hey, potential?) - I mean, running a town built over a dungeon and attracting heroes, managing the enemies that come out, building the town up with facilities for the adventurers? It sounds like a perfect blend of Recettear, Diablo and Dungeon Keeper. But this is not that; Towns is a shoddy, abandoned game with very little to recommend it. It usually comes on sale for 7.49, discounted down from 14.99. It is not worth playing at either price and the fact they want you to pay $15 dollars for an abandoned game is repulsive. You shouldn't be paying for abandonware - speak with your wallet and say no to Towns.
NOTE: Steam shows 0.1 hours on record but I know for a fact I played at least a day of this - it felt longer, honestly, but trust me you don't need a whole day to see the flaws in this one.

What an odd game! I'm really on the fence about whether or not to recommend it, so I've decided to recommend it but with a huge caveat.
Firstly, this is the most mindless game I've ever played in my life, and I started playing video games in the 80s. Even mindless clickers involve the player more than this game does. There's literally nothing to do except for moving right and left and upgrading your stats. Combat and looting are automatic, and even your stats max out or become redundant at certain points, minimizing the value of upgrades.
I found no obvious benefit to a speed in excess of 100, and while your critical stat allows you to keep dumping gold into upgrades, it goes no higher than 100%. I wasted a lot of loot before figuring that out. I also found no benefit to an excessive attack stat. There came a point where I just started dumping all my loot into defense, because that was the only stat that made any difference to me after the critical stat was maxed.
This is not a game for someone who is looking for storyline or character development, because this game includes none of either. It's also not a game for someone looking for clear objectives or an endgame. At the time of this review, I've defeated the dragon 55 times, and the game hasn't finished. In fact, I don't think there is a finish line to this race. I've unlocked 100% of the achievements, and my stats at this point are: level 106; attk 180-359; crit 100; def 1376; and speed 126. I have no doubt that there is either no completion point to the game at all or that the ceiling is so ridiculously high as to call the sanity of anyone who would attempt it into question.
The graphics could be a lot more clear and defined, especially since you're dealing with increased speeds, and the soundtrack is just average. There's not a single element that would motivate me to continue the game at this point, and I see zero replay value.
That being said, the game does what it's meant to do very well. The controls are responsive, and no tutorial is necessary. It's an obvious choice for someone looking for an easy 100% game, but beyond that, there's not much else to say about this game. It offers no other challenge or benefit that I'm aware of. For me, it wasn't even entertaining. It was just something that I persevered through thinking that I was nearing the end.
So my caveat is this. I recommend the game but only for casual gamers looking for a mindless game requiring absolutely no skill, or achievement hunters possessing a great deal of patience.

If you have even the smallest interest in this series, you should get it. The price tag is not too high at all for the contents you get. You get 4 different classes to play with. They play differently, so you basically get 4 in 1 games. The game is fun, and enjoyable both Offline, and Online. Still, there are something that you should know:
Is 4.1 a grindy, mindless shooter? It depends. IMO, it is 'not' the grinding game, but can be play as one. The mindless part maybe true, but it is the mindless shooter on lower difficulties especially for Offline Missions. Online missions, on higher difficulties are not.
Back to the grinding, each class has its own progressions (missions on 5 difficulties), armors and weapons (loot drops). These loot drops can be earned as you progress through missions on each difficulty. They are limited to missions, and difficulties
However, these missions can be played in any order as long as you have unlocked it, by playing through them once as any class on any difficulty. This is where the grinding is.
Players, that want to get strong fast, and easy, will be playing certain missions on certain difficulty over and over to grind for armor, weapon drops. That is very BORING, and killed the very objective of the game, progressions.
These players, apart from their equipments, often lack the skills/knowledges they need to play with others especially on higher difficulty. Some are series vet, which is fine for me as they are fun to play with, and know their parts, but there are lots of new players playing this way. These guys are annoying. They don't communicate, and make things harder than it should be.
I have been playing from Normal, and almost onto the Hardest for my Wing Diver. I have done zero farming. I haven't replay any mission unless, got wiped > restart. I don't have any problem with current armors / weapons that cannot finish the Online Missions with my friends who do similar thing. (Online missions are harder than offline.)

I went in knowing this is a community mod. I come out thinking this was an official DLC. Portal Stories: Mel is such a well made mod that I had several reality checks while playing. The voice acting was terrific, the asthetics were on point, the story was simple yet enticing, and the puzzles were brutal. While this is an mod for Portal 2, it does not feel like one, rather a sequel and/or a completely new game. This is most apparent in the test chambers.
The level designers really out did themselves with the puzzles. Few were quite simple, while others are incredibly brutal. The proceeduce and execution of the solution is very important. There are times where I mess up a single step, and had to go all the way back, almost to the beginning, and redo the puzzle. There are also multiple times where I had to spend upwards of (I think) 20 minutes just thinking, something I did not have to do for both official Portal games. This is also the reason dispite being a shorter game than Portal 2, I spent more time completing it (8.3 hrs for Portal 2. 9.7 hrs for Portal Stories: Mel).
There are several elements that differentiates the test chambers from this game and Portal 2, such as the inclusion of two new types of Material Emancipation Grills, the requirement of two Weighted Storage Cubes to open the exit, and the innovative incorparation of purposely destroying the cubes as a solution to the test chambers. These new additions may not seem much, but it changes the player's approch to the test chambers at a fundimental level.  The test chambers require the players to think outside the box and plan ahead, one can not simply enter a test chamber and "wing it".
Overall, Portal Stories: Mel is a fantastic addition to the Portal games, and it is the first mod that I reconize as an unofficial-offical Portal game. The levels are challenging yet never exausting, and the story is a brilliant prequel to Portal 2. For those that are an experienced and enthusiastic player of the Portal series, this is a
. Also, due to the story being set between Portal and Portal 2, we get to experience what happened to our beloved cake:
10/10 would play again. Not going to spoil the ending for you cucks. 54 minutes. Worth it.

When the Roman Emperors grew very vain and luxurious, they used to have this sand made ornamental with metallic filings, vermilion, and even powdered precious stones; but it was thought better taste to use the scrapings of a soft white stone, which, when thickly strewn, made the whole arena look as if covered with untrodden snow. Around the border of this space flowed a stream of fresh water. Then came a straight wall, rising to a considerable height, and surmounted by a broad platform, on which stood a throne for the Emperor, curule chairs of ivory and gold for the chief magistrates and senators, and seats for the vestal virgins. Next above were galleries for the equestrian order, the great mass of those who considered themselves as of gentle station, though not of the highest rank; farther up, and therefore farther back, were the galleries belonging to the freemen of Rome; and these were again surmounted by another plain wall with a platform on the top, where were places for the ladies, who were not (except the vestal virgins) allowed to look on nearer, because of the unclothed state of some of the performers in the arena. Between the ladies' boxes, benches were squeezed in where the lowest people could seat themselves; and some of these likewise found room in the two uppermost tiers of porticoes, where sailors, mechanics, and persons in the service of the Coliseum had their post. Altogether, when full, this huge building held no less than 87,000 spectators. It had no roof; but when there was rain, or if the sun was too hot, the sailors in the porticoes unfurled awnings that ran along upon ropes, and formed a covering of silk and gold tissue over the whole. Purple was the favorite color for this velamen, or veil; because, when the sun shone through it, it cast such beautiful rosy tints on the snowy arena and the white purple-edged togas of the Roman citizens.

The main campaign is pretty short and I'm really bad at this game.
...so why am I thumbing it up? Well...the main mechanic (drifting a car) has a learning curve that is fun to do. Yes, I slam in every wall I can find and even some more, but Absolute drift doesn't beat me over the head with it. Rather the contrary: the way everything is set up, this is more like a playground than you having to be somewhere. And if the campaign was longer (even twice the size wouldn't be called big), I'm sure I would have gotten better (I mean...I started out as "absolutely terrible", so I made progress ;) ).
The atmosphere is what you get in the preview: minimalistic (near abstract) visuals and an absolutely awesome soundtrack. I absolutely like it.
The thing is that I'm not sure who to really recommend it to. Top down racers were always hard to handle (I mean...I loved super off road on the SNES exactly because inevitably someone of the group would drive COMPLETELY off), and with no other car in sight, this game is like the test drive for these other games.
There's certainly mastery in here. I just think I didn't come close to it (I usually ended the races throughout the game in the bottom 10%). For those who find mastery like this engaging, I guess? :-)

There are a lot of good things to be said about Shovel Knight.  It is an inventive and well-crafted platformer that combines modern design elements with retro 8-bit graphics.  I would recommend this to anyone who likes very challenging platformers and liked old games like Mario Bros.
However, I would not recommend this game to people like me.  Although I've played some good platformers such as Rayman Legends, I didn't have a console when I was growing up and have no nostalgia for old games.  However, I picked up Shovel Knight after reading many reviews which called it the best game of 2014.
From my perspective, the game was usually just frustrating.  The final screen told me I died 330 times in the course of finishing this game.  I believe the vast majority of those were insta-kills, from falling.  The timing required is very precise---in many situations if you press the button a split second too early or too late you will be killed instantly.  Furthermore, if you take any damage from an enemy, they will often push you back, leading to another fall..  When this happens, no matter how much health you have, you die and will lose gold and be set back several screens.  No matter how much gold I started with, I rarely had any gold by the time I first got to a boss.  This made most of the game just depressing, as I felt the more I played the less gold I had.  Without gold, I couldn't buy many upgrades, which in turn made the next level even harder.
About my skill level, I guess I'm below average, but I don't think I'm that bad.  I loved Dark Souls for instance, but I feel Shovel Knight is even harder because there are fewer strategies and routes available, gold is easier to lose permanently, and most deaths come from insta-kills.  Also Dark Souls I felt was more atmospheric and included more RPG elements.  It's one thing to die in Dark Souls 15 times in a row in a tense battle with a huge Dragon.  It's another to die in Shovel Knight 15 times in a row just because you didn't manage to jump from one moving platform to another.
I think someone good at platforming would enjoy this game, but I think it's too hard to recommend to the average person.  If the developers added an easier difficulty setting I would recommend it whole-heartedly.

Like other "incremental games", this seeks to allow you to pour hours of your time grinding away levels to upgrade your character in order to defeat endless waves of enemies and bosses with no end in sight. How it actually falls short of this goal in such a simple genre is incredible, really.
As some reviews here have said, the game is simply too easy. You hit the end goal far too quickly, and your goal then becomes a mission to collect all of the achievements. I was able to collect all of the achievements the game had to offer in a few hours time... making continuous play pointless, but that's not entirely why.
I don't think the game developers actually expect people to play this game for longer than an hour. You VERY QUICKLY hit a point in the game where your levels no longer go up visually, as though they didn't think a counter that works was necessary. Like saying "Nobody is going to max this skill, so who cares?", but you should care... because you can max the skill in under 30 minutes.
The levels don't have enough variety either. I mean you can't expect much from these incremental games as it is, but when you start reading "you've defeated the dragon 42 times", being the end-boss, it's really depressing.
There also comes a point where you gain so much coin from each level run, that you can honestly beat the final boss, load the next difficulty tier, and then jump straight to the end boss and kill it again... and again... The more you play, the easier it gets, which is typically the opposite of what these games are supposed to be about. You gain exponentially more coin which means you can upgrade exponentially faster. There is a COIN MAX of 99,999 and each upgrade costs 9,999 and will never cost more, no matter how much you've upgraded them. Again, they don't expect that you're going to play this game very long, so why increment higher than 9,999?? Yeah.... When you can gain 9,999 coins from hitting a mere few enemies, it's not hard to upgrade yourself beyond the capacity of the game.
While the game is too easy and runs out of runway too early, there are also certain things that annoy me after the 40th time too. Once I've beaten the dragon boss 40 times, you can stop SLOWLY giving me the message about the increase in difficulty and you can stop SLOWLY showing me that I've unlocked another miner, and you can stop showing me that same loading screen to take me to the levels because I'm just trying to get through it so I can jump to the final boss again and beat him in 5 seconds flat.
The miners... I reminded myself of these useless things. In the early game, once you beat it you unlock a coin miner which can, quite obviously, mine coins for you while you're away. The more you unlock, the more coins you unlock. Remember the coin issues I talked about earlier though... when you're making the max 99,999 coins within a few minutes, what exactly is the point of having several dozen miners also generating a max 99,999 coins for you?? Yay I can do about 20 upgrades to my defence and get through the end boss 5 more times for ABSOLUTELY NO REASON!
And this is my last point: With other incremental games, they're difficult enough that you feel like if you sit there grinding, ultimately you'll reach an end result that is awe inspiring. You can unlock heroes to help your DPS, you can "prestige" your character to reset all levels and grind from scratch, unlocking skills as rewards for hours of play, but with this game there's no point! You hit the end within the first half hour, and you can reach the point of no more level gain within the first hour, and you can collect every single achievement (the hardest being level 100) within a few hours of play leaving there absolutely zero reason to keep going. You're as strong as you ever need to be, and you can safely uninstall the game never to look back.
Of course it's a pretty cheap game on Steam, but this should seriously be a free app.... It's not worth the sale price and CERTAINLY not worth a full pricing.

Earth Defense Force 4.1 is a B-movie-lover's dream game. Giant bugs, robots, UFO's, massive firepower, cheesy one-liners, action-packed... it's all here, baby, and it's bloody glorious!
Earth Defense Force 4.1 has the giant monsters of B-movies and the cheesy humour along with it. House-sized bees and spiders, 10-story robots, groups of soldiers singing while moving from one objective to the next, dozens of trails left in the sky after rockets find their target, large UFOs slowly crashing into a fireball of destruction, monster ants flinging NPCs or my character for miles with arms and legs flailing as we somersault through the air awaiting our final landing spot: it all just puts a giant grin on my face.
The 4 classes in Earth Defense Force 4.1 were all fun to play, some a little more than others, but your mileage may vary. For e.g. the Wing Diver has a jet pack and is great at hit and run tactics and collecting loot sprawled all over the battlefield, but she has the lowest armor of all classes making her more of a glass cannon. Want a little more beef and fire power? Play the Fencer who wears Fallout-style power armor and has the capability of wielding tank-like cannons in each arm.
I was a big fan of the fact each class comes with their own set of weapons I needed to find and unlock, half of the fun was experimenting with each new weapon, experiencing its strengths, weaknesses, and quirks. After getting a good feel for each weapon, it was fun playing with optimal weapon pairings for each mission!
All of this fun can be shared with 3 other players in online co-op. I found myself thinking back and laughing at the fantastic memories and stories generated by Earth Defense Force 4.1 based on the experiences I had with friends and random players online. The game produces so many epic “wow” and “what the f*&$! is that?!” moments it makes it difficult not to recall them.
Imagine building-sized robots stomping towards you while massive alien motherships drop 100's of giant ants, all while dodging a barrage of lasers and alien bee stingers.
One of my favourite memories so far was the surprise mech called in by a teammate during a mission where giant red ants storm the beach we were tasked to defend. During all the carnage, one of our online teammates stops firing and says, “Don't worry guys, I got this.” I looked up to the sky to find a huge Pacific Rim sized Mech Warrior being choppered to the beach, lands with such force the sand kicks up, momentarily blinding my view of the impending ant swarm. Then my teammate enters the mech and starts stomping the ants like a slow moving angry child throwing a 1000 ton temper tantrum. All the while, the ants swarm the mech, crawling all over and up and down the hulking armored body. I took the opportunity to pull out my rocket launcher and start firing at the ants, watching them fall off the mech in droves. This was such an incredible moment.
I don't kid myself, Earth Defense Force 4.1 has many glaring issues, the menu UI, lack of VoIP control options, sluggish vehicle movement, slight frame drops during gigantic explosions with 100's of enemies on screen, less-than-impactful weapon sounds, and a host of other bugs (not of the insect kind!). Yet, it remains one of the most fun games I've played in 2016, slowly creeping up the ladder of my top 5 games of all time. It's the type of blissful, mesmerizing fun I have not had in a long, long time.

Portal Stories: Mel is the perfect addition to any Portal fan's library. I've played Portal and Portal 2 (beyond completion, even trying to speedrun portal 2) and I loved those, so, I thought I would give Mel a try. Trust me, I was not dissapointed.
First off, I would like to say that I would spend at least $5 for this as a DLC. This game is amazing and I find it outrageous that it is free.
Next, one of my favorite things about this game is that it is beautiful. The art is never repeated and every test feels unique because of the way it looks. On top of that, the mod is very well made, meaning that I haven't found any major glitches through regular gameplay, although some small clips here and there frustrate me when I'm on the verge of clearing a puzzle. Finally, this game has a great soundtrack, enhancing the atmosphere everywhere you go.
So far, the story has been great. It always leaves you so anxious to find out what will happen next, no matter what it is. The various voices that speak to you always leave hints as to what will happen next (or what happened), making you think of many different outcomes to the game.
You should get this game, although beware of certain things.
1. THE DIFFICULTY CURVE
I understand this is a mod and that it is meant to be for players who have played and finished Portal 2 but this game takes "hard tests" to another level. Right off the bat, the tests are difficult. I found myself having trouble clearing the second 'real test' and being confused about where to go. There is absolutely no learning curve, either you know what to do, or you don't. I don't recommend this to people who aren't generally good at video games and puzzle solving (not just portal).
2. THE DIALOGUE/ VOICE ACTING
There is WAY too much dialogue. Every single moment in the story, whether it be entering a test, solving one or even just doing anything progressive, there is dialogue. A few times during the game there was overlapping dialogue simply because I pushed a button or walked through a door, which was quite annoying. Also, the voice acting. I would like the voice acting, if it wasn't for the fact that Virgil speaks ALL THE TIME. His accent can be entertaining at first, but the overuse of dialogue makes his voice get on my nerves.
8/10
+ Great look and sound
+ Compelling story
+ Excellent mechanics
- Annoying dialogue
- Terrible learning curve

There are a lot of good things to be said about Shovel Knight.  It is an inventive and well-crafted platformer that combines modern design elements with retro 8-bit graphics.  I would recommend this to anyone who likes very challenging platformers and liked old games like Mario Bros.
However, I would not recommend this game to people like me.  Although I've played some good platformers such as Rayman Legends, I didn't have a console when I was growing up and have no nostalgia for old games.  However, I picked up Shovel Knight after reading many reviews which called it the best game of 2014.
From my perspective, the game was usually just frustrating.  The final screen told me I died 330 times in the course of finishing this game.  I believe the vast majority of those were insta-kills, from falling.  The timing required is very precise---in many situations if you press the button a split second too early or too late you will be killed instantly.  Furthermore, if you take any damage from an enemy, they will often push you back, leading to another fall..  When this happens, no matter how much health you have, you die and will lose gold and be set back several screens.  No matter how much gold I started with, I rarely had any gold by the time I first got to a boss.  This made most of the game just depressing, as I felt the more I played the less gold I had.  Without gold, I couldn't buy many upgrades, which in turn made the next level even harder.
About my skill level, I guess I'm below average, but I don't think I'm that bad.  I loved Dark Souls for instance, but I feel Shovel Knight is even harder because there are fewer strategies and routes available, gold is easier to lose permanently, and most deaths come from insta-kills.  Also Dark Souls I felt was more atmospheric and included more RPG elements.  It's one thing to die in Dark Souls 15 times in a row in a tense battle with a huge Dragon.  It's another to die in Shovel Knight 15 times in a row just because you didn't manage to jump from one moving platform to another.
I think someone good at platforming would enjoy this game, but I think it's too hard to recommend to the average person.  If the developers added an easier difficulty setting I would recommend it whole-heartedly.

This game is the perfect example of two concepts.
The first is difficulty vs. tedium. There is no difficulty in this game Anyone can beat it, given time, without the use of any skill whatsoever. I leveled up 20 times with my back to the screen while carrying on a conversation by idly moving the joystick back and forth.
The second concept is the awarding of arbitrary milestones as an incentive to continue "playing" something which contains no actual gameplay whatsoever. I admit, that's what made me spend three hours in this game, even though it was a joyless experience after the first runthrough. I had to grind up to level 100 because that's the game's only real measure of "completion." Upon reaching that stage, I felt relief that I could stop playing without feeling that I'd "given up."
To be fair, this is all disclosed in the game's description, and the price point is fair for what it is. Clearly many people enjoyed it, and there's nothing wrong with that. But I can't stand the thought of someone playing this while in the back of their mind remembering that I recommended it.

Earth Defense Force 4.1 is a B-movie-lover's dream game. Giant bugs, robots, UFO's, massive firepower, cheesy one-liners, action-packed... it's all here, baby, and it's bloody glorious!
Earth Defense Force 4.1 has the giant monsters of B-movies and the cheesy humour along with it. House-sized bees and spiders, 10-story robots, groups of soldiers singing while moving from one objective to the next, dozens of trails left in the sky after rockets find their target, large UFOs slowly crashing into a fireball of destruction, monster ants flinging NPCs or my character for miles with arms and legs flailing as we somersault through the air awaiting our final landing spot: it all just puts a giant grin on my face.
The 4 classes in Earth Defense Force 4.1 were all fun to play, some a little more than others, but your mileage may vary. For e.g. the Wing Diver has a jet pack and is great at hit and run tactics and collecting loot sprawled all over the battlefield, but she has the lowest armor of all classes making her more of a glass cannon. Want a little more beef and fire power? Play the Fencer who wears Fallout-style power armor and has the capability of wielding tank-like cannons in each arm.
I was a big fan of the fact each class comes with their own set of weapons I needed to find and unlock, half of the fun was experimenting with each new weapon, experiencing its strengths, weaknesses, and quirks. After getting a good feel for each weapon, it was fun playing with optimal weapon pairings for each mission!
All of this fun can be shared with 3 other players in online co-op. I found myself thinking back and laughing at the fantastic memories and stories generated by Earth Defense Force 4.1 based on the experiences I had with friends and random players online. The game produces so many epic “wow” and “what the f*&$! is that?!” moments it makes it difficult not to recall them.
Imagine building-sized robots stomping towards you while massive alien motherships drop 100's of giant ants, all while dodging a barrage of lasers and alien bee stingers.
One of my favourite memories so far was the surprise mech called in by a teammate during a mission where giant red ants storm the beach we were tasked to defend. During all the carnage, one of our online teammates stops firing and says, “Don't worry guys, I got this.” I looked up to the sky to find a huge Pacific Rim sized Mech Warrior being choppered to the beach, lands with such force the sand kicks up, momentarily blinding my view of the impending ant swarm. Then my teammate enters the mech and starts stomping the ants like a slow moving angry child throwing a 1000 ton temper tantrum. All the while, the ants swarm the mech, crawling all over and up and down the hulking armored body. I took the opportunity to pull out my rocket launcher and start firing at the ants, watching them fall off the mech in droves. This was such an incredible moment.
I don't kid myself, Earth Defense Force 4.1 has many glaring issues, the menu UI, lack of VoIP control options, sluggish vehicle movement, slight frame drops during gigantic explosions with 100's of enemies on screen, less-than-impactful weapon sounds, and a host of other bugs (not of the insect kind!). Yet, it remains one of the most fun games I've played in 2016, slowly creeping up the ladder of my top 5 games of all time. It's the type of blissful, mesmerizing fun I have not had in a long, long time.

In a market saturated with videogames that try to take themselves seriously (Not that I have a problem with that), EDF4.1 is a pleasant break. Combine massive swarms of massive enemies, hundreds of devastating weapons and 4 unique classes with unique playstyles, and sprinkle in cheese dialog and 'B-Grade' story and you get Earth Defense Force 4.1. The only thing that could make it better is some kind of modding support so I can create truly bizarre and devastating weapons that make the stock ones seem sane. And even then the publisher has released a statement that implies that some kind of modding support interests them. The developers clearly had fun when making this game, and it shows.
For a port, it performs splendidly and the control scheme is very comfortable with a keyboard and mouse. I was expecting extreme lag issues, but it works just fine on my slightly old computer. While the developers and publishers have been pretty silent on issues and questions in general, one must consider the language barrier as they are based in Japan. It does not appear they have a professional translator able to relay every report sent their way yet.

One of the best FPS experience of the past few years. Don't be fooled just because it's made by Ubisoft. The game is tense, difficult, but ultimately fun to play. It has multiple issues regarding latency and general connection issues. In addition, the game has some of the most unique bugs I've ever seen (if you go to r/Rainbow6, you can see what I mean). Despite all of that, it's an amazing game.
Although I must warn you, this game has a deep learning curve. You will want to learn the map inside and out. There are strategies that are superior for defending that you should learn ASAP. If you're starting out, don't be intimidated if you die a lot. Because you WILL die a lot. You will probably face people better than you (since the matchmaking system in this game is bad) but they will most likely help you out if you ask.
Also, play with a mic. This game is team-oriented (moreso than any other AAA game) and you will want to talk with your teammates. I would argue that it's almost mandatory.
In the end, my relationship with this game is best described as "abusive". It has so many issues (such as hit-reg, matchmaking, etc. Heck it would take a while for me to describe them all). But it is a solid game that will get your heart pumping and getting you to sweat ♥♥♥♥ing ponds. That experience is so good that you will ignore the problems that I and other players have with the game.
NOTE: I would strongly advise against getting the Starter Edition. It bumps the cost of operators so you have to grind about 2x more just to unlock them. I recommend getting the base game. It'll save you a bunch of time.

Fun little game that is surprisingly hard to master.
Though 100%'ing the game and achievements can be done in a single sitting, the quick climb to becoming a "drift master" is a good challenge. Cars are loose and easy to drift but hard to control. But controllable they are! This results in it feeling quite satisfying when you string together some tricks and turns and get your combo score flying high. But it can be quite frustrating when, more often than not, you don't keep control. The art and music combo is almost hypnotizing as you get mesmerized. But losing control and crashing your vehicle keeps you grounded in reality.
It really could have used a bit more depth. Overall suffers from that feeling of input lag just by it's style of driving. But this bogged feeling, whether my imagination or not, extends to the menus as well. Things could've been more crisp in that respect. And it is quite short. 2.3hrs to 100% for me. Not even enough time to "farm" all the Steam Cards. I don't feel the need to beat my scores so I don't really see any replayability here. It could've used some sort of racing mode with NPCs or local versus. Would've been a great callback to a MicroMachines or OffRoad feel. Spoiler warning; The ending dialogue hint towards a rally themed sequel gets my nerd senses tingling and I hope to see that realized one day as the base here is exceptional.
There's definitely something here. Maybe not a ton, but something. Fun to be had for an afternoon. A perfect bundle game but might have trouble standing up to scrutiny as a lone purchase.

If you mastered Portal 2 and need a smart extension with challenging puzzles, this is 100% the mod for you. I loved so many things about this game; the story, the puzzles, the humor, and the self awareness that only the Portal community could have. However, every good game has its flaws. The custom animations weren't perfect, the cutscenes had a big motion blur and the camera liked to sway back and forth, and the core seemed to have one animation segment and didnt feel as "organic" as Wheatley's animations were. These are more like blemishes than real problems, but I did have a big problem with the final boss. While the actions leading up to the boss fight were smart and well thought out, the final setting of the fight wasnt too great. (SPOILERS)
Another small problem is how sometimes the switches didn't stand out among all the wreckage, but that might just be me being tired. Otherwise, this was amazing, and to leave on a high note, I absolutely adored the subtlety during the puzzles, where you weren't sure if the solution you think is the actual intended way of playing, and how literally every square was placed with great thought.
tldr: This was an amazing mod that extended everything i love about the previous Portal games, I absolutely recommend this.

When I first clicked the "Install now" button I didn’t really know what to expect, I mean sure the game has tons of positive reviews but still it is listed as just a mod made by people that have nothing to do with Valve and even worse it is free. So, my hopes were really not that high for this one, but since it was free and having nothing to lose I decided to give it a try.
So, after having tried and also beaten the game let me start by saying that this is not a mod, but an actual DLC which has nothing to envy from an official DLC by Valve. It really has everything, a brand new story with the elements of "being chased" and "running for your life" also be as much present as with the original game, new unique puzzles that force you to think outside of the box, a lot of new models and textures, surprisingly good voice acting and finally, about the same amount of gameplay as the original game.
The puzzles are objectively more difficult compared to the original game and as someone coming from just finishing Portal 2, this was something that I really enjoined. As I said before, many of the puzzles force you to think outside of the box. Some of them at first glance may appear to be just impossible, but as you continue to explore the area and trying different things, everything just comes together and you finally get the solution.
One thing also worth pointing out, is that the game wastes no time explaining the player how everything works. Even the first puzzles are already arguable that they are harder to solve compared to many of the later puzzles on the original game. This is really good from the perspective of players just coming from having beaten Portal 2, but on the other hand this might also seem like a plot hole to many. Mel grabs a fully functional portal gun from the very beginning and somehow immediately knows how portals work with momentum. But again, someone could argue that at this point she doesn’t have any other options, because she is trapped in an old building and the only thing that exists there and could help her escape is this portal gun.
The story is also quite rich and the developers do a great job sticking everything together with the events of the original Portal and Portal 2, even though the events take place on a different timeline and with a different protagonist.
So, to summarize. In my opinion, this games is probably the closest someone can get to playing Portal 3, it has its own unique story and does a great job unraveling it. I hope to be proven wrong, but I really believe that Portal 3 is never going to come out. After all this, it's really hard to me to realize that this gem is actually free, if you are a fan of the Portal series you absolutely have to play it, trust me you won’t regret it.

My playtime is a bit low on Steam, but I've been playing this game for hours on end on my 3DS.
This game is sort of like the lovechild of Mega Man, Duck Tales, Zelda II, and Super Mario Bros. 3, but at the same time it proves to be very original. Take for instance the game's death system; rather than losing lives, you lose a certain percentage of your money and restart at a checkpoint, but if you make it to your place of death, you can try and reclaim your lost gold, which is split into 3 flying bags that may or may not be possible to earn back without dying again, thus despawning the last death's bags and taking away more money. You can also destroy checkpoints, granting you a bit of extra money but disabling that particular checkpoint until you beat the level or go back to the map screen. It's simple, but so much more fun than a life system, and much less disheartening. There's a TON of other stuff, but it's better to experience the game rather than have it explained.
If you're looking for something nostalgic or a really solid platformer, Shovel Knight will likely be a favorite of yours.

EDF is like the old Godzilla -- you can clearly see the zipper on the suit, it's obviously made of rubber, and none of the joints bend in the right ways, and all of those things are what make it timeless and endearing. EDF purposefully doesn't try to get everything right in its presentation, but it isn't a parody of bugginess like Goat Simulator. Instead, it's found genuine charm in imperfection, and it knows its rock solid and hectic gunplay will overcome the strangeness of seeing a giant ant stuck inside a lamp post now and then. EDF is confident that it's fun, and knows that that trumps all else.
Beyond the thematic and technical camp, EDF has a well tuned difficulty curve and some extremely thoughtful challenges requiring both tactics and proper gearing. Co-op is wacky fun as well -- picture playing L4D against Power Rangers villains and you'll have a fairly good idea of what you're in for.
Definitely recommended.

I've played the game enough now to have a solid opinion on it.  I recommend this to anyone who loves run and gun, asymmetrical class archetypes and general destruction and decimation of entire city blocks.  It has fantastic(and active) co-op campaigns with plenty of replayable challenge modes to try.
Pros:
-Replayable
-Upwards of a hundred missions with many different enemies to fight
-Challenging in a good way
-Asymmetrical class gameplay where every class brings something good to the table
-Highly Destructible environments, buildings and vehicles go up in flames and crumbles
-Fast paced, hectic gameplay with most missions averaging between 5-20 minutes
-Hundreds of guns to choose from
-Runs well
-Co-op and splitscreen work flawlessly
Cons:
-The menu and UI are controlled via wasd and the mouse has a weird draw on the selection(move your mouse and you may select the wrong thing)
-Limited options menu.  Basically all you can change are vsync, AA and ratio/fullscreen and windowed.  No borderless here.  There are key rebindings but some seemed to be missing, but that could have just been me missing them.
-Controller is sometimes fussy with splitscreen, even using a proprietary xbox controller
-Dated graphics, though great taken as a whole are pretty much PS3 level of quality.  This REALLY shouldn't deter you, though.
-The picking up of items and armor isn't completely intuitive.  If you kill the last enemy and haven't managed to grab everything(especially difficult for air raider and mostly ranger due to their limited mobility) you're pretty much SoL for whatever dropped.
-Many items are fun but just aren't useful.  There are literally hundreds of guns to pick from but many are just so unwieldy that they're immediately outclassed.  This isn't surprising given the sheer number of available loadouts  but it's still a con.
In summary I think this is a great game but it's definitely not for everyone.  I love looting and killing things in interesting ways and this game has that in spades.  The classes are all unique and fun to play in their own way.  You can always bring something useful to the team and your loadout can heavily determine your success in a particular mission.  The game doesn't swamp you with bulletsponges but rather enemies that are legitimately dangerous.  Their health DOES go up with difficulty but it's hardly ever an unreal amount that can't be overcome by using the right weapons and strategy.
This game basically took the premise
and ran with it.

Absolute Drift is a lot of fun.  Once you get a hang of the controls, you'll be drifting along effortlessly and feel just a little bit like Fujiwara Takumi.
The game has 3 modes: Drift Track, Driftkhana, Mountain.  Each presented in a clean, minimal look and feel, which in my mind, enhances your experience since there's no distraction from what this game is about: Drifting.
Drift track is simply what is says: a track to drift around.
Driftkhana can be said to be a timed playground with boxes to knock over, demarcated areas to spin in, make doughnuts and just in general do as many drift tricks as you can in the set amount of time.
Mountain is similar to Drift track, only the "track" mimics a mountain downhill where you traverse it from end to finish.
The aim in each of the modes: score the as many points as possible.
At first this is quite difficult as you get to grips with the car and the handling.  But the controls are forgiving, as are the physics.  Soon you'll learn the limits of the car and the ins and outs of the handling and physics together, throwing the car around like second nature.
Furthermore, connecting all of the events, are hub areas (5 in total), each containing between 18 and 25 missions to complete.  Complete all missions in an area to unlock the next.
You can also access all of the events from the main menu and jump straight in if you like ( no need to unlock them first ).
Absolute drift is great for simply relaxing and pouring out any stress you have into the satisfying act of watching a micro-machine sized car, drift around corners, boxes, containers and trains.
Highly recommended.
NOTE: Absolute drift is purely a singleplayer experience.  Don't approach if you this is a drift racing game.
