There's a lot of praise for this game.  I really can't agree with most of it.
Performance is fine, controller support is fine, keys are rebindable and so forth.  Aesthetic wise the game does pretty well with pixel art.  There isn't really anything beautiful in level design but character and enemy design is robust and expressive.  The music isn't annoying, but I find it hard to really get much into chiptune-esq music usually, so aside from town tunes I can't recall any specific piece of music.
The problem of the game, that major factor that I can't get behind, is the level design that composes the whole of the gameplay.  There is no challenge in ANY of the monsters you encounter in a level.  The game gives you two full health restores, plenty of health drops, and an item which makes you invulnerable for 3 seconds.  The only challenge is in the excessive amounts of instant death pits and any spikes which can't be avoided by using the item which makes you invulnerable for 3 seconds.  Levels are divided into 3 to 6 sections with checkpoints between each and a boss at the end, but the spacing is annoyingly inconsistent.  The start of the stage has many screen transitions to a checkpoint, and the end always has few.  Thus you will have to replay four or more screens only to die once more to an annoying platform-over-death-pit puzzle, and then at the end you will do one or two screens over an easy puzzle to a check point.  Bosses are utterly trivial at the start of the game, and then the very last two introduce instant death pits and spikes into their attack patterns.  And then at very end, you have a boss rush.  Guess where the only challenge lies?  You guessed it, with the two that have instant death phases.  Last boss where her attacks create and destroy platforms?  I never died once to damage, but 20 or so times to instant death pits.
Other minor gripes: Levels are more or less one directional.  There are one-screen side paths that lead to money, but money becomes useless about halfway through the game because you'll have bought everything already.  Dying makes you drop some money similar to dark souls, but not enough that I ever felt like I had to care, thus what was the point in the first place except to encourage you to risk another instant death?  Most items you acquire are useless because combat is not threatening.  I use the three-second-invincibility about 90% of the time, and only two of my six or so attack items the other 10% of the time.  The game gives you bottles to fill for free at a pond (more or less a town) with one of three free potions, but then puts NPCs at the start of levels with potion refills before you have any legitimate reason to use them.  Why, just in case you both forgot to refill them and also forgot that you can exit the level from the escape menu?
Maybe it's because I didn't grow up wih mario and the like, but I don't have any tolerance for this.  Instant death is not fun.  It is pattern memorization, with a failstate for failure to execute.  This is no different than something like Super Meat Boy, just masking itself as some other kind of genre by giving you enemies who don't instant kill you and a health bar.

Some of the bugs are well known to Ubisoft, but they never provided patches as I've learned on some message boards.
UPlay worked on my playthrough (others weren't as lucky), but I still don't understand the need for a double DRM. Being forced to make an account for playing offline really got on my nerves.
This game was also very prone to crashes and Alt-Tabbing out of it was completely out of the question.
Whereas in AC 2 you visit different cities, in this game you just remain in Rome. This and the repetitive missions killed most of the replay value.
All in all I'd give this game 3 out of 10 points mainly for the story and the whole climbing and stealth mechanics - if that's also what you love about the AC series I'd reccomend you to buy AC 1 and leave it at that.

, this PC port of a former PS4 exclusive came pretty much out of nowhere.
like
, however, this PC port is remarkably solid. Barebones, sure, as is (sadly) to be expected from a Japanese budget game, but other than suffering from a severe allergy to AMD processors, as well as the usual interface laziness, it comes without too many hiccups. It also runs fairly well on lower-end hardware (as it rightly should, given the lo-fi visuals, but that hasn't stopped a lot of last-gen port from far more prolific publishers that shall not be named to run worse than the bowel contents of a constipated sandworm). The game itself doesn't need much in terms of description. The series has a cult following for good reason, and
is arguably the best game in the series so far. By releasing it on PC hardware, Sandlot have made a lot of folks happy, including myself. The price tag may be a bit steep - I got it as a surprise gift from a friend, so I really can't complain - but I'm quite sure there will be enough sales to make the mandatory acquisition of this glorious masterpiss of craftsman$hit only a matter of time for anyone interested. Overall awesome short game.
Everyone that is into drifting should get this game!
The minimalistic looks combined with impulsive soundtrack invite you to drift in the small open world.
You unlock the different stages of the game by completing challenges like drifting between certain buildings or doing donuts around trees.
I'm having a tremendous amount of fun only by doing that and trying to obtain the perfect flow and seeing the smooth lines the tires leave behind. Topping your Highscore in one of the Driftkhanas resemble those in Dirt 3 and ain't any inferior.
Each of the 6 differnt cars distinguishes from the others in terms of maneuverability and torque so you can pick the one that suits your skill best. No matter what car you pick you will still have a hard time knowing the point when you have to countersteer or back down on the throttle.
But achieving the perfect combination of drifts will reward you with an emotion, that is just as plain and straightforward as the game itself. . . PURE JOY!
The content is slim and you can easily finish the game in under one hour.
Mastering the arts of drifting will take you much longer and i can only speak of myself but this game was more fun than almost every racing game i played in the last year.

Trust is put to the test in Deceit, a horror FPS where players are stranded with a group of players. One-third of the group is infected with a virus that transforms them into vicious man-eating creatures. The goal of the infected is to wipe out the humans, while the non-infected seek to escape. Each match consists of three rounds, with phases of darkness called blackouts where infected players prowl using night vision. Actions are perceived in twisted ways, adding to the deceitful atmosphere between the group. Players must make decisions about who to trust and who to be wary of while walking around the dark with a gun in hand. Earn currency in each match that can be used to purchase items in-game.I recommend this game!!!!

Overall a great, refined game!

So, if you have been on the internet in the last decade, You've probably seen a guy named slenderman. Many proclaim that slender is the scariest game there ever is, was, and will be, but those people probably havn't played Amnesia: The Dark Descent. There are plenty other video games such as SCP: Containment Breach and Which that compete with this title (Horror wise), but this game is MUCH more interactive, and in most cases, fun. Slenderman is easy to outrun... probably because he doesnt "Chase" you. The monsters in this game chase you, and there 2X faster than you, and can break doors down and kill you with just 2 hits. Not to mention that these monsters (the gatheres), are as creepy as mess. Just opening doors is fun, due to the fact that you have to make a litteral motion with your mouse to open it. The game has some unique properties most horror games dont. When you stay in the dark to long, your Sanity will drain. Sanity is pretty unique to the game, and will mess with your brain by fainting, seeing random things on your screen, bluring out, and randomly falling on the floor when it gets low. A lot of developers for horror games have found it to be more unnerving if you cant defend yourself against the enemies. Amnesia is a perfect example of this, as all you can carry is a lantern. You don't just wake up in a forest and go to find random pages scattered about, but the game has a plot. You play as daniel, the protagonist, who wakes up in a mansion of some sort, not knowing why the mess he's even there. Escaping is the main goal, but the developers warn you that the game should'nt be played to win. This is probably my favorite Horror title, due to its high amount of interactive controlls, jump scares, monsters and the abillity to download custom games and play offtrack of the story mode. As of I, I give this a 4.3. I recomend this to anyone who does'nt mind getting scared to death, otherwise, you'll waste your money on a game that you will  never play.

EDF is quintessentially the lovechild of Starship Troopers and War of the Worlds with a glorious amount of visually satisfying explosions and guns. Take your own army into battle against giant insects and ravagers that descend from space once again. Command your troops to sing on command as you cram a rocket launcher down a giant spider's stupid face. Roll constantly as a Ranger to Dark Souls your way to the enemy, whiz around as a Wing Diver like a magical girl out of an anime, bombard the aliens using artillery as an Air Raider, and be the dual minigun wielding badass Fencer that you want to be.
All in all, this game is pretty neat to play on your own, but really shines when you play with friends. I give this an EDF out of 10. Make the Earth great again.

Resident Evil 5 is not a horror game and is very similar to its successor Resident Evil 6 in that it is most like a co-op action game with horror/gore elements.  While the game plot can often be nonsense and despite some utterly ridiculous boss fights, the game is reasonably entertaining, and very attractive, being almost a decade old now.  While Resident Evil 4 purists may scorn or dislike RE 5, the truth is that the games are remarkably similar.  The key with this game is to find it on a hefty sale to counteract the limited replayability/value and to play it with a friend, which is sure to produce ample laughs.
A nice action TPS if you can find it on a Steam sale.

I had so many friends calling out to me; telling me to play this game. I heard so many stories of the wandering Blue Knight and his odd choice in weaponry, and how this game mixed so many genres into one beautiful package. I didn't even watch the intro to the game...I just bought it.

Is the game too easy? Well no one is FORCING you to get all those sweet upgrades! Too hard? Just stop by your local apple fishing pond to chug down some of its liquid offerings and you'll be happily pogo-ing off the tops of your enemies heads without a care in the world!
Even once you beat the game, you'll find yourself wanting to play it again and again. Whether it be to try and best your own time or the times of your friends, or just so you can go back in and see if you can ever beat Plague Knight with no items and without getting hit...yeah, I know other people have probably done that...show offs XD

Loot Hero DX was orginally for android devices, with the way it plays the game is obviously ported over from mobile almost straight to Steam and then sold at a price after they add some other features to the game in the Steam version. This game is very grindy, so if you don't like games where it requires you to grind for money and exp then you're not going to like this game.
First thing I think that most people will want to know after reading the introduction of this review is what's the difference between Loot Hero DX on Steam, and the free to play version called Loot Hero. According to the developer, the main purpose of putting it on steam and putting a price on it is the graphical side of the game, full screen 60 fps (the android version consists of small window with 30fps) better effects and a "facelift." I'm not really sure what the developer meant by a "facelift" but they have added a few more levels and a miner thing whereby you save a miner everytime you kill a dragon and they will collect gold for you over time. Now that's out of the way, I will briefly explain the way that this game is played. Basically there has been a dragon that has taken over the lands and you, the hero, have to kill it. You will be required to go through a few levels before getting to the dragon, whilst upgrading 4 main things a hero needs. Attack, Critical, Defense and Speed. After killing the dragon once, takes maybe 30 minutes or so you now have to do it again, but on a harder difficulty. This is basically the whole game. What are my thoughts? The game to begin with was fun, collecting exp, leveling up, upgrading my items over time and just generally running into enemies by killing them. After beating the dragon the first time, it did really restrict the replay value of the game a bit. But, I pushed on to defeat the dragon once again. 3 hours passed, I had totally lost interest in this game. It becomes a drag of constant leveling up and upgrading your items until you can kill the dragon over and over again. The game has some really great music when you are killing enmeies, and the slightly destructable enviroment was rather nice. But as you played more, and came back to the same levels they got boring, and I just felt no need to play through the game anymore.
+ Fun at first to play
+ Nice music
+ Killing enemies sometimes destorys enviroment
+ Trading cards & Achievements
- Limited replay value
- Constantly going through the same levels gets boring rather quickly
Although I have stopped playing the game because of it's limited replay value and repetitive gameplay, I still recommened this game. The reason for that is because the game is rather cheap, and the first few times playing the game I really enjoyed it. But now I won't be able to enjoy it because of the constant grind and repetitive gameplay.

I have decided to re-make this review since, originally, I just wrote it because I saw a negative review of this game. So here goes!
Assassin's Creed Brotherhood takes place just where the second game ends, making it a direct sequel. In this game you still relive the memories of your ancestor Ezio Auditore da Firenze. In the real world however, things change a bit. Desmond and the crew have moved the entire operation to Monteriggioni, the town that Ezio's family had earlier lived in. This means that you can, at any given time, exit out of the Animus and wander around in the real world. This is a nice edition, but is sadly not that well made as there are little to none things to do.
The gameplay of this installment has been improved from the previous games. The fighting is well made and you will feel a sense of progression as enemies will be easier to defeat as your skill goes up. Also combos have been introduced, making fighting 2+ enemies will not feel as rubish anymore.
But fighting is only have the game, of cource the climbing has been improved. This is not as noticable though, as it was good in the older games aswell.
This game features alot of quests, aside from the main storyline, that are well fitted into the story and helps you get a better understanding on how Ezio was as a person. The most well made once were the once featuring no one else that your friend, Leonardo da Vinci. He is back with long, well made mission for you to complete. But not only that, he also sells you items that will spice up the gameplay, giving you tons of new options on how to do thing.
Generaly speaking this game is a masterpiece in the Assassin's Creed series. The story is great, you will come to care about the characters, the gameplay mechanics are improved, still same stunning visuals as the last game. Basically a worthy sequel that was not made to cash in on the Assassin's Creed name.

This game features 3 level types: A-to-B mountain tracks, freestyle drift courses, and 3-lap race tracks. The free roam map has additional missions you can perform only once, such as donut around a light pole, drift between buildings, jump over a river, etc.

Despite repeatedly crashing into walls, I really enjoyed playing this game. I enjoyed the game even more once I finally figured out how to drive and drift. I particularly loved driving around the map in free roam and discovering new missions to complete. The minimalistic art style and varied environments provides for a beautiful game that keeps you coming back for more.
Pros
+ Beautiful minimalistic art style
+ Many missions to complete
+ Large soundtrack with ability to skip tracks whenever you want
+ Ramps! Launch your car into the air and spin out of control
+ Customizable car body and paint jobs
+ Controller support
Cons
- Not much replayability once you've completed all free-roam missions
- Difficult learning curve for controls
- Only three types of levels gives feeling of repeating the same thing over and over

Tactical Intervention is a pretty fun game. It's a solid shooter, and fun multiplayer. However, there is a lot or hindrances.
Tactical Intervention is one of those Free To Play, online multiplayer games, yes. But it's also one of those Pay To Win games where you can be stuck with an old♥♥♥♥♥shotgun while an opponent has a fully decked out HK417 to plant bullets in your face. I've been through that a bunch. I feel like they should add a challenge system to give bonus in game cash to allow purchasing of weapons, equipment and etc., mainly cuz it takes ♥♥♥♥ing forever to get cash for said purchases (I've won nearly ten straight matches at one point with positive K/D, and I've only gotten 1,000 GP! Vs. the 55,000 to permenantly own a modern, well balanced assault rifle).
Another big hindrance that breaks the experience is that the spawn points are completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Once, a match has just begun, right. Next thing you know, the entire team is just a few feet away. Or you can spawn on top of a table or railing, being flanked by two other guys! What ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is that? Spawn protection that lasts for three seconds doesn't help, when you spawn boxed in.
There's a lot of weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ but to some it up with +'s and -'s:
+ It's fun and addicting.
+ Pretty cool customization options that expand upon the inventory system of Counter-Strike.
+ Intense shoot-outs across game modes, whether it's Team Deathmatch or a car chase in a Mission game type, plus more.
+ Leaning and Rolling options to be more tactical.
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t spawn points with more disadvantages than advantages.
- Pay To Win ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
- For a Source engine game, it looks pretty bad vs. other Source games, even Source mods. (Minh Le once said in an interview in Game Informer Issue 121 when he was still working at Valve, "I just enjoy designing games in the latest engines, with all the new technological advantages, and seeing how much immersive I can make the experience with better graphics, sound, animation, and game design.") I think Minh Le should examine Dear Esther, or No More Room In Hell, or even Titanfall for ways he can upgrade the Source Engine for Tactical Intervention. The Source engine has come a long way as one of the best engines out there, and It's a shame to see it used like the way it is in Tactical Intervention.
- Rolling should give a accelerated movement, not slow you down or snag you on corners.
Also, some quirks to note:
* The game is almost amusingly and unnecessarily violent. It's like if The Expendables were turned into a game (shotgun blasting away upper torso? Pffft....hahaha!)
* Maybe look to Rainbow Six Vegas for rappeling updates? Rappeling is an interesting feature, but rather rare and very clunky. Controls are really awkward, but it's a good way to set up flanking and suppression options.
* Mission mode is weird, and driving can be improved (look at Half-Life 2, for God's sake! The driving in there was pretty solid!)
* As something in the vein of Counter-Strike, it feels a little outdated. In our modern world of modern world set FPS's, it's hard to remember that Counter-Strike NEVER HAD IRON SIGHT AIMING. I mean, mobility is much improved, with sprinting, rolling, and leaning to enhance and update Counter-Strike's slow pace, but it still feels like there's much more to improve.
Overall, I WOULD NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME UNLESS YOU LIKED COUNTER STRIKE OR REALLY LIKE FPS's ON PC. I commend Mr. Minh Le for making a Counter-Strike 2 in the form of a new name and introducing a plethora of new stuff to seperate it from it's older brother, spiritual predecessor game. But, for the hope that there are substantial updates for this game, there's an ad infinitum amount of stuff he could improve upon that I only scratched the surface of in this review. Maybe in the ultra rare, highly hypothetical case, Mr. Le would look at this review, or the thousands of other NO RECOMMENDATION reviews and take it upon himself and his game development studio to rectify said negatives.

Loot Hero DX is one of a pair of games released by VaragtP that were previously available on smart phone and tablet and have been upgraded for the PC market, now credit where credit is due these games while basic are better than their original counter parts but remain seated in the casual games category with minimum depth. Arguably this doesn't automatically make them poor games and Loot Hero DX certainly has wonderful sprite work and music but overall there is a sense of lost opportunity as its gameplay resembles a clicker game more than the casual action RPG it claims to be.
For those who can't view the video the basic summary is this:
You begin as a knight who moves very slowly and all the game play amounts to is walking left or right bumping into enemies until either you or enemies die. When enemies are defeated they drop gold which can be spent on upgrades to Attack, Defence, Critical hit Chance or Speed however only attack or defence are of any use, you also gain experience points which will eventually level your character which gives pitiful bonuses to these stats in comparison to the bought upgrades.
The enemies do nothing to stop your progress other than act as a blockade and you can stand next to them without fear of been attacked or been pushed back, they also almost immediately respawn once you pass an area so you can grind back and forth through the same line without having to progress in the level.
While there is minor story elements at the beginning the ending is little more that "A winner is you" before shunting you back to the menu and increasing the level of all the monsters and levels.
You do gain a single miner each time who earns you gold while your not playing but because of the small gold cap you soon can earn the maximum amount of gold in seconds at the higher levels.
As I say repeatedly during the review I love the artwork and this could of been made into a nifty little rogue light or platform RPG but if you need something to kill ten minutes Loot Hero DX is ideal but its not much use for anything else.

If I had to give this game an honest review, I'd say this -- For the ones who thought this game was bad, you clearly don't understand the story. And for the ones who rushed through the game without a clue about the story, you shouldn't be reviewing strictly based off of gameplay.
*As for the POSITIVE* I can safely say that being a huge fan of the Resident Evil series, this game ties everything together. From the Co-op, to the physical story, This is probably one of my absolute favorite games of all time. If you played the story slowly, you would have read all the documents that give the player dates and times about the events that have spanned throughout the previous Resident Evils. As you read them, you understand how Resident Evil 5 fits snug in the story from before the game, all the way up to current time.
*As for the NEGATIVE* This game has a 3rd person angle that may throw some people off being a first time player. To be completely honest though, you should be more than comfortable with it after 20 minutes. The only other thing that was a little funky was some of the cutscenes player dialogue - The dialogue and story was just amazing, it really was. Some parts of some cutscenes were very cheesy, but almost humurous. Both of these complaints sort of cancel themselves out though seeing as they don't ruin the game itself.
All in all I give this game a 10/10 due to the very in depth story with characters you can connect to over time. I recommend anyone to go out and pick up a copy of this whether it's on sale or not.

I would overwhelmingly recommend this game, here is why...
I've played many fishing games dating back to Blue Marlin on the NES. This game is the first one that has ever given me a sense of what it is truly like to fish in real life. The environment is beautiful, the equipment realistic, the difficulties of real fishing are present. There are two types of players in this game, the first type goes into it to play a game, the other goes into it to fish. The developers need both types of players to be a success. The game can't be too realistic to where you can play for a few hours and catch nothing, but it also can't be so easy that it feels 'arcadey', because you will lose the players that come to fish. If you want to catch a fish then you can, but if you want to catch a nice fish you will have to work for it, just like real life fishing. There are mechanics occasionally that make it hard to catch fish, but a game that is still early access and is this complex needs leeway to fine tune things.
There are many people that play this game that are in the first group and do not care about learning how to fish, they just want to know where to cast, what to cast with, and what time of day, then they try and can't catch what they were going for and blame the game or the developers. If you take the time to experiment with different lures, different retrieve styles, and cast in places that real fish would hang out then you will catch something, it may take some practice, it may take some persistence, and it will take patience. That is one key thing that makes this game worth my time, the idea that real fishing requires patience, if you don't have that and you wait 5 seconds and nothing will hit your bobber and you get mad and bash the game then you aren't meant to play this game.
On the topic of cheaters, a lot of people say that since there are cheaters in the game, that it ruins their experience. I really don't see how they can do that. One person cheating doesn't change my experience because I can still come into the game and catch a fish, I know how I caught that fish and I can take pride in the fact that I didn't have to cheat to get that fish. The devs have done a lot to curb cheating and sometimes those measures can have false positives. Anti-cheat is a very hard thing to get right and will never be 100% effective.
I will admit that this game can get quite grindy in the higher levels. The official reason for that is so that it will take you longer to do everything there is to do and catch so that the devs have more time to add more content to keep you coming back. But I have been playing for 510hrs at the time I am writing this review and I have yet to catch everything I want to catch and go everywhere I want to go, however I am slightly slower than some. Some say this game is pay to play and it is most definitely not, far from it. I have not paid a single cent to get to where I am, but not that I won't in the future to support the game. Yes you need certain gear to be able to participate in certain areas but you do not need to pay real money to do it. There is a reason why certain maps are level locked and its because you can't start out in the game and immediately go after a 50 pound striper bass or a 40 pound Northern Pike. You start out with access to gear that are only rated for small fish. Its a game, you work up to the big ones, if you don't like that don't play. Some recent reviews are complaining about that because there were limited time events that opened up all the lakes to everyone so they could compete in a tournament for fish anyone can catch. But they chose to go for fish they didn't have the gear to catch. Obviously you can pay for DLC and get better gear early and beable catch any fish that you have the level to catch, such as the 90 pound gar in Missouri. But, that is far from being pay to win because you can just wait till you level up and you can get that gear for in-game currency.

Fishing planet is the new fishing simulator by which all others (if there are any) should be judged.  The depth of detail put into this game is astounding.  From the fish AI to the assortment of rods, reels, tackle, baits, and gear that you can use (all with their own unique stats that factor directly into gameplay as well as real life fishing knowledge), this game has left no stone unturned.  What might arguably be lacking in the visceral thrill of "real" fishing is more than made up for with plenty of meters and indicators to help you keep your finger on the pulse of the fish on the end of your line.  With tournaments, contests, and costs to visit lakes, there's always something to motivate you to learn and get better at catching that certain type of fish.  I've been fishing all my life and I've learned more about freshwater fishing since I downloaded this game than I ever knew before.  If you love fishing, you should really get this game, if for no other reason than to learn from it.

Honestly I'm not even sure where to start with Arma3. I've got just over 150 hours logged at the time of writing this and I feel like I'm still scratching the surface of what this game offers. OK, so pros and cons then, let's KISS (Keep it simple,  stupid)
Pros
- Amazing open world highly detailed military sandbox simulator
- Tremendous modding support offering everything you could ever want from vehicles, weapons, items and equipment to game enhancements and terrains.
- Excellent gameplay mechanics even if the controls take a little getting used to, it's pretty detailed.
- Driving/flying/boating physics are very good considering the scope of this game.
- Land/sea/air based combat mechanics very good in base game and even better with the addition of game enhancement mods like ACE3.
- Base maps offer good variety of terrain to get to grips with, numerous airstrips, towns, villages and other points of interest for highly involved combined arms combat scenarios. Apex DLC very reasonably priced for what it offers and makes a great addition to the base game.
- Eden scenario editor offers full 3D drag and drop map editing with a literal fook ton of other powerful features; from dynamic  weather to complex AI scripting for creating offline and online scenarios and maps, or just to mess around in.
- Fanbase is generally very good and supportive of new players with lots of milsim and more casual squads recruiting all the time.
- Mods are handled via the stock game launcher so no 3rd party software is needed and is easy as he'll to do.
Con
- Heavy on system resources. If you want consistently high fps with consistently high settings you're gonna need a decent amount of horsepower as this game demands alot from both CPU and GPU.
- Weird/bad scripting in online servers can cause some MAD lagging
- Online can be buggy sometimes as can offline play, though I've only had it happen a couple of time where it's been bad enough for me to have to quit out and rejoin
- Occasionally the game will force close due to random errors, usually if you're running a LOT of mods. But typically it is very stable, I have about 25 mods installed and typically it runs very well (i56600k/GTX1070).
- Some of the official DLC is not great for what it costs and offers and is easily outdone by free mods. But it's a really minor point but worth mentioning nonetheless. Pick it up in a sale or as part of a bundle, then it's actually fairly good value for money
~ UPDATED: SERVER HOSTING HEADACHE
Think you gonna make a cool map and just host that so your mates can play? Nope.
Hosting servers so you can play with your freinds and not other randoms is a NIGHTMARE to set up. It requires you to either use UPnP protocols which can put your computer at high risk (no thanks). Or you must create a static IP and manually forward ports for Aram and Steam to your router, which is a real headache.
Think you can just do this from Control Panel? Nope again. You need to use cmd to find out all the relevent information, IPv4 and DNS Severs etc, then isolate the correct DNS primary and secondary if yours defaults to your Default Gateway, Etc etc...
Honesly, if you're not familiar with this stuff expect to spend about 2 hours just researching and finding the info you need to do it. There is just no way to easily host a game for you and your friends right now.
~
For the full asking price Arma3 and the Apex DLC offer potentially thousands of hours of highly enjoyable gameplay both offline and offline and many more hours of learning the powerful features of the Eden editor if that appeals to you. Right now Server Hosting is just ridiculously convenluted and honeslty I wouldn't be surprised if most people just gave up and played in public servers but the issue needs to be addressed by Bohemia as it interferes with the Apex Protocol co-op hosting as well.
That being said, if you can pick it up in a Steam sale it is the definition of a flat out steal for the value for money it offers and the quality of the game overall. If highly detailed, super involving, super fun military land, air and sea combat simulation is your jam, so long as you don't want to host games, then Arma3 is your spoon.

I was surprised to come across a game of this nature. If you love Fishing or Simulator style games then this is a good start. Early levels it is quite fun to learn and to catch fish. But later on it can become a bit repetative trying to gain XP and money. As you level you gain access to better gear and items which is fun. It just starts to feel a bit grindy when you get higher level.  I like how it's setup that there is cost to travel to lakes and to buy licenses, the downside if you need gear from the main store you will lose money traveling back as each lake has a store but not equipped with all gear that the main one has, so the price of these travels, licenses and access per day could use some adjusting. Graphics so far are nice, so is the scenery and sounds of each lake (Birds and what not). I've entered a competition for the first time and can see where others have complained about cheaters. As soon as the competition starts a handful of players automatically were pulling Unique and Trophy fish back to back fast and often.
*IMPORTANT PART*
One thing I do NOT like about this game is the handling of DLC Content. We all buy DLC hoping to enjoy it in game for the duration that we play. Somehow (as I do not recall selling it) one of my reels from the July 4th dlc was sold, after contacting support they did not offer to restore my lost paid gear. I wish that they would make DLC content non sellable or deletable but add extra space to keep them. You are also at the mercy of losing your gear both in game bought and DLC bought to them breaking and no longer being usable. There is also a system of repair where your DLC content needs occasional repair but uses the gold coins instead of the easily obtainable cash in game. I feel for an addition that you paid real money for should have some safety measures in game so one can enjoy what they've bought. I understand a company needs to make money, but when you pay directly to the company for content, you should be able to have safety nets to not lose them or the ability for them to become unusable and have to pay a harder to obtain currency to maintain them.
Minus the previous from preventing me from possibly buying DLC in the future, the game is pretty good for what it is. There is a learning curve, having to match certain reels with certain rods, having to figure out the proper weight of tackle per rod among other challenges. There needs to be more support or even a tutorial system in game to help new players understand things better. It's a work in progress and I appreciate that they are constantly updating and fixing things. I would recommend this game. But I am on the fence about the way they currently handle DLC Content. It's an easy fix and I'm sure the player base would greatly appreciate that, as it does not give any advantage game wise and gives people a secure feeling in buying extra content.

tl;dr - Game is abandoned and overpriced, but if you pick it up for $5 you get your money's worth and have a new game to spend some weekend afternoons playing.
Years ago, this game was fun. Nothing in this game hadn't been done before, but it brought a lot of things together in an enjoyable package, and new content was being brought out that added facets to the idea of managing a town catering to adventurers and trying to survive the dangers of a D&D world. Now, the game is exactly the same. That's the problem; the end of Towns' beta came purely because the dev wanted more sales for less work.
It's really too bad that the development of this game became something of a hot potato due to fewer sales than the original developer wanted. Towns was developing in an interesting direction, and at the end of the updates had started introducing some enjoyably complicated ways to use basic water channels to make tasks easier. However, it never got to a fully mature stage, instead slowly petering out with updates being smaller and much less often. Eventually, after everyone assumed the dev had already walked away, it was pawned off to make a little more money, to someone who promised new updates but never delivered.
A lot of people are saying not to buy this game because it has been abandoned, and at full price I back that up. But I enjoy it still from time to time, knowing full well what kind of game it is. Maybe you will too?
My recommendation to buy this game comes with the caveat that you should look more closely at what it is, maybe scan through the wiki, and see if you might enjoy it. You can always try it out for an hour, then refund it, you know? But for god's sake don't pay $15 dollars for this, $5 at most. Something to stick on the wishlist and pick up during a steam sale.

After 48 hours of this amazing game, I finally got all achievements.
While it was extremely fun and addictive, it was also extremely annoying towards the end. More on this later.
+Pros:
+Fun ''story''.
+Clearing every level feels extremely rewarding since you get a new type of flower every time.
+ALOT of different plants who all do different things and pretty much all of them are viable.
+Fun money system you can use in the ingame shop.
+The zen garden is a fun way to make big money long term.
+Alot of puzzles and challanges that can be really fun.
+Most of the achievements are just time consuming and requires skill and planning.
-Cons:
-No healthbars for enemies or friendly towers. While there are some visual indication of percentage, a healthbar would be so incredibly nice and usefull.
-Not every plant is viable, but I understand its impossible to have all plants at equal powerlevels.
-The 'China shop' achievement had me tilting so hard I had to get help from a friend in the end. It was the only achievement I was missing and it's left a sour taste in my mouth. It's based more on RNG rather than skill, which is terrible for an achievement to be based on.
Overall:
Am I glad I did a 100% clear on this game? Yes.
Would I do it again? Absolutely not.
Will I play this game just for fun in the future? No.
Is it worth full price? Yes.
Do I recommend it? Yes.

I was surprised to come across a game of this nature. If you love Fishing or Simulator style games then this is a good start. Early levels it is quite fun to learn and to catch fish. But later on it can become a bit repetative trying to gain XP and money. As you level you gain access to better gear and items which is fun. It just starts to feel a bit grindy when you get higher level.  I like how it's setup that there is cost to travel to lakes and to buy licenses, the downside if you need gear from the main store you will lose money traveling back as each lake has a store but not equipped with all gear that the main one has, so the price of these travels, licenses and access per day could use some adjusting. Graphics so far are nice, so is the scenery and sounds of each lake (Birds and what not). I've entered a competition for the first time and can see where others have complained about cheaters. As soon as the competition starts a handful of players automatically were pulling Unique and Trophy fish back to back fast and often.
*IMPORTANT PART*
One thing I do NOT like about this game is the handling of DLC Content. We all buy DLC hoping to enjoy it in game for the duration that we play. Somehow (as I do not recall selling it) one of my reels from the July 4th dlc was sold, after contacting support they did not offer to restore my lost paid gear. I wish that they would make DLC content non sellable or deletable but add extra space to keep them. You are also at the mercy of losing your gear both in game bought and DLC bought to them breaking and no longer being usable. There is also a system of repair where your DLC content needs occasional repair but uses the gold coins instead of the easily obtainable cash in game. I feel for an addition that you paid real money for should have some safety measures in game so one can enjoy what they've bought. I understand a company needs to make money, but when you pay directly to the company for content, you should be able to have safety nets to not lose them or the ability for them to become unusable and have to pay a harder to obtain currency to maintain them.
Minus the previous from preventing me from possibly buying DLC in the future, the game is pretty good for what it is. There is a learning curve, having to match certain reels with certain rods, having to figure out the proper weight of tackle per rod among other challenges. There needs to be more support or even a tutorial system in game to help new players understand things better. It's a work in progress and I appreciate that they are constantly updating and fixing things. I would recommend this game. But I am on the fence about the way they currently handle DLC Content. It's an easy fix and I'm sure the player base would greatly appreciate that, as it does not give any advantage game wise and gives people a secure feeling in buying extra content.

I recommend this game buuuut there's a few problems you should know before buying this.
Compared to other versions of RE5 this game does lack some features:
-No split screen. Even the PS3/360 ver has split screen, as does the newer PS4/XB1 versions
-No Mercy Mercenaries mode is single player ONLY
(No Mercy being a previously exclusive PC mode where you'd play mercenaries mode but with the enemy count cranked WAY up)
-VERY narrow field of view. There's a mod to fix this you can find online but I'm not sure it works with both characters, you MAY have to have one or the other installed. This is only made more glaring when I found the PS4/XB1 version has a extra option to widen the field of view.
Positives:
+It's really well optimized, has a benchmark tool to test out your system as well.
+Supports 144hz/unlockable framerate
+Removed Games for Windows Live!!
+ Finally has the DLC featuring a lot of stuff.
RE5 is a damn fun game, if you're playing CO-OP. I've never played single player but I've heard stories of wonky AI. That aside though if you have a friend to play with this game is one of the best co-op games I've played. It's not just shoot all the enemies, you actually have to manage inventory between you and a friend as you're trying to survive which makes for more hectic gameplay.
It's a pretty long game and has a LOT of crap to do. The campaign mode with different difficulty modes, a load of weapons and items to change up the game. Mercenaries mode where you have a ton of levels and characters to play as making every session different.
This isn't the best version but it works well enough and with Games for Windows Live removed there's no more BS keeping you from playing with a friend.
This is a very fun to play game.

This is a really fun game, reminiscent of Drift Legends, a game I used to play on iPhone.
It doesn't hold your hand; it gives you a few pointers, and then lets you get into it.
For most people who play car games on a regular basis, it's easy to get into, but still hard to master. For those who don't play car games, you're probably not going to enjoy it as much - read most of the negative reviews - they complain about not being able to handle. I say, GET BETTER!
Graphically, it's very minimalistic isometric style (even the menu) - much like Kill The Bad Guy - and it works most of the time, except your car can get hidden behind building at times: this is probably the only bit of frustration that could have been avoided had they designed it so buildings get translucent when the car is behind them.
Sounds work - again, very minimalistic, but they work - and the engine sounds are unique as well, not all boring same-as.
Physics are pretty good, and the cars all handle different - some more different than others - you will want to experiment to find which one fits you best (I really liked the Hoonivan).
The only real cons I have are the aforementioned inability to see cars behind buildings, and the listed retail price (I got it for $1, but it's probably worth $5, not the price listed on Steam). I've played about 7hrs, and seen all there is, the only thing to keep me coming back is to increase my scores on levels.
Conclusion: great little drift game, definitely worth playing. It's in a bundle right now, so snap it up.
EDIT: I thought I'd mention it IS playable with keyboard, but A LOT easier to play with a controller, because you really need throttle control (like most car games).

I have played a bit and I think I understand enough to write a review. Here's the skinny:
First off you don't have to pay a dime for anything to enjoy this game. It has, by far, the best payment model of any free to play game i've played. You don't have to spend a dime on anything. Ever. Everything sold as DLC is also sold in the shop.
This does not mean that buying DLC is bad. You get some real bonuses for buying DLC. The number one bonus being that if you buy a DLC package then your rod/reel can never fully break. Second most important bonus is that you can repair most of the DLC items with in game credits instead of in game gold.
Now, before you trip on the Gold/Cash thing this is where the payment model shines. You can earn gold in game and it's not hard or impossible.
Flat out, not a pay to win by any means of the phrase.

+ Local Co-op Splitscreen (A game that lets you couch co-op? What a rarity nowadays)
+ Fun, arcadey gameplay
+ Diverse weapon selection
+ 4 classes with their own pros and cons and specific playstyles and weapon selections
+ Plenty of missions to kill bugs in
+ 5 difficulties that the game entices you into trying: Easy, Normal, Hard, Hardest, Inferno
+ Gain more powerful weapons on higher difficulties
+ Giant mecha that can be operated by the player
+ Diverse vehicles for Air Raider class that are made either for solo play, team play, or both
+ Skin-of-your-teeth moments abound
+ Silly ragdolls
+/- Throwaway, drag-along "plot" that exists purely to introduce the next ridiculous enemy and give you reason to shout "EDF!"
+/- Some classes require the faintest amount of care and skill to use effectively (Fencer - Dash-canceling; Air Raider - Getting into the vehicle fast enough to prevent dying/Knowing what vehicles are best for certain missions; Wing Diver - Stop running into giant insect hordes with no energy management)
+/- Some missions are absolute hell for specific classes
+/- Odd spikes in difficulty [PERSONALLY] (I'm looking at you, Monster Party)
----- Armor grinding; Will explain below
- Online multiplayer has almost died out; You can find a small handful of games that aren't in moonrunes
- EDF 5 does not have confirmed PC release :(
- Some dodgy weapon balancing hither and thither
- The game ends at some point and you will eventually have to stop playing
EDF works fantastic with either controller or KB+M, which is something you might not expect from Japs when porting to PC if you've played some of the more notorious ones. It's non-serious, all-fun as you shoot explosives at giant ants and giant spiders and watch them all go boom. There's not much to say, personally. There is a fair amount of skill that you can use on certain classes, but in the end, it's at its best when played to kill time with friends. It's fantastic to binge on because of the fun it offers, and it's great on those offdays when you say to yourself "Man, what do I even want to do today?"
"Armor" is your character's health. Armor is gained by a ratio; Each class has a different ratio as well. Without drawing the actual numbers, 2 boxes of Armor = 1 actual Armor for Ranger, the "basic" class that carries over from other EDF games. 4 boxes of Armor = 1 actual Armor for Wing Diver, the mobile and squishy class that focuses on manuevering through the air. These boxes of Armor have a
of dropping from all enemies in the game. Other things that can potentially drop are: Small Healthpack, Large Healthpack, and Weapon Boxes. Armor gain is not affected by difficulty. This means that you gain the same amount of armor per crate regardless of difficulty. 2 crates = 1 Ranger armor whether Easy or Inferno. You start off with a measly amount of armor, which is to be expected. You are recommended to have ~5000 armor for Inferno, roughly. Armor gain does not transfer to other classes; If you have been playing Ranger throughout the whole campaign and got 5000 armor somehow, your untouched Wing Diver will still have ~200 armor that you will have to gain all over again; probably by going through the Normal/Easy difficulty campaign all over again, but with this class.
This isn't necessarily bad; It encourages you to keep playing the game with these different classes until you gain both familiarity with the class as well as sufficient gear and armor. The problem is that armor farming is a slow process even at its most grindiest. And you have to do this with every single class. It is the most unfun part of an otherwise great game. The only workarounds are farming specific missions or using a cheating tool to modify your armor; obviously, neither of these are great. It is simply a sad reality.
Yet still, the game shines as a prime example of how to make a fun game in all other aspects. There's not much balancing for multiplayer and even singleplayer can seem a bit iffy sometimes. It takes experimentation to know what weapons to use on what missions against what enemies, but it's not impossible to understand. Sadly, some weapons are really mediocre compared to others and may tempt you to use these overall better choices, but this is not the whole case.

Plants vs. Zombies is a simple tower defence game that has you collecting sun to plant flowers, vegetables, and fruit plants in a 5x5 grid to combat the invading zombie hordes. Each plant has its strengths and weaknesses just as the zombies do. With a limited number of seed packets, you need to figure out what plants you will need to take in with you to take down specific zombies. For example, Headband Zombies will jump over your defences so you’ll need a Tall-nut for it to faceplant into or a Magnet-shroom to take away its metal pole vaulting stick. The game slowly introduces you to each unique plant and zombie type along the way so you are never overwhelmed with your options. The game likes to throw fun mini-games and puzzles at you every few levels to break up its pacing.
The main story mode will set you back roughly 3-4 hours while the puzzles and mini-games will take another 2-3 hours. After the main story is completed an advanced story mode is unlocked with one of the game’s characters picking some plants for you, giving you a harder time trying to figure out how to use the seeds given to you to combat the waves of zombies. If you’re a casual player, i’d recommend playing through the story mode once. If you like a challenge, i’d recommend playing through both story modes and finishing all the puzzles and mini-games.

This game is not for everyone, but if you like trying out experimental game concepts and ideas there is a gem here to be had.  If, however, you are looking for a fully fleshed out game with lots of immersion, choices, quests, story or depth then this game is probably one to pass by.
Perhaps the king of casual gamers, there is some satisfaction in the mindless left, right, left action which results in the demise of hordes and hordes of baddies.  And . . . that's it, that's the whole game.  Move your mouse to the left of the screen your hero moves left, move it to the right and he moves right.  Stop on screen at a shop and you can tweek a few stats: attack, crit, armor and speed.  You play through ten levels each with a "boss" (more on that later) at the end, and after the tenth level is completed the difficulty slightly increases and you replay through all the same levels over again.  This continues on until you get bored and stop playing, or for many, until you reach level 100 and get the last Steam achievement.
Why this works:  Mindless fun can be fun!  Plus you do get to plow through hordes and hordes of enemies in mere seconds.  And you can watch TV while you play and only glance back at the computer from time to time while grinding to that level 100.
However, what doesn't really work is that there isn't any real game after that.  It really feels like a good first level for a much grander game, but it just stops there and then repeats itself.  Even with the ability to up skills I soon discovered that I really only had to up my armor skill to be able to beat any levels that momentarily detered me.  Also, bosses were pointless.  They aren't stronger than the other monsters in the level, at least not by enough of a margin to be noticable, so if you can sail through the level, the boss will be a one hit kill.  Plus there were a few balancing issues I came across; either I could sail through the level without a hitch including the boss, or I was beaten by the first three monsters I encounted.  There were no inbetween challenging levels.  I could either beat the level outright, or I repeatedly died and had to go out and replay the previous level until I had accrued enough gold to buy enough armor to sail through the next one.
Then the main trouble I had while trying to level my hero up to 100 was that the levels never got any longer.  So, most levels are easy to beat in about 15 to 20 seconds, but you need to really grind the experience to level up your knight, meaning there were many times when I inadvertently finished a level instead of swinging back and forth to gain experience for my guy.  And finishing a level in only a matter of seconds means that the load times to go back to the main menu and then back into the levels seem much much longer than they actually are.  It would have been really helpful to lengthen the levels as they got "harder" then to just have them be exactly the same every time.
I should mention that everytime you beat the 10th level boss you save a miner who then goes and mines gold for you, apparently even when you are not playing the game.  While this could have been a charming aspect of the game it actual was 100% pointless.  Most people will achieve 80% of the achievements in the first hour and then it becomes a grind fest for the last 2 leveling up achievements which really only take 2 or 3 more hours.  So, having a person mine gold while you don't have the game running isn't neccessary as you will probably play through the whole game in your first session.  Also, your gold maxes out at something like 999,999 or so which really only takes 40 to 60 seconds to accrue while playing in game, so the slow pecking away the miners do to get you 20,000 gold after 10 mins isn't even noticable, or needed.  Perhaps some other system of freeing different townsfolk to collect would have been a better end-of-level reward.
All in all, I really did have fun playing this game, but its limitations means it really is for the experimental gamer.  If the previous description of the game did not deter you, then by all means I encourage you to purchase this game and try it out for yourself, because it really has a unique game design to it, but just know ahead of time that it isn't going to give you much more than that.

There is nothing hidden in the gameplay of this game.  What you see is what you get.  Repeatedly used models of a small number of enemy types used over and over again to create massive battles.  Despite that, the gameplay is very addictive for those who enjoy the destruction and havoc during each mission.  The game has a large assortment of weapons for each class, all of which need to be unlocked by playing progressively harder missions.  This ends up being a very long grind to get the weapons you want, but the missions are such pure mayhem and chaos that while some missions might feel similar, varied level design keeps the gameplay fresh.
On the technical side, the port is very solid, though the keyboard controls feel VERY shoehorned in.  They work, but not as well as a controller does, especially the fencer and air raider.  These two classes have an abundance of weapons that need to be finely adjusted, but to give them weight, their aim is slow to move.  This makes you FEEL as though you are aiming an enormous cannon, but while the controller just holds the stick upwards, the mouse has to continually move upwards, and most likely be picked up and placed lower on the mousepad to continue moving up.
Anyway, I'm ranting.  Expect nothing more than the trailers, campy one-liners and scifi tropes included, but expect a nigh-endless amount (despite about 95 missions, online only missions included), especially with friends (limit is four).

Remember how fun and awesome Resident Evil 4 was?
The terrible plot....the awful one liners from Leon..... How terribly written the dialogue was between characters....and the silliness/charm of the Merchant, or the interactions with Ada/Louis/Ashley?
No time for fun now....we have to be gritty and serious....this all has to be taken very seriously, because resident evil traditionally has never been tongue and cheek right?
Resident Evil 5, feels like a big step backward from the foundations that the previous game left Capcom to work with.
Whilst the engine itself is fairly nice to play in, and the framerate is very good consistantly (in fact, years ago, it was the first major title I got to see in 60fps+ and I found it impressive for the time compared to how well most other games ran).
The problems lie in 2 different places, and it is odd...
.............Some spoilers ahead............
Firstly the Content itself....
This games story, and the motivations for the antagonists ((strange looking white guy, some lady who works with him? (I think, or it maybe a partnership of oppertunity?) and Wesker)), are incredibly vague. Whilst it doesn't bother me too much on Weskers part as he's the mega evil series antagonist who does a lot in the background we don't see anyway, the other two antagonists have a lot to do with the "story" of why Chris is running around doing what he is doing, and all we get are vague references to "sample" and "outbreaks" blah blah blah. Whilst in some cases this could be considered standard resi, it was also done with characters we liked, had a charisma or charm to them, and with amusing voice acting, fans of the series can accept that. Similar screenplay coming from generic BSAA meat heads we've never met before, or flat boring antagonists whose voice actors sound bored doesn't cut it.
We are also shamelessly treated to some "important" "plot" points regarding Jill, but they are dangled in front of us in a way that felt a bit strange, Chris having memory flashbacks (honestly I never thought he was that deep) to an incident involving Jill that seems to have some importance as to why she turns up in this game....the you realised soon after the game was released that Chris was in fact watching the trailer footage for the upcoming DLC in his flashback *smirks*.
The only parts of this game where characters had any charisma about them, were scenes with Wesker. Honestly, if it were not for Wesker, I wouldn't have finished this game even once, it would have been too flat and boring. I will also genuinely concede that Wesker shouting "CHRIIIIIIISSSSSSSSS!!!" is possibly one of the most laugh out loud moments any resi game has given me, but it isn't much worth the hours upon hours of boring you have to put up with to get there.
Now the second major point I would like to bring up is the Single/multiplayer aspect.
Everything i've said about this game refers to mostly playing it with a friend online, and we must have finished that game several times together, and it was fun, though mostly for the stupid things you do ingame/say to eachother whilst playing with someone you know.
I can't really say much about the single player other than when I last played it with the intention of finishing it on my own on a harder difficulty, the computer controlled ally was so broken. They wouldn't do anything they were supposed to which made certain sections of the game impossible to progress through. It is possible it might be fixed now, it has been a long time since I last went through this game start to finish.
I did in a bundle, buy the DLC story... it was cheap, and I was curious, but honestly, I played maybe like 10mins of it before getting bored and just playing the HD remake of 1 instead. Since resident evil 1 / Code Veronica, Chris Redfield seems to be on the steroids and increased his hunk factor by 400%..he is more muscle than man....twisted and..(hah).
When you add up and consider various elements of the resident evil franchise, all I can really think of is this...
Leon...Resident Evil 4....Killing a chicken...equipping its egg to throw at someone...somehow doesn't feel out of place with the previous 3 games in mind. Everything in Resident evil 5 feels out of place when thinking about the previous titles. In my minds eye, I can see the progression from Leon in res2, to leon in res4. What I fail to grasp (in the context of this game) is the small concept of young adults who entered the Spencer Mansion all those years ago and had a small, narrow story adventure about zombies, now being world biological terrorist fighting squad trying to tie in ideas from a bad movie franchise, with crappy rail shooter sections thrown in for apparently "why not?"which all concludes with a fight in a volcano.
I did not enjoy this product as a "resident evil" title.

The influence from classic NES games like Castlevania, Ducktales, Mega Man, Super Mario Bros. 3, and Zelda II blend perfectly to make this game. Even though it bears similarities to those games, its execution feels brand new as opposed to a straight rip off. Is the Shovel Knight an Perfectly Realized Ultimate Savior and Most Supreme Indie Game of All Time™?
Is this the must have for everybody?
Is hype real?
No. Definitive no. But that doesn't mean that this game is bad. It's pretty far from it actually. Shovel Knight is an extremely well polished 8-bit retro throwback, that checks all the objectives of great 80s platformer. Visuals are pretty spot on, sountrack is not bad and game really plays well. Unfortuntely it misses a massive points for lack of originality. This is basically an "Mega Man with a shovel", at least the core gameplay that is. Gimmicks are from MM. Character speed and jump height are from MM. Enemies are heavily inspired from MM. Even some particular screens of the levels are pretty copy-pasted. I would forget this completely, but unlike other recent platformers that are wrongly accused for lack of originality, Shovel Knight could really use some more charm and unique flavors in gameplay and presentation. it doesn't mix many concepts and doesn't add anything new. It realizes one concept and nothing else. Fortunely this concept is realized pretty well.
This game is also not for casual players. While this isn't particularly hard game, it offers no difficulty settings and 80s One Hit Death Spikes are plenty, sometimes amping up frustration. Luckly those moments are not that prominent in comparison to the whole game. Otherwise it goes smooth with 60FPS, clevel boss designs and satisfing enough gameplay.
No. Hype isn't real. I played some better platformers recently, but Shovel Knight is still a not bad experience. It's pretty much worth $15, but I would suggest taking it, like me, with at least -33% discount. Be a fan of platformers and don't expect miracles and you should be fine.

There is nothing hidden in the gameplay of this game.  What you see is what you get.  Repeatedly used models of a small number of enemy types used over and over again to create massive battles.  Despite that, the gameplay is very addictive for those who enjoy the destruction and havoc during each mission.  The game has a large assortment of weapons for each class, all of which need to be unlocked by playing progressively harder missions.  This ends up being a very long grind to get the weapons you want, but the missions are such pure mayhem and chaos that while some missions might feel similar, varied level design keeps the gameplay fresh.
On the technical side, the port is very solid, though the keyboard controls feel VERY shoehorned in.  They work, but not as well as a controller does, especially the fencer and air raider.  These two classes have an abundance of weapons that need to be finely adjusted, but to give them weight, their aim is slow to move.  This makes you FEEL as though you are aiming an enormous cannon, but while the controller just holds the stick upwards, the mouse has to continually move upwards, and most likely be picked up and placed lower on the mousepad to continue moving up.
Anyway, I'm ranting.  Expect nothing more than the trailers, campy one-liners and scifi tropes included, but expect a nigh-endless amount (despite about 95 missions, online only missions included), especially with friends (limit is four).

RE5 is still one of my favorite Resident Evil games in the series.
While it is different from the original trilogy, going with the same 3rd person view approach as Resident evil 4 but having next to no puzzles in the game, the action and mechanics behind the levels are still interesting. It's especially good in co-op mode as this is where the games development focus was which unfortunately leaves many flaws for single player, particularly on the hardest difficulty 'professional' where the AI will get itself killed in 1 hit constantly without any regard for thier own safety.
The storyline is interesting and the cinematics are impressive to watch although they do stray a bit from the typical resident evil style, heading more into an action genre. This game finds a sweet spot balance between survival horror and constant action but may not please people who wish for more or less of one or the other.
The game features a progressive upgrade system similar to Resident Evil 4 where you find treasures and gold, then use them to purchase new weapons or upgrades for weapons. You can store more than enough weapons ammunition or items at the inventory management screen between missions and this inventory will remain with you through your entire journey through the difficulties. Starting on easy means you will be better equipped when you reach higher difficulties.
The game has a good amount of content that you can get a lot of hours from and was very well optimized making it well worth the pricetag at release. Now it is a steal if you have never played it.
While the game does lack the ability to move/strafe while shooting, I couldn't class that as a negative as I found the game to be very well balanced and designed around the lack of that mechanic.

Ah, the Resident Evil franchise: a series of games which changes genres faster than I can type "zombie."
Zombie.
See?! It just changed genres! What the hell! I was being chased by a bald guy in a trench coat earlier this morning, and now I'm chasing a longcoat-wearing blondie who wears sunglasses indoors!
But what did you expect from a name like "Resident Evil"? It was acceptable with the first game, since it took place in a mansion. Then they moved to a whole city, and then a country; now it's set in the African continent, and we really should've gotten the memo with the second game.
So, Resident Evil 5. What's new? Well, this is the first RE title with co-op; which means that you better play this with a friend, or suffer the consequences of an unreliable AI, which serves the same purpose as Lydia from Skyrim: carrying extra baggage. Do you remember how to conserve ammo in RE4? You either run through the ganado horde, or stagger them with a bullet, then come up close with the knife, right? Now there are new melee mechanics, where you can deal damage if you're close to a staggered (or grounded) enemy. Thanks to that, the knife has been relegated to the role of box cutter. The manual save typewriters and the item box had been replaced by a checkpoint system and end-chapter shop respectively. Overall, it's almost the same as RE4, with fine-tuned mechanics to support the faster-paced, action-oriented gameplay.
And there you have it.

Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood continues right where Assassin's Creed II finished, so if you haven't played Assassin's Creed II I'd highly recommend playing that game first. Not only was it a good game, but it's almost essential at this point to play it so you can understand the story. This may not seem important, but for me the story is the most intriguing element to the entire franchise.
The gameplay continues to improve game-on-game, but it's pretty much the same mechanic we've seen since the first Assassin's Creed game. Sure they've removed the terribly rigid design to the missions where you MUST scale this tower before you can do anything else, and I'm personally grateful they did this. However, overall the gameplay isn't that amazing. It's fun, sure, but at the same time it's played it's course now. Don't get me wrong, you can still scale the towers to remove the fog of war, but now it's optional.
In fact it works well within what is slowly becoming a very sandbox style world, and this is another area of the game I'm starting to enjoy with each Assassin's Creed game. Ubisoft seem to be aware of what people enjoyed from Assassin's Creed II and disliked from Assassin's Creed and have done a good job of doing more of the same, and removing the offending elements of gameplay.
Gone are the insane amount of collectibles, and instead we have more Tombs/Lairs to explore, Glyphs to discover and solve and an entire city to manage. While these elements aren't essential to complete the game, and at times they don't seem to to do much to the story at all (and I personally found the city management side of the game to be over before it begun), it's nice to see that there are options there for people who wish to slow things down and invest into the Assassin's Creed world.
It's not all roses though, there are a few elements to Brotherhood that confused me. I'm hooked into the story, I want to know more, I want it to expand and progress, and sadly Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood never truly felt like it got going. It felt that it was one long prelude into Assassin's Creed: Revelations, with most of the Memory Segments feeling more like tutorials for the new gameplay mechanics or refreshing into franchise staple gameplay mechanics (most of which any Assassin's Creed fan would hopefully already be aware of). It's a minor fault, and if anything it's something of a Ubisoft Trademark to have excessive gameplay hints/tips/tutorials throughout the game.
It doesn't really distract from the game, but it does slow down the buzz and adrenaline that has built up after the huge climax to Assassin's Creed II. Now that I've finished the game, I'm not too concerned about the lull as I can fool myself enough to believe it was perhaps intentional pacing to bring you backdown to build you back up for Brotherhood's ending (which was decent).
Yet, I'm still left feeling 'what really happened' during Ezio's memory segments. I know who the main target was within the story, but you have so little interaction with them directly that you don't really focus on them (unlike in Assassin's Creed II where The Spaniard is referenced and featured in most segments).
Sadly there is one element to the game that is lagging behind Assassin's Creed II and that's the soundtrack. I was convinced it was a new composer as it just felt alien compared to the previous work of Jasper Kydd. I just couldn't connect to it.
Also, once again the character modles have changed ever so slightly but strangely noticably. A minor point of annoyance.
Overall Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood is a fun game, and somewhat fast paced (almost to the point where it feels like it's over before it even begun). If you're hooked into the series by this point I'd recommend buying Brotherhood as it continues the story in an easy fun game. If you didn't really enjoy Assassin's Creed II, I think it's best you bow out of the series now and leave Brotherhood, as it's more of the same.
The characters are slowly developing, and the plot is thickening. I also know that some people don't enjoy the 'future tech' side of the game, namely the areas outside of Ezio (such as being Desmond and the whole Animus side of world). I personally enjoy the mix of history and Sci-Fi within the game, so I don't find this to be a problem; however for those who do find it a problem there is a somewhat large/significant portion of Brotherhood that centres around the 'adventures of Desmond', so again it might be best to avoid Assassin's Creed Brotherhood.
