Shovel Knight gets a lot of praise, which is not for no reason. Many would call it 'nostalgic', but I personally think it's great in it's own way; aside from the classic graphics and recognisable soundtracks many will recognise from the bit-era.
In short:
GOOD
+ Nice ol' iconic platforming, defeating your enemies, aquiring ways to defeat said enemies... a great formula done almost perfectly and with a bunch of new engaging ideas!
+ Level design and atmosphere. It's a small game, but filled to the brim with personality. You'll see a lot of old themes like the 'halloween/undead' stage and the always hated ice-stage, but also a lot of fresh mechanics and themes for such a simple platformer.
+ Bosses deserve their own mention. I always love games with good bosses. I know many feel the same, so here ya go. Definite plus.
+ Though simple, the story is actually pretty intruiging. You might see all the twists coming, but they still do their own original thing with it. Which is why I like the Shovel Knight and Shield Knight characters quite a lot. It's extremely solid, and open for many new stories to build onto it.
+ Soundtrack also deserves it's own mention. Though all the iconic sound effects are the way we know them, the music really is the gigantic lovely cherry on top.
+ There are multiple ways to play the game to give yourself more challenge, and the game also comes with a few achievements to hint at some of these other plastyles!
NOT SO GOOD / COULD BE IMPROVED
- I played it on a keyboard but I admit it would probably be FAR nicer with a controller. So if you don't have one the controls might be a bit annoying.
- Relatively short. It has pretty good replayability, but somehow you still feel like they could've done so much more. Especially when you look at the Mario3-esque overworld map going on.
(Scratch that, with Plague and Spectre now on the roster it doesn't feel so short any more)
- Instant-death spikes? Yes. But it's about the worst kind; the sideways ones. Slip one pixel to much to the left at a snail pace? Dead. It's reaaally something platformers should abolish for some more creative ideas. Dying to a boss at a difficult fight is challenging and fun. Doing an entire section of platforming without a scratch and dying right before a checkpoint? Frustrating.
- Though I earlier praised the music. It tends to change to another version EVERYtime you enter another section of a town or something. Normally, this is great, gives every section it's own feel. But here it's actually taking away the atmosphere it's supposed to give because it keeps switching every 4 seconds when you're running through the towns.
And that's basically it aside from some personal thoughts. I could be getting a little bit ahead of myself by saying Shovel Knight, the character, would be perfect lined up to the likes of Mario and Sonic. If only in extremely iconic design and the world his character lives in. Extremely simple, but very recognisable and engaging.  For example, I wouldn't be surprised to see him or Shield Knight in Smash Bros, things like that. I'd personally love to see far more of this, so I hope the team is planning on expanding this fun world of knighthood and I recommend this to any one who's up for a good old school challenge!
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EDIT FOR PLAGUE OF SHADOWS UPGRADE:
Instead of just being a new playable character, Plague Knights gets his own complete story with both old and new characters part of the play. Some things remain the same like choosing what level you want to do from the map screen, going to town to get your upgrades and tons of places to explore to find hidden treasures. There are multiple challenges to complete and most of the enemies and room layouts will look familiar to you.
Plague Knight as a character, however, is completely different. His method of attack is indirect, using projectiles and his jumps are way more acrobatic. This might sound like he is more powerful, and therfore easier to play but nothing could be further from the truth. Plague Knight is so different from Shovel Knight, you will probably have to unlearn all your muscle memory and on top of that have to deal with far tougher jumps and stunts to get through the levels.
If you manage to be patient and get good at controlling him however, he might become one of the most fun-to-play character you've ever played in a 2D sidescrolling platform game. Time his jumps right, and he can blast & fly through the levels at an amazing pace, so he's obviously well-loved by the speedrunning crowd this game has. On top of that he does not find 'relics' to aid him in his adventures, but rather you can mak crazy mixes of different potions to make your own favourite secondary weapon depending on the level you want to do.
All in all. This is the best free update I have EVER AQUIRED for ANY GAME ever. I'm not sure if I could put a price on this, but I would definately pay another 20 bucks for something like this. Which is a testament to what an amazing crew the Shovel Knight dev team is.
I, for one, don't think I'll ever master Plague Knight completely. And those final achievements I might never get are painfull for a completinoist like me, but nevertheless I love this everything about this update. Especially the ending <3
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EDIT FOR SPECTRE OF TORMENT UPDATE
Wow. We're getting spoiled here. By this point, this game has increased it's size by about four times what the original game was, and we're still not getting charged extra. If Gabe Newell is the god of gaming, then Yacht Club is our Jezus.
But enough praise to the devs, Spectre of Torment is an update similar to Plague Knight's time in the spotight, but once again with it's own story. This time a bit more grim then the last, as we learn the backstory of the gloomy Spectre Knight who could be called the complete opposite of the jovial Plague Knight. Aside from that you have new characters, new games, new challenges and a whole new character to master.
Spectre Knight plays more similar to our original protagonist Shovel Knight, using direct attacks and also using relics, now called 'curios', as secondary weapons. There's a bit more acrobatics involved then with Shovel Knight, but less then Plague Knight had to deal with. Spectre has his own interesting quirks. His wall scaling, air dashing and ability to grind rails with his scytche all add to another unique adventure.
There are some new enemies, some old. Some old ones with new patterns/abilities, and the adventure once again feel fresh enough to really sink your teeth into. You also now have the complete freedom to choose in what order you do which stage and plenty of replay value if you wish to find more treasure, some secrets or simply want to improve your time or skill.
I do have to mention I've not completely finished this playthrough yet, but I'm confident all that's written here will hold strong. Bless you Yacht Club games, for giving us so much for so little~

Tactical Intervention is a free-to-play Counter-Strike clone (right down to the Source engine) that looks like it was made 15 years ago. Production values are weak even for that time period--part of it is clearly designed to appeal to people with slower computers, and part of it is just bad design. The gameplay is mediocre and fairly imbalanced, with players who paid in or accumulated long hours clearly having an advantage, but the action is fast, constant, and satisfyingly gory in a way that Counter-Strike isn't. Blood sprays around liberally and shotgun kills and other high-powered weapons cause limbs to burst apart.
Teams that utilize basic tactics by always trying to control the high ground/choke points and using spotters to track where the enemy team is moving will win every time. Teams respawn together on a timer so it's relatively easy to stay coordinated without even chatting. Just cover your buddies.
When you reach level 2 you will have enough in-game funbucks to buy about two permanent upgraded items, and after that you will be expected to either buy yet more superior equipment via microtransaction or grind levels for a very long time--so choose wisely. The vast majority of players are not paid in, but those that have paid money are typically about 150% as powerful as a free player. Free-to-play games with a microtransaction system should be smarter than this by now, but Tactical Intervention is not exactly a cutting edge game.
The game's one real highlight is its escort missions, which add in drivable cars with extremely suspect physics and an almost total inability to aim your weapon from inside the vehicle, resulting in total chaos when both teams have to deliver a macguffin to an objective point and kill each other along the way. It's basically a low-rent Counter-Strike Meets Mario Kart and like the rest of the game, it has a certain moronic charm.
If you have a kid who you want to play games with but will be too easily frustrated by Counter-Strike players, or you want to have a night of goofing around with friends who enjoy gaming trainwrecks like this, by all means give Tactical Intervention a try. Otherwise, rest assured this game is bad but amusing.

This game has very nice art and music, but neither of those can save the game itself from being one of the dullest experiences I've ever had.
Gameplay is thus:
1. Enter a level.
2. Hold right. Maybe go back and forth a bit to farm for money and XP.
3. Repeat until monsters are too strong to easily pass.
4. Buy upgrades (+atk damage, +crit chance, +def, +movement speed) at one of the multiple shops in each level(You can't do this on the level select screen). If you don't have enough money, go back to an earlier level and grind for it.
5. Hold right some more.
That's it. There is no end goal. Well, the first time you play, the goal is to kill the dragon at the last level, but you can do that in half an hour, max. After that, you just play through the same levels again at a higher difficulty, and beat the dragon again.
Then you do it again.
And again.
And AGAIN.
NOTHING changes, except the numbers.
Every time you beat the dragon, the game tells you the difficulty has gone up and encourages you to keep playing. However, there's literally no reason to. Defeating the dragon is the only goal given to you, and you've already done that. You've seen the entirety of new content the game has to offer at this point. Why do the same thing over again? Here's a hint: There is no reason. Exit the game.
What about the achievements? Well, the only ones you'll be missing after beating the game once will require you to do the same♥♥♥♥♥♥listed above over and over again for hours. It won't be worth it.
Avoid this game unless you love being bored senseless and then patronized.

I've had tears of joy playing this game to completion, which is a rarity, I will say.
Absolute Drift is a top down, minimalistic stunt driving game. Your goal: become a master drifter, by refining the art of
controlling oversteer and burning rubber.
For the aesthetics: it's low poly, simple graphics, with most buildings and roads left white and untextured. Objects of interest are coloured red, blue or yellow. Your car leaves behind skidmarks wherever it goes, whether you slide or not, which allows for impressive drawings on tarmac, or a nice spiral when you catch some big air.
The soundtrack is a relaxing, upbeat electronic and DnB by Nyte and C41 respectively - which fits the near zen-like atmosphere of the game. Cars have simple, but distinct engine noises, with more subtle transmission whine or turbo flutter.
The gameplay is the purest I've seen in modern driving games. It's you, your car, your skills and the track. Whether free-roaming, doing driftkhanas or mountain drifts, almost everything revolves around getting your back end slideways and very, very smokey. You have a selection of 6 cars to choose from, each performing differently from one another - some are heavier, some are more stable, some are more tail happy. All can be repainted and given a little livery. You'll spend most of your time
drifting in an open-ended hub world, peppered with missions to perform - stuff like "drift between this and this" or "donut around this". Finishing the campaign takes around 1.5 hours, but you also have specific tracks - the aforementioned driftkhanas, mountain drifts and circuit drifts, containing Steam leaderboards that will push you to improve your scores.
Let's not beat around the bush; the game is hard. The handling is intentionally challenging. Unless you're careful, it doesn't matter whether you use the gamepad or the keyboard, you WILL spin out and hit walls, and the game knows it. There are several difficulty settings to pick from, which change how grippy your car is, but above all, mastery of counter-steer, weight transfer, grip limit, torque and gearing is paramount to any decent drifting in this world. This results in one of the most satisfying moments I've ever experienced in videogames: the flow of stringing together perfect drifts through a tight and twisty track, losing as little momentum as possible and rocketing to the top. The execution of the handling is absolutely STELLAR.
The game has finally been upgraded to the Zen Edition, bringing forth a new event type - Midnight Drifts, which are really really challenging! In addition, you have Event Challenges to unlock said Midnight Drifts, REPLAYS and GHOSTS on the tracks! This is the kind of free content that will exponentially boost the game's longevity, even if a level editor or proper multiplayer still don't quite exist yet.
I'd liken this game as the Portal of driving games: a clean art style, a short campaign that doesn't overstay its welcome, if it's not over too quick, a dash of humour and one of the best (top down, minimalistic, very very slideways) driving experiences I've had in my long years of driving/racing games.
Get it ASAP if you like/love cars, but even if you don't it's worth a try for the experience and the challenging but rewarding gameplay.

---Edits for updates can be found below :)---
Shovel Knight gets a lot of praise, which is not for no reason. Many would call it 'nostalgic', but I personally think it's great in it's own way; aside from the classic graphics and recognisable soundtracks many will recognise from the bit-era.
In short:
GOOD
+ Nice ol' iconic platforming, defeating your enemies, aquiring ways to defeat said enemies... a great formula done almost perfectly and with a bunch of new engaging ideas!
+ Level design and atmosphere. It's a small game, but filled to the brim with personality. You'll see a lot of old themes like the 'halloween/undead' stage and the always hated ice-stage, but also a lot of fresh mechanics and themes for such a simple platformer.
+ Bosses deserve their own mention. I always love games with good bosses. I know many feel the same, so here ya go. Definite plus.
+ Though simple, the story is actually pretty intruiging. You might see all the twists coming, but they still do their own original thing with it. Which is why I like the Shovel Knight and Shield Knight characters quite a lot. It's extremely solid, and open for many new stories to build onto it.
+ Soundtrack also deserves it's own mention. Though all the iconic sound effects are the way we know them, the music really is the gigantic lovely cherry on top.
+ There are multiple ways to play the game to give yourself more challenge, and the game also comes with a few achievements to hint at some of these other plastyles!
NOT SO GOOD / COULD BE IMPROVED
- I played it on a keyboard but I admit it would probably be FAR nicer with a controller. So if you don't have one the controls might be a bit annoying.
- Relatively short. It has pretty good replayability, but somehow you still feel like they could've done so much more. Especially when you look at the Mario3-esque overworld map going on.
(Scratch that, with Plague and Spectre now on the roster it doesn't feel so short any more)
- Instant-death spikes? Yes. But it's about the worst kind; the sideways ones. Slip one pixel to much to the left at a snail pace? Dead. It's reaaally something platformers should abolish for some more creative ideas. Dying to a boss at a difficult fight is challenging and fun. Doing an entire section of platforming without a scratch and dying right before a checkpoint? Frustrating.
- Though I earlier praised the music. It tends to change to another version EVERYtime you enter another section of a town or something. Normally, this is great, gives every section it's own feel. But here it's actually taking away the atmosphere it's supposed to give because it keeps switching every 4 seconds when you're running through the towns.
And that's basically it aside from some personal thoughts. I could be getting a little bit ahead of myself by saying Shovel Knight, the character, would be perfect lined up to the likes of Mario and Sonic. If only in extremely iconic design and the world his character lives in. Extremely simple, but very recognisable and engaging.  For example, I wouldn't be surprised to see him or Shield Knight in Smash Bros, things like that. I'd personally love to see far more of this, so I hope the team is planning on expanding this fun world of knighthood and I recommend this to any one who's up for a good old school challenge!
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EDIT FOR PLAGUE OF SHADOWS UPGRADE:
Instead of just being a new playable character, Plague Knights gets his own complete story with both old and new characters part of the play. Some things remain the same like choosing what level you want to do from the map screen, going to town to get your upgrades and tons of places to explore to find hidden treasures. There are multiple challenges to complete and most of the enemies and room layouts will look familiar to you.
Plague Knight as a character, however, is completely different. His method of attack is indirect, using projectiles and his jumps are way more acrobatic. This might sound like he is more powerful, and therfore easier to play but nothing could be further from the truth. Plague Knight is so different from Shovel Knight, you will probably have to unlearn all your muscle memory and on top of that have to deal with far tougher jumps and stunts to get through the levels.
If you manage to be patient and get good at controlling him however, he might become one of the most fun-to-play character you've ever played in a 2D sidescrolling platform game. Time his jumps right, and he can blast & fly through the levels at an amazing pace, so he's obviously well-loved by the speedrunning crowd this game has. On top of that he does not find 'relics' to aid him in his adventures, but rather you can mak crazy mixes of different potions to make your own favourite secondary weapon depending on the level you want to do.
All in all. This is the best free update I have EVER AQUIRED for ANY GAME ever. I'm not sure if I could put a price on this, but I would definately pay another 20 bucks for something like this. Which is a testament to what an amazing crew the Shovel Knight dev team is.
I, for one, don't think I'll ever master Plague Knight completely. And those final achievements I might never get are painfull for a completinoist like me, but nevertheless I love this everything about this update. Especially the ending <3
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EDIT FOR SPECTRE OF TORMENT UPDATE
Wow. We're getting spoiled here. By this point, this game has increased it's size by about four times what the original game was, and we're still not getting charged extra. If Gabe Newell is the god of gaming, then Yacht Club is our Jezus.
But enough praise to the devs, Spectre of Torment is an update similar to Plague Knight's time in the spotight, but once again with it's own story. This time a bit more grim then the last, as we learn the backstory of the gloomy Spectre Knight who could be called the complete opposite of the jovial Plague Knight. Aside from that you have new characters, new games, new challenges and a whole new character to master.
Spectre Knight plays more similar to our original protagonist Shovel Knight, using direct attacks and also using relics, now called 'curios', as secondary weapons. There's a bit more acrobatics involved then with Shovel Knight, but less then Plague Knight had to deal with. Spectre has his own interesting quirks. His wall scaling, air dashing and ability to grind rails with his scytche all add to another unique adventure.
There are some new enemies, some old. Some old ones with new patterns/abilities, and the adventure once again feel fresh enough to really sink your teeth into. You also now have the complete freedom to choose in what order you do which stage and plenty of replay value if you wish to find more treasure, some secrets or simply want to improve your time or skill.
I do have to mention I've not completely finished this playthrough yet, but I'm confident all that's written here will hold strong. Bless you Yacht Club games, for giving us so much for so little~

Not much has actually changed in this version of Assassin’s Creed. Ezio has most of his weapons from the beginning with a few slight tweaks including stronger poison, parachute, poison darts (which are a lot of fun to shoot at the enemies by the way), a crossbow and a heavy sheath that allows you to carry larger weapons instead of having to pick them up and drop them. The game is still a free running action adventure sandbox game, but there is no more emphasis on the guilds and a new mechanic in which allows Ezio to train new assassins that he can call and use whenever, with a limit of course.
When you destroy the Borgia towers, I will explain the Borgia later, you can train one assassin per tower for a total of 13 assassins. The player can then send these assassins on missions in order to level them up to what this game calls master assassins. A nice aspect of this is that when there are a lot of enemies you can call in some assassin’s and they easily can take care of the them, take note, it was a whole lot of fun calling in all 7 that I could at a time.
One more change between these two iterations is the combo and fighting system. In Brotherhood you can now dual wield allowing a lot more options during a fight. They have added a whole bunch of new finishing moves and combos to your combat repertoire. There is a lot less bugs in this game as well though I was playing it long after the release so they could have easily patched it by now.

The story continues where AC2 left off. Ezio returns home and decides that his days as an assassin are done and wonders if he should have killed  Pope Rodrigo Borgia. Shortly after, Monteriggioni is attacked by Cesare(pronounced Ches – er – á) Borgia (Son of the Pope) and Mario Auditore is killed in the process. Ezio decides to return to Rome and rebuild the Assassin’s Guild/Brotherhood (hey look the name of the game) and take down the Borgia threat. Eventually after about 4 years of destroying Borgia strongholds, resources, and the like, he takes them out of power and discovers the location of the Apple of Eden that was taken from Leonardo da Vinci.
The whole reason for Desmund to follow this time period of Ezio’s life is in order to find the location of the Apple of Eden themselves and the Grand Temple. The characters in this game are a lot stronger than in the AC2; in fact the Pope’s kids even have an incestuous relationship that drives Cesare in trying to conquer all of Italy. These characters were all based on actual historic people which makes the story even more compelling.

I didn’t talk much about controls in the last review so I figured I should make a mention of how this game is played on PC. A lot of the controls rely on a mix of  4 or 5 different keys. While in combat and locked onto an enemy, if you hold the right mouse button down you will parry an attack. However right after you parry, if you click the left mouse button you proceed to do a counter attack which (unless the enemy is especially good at defending against) will do a finishing move that will kill that enemy.
If immediately after your finishing move you click the left mouse button again and a direction, you can do another finishing move that will continue until you either miss or run out of enemies you can perform the move on, this is called a chain attack.  Also, using ‘Q’  allows you to change your weapons and pressing spacebar while holding the right mouse button will kick your enemies. When you are in free run mode, right mouse does a sort of fast run and holding space allows you to scale walls and move faster up said walls. The shift key allows you to drop while climbing and if you are falling, it also allows you to catch a ledge and stop. These are most of the standard controls apart from ‘wasd’ to move around and mouse to look around.

As for the graphics they are still very nice, even for a 2-3 year old game and are a slight improvement over the second game. On top of that, the architecture of the buildings and the design of Rome was very well done and close to that of what Rome might have been like in the early 16th century. The sound and voice acting is still top notch and is over looked in a game like this where the voice actors have to try and use strong accents and mix the languages between English, Old Italian and French.
Overall this is a much improved game, however it felt to me like the story just didn’t stick with me as well as AC2 or Revelations (which was my favorite out of the trilogy).

This game is so much ♥♥♥♥ing fun if one of two requirements are met; 1. if everyone has a mic and 2. if everyone speaks the same language.
As I am from the US and from the west coast, the times I can play this game and have a blast are during the day. After 11pm the matchmaking starts to get weird. Can still be fun, but I tend to run into more people who aren't using mics, or who don't speak english. It's not the worst thing, it's just not as fun. The fun part is lying to people and pretending you are not infected, or figuring out who is.
In my short time with the game I have only played with one griefer and he called me out as infected right away because the rest of the guys were in a group. I don't know why they thought they would. Maybe grinding xp. It's dumb. For the most part I get some really good games going.
So far this is the best multiplayer experience I've had all year. I wish I would have discovered it sooner.
Just be sure to have a mic before jumping in, or else you are going to wonder where all the fun is.
Before I forget, there are a lot of interesting mechanical ideas at play here as well. The respawn system is tough to get your head around at first, but makes total sense after a few matches. Also the way items work is pretty innovated. You have to solve short challenges to get the item in question and they can be stolen. The blood mechanic is fun and hearing someone gulf blood while seeing two people walk out of the room leads to interesting, these two are infected, scenarios.
I've convinced everyone in the lobby to murder and execute someone because I heard them drinking blood. As he leaves the game he starts telling us how wrong we are. Turns out we are and still have to deal with two infected.  Then we can flip it and convince them all to execute someone and it's one less for you to kill before the innocent players make it to the end.  It's a game full of stories. It's so ♥♥♥♥ing great.  I am so stoke as well because the playerbase is growing everyday since the f2p move.
Your mileage may vary depending on if you have a mic and how comfortable you are talking to strangers. It's so good though.
edit:  Also sometimes you will join a game where everyone is grouped up and on discord talking to each other, so you are just in game talking, but with no responses. It relies to heavily on voice chat and other people to be ridiculous fun. For the most part i get 1 bad game for every 10 play if I am playing during the peak period. As soon as it's too late, or too early and people stop speaking english and or using mics, the game loses a lot of it's luster. Still worth a try.

Make it so you don't fight the same boss 45 times (yes, 45), make it less grindy in the later levels, add more equipment/stat options (Right now it's str/crit/def/spd and only def matters after a while), add mini-games, survival mode, anything to break up the monotony of doing the same thing 45 times.  Just so happens I paid $0.25 for this and I still wouldn't recommend it.  For achievement hunters though, if you're willing to brave the monotony it's not too hard to level up your speed, crank it up and go back and forth for a few hours.

There are no tutorials, the game explains itself through level design.  There is no hand-holding, there's just you and what skills you can bring with you.  There is no level or equipment grind, no gear to make your life easier and no cheap tricks to win the day.  Much like the games of old, it's all on you to make it to the right side of the screen.
This game embodies everything that made the NES classics the NES classics.  The music, the air-tight controls, the aesthetics and the sometimes brutal, skill-based difficulty, and even the "menu lag" that was commonplace because of a lack of available frames to make the menu look to be opening smoothly.
If you're a fan of skill-based platformers, or a veteran of the bygone eras when games like Castlevania, Metroid, Zelda and Mario were the undisputed champions of the CRT screen, you will find absolutely nothing here to be disappointed by.  This game is the "Golden Age" of NES platforming in its rawest form, and even the achievements will keep you hunting for that perfect playthrough in ways you'll find unusual and challenging, extending your playtime with more than just a frustrating, pointless collection-fest.

This game has some issues. I haven't played much of the game, but these issues are clear and apparent within the first few minutes of gameplay.
The tutorial goes from peaceful control learning... To suddenly throwing you into the gameplay at a super-fast pace and you dying. That's okay... for some people. I'm one of those kinds of people, but not everyone is.
Secondly, the game's SUPA TECHNO LIGHTING screws with the gameplay. The effects hide an enemy somewhere and then you die.
By the way... The nice British narrator swears every time you die. He says t**, a**, and a number of other things. This is utter mindless garbage. Swearing is OK, but please make an option to NOT have it. Some menus even have curse words like d*** right on them (Peaceful mode says "Throw in your god d*** towel." Are you joking me? Nothing lets you know this game has that. Nothing. The game looks fine for kids, the tutorial is fine, then the game decides to showcase lots of cursing. The issue I have with this is that there is no "noswear" option, no warning of this, and it is always constant and blatant. Goodness.
Back to the gameplay.
Everything in this game will kill you within a small number of hits. Lasers or ships alike, they will kill you. Instantly, on the lower levels. Once you start upgrading stuff, you will start making it to bosses... Maybe... And then you will die. Half of the "enemies" on screen cannot be killed, half the objects cannot be destroyed. Most stuff you have to drill through. By the way... THE TUTORIAL MENTIONS NONE OF THIS. It gives you a short flying tutorial, and then just says "screw you, MAJOR BLAM BLAM TIME."
And yes. Half the enemies cannot be killed in a twin-stick SHOOTER. This game is more like a runner.
Other gripes. The game's HYPER TECHNO GRAPHICS strike again with performance. On lower cards, it will lag out for a few frames (usually resulting in massive damage / death). No health bar (sure, I'm one hit dead when I start, but could I get a shield bar?). No indication of certain enemies and what they do. Obsessively overintensive lighting that gets in the way (such lighting can be done without messing up the gameplay. Try Beat Hazard Ultra). Swearing is annoying as anything. Narrator repeats the same few lines (and I like his voice! They botched him up.) This game is not only difficult, but also punishing and annoying in almost every way. Game gives no indication or lesson on what will kill you, and with how obsessively good the AI is, you will never know.
So do I recommend this?
If you're a child, no. Lots of swearing.
If you're someone looking to cause carnage... No. The only carnage is your own.
If you're someone who doesn't have the best gfx card. Nope, lag will kill you.
If you're looking for a good experience of skill... Nope, this is just punishing.
The list goes on.
If you are someone willing to put up with a game punishing you for buying it, with constant swearing at you and yelling at your incompetence (half of which is helped by the bad mechanics and lighting) and are willing to die over and over and over and over, with almost no reward... Maybe I could recommend it then.
Seriously... Developers, there are good and fun experiences that are fast-paced. Yours is too fast, and not willing to slow down and get a player pumped before the pain. And honestly, put in some indication that you don't give a darn about cussing, so some kid doesn't have "t**" and "a**" running through their ears constantly, until they say it in front of their parents and then get their games taken away.

Loot Hero is an interesting twist on the "idler" games as you get the feel of one, but it's a bit more interactive...only slightly.  You can handle everything with the mouse (or apparently a gamepad?).  Hold down left mouse button (LMB) on one side to make your character run that way and plow through anything in the way.  Hold LMB on the other side of the screen to go that way (enemies respawn).
Every so often is a "town" or something that tops you off as you get to it and acts as a loot magnet for the section you just ran through.  Here you can upgrade attack power, crit rate, defense, and speed.  Overall pretty simple and rather amusing to get into.  You'll see everything in short order as there are only so many levels before the Dragon.  Kill it and it acts as a reset...sorta.  Everything is supposed to scale from that but eh.
I have about 3.5 hours in the game and got 100%.  You can get the majority of the achievements in the first 40 minutes or so, and really see the game in the first 10 minutes (as others have said).  The rest of the time is just for the really grindy achievements that ended up with a LOT of dragon kills.
Overall I liked it to spend an afternoon on, but that's about it.  Not sure if worth the $2.99 so keep an eye out for a bundle like I did (there have been a few) or decent sale.

Call of Duty: WWII tells the personal story of soldiers forming a tight bond while also delivering a panoramic view of a war where the cause was good but the fighting was brutal.The squad fights through a dozen horrific battles in the single-player campaign. Each one is like its own nightmare. You crawl up Omaha Beach through withering fire. You drive a jeep through enemy lines. You face an artillery ambush that shatters the trees above you. You learn to stick with your comrades and make the ultimate sacrifices for them. During the battles, you are called upon to do heroic actions, like dragging a fallen soldier to safety, capturing enemies instead of shooting them, or escorting a little girl away from the fighting. Such acts of humanity take place against the backdrop of a war that was brutal in almost every way, from the collateral damage on civilians to the mistrust it bred among the conquered populations.
The return to World War II has slowed the pace of multiplayer. You have time to think about your survival, to take your shots, and to hide behind cover when necessary. This is good for players with rusty reflexes.
There are also more ways to practice to get better. In the Headquarter social hub, you can play one-on-one challenges and practice how to use Scorestreaks or weapons. All of that means that you’ll have a better experience as you go from noob to a veteran.
War Mode stands out in particular because you aren’t just out for the kills anymore. Like Electronic Arts’ Battlefield shooters, War has multiple objectives that you have to take in order to win. Each match has two halves, and you switch sides at halftime. To succeed in this match type, each player must fulfill a crucial role. The emphasis isn’t on the kill-death ratio at all. It’s the best part of multiplayer because it forces players to find and fulfill a role in order to win.

TLDR:
Campaign- fun but short
Multiplayer- fun if you get past stg and bar spam and if you play more than TDM/DOM
Zombies- dumbed down from treyarch but still very entertaining
The single player for this game is very short and can sometimes be very hard to control but it is a very fun campaign, keep in mind that you don't go through the same types of missions as earlier cod games set in World War 2 in this game you only fight on the western front instead of goin around through all parts of the war like in World at War.
The multiplayer is extremely fun with having sunk over 90 hours into it and being at this moment 3rd prestige this game still seems to be thriving with peek player counts at around 15,000 players most days and the low end at around 7,000 players, so it it very easy to find a match in gamemodes that are not as popular. The game would be very boring if it didn't have war because there are only 9 multiplayer maps for all gamemodes except war and special made maps for war, if you are planning on just playing TDM or Domination you may not have as good of an experience. There are some really fun guns to use in this game like the m1a1 carbine and the thompson or the kar98k, but the game is dominated by people using the stg and the BAR but the game does have a very wide variety of guns to use that are pretty much made for every playstyle.
The zombies is dumbed down from treyarch zombies but is still extremely fun to play especially if you have a group of friends to play with. Along with that there are two easter eggs in the first map where one is a guided sort of mission like easter egg while the other one is a complete easter egg with no help at all. once you beat the guided easter egg you do get another map to play but it is just the prologue map.

So...where to begin. This game I remember seeing back in 2011 on YouTube and I thought it was pretty cool. Found it on Steam when I joined, bought it when it was on sale for like $5. At the time, it was still being worked on, albeit slowly, so I thought "why the heck not."
Looking back now, this game had potential but was left to rot by the devs and since late 2014 has never received a lick of development. It's unfinished, unpolished, buggy and will probably never, ever see what it was to become. It has good features and has a lot to it despite being in its forever unfinished state. The A.I. has always had a mind of its own and is hard to deal with when trying to set up runners, farmers, builders, and traders at the same time. Not having even just one person assigned to just one tiny task could end up causing your settlement to crash without enemies even attacking, simply because someone wouldn't go and make flour so you can bake bread so your dedicated farmers could eat and go harvest more wheat to repeat the cycle.
It's a challenge, but if you're looking for a basic time waster, this game is good for that. I can't recommend it, however, just because of the state it's been left in without further development. If it's on sale for cheap and you like a nice, casual city builder, you might look into it. But for full price, look elsewhere. This game is going nowhere and will forever be that way.

It's a restomod NES game.  It takes the best parts of those old games and expertly blends them into a nearly-perfect platformer.  Even the graphics and sound are carefully designed to highlight the best qualities of the old hardware, but not so slavishly that the rules can't be bent when it suits the enjoyment of the game.
The difficulty is handled admirably.  The checkpoints are smartly placed and death only incurs a mild penalty.  Infinite continues are provided, so difficult sections can be continually attempted without slogging through the entire stage or game again.  Oddly enough, the 4-6 hours of gameplay time is often cited as too short in other reviews, but this game packs considerably more content than any of its inspirations.  In scope and balance, it's arguably superior to those old classics.
If you liked the classic NES platformers from Capcom and Konami, you'll love this.  It's more accessible, looks great, and sounds fantastic.  If you lack such nostalgia, it's comparable to more recent games like Super Meat Boy or BattleBlock Theater.
I've enjoyed every minute of it, and I'd readily call it one of the top games of 2014.

I see a lot of negative reviews mentioning Call of Duty, this is not Call of Duty, it is Counter-Strike. In terms of base gameplay it's average with some aspects feeling cheap, but keep in mind this is a free game. Like most other Free FPS games like the overwhelmingly bad FEAR Online, or even a decent game like Heroes and Generals, it features a pay to rent or pay to buy system for higher end firearms. It's worth noting that there is no "best" rifle or pistol, and that the free weapons can get you by if you're a skilled gamer. The inclusion of vehicles and vehicle missions adds a nice variety to gameplay that Counter-Strike and other games desperately need.
For those of you intending on spending money on the game, if you spend roughly the same on the game you would have a pay-once game like Counter Strike: GO you will be unsatisfied; the overall quality will not meet your expectations, and you'll find yourself getting killed round after round even with your expensive equipment.
TL;DR? Poor Man's Counter-Strike 2, if you want more CS:S or CS 1.6, there is still CS:GO or CS Nexon respectively.

TL;DR: A well-made but fairly pointless grinding game. Only recommended for achievement hunters so you at least get a trophy out of it.
In a traditional RPG you usually start as a low-level character with little to no equipment and the only way to become more powerful is to
kill monsters.
Basically begin with a standard RPG. Take out quests and dialogues, reduce equipment to purchasable stats and reduce the combat to just damage-per-second and make it a side-scroller and you've got yourself Loot Hero. The gameplay consists of three parts: choosing a level, running left and right killing monsters and buying better stats at the towns in-between. There's also a short and pretty meaningless story: a terrible dragon has appeared and you, the hero, has to go and kill it to save the land.
The first thing I noticed when I fired up the game was that there is no keyboard support whatsoever. The gameplay would be totally natural with keyboard, with the only keys being basically left and right (plus some extra keys for buying stuff at towns). I think this is a huge oversight from the developer, this being a PC game after all (even if you can play a version of it on the browser on various sites). After a minute I realized that mouse is functional: the guy runs towards the mouse cursor when click is held. This is fine but not as convenient as keyboard would have been.
Finally I opted for a gamepad, which worked well. Furthermore it proved to be superior to the mouse: a bit more on the reason later. As the gameplay goes, the music and sounds are pretty good and running through and grinding monsters curiously feels quite satisfying. In addition to experience points and gold the monsters drop health and invulnerability potions, the latter of which makes you super fast and almost un-killable so you can easily grind through hordes of monsters with the music flowing consistently with the diamond tornado as the money gets sucked into your loot bag counter in the top-left corner.
At first you have to play each level sequentially but after beating the first dragon you can skip any number of the subsequent levels to go even straight to the next dragon level. Usually you don't want to do that though, unless you have prepared: each level (called aptly Difficulty) is more difficult, i.e. contains stronger monsters than the previous one. It also provides a bit more experience (that is for levels) and gold (for buying better stats) than the previous one. There are different enemies to each level, but game mechanically they are identical, the only difference being visuals and their attack power and health.
Thing is, it is so much more difficult to kill tougher monsters that you'll probably want to grind in a lower level until you can beat it consistently before going to the next one. Later on you can skip a few levels as you will develop an intuition of how powerful monsters you can kill easily. If you do a mistake, you are stuck in the level that is too difficult (well, at least I couldn't find a way to exit a level short of exiting the game). Then you can still grind, as diamonds drop even when hitting a monster once, so a boring left-right-left-right limbo can be issued right next to town for a slow but steady grind for better stats.
You can heal (automatically) and buy stats at towns: there is attack and defence power, better critical strike chance and higher speed available for purchase. Critical strikes cap at 100% although for some reason you could still waste money on them afterwards. Speed seems to have a cap or I just wouldn't notice the slight change of pace after certain point. Then later on the only meaningful purchases were attack and defence power. Your stats get higher also when you level up the character.
The speed upgrade caused some weird things when I got it at high values. I would run and then get stuck at some monsters (because I was not strong enough to kill them immediately), but the screen would continue onwards, leaving the hero and the monsters I was fighting out of the window. The monsters only spawn outside the screen, so then the hero would continuously fight monsters out of sight, usually dying eventually because if he could kill them, he'd pretty much run right through them and not be left behind. This is where I pulled the controller out: with mouse I can't retreat the other way because I can't get the cursor to the other side of the hero who is outside the screen. With gamepad I could at least do that.
A minor bug occurred sometimes when the high speed also made me run straight past the boss monster, presumably because he was not spawned yet as the character ran past him.
By the way, dying is of little consequence: you can immediately revive and continue grinding. You just lose a bit of experience and gold when that happens. It was not too much but enough to make me cautious.
4.5 hours of grinding later I had 100% completed the game achievement-wise (I will still have to idle a bit for cards). I had defeated 38 dragons and thus saved 38 miners. The miners provide gold for you when you're idle, pretty pointless as there's a hard cap of 99999 gold. Frankly, the game was pretty boring. I get the parody of reducing the present-day RPGs to their bare bones of gold and experience grinding but the notion isn't worth a whole game. That said, it's mere 3 €: if you fancy getting a fairly easy 100%, it might be worth it at least when it's on sale. If you can manage, play it while watching a movie or similar. The rest of you: go play something better.

OVERVIEW
Kill baddies with a few clicks of your mouse...And a lot of just holding down the LMB. :D That's Loot Hero DX in a nutshell. You can play it for free, or play this slightly updated version for a few bucks. Is it worth it? Let's see.
PROS
+ Decent graphics.
+ Good music and sound.
+ Cheap (as it should be).
+ Trading cards.
+ Difficulty is scaled reasonably well.
+ Relatively amusing, and great for when you don't feel like putting any effort into a game.
+ Miner system is nice.
CONS
- Too repetitive. A little design finesse could have helped a lot here - adding a bit more story, some randomness, etc.
- The FPS rate drops pretty badly later in the game. It's also a bit slow loading in general.
- You have to go to the main menu to exit the game.
- Slightly glitchy; e.g., sometimes when you go to exit, you'll click, and "Yes", "No" will be left floating over the main menu, and it didn't really exit. It's also had issues where it didn't update the run speed properly. Also, muting the sound still allows this weird clicking noise to occur occasionally, just like normal; plus, the noise when you get knocked out remains present. Code is sometimes present at the end on screen when you beat the last boss.
- You can't upgrade critical past 100%, but it will still take your money.
- It would be nice if you could have it where it just goes from level-to-level instead of having to leave the level and selecting a new one. An infinite mode would also be a nice touch, where it just runs level-to-level in a seamless fashion - one big level that repeats over and over. It would make grinding for level 100 easier.
- Your hero seems to get stuck sometimes; like he slams into the same enemy over and over, and you can't see him on the screen.
- There shouldn't be a gold cap.
- You should be able to mute sound without adjusting the levels.
CONCLUSION
It's cheap, decent, mindless fun, you get trading cards, and you're supporting an indie developer. It will give a few hours of fun over a period of time of your choosing, and seems like something that would be fun to come back to every now and then for some easy-as-heck victory. To me, that's worth it - and if you can get it on sale, even more so.
Thanks for reading my review; I hope it was helpful. Have a great day, and Godspeed!

The levels have great variety from one to the next.  Some don't entirely make sense, but it still makes for a great adventure.  New gameplay styles are introduced often with each level.  Exploration is always rewarded as well.

First of all, just a general comment: I love this game. It has a great, smooth game engine and the controls are fairly easy to me. I have owned this game since August 2015 and have really been off and on with it. I can tell you that once I got a Steam Controller, everything changed, and I loved how the game played with it. Honestly, I couldn't play it on anything but the highest difficulty.
The physics are phenomenal. I don't think I have ever played such an arcad-ey styled game with such realistic physics. It totally replicates real life (or damn near it) and the developer did such a great job with it. From what I have seen, there are no current bugs in the game's physics and I see no reason for the physics to be modified at all.
The graphics are great aswell. I think that the color theme is perfect for the (not so much) "JDM/Dorifto" and (but more) Japan feel. It is a little brutal on the eyes when you're in a dark room or are very tired, but otherwise, it is very fun and keeps you alert. I really enjoy how the tire marks work. They really help when you are drifitng if you need to see if you're angle is going too far (genenrally more than 90º), and they look cool. The graphics, in general, may seem a little bland at times, but it really keeps you focused on what you're doing. Plus, this game isn't really about looks, it's more about the gameplay.
Any kind of controller (I use a Steam Controller) is nearly a must. Keyboard is simply not enough to fully enjoy and get good at this game, but it is still playable. It really sucks that you can't change the controls in game, but the Steam Remapping or something like motioninjoy could help with that.
The actual controlling on all difficulties is great and accurate to their names. The hardest difficulty feels butter smooth and is what I use all the time. If you take your time, you can really learn the game and get good with a car that fits you. I personally work well with "The Original," but who knows what you might be great with. Also, there is always a mixture of challenging yourself, the music, and the map you're on that can give you different moods within the game.
This game is also very fun and easy to get back into and keep with. I think that in general, it may get boring after you completely master (rank 1) all of the maps and finish the campaign, but it would take a long time (probably no less than 150 hours) before you get to that point. At least for me, the game pushes me to try harder and be the best at any map I try. I am currently, as of this review, number 4 on Mt. Nikko with about 300,000 points to go to number 1. It's taken me about 15 hours to get to that point and I don't plan on stopping until I am at number 1.

The point system is very fair and I think I have it figured out, in general. Here's my thoughts:
- This is the general "drifitng score."
- The wider the angle up to a 90º drift is more points
- You get a multiplier based upon how long you have been drifing "continuously"
- If you're going too slow, the points stop adding
- If you go over 90º, the points stop adding
- If you hit anything, except bonuses, your points are summed in the total and you lose your multiplier
- If you stop drifing for too long (I think about 5 seconds), your points are summed in the total and you lose your multiplier
- The closer you are, the more points you get
- The faster you are going, the more points you get
- If you're too far away or "aren't drifitng" near one, it doesn't count
- If you hit one, it doesn't count, but doesn't get rid of your score or multiplier
- If you hit it you get points
- If you don't hit it, you get no points
- Faster and more Sideways you are, you get more points
- If you finish the donut indicated with the increasing red circle, you get more points
- Faster and more Sideways you are, you get more points
- If you hit it, you get no points
- If you finish the spinning indicated with the increasing red circle, you get more points
- There's really no downside to these...
- If you keep getting bonuses, they'll exponentially increase
- If your current score is reset, so does your bonus stack

We were shouting at each other a lot and it was very entertaining.
In my short clips video you can see all the good things I was writting about. We were really having fun and laughing a lot:
And here comes all the criticism I need to share with you. The Steam PC version of Resident Evil 5 has many bugs and complicated mouse+keyboard controls. I don't like quick time events very much. But the weird combinations of buttons in RE5 are unbelievable. Sometimes A+D and sometimes F+V with very short time to react to that. I watched some gameplay on consoles and they only had to press one button on their controllers. It's even more annoying during cutscenes when you sit back, enjoy and don't expect anything.
Another unpleasant moment is when you find out that you as Sheva won't get the steam achivement for finishing a chapter if your partner's game crashes or if you decide to stop playing in the middle of a chapter, save the progress and finish later. Only Chris, the player who host the game, will get it then.
It happened to us that an important enemy with a keycard we needed spawned in an inaccessible area, I was locked in a cage and my boyfriend spent quite long time trying to get there while I was waiting and waiting for ages. We tried it again and this time we only saw his shadow on the floor. I tried to use explosives so we got him down from that unknown place this time and luckily it was on the right side.
Another very annoying moment was the final boss fight where you have to press F as Sheva for almost a minute. Not just that but you have to do it SUPER fast. You kind of need to be like The Flash! I played this game 6 years ago as well and I remember I had to give up back then. It was not possible. On my last playthrough I tried it so many times and I managed to do it only once.. My finger really hurt, so I had to ignore the pain and was lucky my boyfriend didn't mess it up after that so we could continue. Uffff! These moments definitely made us want to ragequit..
RE5 Bosses in general can be very annoying. When you are not doing the right thing - shooting the right spots at the right moments , you are basically wasting your ammo and the game won't give you any more and it won't make you fail either even when you clearly can't do it. You just have to decide for yourself to restart from the last checkpoint.. But in case you somehow manage to do it but you already wasted all your ammo before, good luck to you, because you can't buy ammo directly. However you can buy weapons and sell them so you keep the ammo they had.
Final verdict: Partly recommended! Overall I am very hesitant in case of Resident Evil 5. I am a fan of RE games. I like the coop option of it. But all the bugs are breaking the full enjoyment of it for me. I believe the console version is much better! If you love Resident Evil games and you have the patience to deal with it, go for it! Wait for a sale, please. Don't pay the full price for something what couldn't have bugs fixed since 2009.
Thank you for reading my review! In case you have some questions feel welcome to ask me :)

Although the core gameplay of the Assassin's Creed franchise remains undoubtedly fun, enjoying AC:Brotherhood is made more difficult by an excessive amount of grinding and minutiae.
Despite the lively environments, the game desperately cries out for an improved fast-travel system; at least half of the game is spent running between the start points of the various missions, which quickly becomes tiresome. The game is further padded out by a heavy reliance on collectibles which rarely offer any benefit even if you do catch them all. The conspiracy-laden plot that stretches imagination at times (if /everybody/ is involved in the secret conspiracy, how can they claim nobody knows about it?). The graphics were too subdued and could have used a splash more color; another victim of the "real is brown" design school. And a host of bugs and gameplay issues - including a flaky camera, AI scripting problems and a finicky jumping mechanic that far too often had me leaping to my doom rather than at the obvious target right in front of me - did nothing to improve things.
On the other hand, the combat system was well done, with excellent and numerous animations, as was the parkour climbing that is the heart of the game. The level design were interesting, if too beige, and the voice-acting was excellent. Brotherhood shows that the Assassins Creed franchise remains enjoyable, even if it is growing a bit long in the tooth.

TL;DR Preview: An enjoyable game that improves on its predecessor and introduces a great new multiplayer component is unfortunately brought down by technical issues on the Mac version.
Ah, Roma. A beautiful city filled with the good things in life: wine, women, neck-stabbings... Following up on the much acclaimed Assassin's Creed II, Brotherhood's single player campaign tells the story of an older Ezio Auditore, a master assassin who's home is attacked by the powerful Borgia family, forcing him to relocate to Rome in pursuit of people to pay loving steel retribution to. While you're on your revenge tour, Assassin's Creed Brotherhood offers you the opportunity to train your own army of assassins, raising them from street urchins to your own private army of conspicuously dressed murderers.
While many aspects of the game, such as the free-running system central to the game's mechanics or the counterattack-based combat, have received slight refinement if any real changes at all, the package as a whole feels well-put together. That's not to say no changes have been made, as there are portions of the game which have received noticeable improvements, primarily the visuals. Assassin's Creed II, while a detailed protrayal of Renaissance Italy, suffered from a color palette that at times could be described as downright dreary and washed out. With the move to Rome, AC:B has given Ezio a much brighter environment to commit murder in. Colors are more vibrant, the sun actually shines, and the setting benefits greatly from it. Running around in Rome became a pleasure, not an occasional chore. Characters and character animations have also been improved, and it doesn't always feel as if Ezio spends his time talking with snappily dressed mannequins.
Perhaps the best and most noticeable improvement to the Assassin's Creed formula, however, stems from the new multiplayer mode. Pitting players against each other in a battle of cunning and stabbings in a variety of game modes, AC: B's multiplayer offering you the chance to test your assassin skills against live opponents tests you in a way few other multiplayer games do. While there are several game types to choose from, the highlight for many players will be the Wanted mode. It helps that this mode is the best suited for showing off the potential of the multiplayer component. In this mode, players are made to pursue a designated target around an environment populated with NPCs while they themselves are hunted by another player in one circle of cat and mouse. It's extremely exciting to pull off a perfectly stealthed kill on an unsuspecting opponent, and for this reason alone I could recommend Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood.
While this review may seem to some to be universally glowing, Brotherhood does have issues a prospective purchaser may wish to keep in mind. First, this game was reviewed on the Mac port. While the game has the potential to run just fine, Macs running OS versions Lion and onwards may encounter major technical issues with getting the game to run. The multiplayer component is also barren of players, leading to matchmaking taking very long periods of time to find matches, if one can be found at all.
Note: Portions of this game were played in Steam's Offline mode. As such, total playtime is not accurately represented on Steam.

It's a restomod NES game.  It takes the best parts of those old games and expertly blends them into a nearly-perfect platformer.  Even the graphics and sound are carefully designed to highlight the best qualities of the old hardware, but not so slavishly that the rules can't be bent when it suits the enjoyment of the game.
The difficulty is handled admirably.  The checkpoints are smartly placed and death only incurs a mild penalty.  Infinite continues are provided, so difficult sections can be continually attempted without slogging through the entire stage or game again.  Oddly enough, the 4-6 hours of gameplay time is often cited as too short in other reviews, but this game packs considerably more content than any of its inspirations.  In scope and balance, it's arguably superior to those old classics.
If you liked the classic NES platformers from Capcom and Konami, you'll love this.  It's more accessible, looks great, and sounds fantastic.  If you lack such nostalgia, it's comparable to more recent games like Super Meat Boy or BattleBlock Theater.
I've enjoyed every minute of it, and I'd readily call it one of the top games of 2014.
